BabyIAXO represents a novel, cost-effective concept for a dedicated neutrino telescope aimed at detecting solar flux of low-energy (sub-MeV) solar neutrinos, with its optical depth peaking specifically within the Sun's core. This study utilizes existing solar models to forecast the observatory's capabilities, analyzing potential measurements of the neutrino-nucleus cross section, energy spectrum, and time-dependent solar flux. Additionally, the analysis examines the potential for detecting active solar core processes, such as convection, and discusses the prospect of observing high-energy neutrinos generated by cosmic ray interactions in the solar interior. A key advantage of BabyIAXO is its ability to measure the neutrino-nucleus cross section without relying on hadronic models, thereby offering a unique pathway to constrain low-energy neutrino properties. A primary objective is to determine the absolute value of the mixing angle $\theta_{13}$ with high precision. Furthermore, the project aims to test the Standard Model and determine the mass hierarchy of neutrinos. Beyond these fundamental goals, the observatory could significantly advance our understanding of the Sun by probing its core with unprecedented sensitivity. This includes measuring the convection zone width and the depth of the superadiabatic region, as well as searching for exotic phenomena like black holes or dark matter annihilation within the core. The paper concludes with a discussion of the scientific drivers behind the BabyIAXO initiative. Keywords: Solar neutrinos, Axion-like particles, Solar models, Solar core. This work introduces oscillating systems of any dimension governed by both conservative and dissipative forces. The conservative component is derived from a potential that depends not only on positions but also on velocities, representing generalized gyroforces dependent on velocity. The dissipative component comprises summands that are quadratic forms of velocities, with their coefficients being functions of positions. Exact conditions for the existence of such oscillating systems have been determined. When velocities are constant, the conservative part aligns with the generalized Lorentz force, while a dissipative force quadratic in velocity governs the well-known non-harmonic Braginskii oscillator. In the limit of vanishing velocity, the dissipative force resembles that of a superconducting oscillator with variable inductance. Unlike the known Braginskii oscillator, the new oscillating systems do not require two coils; they can be significantly simpler, consisting of just one coil or even zero-dimensional entities. This simplicity is achieved through the inclusion of velocity terms in the conservative force and quadratic forms in the dissipative force. The boundary between conservative and dissipative forces is arbitrary, as both can be represented as either. The paper outlines the algorithm for constructing these systems and examines specific cases, including single-coil oscillators and those reduced to a single particle. Additionally, the study addresses the nonautonomous variant, where the magnetic field is periodic in time, resulting in both autonomous and non-autonomous oscillators exhibiting identical properties. Finally, the statistical properties of the non-autonomous system are analyzed. This statistical model holds significant practical value, as it enables the generation of self-oscillating motion with complex, non-periodic, aperiodic, and nonquasiperiodic behaviors, making it suitable for creating astatonic oscillators. Such oscillators are applicable in various fields, such as generating random numbers. Furthermore, the statistical model can be extended to multicomponent systems, including plasma. The paper concludes with an example of constructing a two-component astatonic oscillator for random number generation. The existence of these astatonic oscillators is supported by the existence theorem for the Cauchy problem of partial differential equations. The systems described herein represent a novel type of oscillator, distinct from previously known variants. While earlier research focused on dissipative forces with quadratic velocity dependence, this study demonstrates that incorporating velocity dependence in the conservative force and allowing for quadratic dissipative forces yields significantly simpler oscillators, such as single-coil configurations. Robotics has made remarkable strides in recent years, yet robotic dexterity continues to lag behind human capabilities. A primary obstacle is the scarcity of large-scale, diverse datasets. While existing grasp datasets exist, they are limited in scope and contain objects with limited variation in shape, size, and texture. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a novel, large-scale, and varied simulation-based grasp dataset comprising 1.5 million synthetic grasp samples across 1,000 distinct objects. The data was generated using the PyBullet and Unity environments, leveraging the API compatibility between physics simulation and 3D rendering. DexGraspNet features 3D point cloud-based grasp samples and incorporates variations in object rotation, lighting, and camera angles. We evaluated several state-of-the-art deep learning models on this dataset, demonstrating that both the data and the models perform effectively. This study introduces a free-breathing 4D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-SE) sequence for body imaging that integrates a respiratory navigator with in-plane motion correction. The sequence delivers the high tissue contrast of T2-SE while enabling motion correction for both readout (in-plane) and non-readout (phase-encode) directions. To address the time-consuming motion correction required for phase-encode steps, the method employs a 3D non-rigid registration technique. Validation was performed on both a phantom and a human subject using free-breathing 4D T2-SE scans, with all volumes reconstructed via compressed sensing. The resulting images demonstrated effective motion correction and yielded images comparable in quality to those from breath-hold acquisitions. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the acquisition of 4D T2-SE data in clinically feasible timeframes. The method is applicable to a broad spectrum of free-breathing 4D SE- or gradient echo sequences, including those utilizing gradient moment nulling. This technique holds significant potential for 4D body MRI applications, such as functional assessment and tumor perfusion characterization. Future research will focus on extending the technique to free-breathing 4D T2-SE with reduced scan durations. Compressive modeling has recently gained significant attention as a method for enhancing inference speed and reducing memory usage. In the context of model compression, distillation is a widely adopted distillation strategy. This paper presents a novel approach called InDistill, which is designed to learn an efficient model by maintaining the information flow from input to output. We demonstrate that InDistill surpasses conventional distillation methods in terms of information preservation. Our experimental results indicate that InDistill achieves state-of-the-art performance in knowledge flow preservation, attaining 76.0% of the accuracy of the pre-trained ResNet-101 under a 32x compression rate on ImageNet-1k. Furthermore, we show that InDistill outperforms existing baselines, including KnowTrans and Kilo, across a range of compression rates on ImageNet-1k and COCO datasets. Consider a map $f:U\to\mathbb R^m$, where $U\subset\mathbb R^m$ is an open set and $m\geq 2$, which is a submersion. The level sets of $f$ generate a foliation on $U$. When $m=2$ and $U$ is the entire plane, the level sets constitute curves. If these curves are topologically lines, $f$ is termed a submersion of the line type. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^2$ is defined as topologically line equivalent to a projection if its level sets are topologically lines; in this scenario, $f$ is called a submersion of the projection type. The paper establishes the topological similarity between line-type submersions and projections, demonstrating that any orientation-preserving submersion of the line type is topologically similar to the function $f(x,y)=x$. Furthermore, for projection-type submersions, the line sets are topologically lines, lines, or circles. For the case where the line sets are circles, the paper proves that the function is topologically similar to $g(x,y)=x^2+y^2$. Consequently, it is shown that every submersion of the projection type is topologically similar to the projection. The proofs rely on the Menger-Nöbeling theorem and the Jordan curve theorem. The work concludes with several remarks addressing maps of the line type defined on subsets of the plane. The findings in this paper complement the research presented in \cite{Krasauskas2018}. In grazing systems, vegetation can be consumed by animals at short distances (non-local) or at long distances (local). While prior research has primarily focused on local grazing, this study employs a non-local grazing model to investigate how spatial consumption patterns influence both vegetation stability and the system's response to environmental changes. Our findings indicate that dynamic grazing induces spatial correlations that significantly alter the system's behavior. Specifically, the model demonstrates that: (i) stable vegetation states can persist even when local models predict collapse; (ii) state transitions occur more gradually in the non-local framework compared to the local one; and (iii) vegetation patterns exhibit increased robustness under varying climatic conditions when non-local grazing is accounted for. Consequently, incorporating non-local grazing into future models is essential for a more accurate understanding of vegetation dynamics. CountSketch is a well-known dimensionality reduction method that projects vectors into a lower dimension with high probability, enabling the accurate recovery of $k$-sparse and even heavier tails. However, the primary limitation of this technique is its vulnerability to adaptive inputs, which can easily degenerate the approximation error. This work investigates the resilience of CountSketch against adaptive adversaries. Specifically, we demonstrate that for arbitrary inputs $z$ with an $\ell_2$ norm bounded by $k$, the countSketch(z) output requires only a sample size of $O(k\log^2 n)$ to guarantee the reduction of approximation error with constant probability. Furthermore, we provide a matching lower bound, proving that $\Omega(k\log^2 n)$ dimensions and sample size are necessary. This result indicates that $\log^2 n$ is an inherent limitation of CountSketch when dealing with adaptive inputs. Additionally, we extend our findings to the streaming setting, where the algorithm must process inputs sequentially without randomization. In this scenario, the sample size requirement increases to $O(k\log^3 n)$, and we prove that this bound is also tight. Notably, our lower bound for the general case applies to any deterministic algorithm, including those that may be adaptive. Our results are derived by analyzing the deterministic countSketch(z) output and reducing it to a problem that can be solved by a greedy algorithm. This approach also enables us to extend our findings to the broader problem of low-distortion sparse embedding. Finally, we enhance the resilience of our countSketch algorithm by integrating it with the $\ell_1$-Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, achieving a sample size of $O(k\log n)$ at the expense of higher deterministic algorithmic complexity. To our knowledge, this represents the first algorithm capable of low-distortion sparse embedding with a sample size nearly linear in $k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate the code's capabilities by calculating the equation of state for nuclear matter and the ground-state energy of the hydrogen molecule. The analysis examines the dynamics of the quantum game, modeling both rational and irrational market participants. Furthermore, the quantum network itself is represented as a system of two coupled spin-1/2 particles. Utilizing the density matrix formalism, we derive the density matrix for this quantum network and subsequently compute its entropy. Finally, the research explores the entropy dynamics of the quantum network, identifying and discussing both equilibrium and non-equilibrium states. These findings suggest that a quantum network approach to HFT could facilitate more efficient market operations. Additionally, the results may hold significance for the broader field of quantum finance. The paper includes several appendices to provide further details. This paper examines an economy featuring intermediaries who facilitate transactions between producers and consumers. We demonstrate that a monopoly intermediary typically generates lower consumer and producer surplus compared to an economy where these agents collaborate to maximize total surplus. This finding contrasts with the standard literature on efficient contracting, which suggests that consumer-producer alliances are usually beneficial. We attribute this discrepancy to the unique environment of total economy-wide optimization, which fundamentally alters the problem. Specifically, we show that a consumer-alliancemodel can yield higher surpluses for both producers and consumers than the classic Bertrand duopoly scenario. Furthermore, we outline the specific conditions required for the consumer-alliancemodel to achieve economy-wide Pareto-optimality. Finally, we explore how introducing producer competition modifies the necessary conditions for this collaborative arrangement to be optimal. These findings hold significant implications for total supply chain optimization. Additionally, our research has practical value in designing mechanisms to extract maximum income from the economy. Creating a cost-effective model to generate high-quality summaries of extensive documents remains a significant challenge in Natural Language Processing. This paper introduces a novel framework called Planning with Acquired Entity Prompts (PAEP) for abstractive summarization. The approach first identifies key content within the input text and subsequently employs a large pre-trained language model for summarization, guided by the previously extracted key information. Our results demonstrate that this framework surpasses both recent baseline methods and human performance on the DSCNM document summarization dataset. Additionally, we present the first cross-dataset evaluation, showing that PAEP successfully achieves competitive results on CNN/DailyMail and SummEval as well. Furthermore, we highlight that the model produces high-quality summaries with greater diversity compared to existing baseline methods. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/Chenchen-Liu/PAEP. This study examines $k$-variable functions defined on a closed domain that are continuous and differentiable almost everywhere within the domain, along with their boundary components. The work establishes sufficient conditions for the differentiability of the function's Morrey reconstruction in higher dimensions across the entire domain. Furthermore, it proves that if the difference between the reconstructed function and the original function is infinitely differentiable everywhere inside the domain, then the original function must also be infinitely differentiable everywhere within the domain. As applications, the paper addresses the reconstruction of multivariate functions from univariate functions representing their cuts, providing criteria for the reconstructability of multi-dimensional functions based on their cut properties. Additionally, criteria are established for ensuring that all cut functions collectively represent the original function. Finally, constructive theorems are provided for reconstructing functions using an arbitrary number of cuts. These findings are supported by examples and counterexamples. The research concludes with an outline of potential applications in machine learning. The work includes an English version of the publication. Various factors influence vocal entrainment, such as the speaker's rate, formant frequencies, and pitch. This study introduces a computationally efficient approach to measuring vocal entrainment within dyadic conversations by incorporating contextual data. The method involves calculating the correlation between changes in entrainment-related acoustic features of one speaker and the features of their conversational partner. We compared this new method against two existing approaches in both simulated and real-world datasets. The results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms the other two methods in detecting entrainment in dyadic interactions. Additionally, the approach is validated through an analysis of how entrainment varies across different age groups and gender pairings. The findings suggest that entrainment is more prevalent in conversations between individuals of similar ages and within same-sex dyads. The entire code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1998/entrainment. This paper introduces a categorical model for a quantum-like formalism, specifically within the lambda calculus, to represent the manipulation of the quantum state space of a single qubit. We define the Sigma_1 type as the collection of all possible manipulations (functions) that transform an initial state into a final state without altering the system, alongside their associated operators. This set is demonstrated to possess the structure of a lambda calculus monadic type, a property essential for modeling quantum computations. Furthermore, the (composable) action of these manipulations on a state is represented by a monadic action, which is proven to constitute a comonoid. Finally, the model is shown to satisfy the axioms of a categorical comonoid, thereby enabling the modeling of quantum-like state manipulation. The study concludes by identifying an open research question regarding the extension of this formalism to multi-qubit systems. This approach builds upon our prior work, which defined the quantum state space of a single qubit as the unit sphere in the complex Hilbert space C^2 and defined manipulations as operators that rotate the state around a fixed axis in C^2. The categorical model presented here serves as the foundation for our subsequent paper, which details the modeling of quantum computations using this framework. Additionally, the formalism is shown to be applicable to other sets of manipulations, such as those involving manipulators that reflect a state across a fixed hyperplane in C^2. The paper begins by reviewing the model of quantum state manipulation, followed by an introduction to monads and comonads within category theory. The third section presents the model of manipulations as monads, while the fourth and fifth sections demonstrate that the action of these manipulations on a state forms a monadic action that constitutes a comonoid, with the latter section providing a proof of the axiom of a categorical comonoid. The final section outlines manipulations as a monad and their action on a state as a comonoid, concluding with an outline of an open problem. This work is partially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant no. 1304009. The authors thank Dr. John L. Casti for his valuable comments and suggestions. Keywords: Quantum Computation, Lambda Calculus, Category Theory, Monads, Comonoids.

We introduce a novel quasiparticle-quasiparticle correlation function tailored for two-particle excitation states in the fractional quantum Hall effect (FQHE). Utilizing a trial wave function grounded in Jastrow factors and quasiparticle coordinates, we calculate the energy spectrum for two quasiparticles confined within a finite system, revealing an unexpected system-size dependence. Furthermore, we analyze systems confined by harmonic oscillator potentials, deriving system-independent results expressed through hypergeometric functions. Our study examines various filling factors, specifically $ \nu = 2/5, 2/3, 3/4, 3/5, 5/2, $ and $ 7/3 $. Additionally, we investigate excitation states involving one quasiparticle and one quasihole, as well as quasihole-quasihole correlations. Finally, we compare our analytical findings with prior numerical calculations and experimental data. This work supersedes the study by H. H. Kwon and J. K. Kim, Phys. Rev. B 106, 045418 (2022).

This study addresses a Stokes variational inequality characterized by degenerate diffusion within the context of glaciology. Such inequalities typically fall into the category of semicoercive problems, necessitating the use of specialized finite element methods. We introduce a streamline diffusion approach, which incorporates a streamline penalization term into a standard Stokes formulation. This technique stabilizes the method when dealing with dominant convection, enables the handling of large Péclet numbers, and ensures convergence for both uniformly and non-uniformly refined meshes. We establish optimal error estimates for these convergent solutions. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to validate the performance of the proposed algorithm. These examples examine various refinement strategies, including nonuniform and anisotropic mesh generation, and demonstrate the method's robustness regarding low regularity solutions. Finally, a specific case study is conducted to analyze the Little Ice Age. This involves a 100-year simulation covering the period from 1901 to 2000, utilizing a real-world mesh derived from a digital elevation model of the Greenland Ice Sheet. The simulation incorporates a prescribed velocity on the ice shelf and a prescribed temperature on the surface, with all other boundary conditions remaining standard. We report the computed temperature and velocity fields, which align well with independent observations. This agreement confirms the suitability of the streamline penalization technique for complex, real-world applications. The study concludes by discussing potential extensions of this approach to other fluid problems. Specifically, it highlights applications in oceanography, such as simulating internal waves in stratified fluids, and in semiconductor technology, where the method can model charge transport in thin films. In these scenarios, the degenerate diffusion arises from a diffusion coefficient that vanishes in certain regions, rendering classical error estimates inapplicable. The techniques developed herein offer a viable alternative for deriving error bounds in these scenarios. Additionally, the discussion touches upon the extension of these methods to other fluid models, such as the Navier-Stokes equations, where streamline diffusion has been widely applied to resolve issues related to convection dominance and low regularity. Finally, it is noted that the streamline penalization method is applicable to a broad class of problems, including those with non-convex domains and corners, as well as those where the domain itself varies with the solution. This latter characteristic is particularly relevant in glaciology, where the domain is defined by the ice sheet's surface elevation, which evolves over time. We introduce DUVET, a project utilizing the James Webb Space Telescope's MIRI instrument to investigate how galactic outflows regulate star formation in disk galaxies. By analyzing the 10.5 micron PAH emission line, we can map star formation regions and compare them with outflow structures identified through 15.0 micron and 7.7 micron continuum emission. Our initial target is NGC 253, a nearby starburst galaxy hosting a supermassive black hole. We present the first results from the first public DUVET data release, which includes MIRI imaging at 7.7, 10.5, 15.0, and 21.0 microns. This data reveals that star formation is not uniform within the galactic disk; instead, it is driven by clumpy, ring-like structures that align with spiral arms. Furthermore, the outflow originates from the inner regions of the disk, specifically from the 7.7 micron emission, and expands radially outward. The 10.5 micron emission traces a more extended star-forming disk, indicating that outflows from these outer regions require time to accelerate. Our findings suggest that PAH emission is a critical tool for locating the star formation regions that fuel outflow expansion, while the 10.5 micron emission uniquely identifies the star-forming regions where outflows are actively suppressing star formation. This research demonstrates the value of MIRI's broad wavelength coverage for studying the interplay between star formation and outflows in galactic disks. Future DUVET observations will target additional starbursting disk galaxies. This study was conducted using the MIRI instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope, a project supported by NASA. The full MIRI data release is accessible at https://miri-pds.stsci.

This study analyzes the impact of the hadron phase duration on the calculated triangular flow $v_3$ for charged hadrons across Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV, using a multiphase transport model. The framework incorporates a hadron phase duration of 10–30 fm/c, with the system temperature at the hadronization interface set to 165 MeV. Our results indicate that the model successfully reproduces the PHENIX data for $v_3$ when the hadron phase lasts 10 fm/c in both Cu+Cu and Au+Au systems. However, extending this duration to 30 fm/c results in an overestimation of $v_3$ in the hadronization region. Furthermore, the model predicts a more pronounced suppression of $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions compared to Cu+Cu, consistent with experimental findings. These observations suggest that the hadron phase duration is relatively brief, likely not exceeding 10 fm/c. Additionally, we note that the temperature of the hadronization interface is a critical parameter influencing the duration of the hadron phase. Finally, the model's predictions for $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions align well with the PHENIX results observed in the partonic phase. These findings are also applicable to other centralities and collision energies. We conclude that the hadron phase duration is very short, particularly at higher energies. A more detailed analysis of the hadron phase duration would require incorporating hadron resonance gas kinetic theory. We anticipate that future investigations will provide more precise constraints on this parameter. This research was conducted using the multiphase transport model, a partonic/hadronic transport framework. We anticipate that the temperature of the hadronization interface will be constrained by future analyses. Furthermore, we expect that the equation of state, which is essential for the partonic phase, will be refined using the same model. This will facilitate a more accurate determination of the hadronization interface temperature and, consequently, the hadron phase duration. We anticipate that the refined hadron phase duration will be significantly shorter than the value of 10 fm/c used in this analysis. Drawing inspiration from the human ability to multitask effectively, we introduce a framework that enables a robot to execute multiple objectives concurrently. This approach leverages an optimization method to handle the simultaneous pursuit of these tasks. Extensive simulations and real-world experiments were conducted to assess performance across various configurations and conditions. The results indicate that our method achieves a balanced outcome, successfully advancing all assigned tasks even when they conflict. Furthermore, this framework is highly adaptable and can be easily integrated into existing control systems. Pre-training deep neural networks on tasks sharing a subset of layers and training objectives has recently become a standard approach for addressing data scarcity in deep learning. This paper presents an extensive empirical study comparing various pre-training strategies for semantic segmentation, specifically investigating whether general depth estimation offers a stronger performance boost than closely related monocular depth estimation. We demonstrate that depth estimation yields significant gains for semantic segmentation, with monocular depth estimation achieving the best results. Furthermore, we find that the performance improvements from both monocular depth and depth from depth stereo are largely attributable to the depth estimation component, rather than the shared categorization objective. These findings are supported by our analysis of the shared categorical objective and the distinct pre-training performance of monocular depth estimation. Finally, we attribute these outcomes to the similarity in loss functions and output dimensions between depth and semantic segmentation, and we offer insights into the pre-training performance of other potential general encoders. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Depth-Segmentation. This work can be categorized under the theme: Pre-training for Semantic Segmentation. For a specific class of starlike log-harmonic mappings, we derive an estimate for the Bohr radius using a novel methodology. This derived estimate significantly surpasses the standard Bohr radius, which is independent of Bohr's original constant. Additionally, we provide a comparable estimate for the Bohr radius of the corresponding class of elliptically harmonic mappings. In this context, the radii of both the ellipses and the stars involved are treated as general parameters. Our primary focus remains on starlike log-harmonic mappings, where the resulting estimate exceeds the Bohr radius of the corresponding class of elliptically harmonic mappings, thereby reinforcing starlinearity as a more critical condition than elliptical linearity in this context. Furthermore, our result improves upon the estimate established by Mavrovouniotis and Ponnusamy. Finally, the Bohr radius for the class of circular log-harmonic mappings is computed, and the corresponding radius for the class of circular harmonic mappings is determined. In this specific scenario, the estimate for the Bohr radius of the class of circular log-harmonic mappings is strictly greater than that for the class of circular harmonic mappings. This confirms that our findings extend naturally to the case of circular harmonicity. We also establish that the Bohr radius for the class of circular harmonic mappings is precisely $1/3$, which is greater than the Bohr radius of $1/4$ for the class of starlike analytic functions. This demonstrates that our results generalize beyond starlike analytic functions and represent a significant advancement in the field. Our findings are particularly significant because they represent the first instance of such results being achieved for Bohr radii related to the Bohr phenomenon. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, offering robustness against outliers and capacity to detect monotone relationships. However, calculating the exact value of Kendall's tau becomes computationally prohibitive when dealing with datasets containing more than a few hundred data points. Consequently, researchers typically rely on Monte Carlo approximations to estimate the p-value for testing the significance of Kendall's tau. This study introduces a collection of methods designed to determine the exact or highly accurate p-value with a controlled failure rate, even for large-scale datasets. These approaches are grounded in techniques for reducing sample size, including the nearest neighbor chain algorithm, and utilize the concept of effective sample size. The proposed methods are evaluated through simulations and case studies focused on climate change. Additionally, all methods are implemented in the R package `kendalltest`. Finally, a web-based application named `kendalltest.org` allows users to easily access the package's functionality. This paper introduces a suite of algorithms for calculating the exact distribution of Kendall's tau, enabling robust hypothesis testing and confidence interval estimation. These methods rely on computing the effective sample size, a metric that quantifies the maximum number of pairwise comparisons necessary to estimate population parameters within a specific tolerance. The efficiency of these approaches was validated using datasets from climate change research. The implementation is available in the R package `kendalltest`, with a user-friendly web interface provided by `kendalltest.org`. These tools enable users to compute exact p-values for permutation tests of Kendall's tau, determine confidence intervals for population Kendall's tau, and assess the accuracy of common approximations. The methodology employs pairwise coarsening, drawing inspiration from the nearest neighbor chain algorithm, to reduce the count of pairwise comparisons. The paper details the theoretical underpinnings of effective sample size and its application to inferential tasks involving Kendall's tau. Furthermore, it demonstrates how to calculate population Kendall's tau and its distribution exactly, even when the effective sample size is unknown. The study also addresses scenarios where data are missing at random, allowing for the estimation of population Kendall's tau by conditioning on observed data. Finally, the paper illustrates how to leverage network structures to reduce the number of pairwise comparisons needed to estimate population Kendall's tau. The computational implementation was developed using the R packages `kendalltest` and `kendalltestR`, alongside the `kendalltest.org` web application. The rapid proliferation of connected and autonomous vehicles (CVs) has created significant challenges for processing and data privacy. To address these issues, this paper introduces a privacy-preserving edge intelligence framework designed for automotive networks. This system integrates two core components: Secure Aggregation (SA) and Differential Privacy (DP). SA enables the secure combination of data from multiple vehicles without exposing individual inputs, while DP ensures robust privacy guarantees by managing data sensitivity and uncertainty. The proposed framework is tailored for a scenario where a group of vehicles shares private data with an edge computing node to facilitate intelligent decision-making. Simulation results demonstrate that the framework effectively safeguards user privacy while maintaining high system utility. Furthermore, the outcomes indicate that varying the number of vehicles participating in the secure aggregation process can enhance privacy protection and reduce the computational load on the simulation simulation server. Ultimately, this framework holds promise for intelligent applications within automotive networks. A detailed description of the framework can be found in our technical report [1].

We introduce a novel manifold called the Euler characteristic manifold. Its coordinates consist of the Euler characteristics of various manifolds obtained by performing surgery on a given manifold along one specific diffeomorphism class of codimension-one spheres. We demonstrate that this manifold is countable and possesses a homology manifold structure. Furthermore, we establish that two manifolds have identical invariants (such as fundamental groups, Heegaard splitting genera, etc.) across all possible sphere surgeries if and only if they occupy the same coordinate location within the Euler characteristic manifold. Finally, we provide the specific invariants for several manifolds in dimension three or higher, which were previously unidentified or unclassified in existing literature. This paper serves as a preprint for the first volume of our ongoing book series on the Euler Characteristic Manifold. Subsequent volumes will detail the manifold's tangent and normal spaces, develop calculus on its surface, and utilize these tools to discover new manifolds. In the first paper of this series, we demonstrated that the facet rotation simplex method, introduced by P. Belotti and S. Vial in 1979, features a polynomial iteration bound when applied to linear programming problems with sparse matrices. In this study, we demonstrate that for dense matrices, a linear iteration bound is unattainable. Furthermore, we provide computational evidence suggesting that the method may exhibit a superlinear iteration bound. Additionally, we present evidence indicating that the method could possess a quadratic iteration bound. Finally, we extend these results to the revised criss-cross method, which is a specific instance of the facet rotation simplex method. The terminology and notation employed here align with those established in the companion paper. In that work, we defined and investigated several graph-theoretic concepts; in this paper, we apply those concepts to generate combinatorial proofs of the assertions made. This approach contrasts with the analytic proofs presented in the earlier study. We also outline a proof strategy for the superlinear iteration bound that relies on techniques analogous to those used for quadratic matrices. However, for matrices where the average degree is high, this strategy fails, and we conjecture that an analytic proof for the quadratic iteration bound in such scenarios is likely impossible. To address this, we propose an algorithm based on the facet rotation simplex method and offer a sketch of its analysis. We demonstrate that this algorithm achieves a quadratic iteration bound for linear programming problems with arbitrary matrices. Our algorithm adheres to the same rules for selecting the entering variable as the facet rotation simplex method, differing only in the selection of the leaving variable. We also present an alternative analysis of our algorithm, which relies on the same graph-theoretic concepts and generates the same combinatorial proofs regarding the lack of a linear iteration bound for dense matrices. This alternative approach may be more intuitive than the one we previously presented. Finally, we provide an outline of the proof for the quadratic iteration bound for the algorithm. The extension of these results to the criss-cross method follows from the initial section of this paper. We also present an outline of the proof for the quadratic iteration bound for criss-cross method variants. For an associative graded ring $R$ where elements of degree $-1$ form an $R_+$-regular sequence, and a space $X$ within the pointed homotopy category of $R$-modules, this paper computes the $R$-module structure on the $NK_1$ group of $R$'s unitary collection over $X$. Specifically, the structure of $NK_1(\mathcal{U}_{X})$ is shown to be isomorphic to $(\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}R_{-i})\otimes_{R}X\otimes_{R}R_{-1}$, where $\mathcal{U}_{X}$ denotes the unitary collection associated with $X$. This result extends the computation of $NK_1$ unitary categories, previously established by D. Bak and the second author, to the relative setting. The proof relies on the resolution of $-1$ graded modules proposed by J. Axelrod and S. Freed. Furthermore, as a consequence, the universal universal $K_1$ space $\mathsf{U}K_{1}(R)$ is identified as $S^{1}\wedge_{R}R_{-1}$, which aligns with the $K_{1}$ space of the graded ring $R$. Finally, the paper presents several applications, including the calculation of $\pi_{1}(\mathcal{U}_{X})$ and the derivation of a universal $K_{1}$ space for $R$-modules. Additionally, the dimension of $\pi_{0}(\mathcal{U}_{X})$ is determined by the rank of $X$ as an $R$-module. These findings generalize earlier results by D. Bak and the second author. The methodologies employed in this study may also be applicable to other algebraic structures. Finally, the authors acknowledge the valuable contributions of the anonymous referees, whose suggestions regarding the relative $K_{1}$ space of monoids and the $\pi_{1}(\mathcal{U}_{X})$ for $X$-modules significantly enhanced the paper's quality. This work investigates the impact of off-shell contributions on extracting the top quark mass from $t\bar{t}$+jet ($ttj$) events. We develop an analytical formula for the $W$-boson propagator that maintains a finite width at zero distance, ensuring a correct asymptotic behavior of $1/q^2$. This expression is subsequently applied to the matrix elements governing $q\bar{q}\to t\bar{t}+j$ and $qg\to t\bar{t}+q$ processes. Our findings indicate that incorporating off-shell effects in the $W$-boson propagator can alter cross-section predictions by up to 10% for $ttj$ events. Furthermore, we observe that these effects are more pronounced in $q\bar{q}\to t\bar{t}+j$ compared to the $qg\to t\bar{t}+q$ channel. Finally, we demonstrate that including off-shell corrections can enhance the precision of the extracted $m_t$ value by approximately 1%. These results are particularly relevant for the ATLAS and CMS measurements of the top quark mass at the LHC. Our approach can be extended to other $t$-channel processes to include $W$-boson off-shell corrections. Additionally, the off-shell corrected matrix elements presented here are available in the public software tool \texttt{CompHEP}. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has recently emerged as a promising approach for autonomous driving, yet it faces significant hurdles, including the need to model complex driving environments, define appropriate state and action spaces, ensure training stability, and incorporate safety into the learning process. This paper reviews recent advancements in DRL-based autonomous driving, specifically examining the recently released OpenPAE Driving dataset. The dataset's realistic simulation environment and carefully designed state and action spaces facilitate the training of robust driving policies. Furthermore, we introduce a novel safety-aware DRL framework to enhance training stability and enable safe driving behaviors. Our system demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods, successfully navigating various challenging scenarios found in the OpenPAE Driving dataset. Additionally, the proposed approach is versatile and can be applied to other driving datasets. Open-source implementations are accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1998/Safety-Aware-Deep-Driving. The comprehensive OpenPAE Driving evaluation code will be released shortly. We hope this work contributes meaningfully to the field of autonomous driving. All related code and data will be made publicly available. Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs) are designed to shorten the time required for running Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs). Among these, asynchronous parallel EAs offer performance benefits by enabling the continuous generation of offspring without waiting for the master node to evaluate worker-evaluated individuals. However, standard parallelization methods inherit the same issues as standard EAs, including evaluation time bias. This problem is particularly pronounced in asynchronous multi-objective EAs, where algorithms are increasingly utilized. To address this, we introduce a novel selection mechanism that reduces the impact of evaluation time bias in asynchronous multi-objective EAs by selecting parents based on the age of evaluated individuals. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed mechanism outperforms both standard synchronous and asynchronous parallelization approaches. Additionally, the method is straightforward to implement and incurs no extra computational cost. The study includes 156 experiments across 21 objective functions, comparing three PEA implementations. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/eduardo-oliveira/ParetoFronts. These findings indicate that the proposed mechanism is highly effective for generating high-quality solutions in asynchronous multi-objective EAs. Furthermore, the approach is versatile and can be applied to any multi-objective EAs, including those that do not rely on EAs. The research was conducted by Eduardo M. The microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 was identified through the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) survey, with follow-up observations from the Keck Adaptive Optics (AO) system yielding high-quality light curves. Analysis of these curves revealed a planetary anomaly, and the data were modeled using both the lensfit algorithm and the Bayesian analysis tool BAYESAL. Both methods identified a single planet, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434B, with a mass ratio of $\q = 0.0029 \pm 0.0008$ and a projected separation of $s = 1.19 \pm 0.14$ (where $s$ represents the projected separation relative to the Einstein radius). The mass ratio and orbital separation are highly constrained, whereas the mass and distance to the lens remain loosely constrained. Under the most probable parameters, the planet has a mass of $M_B = 1.9 \pm 0.3 M_{\oplus}$ and orbits a super-Earth star with a mass of $M_L = 4.6 \pm 0.6 M_{\oplus}$ at a distance of $d_L = 2.4 \pm 0.3$ kpc. The planet's semi-major axis is approximately 0.18 AU, resulting in an equilibrium temperature of roughly 10 K. This system is notable for being the coldest super-Earth discovered to date. Additionally, the event is the second to exhibit a planetary anomaly, further suggesting that microlensing may be more sensitive to the detection of cold planets than previously believed. This study underscores the AO technique's capability to detect very cold planets and super-Earths around low-mass stars. Future observations of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 are necessary to constrain the lens distance and mass, which will help determine the planet's precise temperature. Furthermore, the system may be a candidate for direct imaging using the James Webb Space Telescope. This work demonstrates that microlensing can identify a class of very cold planets that are otherwise difficult to detect. The AO method is anticipated to discover more such systems, potentially offering a unique window into the formation and evolution of planets in the outer regions of their systems. The quantum Langevin equation (QLE) and the Lindblad master equation (LME) are fundamental frameworks for analyzing open quantum systems. In many applications, the dynamical generators of the LME exhibit rapid temporal oscillations. Although high-frequency expansions have been developed for conservative oscillations, their validity and limitations regarding non-conservative cases remain unclear. This study investigates these aspects and establishes rigorous bounds for such expansions. We demonstrate that a single term in the expansion is sufficient to capture the quasi-static dynamics of a two-level system, and we construct second-order expansions for general multi-level systems. Furthermore, we derived experimental data confirming these expansions and observed that both first- and second-order approximations align well with the data. These findings are expected to facilitate more efficient simulations of quantum systems with non-conservative high-frequency oscillations. Additionally, we note that the developed expansions can be applied to various other contexts, including the high-temperature behavior of Lindblad generators and the analysis of quantum non-demolition measurements. Finally, our work offers a comprehensive review of the Lindblad equation and Lindblad generators, which may serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the field. Specifically, we provide the first complete characterization of Lindblad operators that generate the maximally mixed state. This characterization is essential for understanding the dynamics of high-temperature open quantum systems. We also highlight the existence of a non-unique class of Lindblad operators capable of driving the system to the maximally mixed state, a phenomenon that may have significant implications for quantum thermodynamics. This characterization is expected to be useful for researchers in this area. Finally, we have made our code publicly available to assist researchers in their studies. Our code, which is based on the Python package QETLAB, is available at \url{https://github.com/etkaya/QETLAB/tree/QLE}. Users can access it by cloning the repository and switching to the QLE branch. This shift causes the zero-field neutron depolarization signal to vanish. The resulting field-dependent changes in the depolarization signal align with the magnetic field-induced shift from a nonmagnetic to a ferromagnetic phase. These observations are consistent with the phase diagram of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reported in prior studies. We conducted a 21-cm neutral hydrogen survey targeting the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 using the NRO VLA. This area is renowned for hosting the Galactic center's most luminous HII region, G176.51+00.20 M, and is believed to contain a massive black hole candidate, G176.51+00.20 I. Our observations revealed numerous HI narrow-line self-emission sources within the region, with the majority located near the G176.51+00.20 I candidate. The HI velocity dispersion of these narrow-line self-emissions was found to be comparable to that of the surrounding molecular gas. Furthermore, the velocity structure of these HI features aligns with the kinematic pattern of the surrounding molecular gas, suggesting they are physically linked to the molecular cloud. We propose that the G176.51+00.20 I object is a massive black hole surrounded by a massive accretion disk. The accretion disk is thought to be composed of cold, neutral gas, and the observed HI narrow-line self-emissions are interpreted as HI gas heated by the accretion process. Additionally, the spatial distribution of these HI features appears to trace the morphology of the X-ray jet emanating from the black hole. This study demonstrates that HI narrow-line self-emission is a viable tool for investigating the accretion processes of massive black holes. Future investigations should aim to detect HI narrow-line self-emission around other massive black hole candidates to further explore their accretion mechanisms. The NRO VLA is well-suited for this purpose, and we anticipate that its future observations will uncover more HI self-emission features near other massive black hole candidates. The data from this study will be accessible at the NRO VLA archive. We demonstrate that the intermediate $\beta$-shift, originally defined by Ferenczi and Preiss, is equivalent to a specific class of greedy $\beta$-systems featuring a gap, a concept introduced by Bugeaud and Mauduit in certain contexts. This equivalence offers a novel approach to analyzing the dimension of these systems. Consequently, we establish a criterion for determining the dimension of an intermediate $\beta$-shift based on the distribution of its return times, a method inspired by preprint arXiv:2001.01000, which generalizes findings by Preiss and Rudolph regarding the dimension of symbolic dynamics on one-sided $\beta$-shifts. Furthermore, we provide sufficient conditions under which intermediate $\beta$-shifts possess the specification property, thereby extending the work of Preiss and Preiss. Finally, we examine an alternative characterization of intermediate $\beta$-shifts through the lens of $\beta$-transformation dynamics, specifically by characterizing the set of discontinuities of their inverse transformation. This analysis includes a unified treatment of various intermediate $\beta$-shifts, such as those associated with Pisot and Salem numbers, as well as algebraic integers of degree 3. Notably, our findings indicate that the distribution of return times for this inverse transformation is, in general, irregular, even when the underlying algebraic number is a Pisot number. This irregularity contrasts sharply with the behavior observed in the one-sided $\beta$-shift. Our investigation is motivated by the intriguing question posed by Preiss: Do there exist intermediate $\beta$-shifts where the set of discontinuities of the inverse transformation forms a set of measure zero? Our results suggest an affirmative answer to this question. To support this, we provide explicit examples of intermediate $\beta$-shifts derived from Pisot and Salem numbers, where the return times of the inverse transformation exhibit regular behavior, resulting in a set of discontinuities with a dimension strictly less than 1. These examples encompass not only Pisot and Salem numbers but also certain Pisot and Salem numbers of degree 4. Additionally, we identify a family of intermediate $\beta$-shifts that arise from a novel class of Pisot and Salem numbers, which we term Pisot and Salem type $\alpha^*$. The existence of this family is established in a separate paper, which also offers a comprehensive overview of the properties of intermediate $\beta$-shifts. Training neural networks for image recognition demands vast quantities of labeled data, a resource that is frequently unavailable in real-world scenarios. Domain adaptation (DA) offers a solution by enabling models trained on a source domain to function in a target domain, particularly when both domains are related. This study comprehensively evaluates various deep DA approaches for image recognition, systematically analyzing their performance across different configurations. We conducted experiments on three benchmark datasets, utilizing eight standard DA methods alongside three recent self-training-based DA techniques. Our findings indicate that simple yet effective strategies, such as training the network jointly on both source and target domains, yield promising results. Furthermore, we observed that semi-supervised DA methods outperform fully supervised ones, highlighting the cost-effectiveness of these approaches. To facilitate future research, we have made all experimental code and data available at: https://github.com/abhishekgupta12345/DA-Review. This work serves as a valuable resource for researchers in the field. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/abhishekgupta12345/DA-Review.

The collection of all such points forms a regular tetrahedron. We aim to prove that the total count of distinct triangles with vertices at these grid points is precisely $2n+1$ times the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{3}$.

To establish this, we first determine the number of triangles formed by grid points within an $n$-level structure. By analyzing the combinatorial properties of the grid, we can derive the final expression. This count encompasses all triangle types, including those with parallel sides, and is consistent with known results in combinatorial geometry.

The final formula, $2n+1 \times \binom{n}{3}$, represents the total number of triangles that can be formed using the grid points as vertices. This result is significant in various areas of mathematics, such as graph theory and combinatorial optimization, where understanding the number of substructures in a mathematical structure is crucial.

In conclusion, the number of triangles that can be formed using the grid points of a tetrahedral structure as vertices is exactly $2n+1 \times \binom{n}{3}$. This proof without words demonstrates the elegance and simplicity of mathematical reasoning and can be used to illustrate the power of combinatorial arguments in mathematics. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have gained significant traction for analyzing graph-structured data, yet their internal mechanisms remain difficult to interpret. This paper introduces the Parameterized Interpreter (PI), a novel framework designed to render GNNs more transparent. By explicitly modeling the roles of individual GNN components, the PI illustrates how these parts contribute to the network's behavior. The framework is highly adaptable, supporting various existing GNN architectures and the graph operators essential to them. Additionally, the PI is versatile enough to be employed as a meta-learning approach to generate models that are either larger or smaller than the original, or as a method to GNN distill large, complex networks into smaller, interpretable ones without compromising performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the PI enables this reduction in size while maintaining a negligible impact on accuracy. The PI is expected to facilitate the investigation of GNN characteristics and aid in debugging these models. The implementation of the PI framework and a suite of GNNs are available at https://github.com/DeepGraphLearning/PI. Furthermore, a comprehensive set of experiments was conducted on the PyTorch Geometric platform. The results indicate that the PI can significantly shrink both the number of parameters and the model size, thereby allowing for more efficient training and deployment. Specifically, the PI can reduce a GNN to approximately 10% of its original size with minimal accuracy loss. This shrinkage is achieved by retaining only the most critical parts of the GNN, making it possible to analyze the internal workings of the network. These retained essential components can be identified to guide future research. The essential GNN parts discovered by the PI are detailed in the paper's appendix. We report a serendipitous gravitational lensing discovery involving the galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420, which exhibits multiple lensed arcs and two substructures, designated as DS1 and DS2. By analyzing the convergence map, we determined the physical properties of these substructures. Our findings indicate that DS1 is likely a dark matter halo with a mass of $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.4} \times 10^{13} M_{\odot}$ located at $0.17^{+0.05}_{-0.04} r_{500}$, while DS2 corresponds to a halo mass of $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.4} \times 10^{12} M_{\odot}$ at $0.35^{+0.08}_{-0.06} r_{500}$. Additionally, we identified a subclump in the X-ray surface brightness profile that aligns with the substructure at 0.35 r500. This subclump's X-ray luminosity is estimated to be $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.4} \times 10^{43}$ erg/s, with a 90% confidence level that it is not a chance alignment. The presence of substructures in both the X-ray profile and mass distribution suggests that the accretion history of RXCJ0232.2-4420 is more complex than previously understood. Furthermore, the mass distribution of the substructures remains largely unaffected by the cluster's merging activity. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings regarding the cluster's formation and evolution. This study underscores the value of combining gravitational lensing with X-ray observations for investigating galaxy cluster substructures. Future research should employ more sophisticated techniques to analyze substructure properties and their impact on the cluster's evolution. Additionally, we recommend further studies to explore the relationship between substructures and the cluster's accretion history. Ultimately, RXCJ0232.2-4420 serves as a valuable case study for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. Legendre Memory Block (LMB) is a lightweight memory architecture designed for deep neural networks. This study demonstrates that training LMB can be accelerated through parallelization by grouping samples based on their Legendre polynomial evaluations. We introduce a method for training this memory block in parallel using a novel data-parallel strategy. Experimental results indicate that a multi-core CPU configuration can achieve up to a 3.5x speedup compared to a single core, with minimal deviation from single-core performance. Additionally, we show that training the entire network with LMB is viable through a new approach called Data-Parallel LMB, which employs a non-trivial sampling method. This technique allows for parallel training of the full LMB-based network without degrading the generalization ability of the resulting model. The proposed Data-Parallel LMB method is versatile and can be applied to other memory-based neural networks. Furthermore, we illustrate that this method facilitates the training of networks on large datasets, such as CIFAR10 and MNIST, that were previously considered too vast for single-core training capabilities. Furthermore, we show the game's applicability to both online and offline social networks, where agents interact to adopt a naming protocol that aligns with linguistic goals derived from their specific network context. Finally, we outline the game's relevance to other real-world scenarios, including language learning and cultural evolution. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently demonstrated significant utility for solving differential equations, yet they often suffer from slow convergence and are highly sensitive to hyperparameters. This study reveals that standard PINNs exhibit spectral bias, favoring low-frequency modes, which slows convergence and creates a risk of getting trapped in local minima. We show that incorporating a momentum term into the PINN update rule mitigates this spectral bias, accelerates convergence, and produces more accurate results. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of how momentum influences the learning dynamics of PINNs. Finally, numerical experiments confirm that adding momentum allows PINNs to converge rapidly and learn high-frequency modes effectively. Consequently, introducing momentum transforms PINNs into a more efficient and robust method for solving both linear and nonlinear high/low-frequency partial differential equations. This study examines a coupled wave system featuring locally disrupted KV damping and coupling, formulated as a coupled hyperbolic dissipative system. We first demonstrate that the energy of the system decays polynomially. Subsequently, we establish the well-posedness of the coupled wave system by employing the Friedrichs extension theorem to construct maximal self-adjoint operators for the coupled second-order elliptic operators within the Dirichlet setting. The proof strategy for polynomial energy decay relies on a combination of the abstract shift semigroup method, the Lax-Milgram theorem, and the Friedrichs extension theorem. Furthermore, we prove that the Kato square root property does not hold in disconnected domains. Finally, utilizing the Lax-Milgram theorem, we derive $L^2$-solvability for specific coupled elliptic operators with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a result that is essential for establishing the polynomial decay of energy. Additionally, the maximum principle is applied to demonstrate that the displacement remains bounded. These findings are achieved through a series of technical estimates, including those concerning coupled elliptic operators, the Kreiss-Lopatinskii condition, and coupled parabolic-dissipative operators. Notably, our results extend to cases involving a Neumann condition. The approach utilized here is applicable to various coupled wave systems, including those with nonlinear damping, nonlinear coupling, or nonlinear disrupted damping. Specifically, this work addresses a gap in the literature regarding coupled wave equations with disrupted Kelvin-Voigt damping, a problem that has not been previously solved. Our methodology is rigorous and rigorous enough to be extended to other related coupled wave systems. Finally, the paper includes several examples of coupled wave systems with disrupted Kelvin-Voigt damping to illustrate the applicability of the proposed method. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive and detailed analysis of the stability and well-posedness of coupled wave systems with locally disrupted Kelvin-Voigt damping, offering a valuable reference for future research in this area. Although model-based reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising avenue for creating data-efficient, generalizable agents capable of handling unseen environments, it frequently depends on ad-hoc heuristics and lacks the ability to explain its learned models. This paper introduces a hierarchical RL framework utilizing inductive logic programming (ILP) to derive symbolic representations from raw sensor data. By employing a top-down strategy, the system decomposes complex tasks into simpler subtasks based on the semantic structures of these symbolic representations. This approach enables the construction of interpretable hierarchical RL models that demonstrate robustness in both generalizing to new settings and recovering from environmental perturbations. Experimental results in robotic navigation tasks validate the efficacy of our proposed method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2002/iLHAM. In summary, we present a novel, data-driven method for task decomposition that yields both high performance and interpretability. Furthermore, our findings suggest that deep model-based RL and symbolically grounded RL can be effectively merged to enhance sample efficiency and robustness. Finally, the application of ILP in RL opens doors for further research into leveraging symbolic AI to create more interpretable and data-efficient artificial intelligence systems. This paper introduces natural Hoare logic, a novel formalism designed to verify the correctness of ordinary programs expressed in computable languages against natural language specifications. We provide a comprehensive abstract syntax and semantics for the language, alongside a proof system for formal validity. Within this system, theorems correspond to assertions in form, while the rules facilitate the construction of formal validity proofs. The approach is illustrated through examples drawn from our previous research on the formal validation of C programs, demonstrating how proofs are developed using the natural language specification language. Furthermore, we implement the syntax and semantics within Nqthm and Coq, and provide a custom Coq library that encapsates the proof system. Finally, we present the formalization of several representative proofs within this framework. Overall, this work offers a foundation for integrating natural language into formal methods, bridging the gap between human-readable requirements and machine-checkable proofs. By providing a formal basis for reasoning about natural language, the system advances the formal validation of software against such specifications. Additionally, the ability to formalize proofs ensures their rigor and minimizes the risk of errors. The resulting system is extensible, allowing for further refinement of the logic and the formalization of additional proofs, thereby supporting the broader adoption of natural language in formal methods. Our findings indicate that the formalization process is straightforward and does not impose significant overhead on existing proofs. We conclude that natural Hoare logic is a viable approach for incorporating natural language into formal methods and propose it as a foundation for future research in this area. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the development of formalizations for natural language specifications, enhancing the application of formal methods to software systems defined by such language. We also suggest that the formalization of proofs will aid in the widespread adoption of natural language within formal methods. The paper includes source code for the syntax and semantics implementations in Nqthm and Coq, along with illustrative examples of valid formulas and proofs. The Coq library is available at https://github.com/ahmed-ayoub/natural-hoare-logic. Canopus is a Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) replica state machine (RSM) designed for cloud environments, featuring a streamlined protocol that reduces network traffic and latency compared to other BFT solutions. However, Canopus currently lacks robustness against node failures and Byzantine behaviors. This paper introduces RCanopus, an enhanced version of Canopus that safely manages node failures and Byzantine faults. We validate the effectiveness of RCanopus through an extensive experimental evaluation. The results demonstrate that RCanopus matches Canopus's performance under normal operating conditions while successfully tolerating node failures and Byzantine faults. Furthermore, RCanopus surpasses the robustness-enhanced version of PBFT, achieving 1.5 times higher throughput and 1.5 times lower latency. Additionally, we implemented RCanopus on Kubernetes and confirmed that it retains Canopus's performance characteristics within the cluster. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address and resolve the issues of unrobustness and Byzantine faults inherent in Canopus. This paper presents Phase I of the first comprehensive catalog of the highest-energy cosmic particles detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory. The catalog features 27 extreme events with energies surpassing 1.00×10²⁰ eV, along with an additional 15 events within the narrow band of 1.01×10²⁰ eV to 1.09×10²⁰ eV, which collectively constitute the sample of 42 ultra-high-energy particles utilized in recent extreme energy statistics. For every event, we provide the shower direction, energy, and arrival time, alongside the complete list of detector stations that measured the event. We also examine the potential significance of clusters of extreme events and their implications for source identification. Furthermore, the event flux is analyzed in relation to the Augmented Eddington model of ultra-high-energy particle sources. A machine learning approach is employed to assess the probability of events originating from the Milky Way, utilizing a new feature set derived from the angular distribution of event constituents. Additionally, we present the two most extreme events, UF6348 and UF764, which were recorded just 1.5 seconds apart, and explore the possibility of them being fragments of a single, much higher-energy event. Deep Object Detectors (OODs) are widely utilized across numerous computer vision applications. However, their inability to provide uncertainty estimates restricts their deployment in safety-critical environments. We introduce BayesOD, the first general framework for uncertainty estimation in OODs by applying Bayesian principles to replace standard feedforward layers. By enabling uncertainty calculation at both the object level and pixel level, BayesOD supports bounding box regression, classification, and instance segmentation. On benchmark datasets, our method achieves competitive performance while delivering meaningful uncertainty metrics. Specifically, BayesOD matches the accuracy of its non-bayesian counterpart, SingleShotDetector (SSD), on PASCAL VOC and COCO, and surpasses it on OHS2017. Furthermore, it generates reliable uncertainty values for both detected and non-detected objects, as well as for positive and negative background pixels. The project's implementation and code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder1992/BayesOD. The source code will be made available upon request.

We introduce a bicategorical framework for morphism-revising, a concept recently proposed by Abramsky and N\'ab\'o as an abstract representation of computational updating. Equipped with appropriate structural properties, this framework carries an intrinsic bicategorical geometry that defines the maximum geometry for revising a specific morphism. Furthermore, we extend the theory to include methods for constructing the geometry of revising a composite morphism, thereby clarifying the conditions under which this construction is universal. To facilitate applications, we develop the theory within a general setting for updated geometry, demonstrating its utility for individual and morphism updating in categories of relations and Set-based relations. We also present a generalized coherence theorem for individual updating and prove, via the Set-based relations model, that the geometry for morphism updating constitutes the maximal coherence structure for that category. Finally, we outline a strategy for applying this framework to other computational categories. In the concluding section, we discuss related work and potential future research directions. This paper extends the authors' earlier work, which presented only the Set-based relations model, by providing a more general theory and a broader application. The development of the theory itself is new. Additionally, the related work section has been expanded to include a discussion of coherence. Consequently, this version of the paper offers a more comprehensive treatment of both theory and application than the previous version. Accurate segmentation of the hippocampus is essential for diagnosing and analyzing various neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. However, the heterogeneous nature of hippocampus images and the diversity of pathologies make this task difficult. Deep learning methods have proven effective for segmentation; this study introduces a novel architecture that integrates four Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to enhance feature extraction and optimize hyperparameters. The proposed model was evaluated on the ADNI and SEEG-hippo datasets, which encompass data from patients with Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. Experimental results indicate that the model surpasses other state-of-the-art techniques, achieving a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.8102 on the ADNI dataset and 0.7508 on the SEEG-hippo dataset. These findings demonstrate the model's superior performance and robustness across different epilepsy and Alzheimer's cases. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/abdallah-ahmed/hippocampus-segmentation}. Additionally, the model is available on Hugging Face at \url{https://huggingface.co/abdallah-ahmed/hippocampus-segmentation}. We examine the mapping of a rotating Gaussian beam through a stationary diffraction grating by solving the time-dependent paraxial wave equation. Our findings indicate that the apparent pigeonholing of transverse modes, typically observed when a non-pulsed Gaussian beam is mapped through a static diffraction grating, does not occur with a transversal mode-gaussian beam interaction. Instead, both the transverse and longitudinal evolutions exhibit significant differences, demonstrating that the transverse and longitudinal motions are not independent. These insights are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we explore the potential applications of this phenomenon. This study utilizes the Geant4 simulation package to analyze the spectrum of secondary cosmic ray particles trapped in low-Earth orbit, specifically for the CRAND (CReosure ANalysis Database) project, which supports the CReosure experiment. Trapped particles are a primary source of noise for the experiment's sensitive components. The research focuses on modeling particle interactions with CReosure's mechanical structure, particularly those striking the outer skin, to evaluate their potential to cause Single Event Upsets (SEUs) and Single Event Latchups (SELs) in electronic devices. The resulting spectra are compared against the AE8 and AE9 empirical models. The simulation reveals that secondary particles generated by cosmic ray interactions within the CReosure mechanical structure are the dominant contributors to the CRAND spectrum. Furthermore, the AE8 and AE9 models significantly underestimate the trapped particle flux, which is critical for assessing SEU and SEL risks. Consequently, this work demonstrates the necessity of employing simulation tools to accurately predict the CRAND spectrum. The methodology is also applicable to other space-based experiments. Future research will expand the analysis to include electronic devices, aiming to quantify the specific SEU and SEL effects. The code used in this simulation will be made publicly available. The final conclusions will be presented at the 35th International Cosmic Ray Conference (ICRC). This manuscript was submitted as a short paper. Low-rank matrix completion focuses on reconstructing a matrix that is assumed to have a low rank. This work investigates the application of differentially private mechanisms to complete such matrices. We introduce the privately completed low-rank matrix (PCLMR) framework, which employs a joint optimization strategy combining the REweighted least-squares (RE) method with the HUBER loss function. Our analysis demonstrates that the HUBER mechanism is optimal for the PCLMR framework when a first-order optimality condition exists. Furthermore, we empirically validate the mechanism's effectiveness in both continuous and discrete settings. Finally, we compare our approach against existing private matrix completion methods, confirming that the HUBER mechanism delivers superior performance. Additionally, we explore the application of this mechanism in privacy-preserving recommender systems. We introduce a unified astrophysical model that describes the extinction, emission, and polarization of the diffuse and clumpy interstellar medium (ISM) using a single set of dust components. This model incorporates "Astrodust," a collection of $10^{16}$ cm$^3$ amorphous carbon grains and $10^{15}$ cm$^3$ silicate grains, which are the primary contributors to the diffuse ISM's extinction and energy emission. Additionally, we model the emission from 11 specific, commonly observed, and isolated classes of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs). Astrodust exhibits wavelength-dependent polarization in both the optical and far-infrared/submillimeter ranges, with a polarization efficiency that closely matches observations. The efficiency of astrodust's emission is approximately 10% that of PAHs, indicating that astrodust acts as the main energy donor to PAHs, while PAHs function as the primary radiators. The astrophysical implications of this model are explored in a companion paper. This work is part of a broader project aimed at modeling the ISM using a minimal set of components. The model's predictions for extinction, emission, and polarization are available through a Python package named "AstroModel" and a RESTful web service called "AstroModel+." The package can be installed via `pip install AstroModel`, and the service can be accessed at https://astromodel-plus.herokuapp.com/. A forthcoming paper will detail the model's predictions regarding extinction, emission, and polarization. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/astro-model/AstroModel.
