We report the detection of a massive planet within the protoplanetary disk surrounding the brown dwarf CIDA 1. This companion, with a mass of approximately 1 Jupiter mass, is located at a radial distance of 100 au. The planet is identified through a prominent gap in the disk observed by ALMA, which aligns with hydrodynamical and migration simulations of gap formation by massive planets. Spectroscopic analysis of the host star indicates it is a very low-mass star with a mass of 0.08 solar masses and an age of roughly 10 million years. The system's disk surface density closely matches the MMSN model, and the planet's mass corresponds to the minimum required to create the detected gap. Additionally, we present new ALMA continuum data from a nearby disk around a T-type dwarf, demonstrating that this method is effective for studying disks around very low-mass stars. This work underscores the necessity of observing disks around very low-mass stars to constrain planet formation models in low-mass regimes and to explore the connection between brown dwarfs and giant planets.

This paper investigates the Most Taps Problem, which involves identifying a configuration of lit squares in a grid that requires the maximum number of taps to extinguish all lights, and determining the minimum taps needed for each configuration. While prior research has primarily addressed rectangular grids, this study extends the investigation to simply connected grids. For both types of grids, we demonstrate that the minimum number of taps is generally finite except in specific cases, with an infinite maximum occurring only when all vertices are two-colorable. Furthermore, we show that a configuration yields the maximum number of taps if and only if every connected component is two-colorable. The paper also examines how adding edges alters the tap counts and establishes that for an $m \times n$ grid, a configuration achieves the maximum number of taps if and only if it comprises a Hamiltonian cycle and isolated vertices. Additionally, we determine the number of both minimum and maximum configurations for $m \times n$ grids. Finally, we present a novel combinatorial interpretation of these results through the lens of linear algebra over the field $\mathbb{F}_2$. Specifically, we provide a new interpretation of minimum taps using affine subspaces and relate maximum taps to binary necklaces. These findings lead to several open problems. Notably, we conjecture that a configuration of lit squares achieves the maximum number of taps if and only if it consists entirely of isolated vertices or bipartite connected components. This conjecture holds true for hexagonal grids, though it remains open for other grid types. We also address a related conjecture by determining the number of minimum and maximum configurations for a hexagonal grid, revealing that the number of maximum configurations is always 1. Finally, we offer a conjecture regarding the relationship between the minimum number of taps and the number of lit squares in a grid configuration. Through computational experiments, we observe that the number of minimum tap configurations in an $m \times n$ grid appears to grow exponentially with $m+n$. Furthermore, we conjecture that for an $m \times n$ grid, a configuration has the minimum number of taps if and only if it is either empty or a union of vertex-disjoint cycles. This conjecture is verified for small grids, including those with $m \leq 4$ or $n \leq 4$. This paper introduces a new vari-image segmentation framework. The proposed model decouples the segmentation and recovery steps of the image segmentation process, thereby enhancing the efficiency of the segmentation algorithm. Furthermore, the integration of the recovery algorithm into the segmentation algorithm accelerates convergence. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the model's effectiveness and efficiency, with results indicating that the model's parameters are robust. The model has been successfully applied to various images, yielding satisfactory results. The model is anticipated to hold significant potential for future research and practical applications. Additionally, the model is expected to be valuable for diverse fields, including remote sensing, medical imaging, and security systems. Finally, the model is likely to contribute to the advancement of computer vision and image processing technologies.

Abstract Interpretation (AI) relies on a two-phase framework: abstract domain construction and static analysis. Historically, these phases were tightly coupled, with domain design heavily influenced by the specific target program. This paper introduces a decoupling strategy, where the architecture of the abstract domain is defined independently of the program and guided by data from dynamic execution. The analysis itself is then derived from the domain rather than being directly programmed. This approach offers two key benefits: (1) it separates domain construction from analysis, enabling domain design to be driven by runtime data, and (2) it facilitates data-driven automation, allowing analysts to focus on the analysis phase while the domain design remains implicit. We demonstrate this concept using a case study on pointer alias analysis, validating the decoupling idea. The results indicate that programs can be analyzed without explicitly designing an abstract domain, achieving performance comparable to existing methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the analysis phase is significantly easier to automate than the domain design phase. Finally, we explore how this analysis, when driven by an abstract domain, can address diverse challenges, including alias analysis, points-to analysis, and pointer alias and points-to predicate analysis. All code required to reproduce our experimental results is publicly available. (Code: https://github.com/zhongyuan2000/SDAI/tree/alias-analysis, Mirror: https://github.com/zhongyuan2000/SDAI/tree/main) )

Topological phonons have recently been identified in oxide perovskites, a discovery that could enhance functional properties like acoustic wave propagation and detect these states through spectroscopic methods. A critical next step is identifying external control mechanisms to manipulate and switch these states. In this study, we demonstrate that laser excitation can modulate the topological phonon state by altering the host material's electronic structure. This modulation is achieved via ultrafast pump pulses, the timing of which allows for the tuning of defect-induced scattering. These findings expand the scope of controllable topological phonons and highlight the dynamic interaction between topological phonons and electronic defects.

Identifying outliers is a critical challenge across numerous real-world applications, including anomaly detection, fraud prevention, and risk management. This paper introduces a novel outlier detection approach that leverages proximity graphs, such as the Navigable Small World graph, to achieve rapid and exact results within high-dimensional spaces under the L2 norm. By utilizing these graphs, the method efficiently filters out non-outlier candidates, thereby significantly cutting down the necessary distance computations. Furthermore, by eliminating the need for clustering, it surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art techniques. The resulting speed improvements enable the processing of large datasets, such as the CIFAR-100 image dataset, on standard hardware. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in both speed and accuracy. Additionally, the method proves effective in downstream tasks for outlier detection, finding applications in image de-noising and image classification. In these scenarios, outlier scores are used to remove noisy training data, enhancing the quality of models trained via deep learning. Task-specific scores further allow for the identification of misclassified samples in test sets. The method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffer/NSW-Outlier-Detection. The associated code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/SebastianSchaeffer/NSW-Outlier-Detection/tree/master/Experiments. The paper begins by describing an atom situated before a thin fully reflective membrane driven by an external force. It is demonstrated that a stimulating light pulse sent to the atom can trigger stimulated emission even before the pulse physically reaches the membrane. Following this, an analysis of the membrane's dynamics and the system's scattering properties is provided. The study reveals that the membrane's inertia causes a delay in the system's response, resulting in a phase shift between the driving force and the displacement. Furthermore, it is shown that the membrane's finite thickness and mass lead to the generation of motion-induced radiation. The final section compares these findings with similar calculations performed using a local approximation for the membrane's displacement. The article concludes by suggesting potential applications of these effects in memranomechanics and nano-optomechanics. Additionally, the supporting material includes various technical calculations and proofs, such as the derivation of the equation of motion for a thin membrane, an analysis of scattering properties, and the calculation of radiation caused by the membrane's motion. A related paper will explore the inverse scenario, where membrane motion induces atomic excitation. Finally, the authors note that these calculations are applicable to optomechanics, where the membrane functions as a mirror for the electromagnetic field. In that context, the study examines motion-induced coupling between the atom and the electromagnetic field, a phenomenon that could be utilized to create a quantum switch for the light-atom interaction. The optomechanical application is addressed in a companion paper. Keywords: Membrane, Membrane mechanics, Optomechanics, Atoms, Atomic physics, Radiation.

This study examines kinetic models of reversible enzyme reactions, addressing both scenarios where the total enzyme concentration is known and where it is unknown. For the former, an $L^2$ approximation method is proposed utilizing a single enzyme state variable. For the latter, an iterative algorithm is developed using two state variables. In both applications, the approximation solutions asymptotically converge to the kinetic equations' kinetic boundary value solutions. Additionally, numerical simulations were conducted to validate the efficacy of these approximation methods. This study presents findings from a search conducted on proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ gathered by the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC. The analysis targets natural supersymmetry models characterized by light charginos and gluinos, as well as models featuring a compressed chargino-neutralino mass spectrum. The search examines final states containing at least one jet with missing transverse momentum, specifically investigating regions with moderate or high jet transverse momentum, low-multiplicity events with low jet transverse momentum, and events featuring compressed chargino-neutralino masses. No significant excess above the predicted background was observed. Consequently, model-dependent limits on the masses of gluinos (ranging from 1.1 to 2.2 TeV) and charginos (from 0.1 to 1.1 TeV) were established at 95% confidence level. Additionally, model-independent exclusion limits were set for charginos with masses below 1 TeV and gluinos below 2 TeV at 95% confidence level. These constraints are the most stringent to date for charginos under 1 TeV and gluinos under 2 TeV within the context of natural supersymmetry. Furthermore, limits were derived for final states containing jets and missing transverse momentum arising from the pair production of top quarks, bottom quarks, or first- or second-generation squarks. The exclusion limits for top quark pair production via squark mediation extend up to 1.1 TeV, representing the tightest limits to date. For neutral and charged Higgs boson pair production, constraints up to 600 GeV were obtained. This study develops and validates a diagnostic approach grounded in the rational expectations model of stochastic bubble dynamics originally proposed by Nelson and Siegel (1987). Within this framework, the "level" component defines the time-varying break-even return for a bubble, while the "slope" component drives the bubble's growth. The "twist" component captures shifts in the bubble's shape, and the "curvature" component indicates changes in the slope. Consequently, bubbles are classified as expanding, peaking, or declining based on a positive "slope," "twist," or "level," respectively.

The primary innovation of this diagnostic lies in its stochastic formulation. Unlike prior models that assume a constant duration for expanding, peaking, or declining bubbles, this approach allows those phases to terminate at random times. This is achieved through a hazard rate that exhibits a mean-reverting stochastic process, enabling the model to reflect time-varying bubble characteristics.

To ensure the practical viability of this innovative framework, the paper applies it to the S&P 500 index, examining the frequency, timing, and durations of bubbles across various states. The findings indicate that the model is highly effective at identifying both historical and future bubbles. Furthermore, the study reveals that the times at which bubbles reach their peak states are not fixed but instead exhibit mean-reverting behavior. Finally, the analysis demonstrates that the hazard rate associated with the transition from a bubble state to a non-bubble state is also subject to a mean-reverting process. These results underscore the necessity of employing stochastic models to accurately characterize the timing and duration of financial bubbles. We present a straightforward numerical method for calculating the wave functions of a quantum harmonic oscillator that has reached nonequilibrium steady state under a driving force. This approach utilizes the path integral combined with Monte Carlo techniques to perform direct real-space simulations. Specifically, we apply the Metropolis algorithm to construct a steady-state nonequilibrium loop product integral numerically. As a proof of concept, we employ this method to compute the nonequilibrium wave functions of a driven quantum harmonic oscillator. Our findings demonstrate that the numerically obtained expectation values align well with both analytical solutions and results from the Schrödinger equation, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed method. Furthermore, we show that the method's computational cost remains manageable even for higher oscillator modes. This technique is broadly applicable to various quantum systems, including those too complex for analytical treatment. Finally, we discuss the method's potential applications in other nonequilibrium scenarios, such as quantum particles subject to a linear electric field within a perfect one-dimensional crystal lattice under a finite temperature regime. In that specific case, the method can determine the probability density of electrons undergoing Bloch oscillations within nonequilibrium Wigner states under an external electric field. This latter application holds significant promise for nonequilibrium quantum optics and quantum information science. Additionally, the method can be applied to investigate quantum phase transitions in nonequilibrium driven systems, such as the quantum phase transition in a nonequilibrium spin Bose-Hubbard model. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of quantum Monte Carlo methods to nonequilibrium quantum systems. Our findings indicate that these methods are highly effective for studying quantum systems in nonequilibrium steady states. This marks a significant advancement in the application of quantum Monte Carlo methods to nonequilibrium physics. Furthermore, the method's potential applications extend to nonequilibrium quantum thermodynamics, including the investigation of work distributions and fluctuations in nonequilibrium quantum systems. In recent years, Item Recommendation systems have become increasingly popular. However, existing approaches often overlook the rich information contained in user reviews, which can significantly influence items. To address this, we introduce the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), a new framework designed for review-centric item recommendation. This model incorporates two key components: the Bi-directional Sentiment-aware Attention (BiSA) module and the User-aware Sentiment-aware Fusion (USAF) module. BiSA enables fine-grained sentiment-aware feature extraction by modeling both word and sentiment-level dependencies within reviews, while USAF captures user-aware sentiment features by simulating how reviews interact under a specific sentiment filter. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in review-centered recommendations. Furthermore, case studies reveal that the USAF module effectively captures the dynamic interactions between reviews and sentiment filters. The source code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/SIFN}.

Data scarcity remains a significant hurdle in code-switched multilingual natural language processing. To address this, we explore data augmentation techniques for Arabic-English code-switched text, aiming to generate new training samples from existing ones. Our approach involves substituting lexical items in the Arabic portion of the co-text with their synonyms or closest equivalents from the SynArabic dictionary. Experiments conducted on the SAQA question-answering dataset demonstrate that this augmentation strategy enhances the performance of state-of-the-art transformer-based models. Furthermore, by fine-tuning BERT and Transformer-XL models using our augmented data, we achieved improved results on the non-Arabic HANS test set, indicating a reduction in algorithmic bias. This paper details our findings and provides the corresponding code. Future research will investigate additional data augmentation methods. Our work is made available to the community through a GitHub repository. For more information, please visit our project website. We welcome inquiries regarding this research. Keywords: data augmentation, Arabic-Code-Switching, bias mitigation.

We demonstrate that any Roelcke precompact collection of homeomorphisms acting on a surface must fix a point at infinity. Consequently, there exists a uniform metric on the surface relative to which the homeomorphisms in the collection are isometries. This point at infinity remains fixed even when the surfaces are replaced by their one-point compactifications and the homeomorphisms are extended to map the point of infinity to itself. Furthermore, if this fixed point at infinity is unique, it can be realized as a point within the surface that is invariant under the action of the collection. These findings are achieved through a novel characterization of the quasi-boundedness of surfaces. Additionally, we show that the quasi-bounded component of an immersed surface within a loop space is not necessarily connected. These results have significant implications for the theory of hyperbolic dynamics. Specifically, we provide a concise proof of a recent theorem by Mañé, which asserts that the set of all homeomorphisms on a surface acting isometrically with respect to some hyperbolic metric forms a closed, Roelcke precompact subset of the homeomorphism group. However, this set is generally not compact. We also establish that the collection of all homeomorphisms on a surface possessing a parabolic fixed point is closed and Roelcke precompact in the homeomorphism group of any hyperbolic surface, yet it is not compact. The proof of the non-compactness in both instances relies on an analysis of the action of the homeomorphism groups on the surfaces. We establish that the quotient map from the homeomorphism group to the quotient of the monad of uniformity is both open and Roelcke precompact. Leveraging this analysis, we derive a characterization of compact Roelcke precompact subsets within the homeomorphism group of a surface. We introduce a new tetrakis-snub dodecahedral subdivision, termed the "tetrahedral mesh," which is specifically designed to cover arbitrary hex meshes for finite element analysis. This procedure is fully automated, functioning as a script within the open-source software Gmsh. The resulting tetrahedral meshes, achieved through Delaunay refinement, consistently attain a quality index of at least 0.45, with an average index of 0.62. Furthermore, we provide theoretical and numerical evidence demonstrating that the optimal tets/hex ratio for this method is exactly 58, a figure that aligns with prior numerical observations. This ratio is derived from a novel formula for the fundamental group of a Heegaard splitting of a 3-manifold. Additionally, the paper includes supplementary findings on this formula. Our results indicate that 58 is the maximum number of tetrahedra required to subdivide a single hexahedron while maintaining a quality index of 0.45 or higher, a number that also represents the count of vertices in the smallest regular polytope in dimension 4. Finally, we discuss the relationship between Heegaard splitting theory and mesh generation. This work was partially supported by the ANR project "TetGen" (Grant ANR-18-CE40-0021). While previous research has demonstrated that pre-trained language models like BERT significantly enhance RE performance, recent studies indicate that combining these models with external knowledge graph (KG) information yields even greater gains. The policy gradient method seeks to identify the optimal policy by parameterizing it within a topological space, utilizing measures such as Lipschitz and continuity to assess how minor shifts in the policy produce moderate or significant variations in the reward. These characteristics are vital for reinforcement learning, where small, unnoticeable perturbations in the policy often lead to substantial differences in the agent's behavior. This work demonstrates that most existing topological metrics fail to capture the intuitive notion of similarity between policies. To address this limitation, we introduce a coarse-grained continuity measure, grounded in an $\epsilon$-transition probability, that effectively captures the similarity between policies. We also provide a metric that ensures this $\epsilon$-transition probability. Our approach is validated through experiments on a robotic manipulation task, which confirm that this metric aligns more closely with the robot's actual behavior compared to traditional alternatives. Furthermore, we illustrate how the Coarse-Grained Continuity Policy Gradient algorithm successfully learns a policy that balances robustness against adversarial attacks with performance. Topological measures play a critical role in reinforcement learning, particularly when dealing with stochastic dynamics and perturbed inputs. This paper establishes a metric tailored for policy search, grounded in an intuitive understanding of policy similarity. The proposed algorithm achieves a robust policy that maintains high performance even under adversarial attacks. Experimental results validate the method's effectiveness in enhancing robustness. Experimental results confirm that the filter effectively stabilizes simulations, maintaining physical constraints like the Jacobian determinant in position and velocity updates. Type-ax (Type-C) quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in black hole X-ray transients are characterized by a single high-frequency component, yet their evolution during the hard state remains poorly understood. This study investigates the evolutionary trends of LMAXI and HXMT in the hard state of MAXI J1535-571. Our analysis reveals that the amplitude of LMAXI and HXMT in Type-C QPOs gradually diminishes as the hard X-ray flux declines. Furthermore, the centroid frequencies of LMAXI and HXMT Type-C QPOs decrease progressively, while their full width at half maximum (FWHM) initially narrows before expanding. Additionally, the frequency ratio (LMAXI/ HXMT) fluctuates between 0.7 and 1.0, and the FWHM ratio (LMAXI/ HXMT) stays below 1.5. These findings indicate that Type-C QPOs in MAXI J1535-571 evolve gradually, a pattern consistent with other Galactic black hole systems. Finally, we explore the potential physical mechanisms underlying these observed variations. Our results suggest that the evolution of Type-C QPOs in MAXI J1535-571 may be driven by a decrease in the accretion rate. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results. This paper investigates cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) from a social perspective, specifically examining how agents react to one another's actions. We introduce a new method termed "transfer empowerment," which employs a variational approach to re-agenting to predict how a target agent will respond to the actions of a source agent. Drawing inspiration from social learning, this proposed social intrinsic incentive facilitates the rapid and reliable prediction and reaction to a partner's behaviors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by showing that, compared to standard MARL baselines, it achieves significantly faster and more stable joint entropy maximization during cooperative tasks requiring mutual response. Furthermore, we evaluate the method's generalization capabilities by demonstrating that agents can infer each other's reactions across various new tasks, even when these tasks differ substantially from those encountered during training. Finally, we illustrate how to construct complex cooperative scenarios by having agents learn to play games like "Tag" and "Pong" using the Social Empowerment Policy (SEP). The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/taehyungkim1229/SEP. Identifying materials through visual cues is vital for numerous applications, including material identification, classification, segmentation, and segmentation-guided rendering. While existing learning-based approaches have significantly improved performance, they typically require extensive datasets and are limited to specific domains, such as wood in computer vision or metals in materials science. This limitation hinders the creation of a universally applicable framework capable of identifying "any material, anywhere." To address this, we introduce a novel framework for material identification that operates with minimal training data and generalizes effectively to unseen domains. Our approach leverages physics-based rendering to generate a few synthetic material views and employs contrastive learning to discover material-specific features. We validate the framework's efficacy in material identification across three datasets: synthetic materials, the MPI-SYNthetik Materials dataset, and real-world wood grain from the WoodGrain dataset. Furthermore, we demonstrate successful generalization to a completely new domain: identifying any wood species from grain patterns. These results confirm that our method effectively identifies materials based on their appearance and texture, regardless of the specific rendering domain. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of their structure, along with related concepts such as strict Lie 2-algebras, Lie 2-groups, and the  categorical analogues of nilpotent and solvable Lie algegebras. As higher-categorical versions of these traditional Lie algebra properties, we emphasize categorification throughout the discussion. Finally, we sketch a potential path toward a higher-categorical analog of the Lie algebra associated with a Lie group. We introduce a new end-to-end descriptor matching approach that operates without relying on keypoint detectors. Our method utilizes a global feature map derived from a convolutional neural network to identify corresponding descriptors. Unlike traditional methods, our descriptors are free-standing and depend solely on global context rather than being centered around specific keypoints. A transformer-based transformer-local cross-attention mechanism enables the integration of local features with global semantic context. Furthermore, a transformer-transformer cross-attention module facilitates the mutual enhancement of global and local features. This architecture yields two primary advantages: first, local features are independent of keypoints, enhancing robustness against invariance-breaking transformations; second, global features are refined by local features, boosting overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate that LoFTR achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmarks, including the Oxford5k, Oxford50k, and MS LoL datasets. Additionally, LoFTR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the KITTI-300 dataset for visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) by over 10%, while offering a 3x speed improvement through reduced computational complexity. The LoFTR method is available at https://github.com/lucasb12/LoFTR. Supplementary material can be found at https://lucasb12.github.io/LoFTR. Keywords: Keypoint-free Local Descriptor Matching, Transformer-based Local Attribute Matching.

This study examines the bias inherent in the Inferred Modulation (IMOD) technique used for solar vector magnetic field data. We demonstrate that the method's assumption of normally distributed input errors is invalid, as it is compromised by the skewness of the modulation distribution and the nonlinearity of error propagation. Consequently, bias is introduced into the imputation process, resulting in a systematic underestimation of the total error in the inferred quenching measurements. To address this, we developed a new imputation approach that eliminates the bias in solar vector magnetic field data. This method is applicable to any dataset where the modulation is skewed or when error propagation is nonlinear. We validated the method using both synthetic and real-world data, confirming that it successfully mitigates the bias in inferred quenching measurements. Furthermore, we applied this technique to historical data from the SOHO/MDI and SDO/HMI instruments to reanalyze the Sun's magnetic field evolution over the past three solar cycles. Our results indicate that the total error in both horizontal field components is significantly lower than previously reported, which has notable implications for solar dynamo models. Specifically, we find that the decay of horizontal fields is more rapid, while their maximum magnitude is more pronounced. These findings suggest that the quenching function within mean-field dynamo models may need adjustment. Additionally, we provide a Python package to facilitate the application of this method to various datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1992/IMOD. Future research will explore the utility of this method for other datasets. The methodology can be accessed via the IMOD package at https://imod.readthedocs.io/. We introduce a straightforward method for identifying metal-poor stars with $[Fe/H] < -2.0$ using Gaia blue and visible (BP/RP) spectra. This approach relies on a simple color criterion defined as $C = BP_{G} - R_{P}$, which is highly effective for stars with masses below $1.0\,M_{\odot}$. For these stars, a color of $C < 1.2$ strongly indicates metal-poor status. This threshold corresponds to a false positive rate of approximately 1% and a detection efficiency exceeding 90%. We have applied this technique to the 100,000 brightest stars within the Gaia Data Release 3. The resulting sample of 1,000 candidate metal-poor stars exhibits a median mass of $0.8\pm0.2\,M_{\odot}$ and a median age of $12.5\pm1.0$ Gyr. This collection of candidates is ideal for future spectroscopic follow-up campaigns, such as the Gaia-ESO Survey and APOGEE, to further refine their properties. Additionally, we demonstrate that these stars are valuable for asteroseismology studies, showing that their oscillation frequencies can be measured with a precision of $\sigma/\nu \sim 10^{-4}$, which is comparable to the precision achieved for stars in the Kepler mission. Finally, we illustrate that the Gaia-100k sample can be utilized to constrain the mass-radius relationship of white dwarfs. By analyzing the Gaia-100k sample, we derived a mass-radius relation for white dwarfs with a precision of $\sigma_{R} \sim 0.01\,R_{\odot}$, which aligns well with theoretical predictions. This study presents a statistical analysis of global blaze seasons, examining the impact of climate change on these events. Data from the US, Australia, and Africa were analyzed to identify trends and anomalies. The forecasting model developed for the US is subsequently applied to the remaining countries, yielding robust results. The analysis indicates that the Earth's average temperature is rising, with the most significant increases occurring in Australia and the US. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that Blaze Season Severity (BSS) will rise in the coming years for all analyzed nations. The forecasting methodology relies on the assumption that, given similar climatic conditions, the BBS of nations with comparable temperature trends will also exhibit similar trends. The study concludes that the proposed model is effective for nations with comparable climatic conditions but is not suitable for application to countries with distinct atmospheric conditions. Additionally, the model's efficacy is contingent upon the availability of data from reliable sources. Finally, the authors suggest that future research should expand the analysis to include nations with diverse climatic conditions to further validate the model. Given the model's strong performance, it is deemed highly promising for predicting Blaze Season Severity globally. The demand for valid psycholinguistic metrics has grown due to the rising popularity of psychological methods in natural language processing. This study investigates the robustness of psychological measures designed to assess morphological complexity. We gathered 14 existing corpus-based metrics and evaluated their inter-correlations. Results indicate that while certain measures are highly correlated, others are not, suggesting they may capture distinct, complementary aspects of morphological complexity. To validate these findings, we conducted a psychological experiment where participants rated morphological complexity for over 1,000 items. Our analysis demonstrates that the highly correlated measures align well with human judgments, whereas low-correlated measures diverge. We attribute this discrepancy to variations in item type, arguing that a diverse selection of items is essential for psychological experiments. Finally, we re-analyzed complex word segmentation data to demonstrate that a combination of morpheme-counting and token-counting measures yields superior performance compared to using either approach alone. Overall, this research provides a critical assessment of psychological measures for morphological complexity, offering a foundation for future development. We investigate gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters, focusing on the substructure signal in the gravitational arc of A2219. By analyzing 1.2 terapixels of Hubble Space Telescope data, we identified 13 new substructures, bringing the total count to 21. Our analysis employs both parametric and free-form modeling techniques. We compare these observational results with numerical simulations of cold dark matter (CDM) and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) using the AREPO code. The observed number of substructures aligns well with CDM simulations but exceeds predictions from SIDM models. This discrepancy suggests that either the mass of the lensing subhaloes is lower than anticipated or that the cross-section for self-interaction in SIDM is lower than previously thought. Specifically, an interparticle cross-section of $\sigma/m \leq 0.1$ cm$^2$/g is required to match the observed signal, which is more stringent than constraints derived from dwarf galaxy dynamics. Consequently, the lensing data in A2219 supports a CDM-like dark matter scenario. We conclude that HST-based lensing offers a complementary approach to studying dark matter interactions in dwarf galaxies, particularly by probing larger mass scales. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gravitational lensing can effectively constrain the self-interaction cross-section of dark matter. Finally, we outline the potential for future HST observations to further constrain SIDM parameters. Model simplification is a critical technique for reducing the computational demands of simulating complex systems. The presented approach begins with a detailed system model and generates observations using various input configurations. It subsequently constructs a reduced model capable of reproducing these specific observations. Crucially, this reduced model is not restricted to being a subset of the original; it can utilize novel input structures to achieve equivalent outputs. The method is currently applied in fields such as software testing, biological modeling, and the analysis of security protocols. Additionally, the paper explores extensions of this technique for scenarios where the detailed system is unknown, including the biological common ancestor problem and a generic framework for creating models from observations. A primary innovation of the approach is its ability to handle partial observations, which are the only data points available in the cited applications. Furthermore, the method is designed to be general and can be adapted to other partially observable systems. Finally, experimental results are presented to demonstrate the algorithm's performance and effectiveness. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/brunopereira/model-simplification. Keywords: model simplification, model reduction, black box modeling, input-output behavior, computational complexity.

This paper introduces M-ar-K-Fast, a novel dimensionality reduction technique that extends the M-ar-K analysis framework. Originally, M-ar-K analysis identified a low-dimensional subspace that jointly maximizes mutual information and minimizes the mean-Kullback-Leibler divergence between the original and reconstructed data distributions. M-ar-K-Fast achieves a similar objective but through a significantly accelerated algorithm. The core innovation lies in replacing the original computationally intensive optimization method with a new, highly efficient approach. This new framework is a variant of the widely used Kernel Fisher Discriminant, which effectively locates the M-ar-K subspace while substantially reducing computational costs. Experimental results demonstrate that Mar-K-Fast substantially accelerates the original M-ar-K analysis without negatively impacting the quality of the resulting low-dimensional subspaces. Furthermore, M-ar-K-Fast exhibits superior performance compared to several existing dimensionality reduction methods. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ahmedelkhatib/Mar-K-Fast. This study introduces a real-time incident detection framework for traffic monitoring by integrating spatio-temporal data from social media posts. The methodology begins with automatic geo-tagging of posts using social media check-in data. Subsequently, posts are filtered by subject and geo-spatially mapped to specific road segments. Temporal features are then extracted from these posts to identify traffic incidents. The system's efficacy is demonstrated through a case study in London, which compares detected incidents against official traffic management data. The results confirm the framework's ability to detect spatio-temporal traffic incidents with high accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be generalizable to other cities, provided that a method exists to map social media check-ins to local road networks. This capability significantly enhances real-world traffic monitoring and analysis. Finally, the paper explores how this technology can be leveraged to improve real-time traffic information delivery to social media users. Keywords: Traffic Monitoring, Incident Detection, Social Media Analysis, Real-time Information Service.

This study establishes results for nonlinear elliptic equations defined on ${\mathbb R}^N$ with data represented as surface measures. As applications, we derive the regularity of measures linked to these equations and analyze the properties of their solutions. Specifically, we examine the case where the function $\varphi$ possesses Dini continuity. Furthermore, we explore the influence of additional smoothness orders on nonlinear elliptic equations and the related Poisson problem. Finally, the work includes various examples and counterexamples to illustrate these findings. Notably, the methodology developed here for nonlinear problems also yields new insights into elliptic equations involving surface measures. Many of the problems addressed here find applications in the study of regular measures. This study employs an evolutionary search algorithm to investigate cobalt-abundant materials within the Y-Co-B system. By defining a target range for the average Co atomic radius, we identified 159 chemically stable compounds meeting this criterion. Among them, 135 belong to the Al$_2$Y$_3$-type intermetallic structure, while the remainder are classified as either complex or simple structures. These findings are corroborated by first-principles calculations, which demonstrate that the average binding energy of the target compounds is superior to that of randomly selected compounds meeting the same conditions. This research not only uncovers promising candidates for high binding energy materials in the Y-Co-B system but also underscores the efficacy of the proposed search algorithm in locating such materials. Furthermore, this work serves as a proof-of-concept for the algorithm's application in discovering Cobalt-free materials in the Y-B system with high binding energy. A comprehensive dataset of 159 compounds is provided in the supplementary material for reproducibility. This study was conducted as part of the Computational Materials Discovery (COMAD) challenge, which was organized by the Computationally Enhanced Materials Discovery (CEMD) initiative. The Computational Materials Discovery (COMAD) challenge is a flagship event in the Computationally Enhanced Materials Discovery (CEMD) series. The COMAD challenge was structured into three parts: (1) identifying cobalt-abundant compounds with a low formation energy, (2) identifying cobalt-abundant compounds with a low volume, and (3) identifying cobalt-free compounds with a high binding energy. In the current display advertising market, second-price auctions are the standard auction format. To prevent excessive budget overspending, bidders typically set their first-price bid amounts, constrained by a maximum budget. This leads to a sequential bidding process where budgets are allocated dynamically, requiring adaptive bidding strategies. This paper introduces a new online bidding strategy that adjusts bid amounts based on the bidder's risk appetite, ensuring the budget is not exhausted. We rigorously analyze the bidder's risk and derive an upper bound for expected revenue loss, demonstrating that it does not exceed a specific threshold determined by initial risk levels. Furthermore, we establish an optimization problem for parameter tuning and propose a method to address this challenge. Experimental results using real-world data confirm the effectiveness of our proposed strategy. Finally, we release our code and data to the public to facilitate future research. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We introduce a novel adaptive bidding strategy grounded in risk appetite, offering a theoretical guarantee on expected revenue; (2) We provide a practical tuning approach for strategy parameters, enabling straightforward implementation; and (3) We validate the strategy's superiority over existing methods through real-world experiments. Our code and data are available at: https://github.com/Chenchenchenchenchen/ARAB. Wigner negativity is a fundamental characteristic of Wigner functions that enables witness-based quantum enhancements in various computational and communication tasks. Although it is established that wigner-negative quantum states offer an advantage in quantum transport, the link between such advantages and wigner-negative quantum guidance remains unclear. This study investigates the quantum transport of both wigner-positive and wigner-negative quantum guidance, demonstrating that wigner-negative quantum guidance is essential for achieving quantum enhancement during particle transport. Furthermore, the results show that the quantum enhancement provided by wigner-negative quantum guidance surpasses that of wigner-negative classical velocity distributions possessing identical negative capacities. These findings provide a fresh perspective on the role of wigner negativity in quantum transport and offer critical insights for designing information carriers capable of optimizing quantum transport performance. Additionally, the study examines the connection between wigner negativity and interference in quantum transport, revealing that while both wigner-positive and wigner-negative quantum guidance distributions can generate interference, wigner-negative distributions produce more significant interference, thereby contributing more substantially to quantum enhancement. In secure quantum key distribution, raw key generation relies on random numbers derived from a seed. When the seed exhibits random non-uniformity, standard security proofs are insufficient. This study revisits random limit analysis within the security framework of quantum key distribution. We derive a secret key rate formula that accounts for the random limit analysis of privacy amplification utilizing an imperfectly random seed. Furthermore, our findings are applied to unconditional quantum key distribution based on phase-encoding phase-contrast interferometry, demonstrating the security analysis of a quantum random access memory that is uniformly random but not perfectly so. The proposed method is general and can be extended to other quantum key distribution protocols involving non-perfect random resources. Additionally, the results of this analysis may prove beneficial for other fields such as cryptography and information theory. This paper explores the concept of timelike (or pseudo-) Bertrand curves within a semi-metric space, which generalizes a Riemannian space. A Bertrand curve is defined as one where each arc has a corresponding isobaric curve sharing the same arc length parameter; the difference in their principal radi of curvature remains constant. We demonstrate that all known examples of Bertrand curves are actually special cases of these timelike variants. Furthermore, we establish that a necessary condition for a curve to be a Bertrand curve is that it must be either a geodesic or a curve of constant curvature. Finally, we derive the canonical equations for a four-dimensional semi-metric space and illustrate their application through specific examples. The concept of timelike Bertrand curves is applicable in both theoretical and practical research regarding the geometry of the physical universe. Additionally, the theory of F-Bertrand curves in an F-space can be developed using analogous methods. Keywords: Semi-metric space, isobaric curve, timelike Bertrand curve, F-space.

This study examines the distribution of the sampled value of a Feller process at the time of coalescence within state 0. Initially, we establish coalescence and sampling properties for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as a warm-up, then extend these findings to the more general Feller class I process. Finally, we present a further generalized result applicable to weakly Feller processes.

To achieve these results, we first develop an alternative approach to calculating the joint distribution of the coalescence time and sampled value for an absorbing diffusion, specifically targeting non-negative values. This method is then applied to an asymmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$, which is closely associated with one-dimensional Feller processes. Subsequently, we derive the corresponding results for a Feller class II process representing an asymmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}_{\neq 0}$, and briefly extend these findings to a broader category of reflecting diffusions.

The primary analytical instrument employed is the joint $q$-transform of the joint density of the coalescence time and the sampled value. We demonstrate that the $q$-transform of the desired joint distribution corresponds to the difference between the $q$-transform of the density for a diffusing particle and that of the Green function for a killed particle. This relationship holds for a wide spectrum of one-dimensional diffusions. Additionally, for symmetric diffusions, we show that the joint $q$-transform of the coalescence time and sampled value for two particles can be expressed using the joint Laplace transform of the range and position of a single particle.

By applying this framework, we successfully recover the known coalescence and sampled value distributions for the classical Brownian motion. We also generalize these results to all symmetric Feller processes on $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ with a non-zero drift, as well as to certain diffusion processes on $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ that are not necessarily related to random walks.

**Keywords:** Feller process; coalescence time; sampled value; asymmetric random walk; q-transform; Laplace transform; range; position.

Recent years have seen a surge in theoretical proposals for fundamental quantum information processing tasks involving multi-photon states. This study derives a diagrammatic scattering matrix method for one-dimensional waveguide QED systems featuring a single quantum emitter, applicable to arbitrary incoming multi-photon states. The proposed method is demonstrated through examples including two-photon and three-photon Gaussian states, as well as two-photon Fock states. These results demonstrate that the diagrammatic method offers significant computational efficiency compared to traditional approaches. Furthermore, the findings are directly relevant to fundamental research initiatives concerning quantum information processing with multi-photon states. Dark Matter may possess intrinsic spin, which could be detected through nuclear recoil experiments. In this study, we derive the first scattering cross-section for spin-dependent interactions between relativistic, incident, polarized Dark Matter and stationary, spinless nuclei. Our findings demonstrate that at sufficiently high energies, the scattered Dark Matter can exhibit polarization opposite to that of the incident state, while the recoil nucleus may also become polarized despite lacking initial spin. These phenomena are most pronounced at energies where the scattered Dark Matter is highly relativistic, a regime potentially accessible to future accelerators. This research is particularly pertinent to experiments utilizing polarized targets, such as YAP, which employ $^{171}$Yb nuclei, and it also has relevance for direct detection experiments employing natural germanium targets, where accelerated Dark Matter could scatter off the minor spin-dependent component present in natural germanium isotopes. Furthermore, we illustrate that a combination of direct and indirect detection methods could constrain the parameter space for spin-dependent interactions with polarized nuclei, even in the absence of experimental data. This approach is particularly applicable to scenarios involving velocity-dependent cross-sections, where accelerated Dark Matter explores a parameter space inaccessible to Galactic Dark Matter. Finally, we provide the Fortran code used in this work, which can be adapted for broader use. This code is especially useful for computing the partial partial spin-dependent structure functions for any given nucleus. These findings are especially relevant for the upcoming CHASE experiment, which aims to investigate spin-dependent interactions of accelerated Dark Matter. CHASE will employ a radio-frequency quadrupole (RFQ) to accelerate Dark Matter within a magnetic field, utilizing a liquid $^{171}$Yb target to measure the polarization of both the scattered particles and the recoil nuclei. This dual measurement approach offers a unique method for characterizing spin-dependent interactions, particularly those with velocity-dependent components. Furthermore, CHASE will be capable of measuring the polarization of scattered Dark Matter, providing valuable data for understanding the spin structure of Dark Matter. This ability to measure Dark Matter polarization is crucial for constraining the spin-dependent parameter space, even in the absence of current data. Our results indicate that the cross-section for spin-dependent interactions may vary with the Lorentz factor $\gamma$, a possibility supported by theoretical models. This paper introduces a delay-enhanced variant of conventional delay-cooperating (DC) detection for continuous phase modulation, achieving a 3 dB improvement in detection gain across all delay values. By applying maximum ratio combining to the differential outputs of the receiver, this maximum ratio combining (MR) detector surpasses DC detection across every delay value, surpassing the local optimality of DC detection regardless of the delay parameter. This advantage stems from the fact that the autocorrelation of the differential filter's output is strictly positive for any delay, thereby ensuring robust detection performance. Simulations confirm that the proposed MR detector outperforms DC detection in terms of bit error rate. Furthermore, the paper establishes a closed-form expression for the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain of DC detection with respect to delay and identifies the associated crossover delay. Finally, the study examines the trade-off between SNR gain and the BER crossover delay for various delay values. These findings are applicable to all conventional CPM schemes. The MR detector is also implemented in specific digital CPM scenarios, such as MSK, to further validate its efficacy. Additionally, the concept of delay-enhanced DC detection is extended to non-digital CPM schemes, including minimum energy CPM, minimum side lobe CPM, and raised cosine CPM. The analysis demonstrates that the MR detector yields a consistent 3 dB SNR gain across all delay values for these analog CPM modulations as well. Finally, the paper establishes a closed-form expression for the SNR gain of DC detection relative to delay for these analog CPM schemes, noting that the SNR gain converges to 3 dB as the delay approaches infinity. The results indicate that the MR detector outperforms DC detection up to a crossover delay, which is identified for each specific scheme. The paper concludes that the proposed MR detector is locally optimal for all considered CPM schemes at the crossover delay. Additionally, the SNR gain of DC detection is observed to be monotonically increasing with delay for both digital and analog CPM schemes. These conclusions are derived from the closed-form expression of the SNR gain, which is shown to be independent of the transmitted signal. The findings suggest that the MR detector is globally optimal for all considered CPM schemes. Finally, the paper discusses the computational complexity of the DC and MR detectors and their associated implementation trade-offs. The results indicate that the MR detector is more suitable for high delay values, whereas DC detection remains preferable for low delay values. Reward learning (RL) represents a promising approach for automatically deriving rewards from demonstrations, thereby eliminating the need for manual annotation. However, existing methods often demand substantial computational resources and lengthy training periods. This paper introduces VACOR, a visually assisted cluster ranking technique that leverages pairwise comparisons to identify clusters of similar states. By training a reward model on these selected states, VACOR achieves accurate generalization to unseen states while significantly reducing the number of parameters and computation required. Furthermore, we develop a visual explanation framework that renders the learned rewards interpretable, facilitating the creation of more effective reward models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both generalization accuracy and efficiency. This study employs light-cone quantization to derive the nucleon light-cone wave function within noncommutative space-time, revealing an explicit dependence on the noncommutative parameter $\theta$. Utilizing this wave function, we calculate key nucleon structure characteristics, including the number of partons, Dirac and magnetic moments, and the radii of the nucleon, %Dirac, and %magnetic, all as explicit functions of $\theta$. This study examines the Toric code model on a Kagome lattice, which exhibits geometric frustration, and its extensions incorporating next-nearest-neighbor interactions. These variations demonstrate distinct topological orders, with some lacking a ground state degeneracy that scales with system size. By employing the algebra of string operators, we investigate how ground state degeneracy, the count of topologically distinct strings, and string energy contributions interrelate. Furthermore, we analyze string operator effects within a model featuring ferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor interactions, revealing that these forces generate new types of strings. Finally, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the emergence of a new topological phase, characterized by ground state degeneracy proportional to the system size, based on string energy considerations. This phase is defined by a closed geometric line, termed "geometric loops," which are not topologically protected. Additionally, we explore the influence of these geometric loops on string energy and propose methods for manipulating ground state degeneracy through local perturbations. Our findings are validated through exact calculations on small lattices and numerical analyses of a single infinite graph. These results offer a novel framework for investigating topological order in frustrated systems. Specifically, they elucidate the relationship between strings and loops in the Kagome Toric code, a relationship previously unexplored in the literature. Consequently, our research establishes a new foundation for the study of topological order in geometrically frustrated systems. To demonstrate the utility of our theoretical framework, we apply it to the Kagome Toric code model, revealing that its phase diagram is more complex than previously believed. We identify multiple phases, each defined by ground state degeneracy per unit cell, accompanied by phase boundaries determined by string energies. Our analysis indicates that these phases are separated by first-order phase transitions. Additionally, we examine the potential for geometric loops to serve as new resources for quantum computation. Finally, we outline several promising research directions for future investigation. We examine extensions of random band matrices involving complex perturbations of finite rank. These models combine a large number of weak interactions with specific particles that participate in strong interactions. When the size of the perturbation matrix scales as $1/\sqrt{N}$, the spectrum remains essentially identical to that of the unperturbed random band matrix model, yet the particle number and eigenstate occupations are significantly altered. In the limit of large matrix size, both the unperturbed model and these variants can be approximated by sigma-models. We present the sigma-model approximation for the fourth moment of the overlap between particles and Anderson-Davydov states in the XXZ model perturbed by a finite-rank matrix. This approximation is valid when the perturbation strength scales as $1/N$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the approximations for the third and fifth moments of this model align with those of a corresponding four-component model, which is a variant of the two-component model previously analyzed in this context. The study of these models is motivated by their potential to describe perturbations of weakly interacting Bose gases characterized by random couplings. Additionally, we explore a perturbation scenario applicable to the four-component model, which also corresponds to the fourth-moment approximation of a specific perturbation of the XXZ model. Finally, we discuss the applicability of these models to perturbation strengths scaling as $1/N^{1/2}$. This case is particularly relevant for understanding the Bose-Einstein condensation transition in perturbed interacting XXZ models. We analyze the behavior of the first moment of the perturbed XXZ model in this regime, showing that it is well-described by the four-component model. We also provide a brief discussion of the two- and one-component models, which are relevant for very large perturbation strengths. Throughout the text, we reference the findings of this work alongside our previous studies. We conclude by outlining several open questions. This paper serves as a companion to [1-10]. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical factor in the deployment of machine learning models. However, the current state of the art lacks a precise definition for this concept, and existing evaluation methods are limited to qualitative approaches. This paper introduces a framework for interpreting machine learning models based on the hypothesis that an interpretability model corresponds to how humans learn these models. The proposed framework is evaluated through a series of experiments, culminating in the introduction of the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS) as a metric to quantify algorithmic interpretability. The study aims to provide both a theoretical and practical foundation for the interpretation of machine learning models. The proposed learning-based interpretability model and the CCS are anticipated to offer valuable insights for the evaluation of machine learning models. Outlier detection is a critical challenge in data mining, with Isolation Forest (iF) emerging as a leading unsupervised technique. Despite its widespread adoption, iF faces significant performance drops when applied to modern, efficient machine learning models characterized by large parameter counts, small feature spaces, and low inference precision. These advances are essential for deploying AI in resource-constrained environments, such as edge computing. This study demonstrates that iF can be enhanced in such settings through two primary strategies: (1) integrating modern model compression techniques to reduce feature space dimensions, and (2) formulating outlier classification as an optimization problem to derive optimal supervision signals. Our findings indicate that iF, when optimized through these methods, achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning models. Furthermore, we validate the iF framework's effectiveness across diverse domains, including industrial fault detection, satellite image analysis, and medical diagnosis. Finally, all code and datasets are made publicly available to foster future research and development in this area. This paper introduces a new parameterization for the Poisson process tailored to extreme value analysis. By leveraging the relationship between point processes and their max-stable counterparts, we construct a novel max-stable process whose associated Poisson process is a Poisson-driven point cloud within $\mathbb{R}^d \times [0,1]$. The resulting intensity measure features a conditionally Pareto tail integral, making it compatible with standard extreme value models. We propose a new parametric family for Poisson-excess measures that extends the generalized Pareto distribution to higher dimensions, offering a convenient way to characterize marginal tail behaviors. This approach facilitates the development of max-stable processes with specified marginal tail distributions and enables the simulation of multivariate extreme data. Furthermore, we develop a novel reparameterization technique to link these Poisson process representations with max-stable distribution functions. This framework supports efficient likelihood-based estimation and provides a method for recovering max-stable parameters from simulated data. Finally, we evaluate this reparameterization using a finite sample of simulated data to demonstrate its effectiveness. The proposed technique is designed to be easily adaptable to any Poisson-driven point cloud that adheres to standard extreme value models. This paper outlines our system for the shared task "Commonplace Medical Event Texts to Knowledge Graphs (COMET-ATOMIC 2020)" at TACL 2020. The goal involves accepting brief clinical trial descriptions and annotating them with ATOMIC commonplace knowledge graph concepts to identify relevant medical events and their structures. We present a novel approach combining a symbolic method, which leverages the ATOMIC knowledge graph and event chunking, with a neural method, which utilizes a pre-trained medical language model. Both approaches achieve state-of-the-art results, with the symbolic method leading in the original dataset and the neural method excelling in the fold-over dataset. We conclude by discussing the system's strengths and limitations. The code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/med-nlp/COMET-ATOMIC-2020. This publication is based on a system entry into the shared task COMET-ATOMIC 2020, which was held during TACL 2020. The task requires taking a short text describing a clinical trial and labeling event mentions with event concepts from the ATOMIC database (Sap et al., 2020). The symbolic method employed in this paper uses a rule-based approach to map the input text to a knowledge graph, utilizing the ATOMIC database as a knowledge base and a state-of-the-art chunking tool to identify text segments for graph concepts. The neural method employs a transformer-based language model trained on biomedical text, fine-tuned on the task. The evaluation dataset consists of two subsets: an original test set and a fold-over training set. The original test set includes 1,000 texts, each annotated with event concepts from ATOMIC. The fold-over training set consists of 10,000 texts annotated with event concepts from MedMentions (Miyao et al., 2019), a medical event graph built on the Medical Mentions Ontology. The evaluation metrics consist of the F1 score for the text label and the F1 score for the entity label. The system achieved state-of-the-art results on the original test set with an F1 score of 0.502 (compared to 0.482 for the best prior system) and on the fold-over training set with an F1 score of 0.525 (compared to 0.480 for the best prior system). This study outlines a data reduction pipeline designed for the Hi-GAL survey, which targets cold molecular gas and star-forming regions at a resolution of 4.5" using the HIFI instrument on the Herschel Space Observatory. The pipeline incorporates a radiation transfer model to correct the observed line profiles for continuum emission, thereby generating line profiles suitable for scientific analysis. Additionally, it produces line maps at the full bandwidth and provides line profiles for every line map within a specified spectral range. A primary innovation is the creation of line profiles for every line map across a defined spatial region. The pipeline's efficacy is demonstrated using H23CO and N2H3D+ data from the Hi-GAL survey's central region. The resulting line profiles are shown to be ideal for calculating integrated intensities and performing kinematic analysis. Furthermore, the paper discusses the advantages of generating line profiles for every line map within a defined area, which facilitates a more robust kinematic analysis. Finally, this work serves as a foundation for developing a unified data analysis framework for the Hi-GAL survey. The pipeline is accessible at https://github.com/Hi-GAL-Survey/HiGAL_Pipeline.

**Context.** The presence of a metallicity spread in globular clusters (GCs) has been a subject of intense debate for over a decade. While some studies have reported such spreads, others have found results consistent with a single metallicity. This debate has intensified following the introduction of new methodologies, including high-resolution spectroscopy and asteroseismology.

**Aims.** We present high-precision abundances for iron and iron-peak elements (Mn, Ni, Co) for 10 red giant branch stars in NGC 2808, utilizing both high-resolution spectra and asteroseismology. Our analysis aims to determine whether these stars exhibit a metallicity spread.

**Methods.** We conducted a detailed asteroseismic analysis of the stars, deriving surface gravity ($\log g$) and effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) with a precision of 0.05 dex and 10 km s$^{-1}$, respectively. These parameters were combined with photospheric spectra to determine surface abundances of iron and iron-peak elements.

**Results.** We confirm a metallicity spread of 0.02 dex in NGC 2808, with a 95% confidence level. The observed spread is primarily driven by variations in the iron-peak element Ni. The correlation between $\log g$ and $T_{\rm eff}$ aligns with stellar evolution models.

**Conclusions.** Our findings support the hypothesis that NGC 2808 hosts multiple stellar populations. The spread in $\log g$ values is likely due to the stars' differing evolutionary stages, whereas the spread in $T_{\rm eff}$ and chemical abundances stems from their distinct initial chemical compositions. The high precision of our $\log g$ measurements suggests that the observed $\log g$ spread is intrinsic to the cluster. This result is consistent with the hypothesis that these stars formed from a primordial gas cloud containing a range of metallicities. Our results also reinforce the conclusion that the temperature sensitivity of NGC 2808's red giant branch is low. Finally, the observed correlation between [Ni/Fe] and [Fe/H] indicates that NGC 2808's first-generation stars formed from a primordial gas cloud with a non-negligible spread in nickel abundance. Investigating particle transport within confined geometries offers significant insights into fundamental physical, chemical, and biological processes. In single-file systems, particle translocation is primarily driven by the dynamic rearrangement of excess free entropy. This study examines one-dimensional single-file diffusion by modeling particles as hard spheres moving within a channel subject to an external potential. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we analyze the duration statistics for the first exit of particles from a biased region. Our findings reveal that these translocations can be categorized into two distinct regimes: a rapid regime where particle rearrangement is negligible, and a slow regime where rearrangement is essential. We demonstrate that entropic forces can be derived from the correlation between the translocation particle and the surrounding system. Furthermore, our results indicate that the concept of entropic attraction is applicable in the rapid regime. Finally, we establish that the first exit time statistics adhere to a scaling law, with the entropic attraction length serving as the characteristic scale for the potential's decay. These insights are validated by comparing our results with analytical calculations. Our comprehensive findings offer a robust framework for characterizing single-file transport phenomena. Additionally, the proposed methodology for analyzing translocation times and entropic forces is applicable to a broad spectrum of potential functions and particle sizes. Finally, this study serves as a foundational reference for future investigations into complex biological transport mechanisms. Measurement in quantum mechanics is a fundamental yet intricate process that has been the subject of extensive study. While various formulations of measurement exist, they often lack a unified approach to defining the information gained through measurement. This paper introduces a consistency criterion for measurement inference, utilizing quantum Bayes' rule to determine the updated state following a specific measurement outcome. We demonstrate that the consistency condition is equivalent to the continuity of quantum Bayes' updates, ensuring that the sequence of inferring and verifying does not alter the final inference. Furthermore, we examine the consistency condition across several well-known measurement definitions, including von Neumann, weak, and quantum trajectory measurements. In each case, we clarify the fundamental assumptions regarding information definition and reveal the necessary and sufficient conditions for consistency. Additionally, we propose a general definition of consistency that remains independent of the specific measurement formulation. Finally, we explore the relationship between consistency and information in the context of repeated measurements. These findings provide a robust foundation for developing a theory of quantum information that is free from the traditional conflicts between complementarity and reality. Additionally, they offer valuable insights for designing new measurement types and interpreting their results. This work is presented as a supplement to our previous publications [Phys. Rev. This work reports initial findings regarding the small-system limit of the equation of state (EOS) for a finite volume $V$ and particle number $N$. Utilizing finite-size scaling (FSS) techniques, we demonstrate that the pressure $P$ approaches zero as the $N/V$ ratio tends to infinity, whereas the ratio $N/E$ converges to a positive constant. We analyze the large-$N$ limit of the small-volume EOS by employing the grand-canonical ensemble and expressing thermodynamic quantities as finite grand-canonical partition functions. By applying Stirling's approximation to the infinite limit, we derive an EOS resembling that of an ultra-relativistic (UR) Bose gas, characterized by $S = 3P = E/3 = NE$. However, we identify a systematic deviation from this UR behavior, which we attribute to the finite bag constant $B$. This deviation is quantified by the deviation function $D = E - 3P + 3B$, which we examine using the UR EOS as a baseline. Our results indicate that the critical point of the QCD phase diagram is not scale-invariant, leading to a deviation from UR behavior that is more pronounced near the critical point. Consequently, the deviation function $D$ scales with system size according to universal critical exponents. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the UR EOS in small systems, the definition of the small-system limit, and the potential for UR behavior to persist in systems smaller than the critical correlation length. Furthermore, we extend the UR analysis to the baryon chemical potential $\mu_B$, showing that the system exhibits UR behavior up to $\mu_B \approx 100$ MeV before deviations emerge. This result aligns with the UR small-system limit of the QCD phase diagram, where the critical point is characterized by $\mu_B^c = 0$ and $T_c^c = 208$ MeV. The UR EOS is expected to hold in the limit of large $N/V$ and small $\mu_B/T$, with the latter condition being satisfied at energies above the collision energy of $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 7.7$ GeV. These findings suggest that the UR small-system limit of the QCD EOS is relevant to the LHC but not the RHIC. Let $H^*(BG_q;{\Bbb F}_2)$ denote the mod-2 cohomology algebra of a finite group $G_q$, where $G_q$ is the subgroup of $GL_q({\Bbb F}_2)$ preserving a non-zero vector. We demonstrate that for any positive degree $n$, the Steenrod algebra $\mathcal A$'s action on $H^*(BG_q;{\Bbb F}_2)^n$ leaves an invariant subspace $U_q^n$. Furthermore, we establish that the direct sum $\bigoplus_{q=2}^\infty U_q^n$ is both non-trivial and infinitely generated. This finding contrasts with a conjecture by Broto and Santhanam, who posited that the direct sum of minimal transitive permutation modules for symmetric groups could not be generated by a finite number of elements. Their conjecture was subsequently refuted by Broto, Santhanam, and Shulman, who identified such a module isomorphic to $\bigoplus_{q=2}^\infty H^*(BG_q;{\Bbb F}_2)^n$. Consequently, it follows that $\bigoplus_{q=2}^\infty HU_q^n$ constitutes a counterexample to that specific conjecture. Additionally, for $n=1$, we explicitly identify all indecomposable $\mathcal A$-modules $U_q^1$ and their direct summands. We also provide the explicit structure of the $p$-primary component of $\bigoplus_{q=2}^\infty HU_q^1$ when $p$ is an odd prime. Finally, we examine the case $n=0$ and offer a partial resolution. These findings are supported by a computer search conducted using the Macaulay2 package Nemo. Future space telescopes are expected to conduct Lyman-$\alpha$ surveys to investigate the evolution of galaxies and the early Universe. To isolate Lyman-$\alpha$ emission from Lyman-$\beta$ emission and the continuum, a Lyman-$\alpha$ filter is essential. This study presents the design and laboratory characterization of a 100~cm$^{-2}$ LiF XR-500 thin-film interference filter, designed to serve as a prototype for these surveys. The filter was fabricated at the University of Liège and tested using a SpectraPhysics 3900 Ar$^{+}$ laser. Results indicate that the transmission peak reaches 70% at 514.2 nm, with a full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) of 0.3 nm. Furthermore, the Lyman-$\beta$ and continuum transmissions are both below 10% at 486.1 nm and 500.7 nm, respectively. These findings suggest that the LiF XR-500 filter is a viable candidate for future Lyman-$\alpha$ surveys. This paper addresses the graph symmetric problem within a distributed framework by introducing graph filters designed to achieve Graph Symmetry. Leveraging the unique properties of graph filters, we develop distributed algorithms capable of generating these filters in a fully distributed setting. Consequently, our proposed filters enable the realization of graph symmetric systems in a distributed context. Numerical simulations using the complete graph dataset demonstrate the performance of these filters, confirming their suitability for distributed deployment. Additionally, the communication overhead is analyzed, showing that it decreases as the word length of the generated filters is reduced.
