The electronic transport properties of a macroscopic film composed of single-crystalline armchair carbon nanotubes were investigated using a four-point probe technique. Under low-bias conditions, we observed a phonon-assisted electronic conduction pathway occurring between adjacent nanotubes. This conclusion is supported by comparative analysis of the electronic characteristics under both high and low temperatures, as well as the observed modulation of phonon-assisted conduction when applying a transverse magnetic field. These findings offer a promising avenue for developing electronic devices that utilize the unique quantum properties of carbon nanotubes. Furthermore, this study establishes a foundation for future investigations into phonon-assisted phenomena, such as the spin Hall effect, within carbon nanotube films. To achieve this, we have engineered a high-quality transverse magnetic field setup featuring a lateral magnetic field gradient reaching up to 1.5 T/µm. This configuration is specifically designed to facilitate the detection of transverse voltage signals, thereby enabling the analysis of transverse charge and spin transport phenomena in these nanostructures. Finally, we propose a theoretical framework to interpret the experimental data. Our analysis indicates that the phonon-assisted conduction mechanism is primarily driven by electron scattering from acoustic phonons. Additionally, the observed transverse voltage modulation in the magnetic field is attributed to the Lorentz force acting on the electronic current between the nanotubes, with the acousto-magnetoresistance effect playing a secondary role. These results provide compelling evidence supporting the occurrence of phonon-assisted electronic conduction between carbon nanotubes within the film. By leveraging the distinctive quantum transport phenomena of carbon nanotubes, this research paves the way for the design of novel electronic devices. Specifically, the identified acousto-magnetoresistance effect could be utilized to create sensitive acoustic wave sensors. This potential is demonstrated by the detection of minute changes in the magnetoresistance ratio resulting from variations in the acoustic phonon flux. The proposed device is expected to exhibit a sensitivity of 10⁻⁴ F/µm, representing an improvement of three orders of magnitude over existing acousto-magnetoresistance sensors. This advancement is achieved by employing a high-quality, single-crystalline nanotube network as the sensing element. Additionally, the strong coupling between phonons and electrons in carbon nanotubes enables the observation of a magnetophonon resonance effect. This resonance was detected as a distinct peak in the differential resistance of the nanotube film at low temperatures under a longitudinal magnetic field.

This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering algorithm designed for high-dimensional data containing outliers. Drawing inspiration from the traditional k-Means method, it incorporates fuzzy logic to mitigate the detrimental impact of outlier data points. Furthermore, the approach utilizes entropy to assess feature relevance, dynamically assigning weights to dimensions to enhance clustering quality. The method was validated using both synthetic datasets and real-world data from the UCI Machine Learning repository. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed algorithm surpasses existing fuzzy clustering techniques in terms of accuracy and precision. Additionally, its high computational efficiency makes it suitable for deployment in high-performance computing environments. A web-based interface has also been developed to facilitate user-friendly access to the algorithm. The source code and a web interface are available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/EF-Means. Users can access the algorithm by entering a CSV file via a form on the interface; upon submission, the algorithm executes and the results are displayed automatically. The interface supports clustering for data files with a maximum size of 1 MB. The algorithm operates within 10 seconds for datasets up to 10,000 rows and 20 columns, and within 30 seconds for datasets up to 100,000 rows and 5 columns. Future enhancements will include support for larger datasets and increased column counts. Keywords: Fuzzy Clustering, High-Dimensional Data, Outliers, Fuzzy C-Means, k-Means.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, comprising a gating network that chooses from $k$ expert functions, are foundational in machine learning. Although recent research has established that certain continuous MoE structures are efficiently learnable from noisy labels, the discrete-activation variant remains an unexplored territory, with existing methods failing to offer both efficiency and robustness against noise. This paper addresses the MoE learning problem under discrete gating activation and introduces a novel, efficient gradient descent framework capable of global convergence. Our approach integrates two key components: (1) a computationally efficient method that provably drives the gating network to a stable state, and (2) an algorithm that guarantees the model's convergence to the true structure. We further extend this work to the multi-task learning setting and provide a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's convergence and sample complexity. Extensive experiments confirm the practical effectiveness of our proposed methods. Code is available at: https://github.com/Chenchen-Zhao/MoE-Expert-Selection.

These notes offer a self-contained introduction to chip-firing games on weighted directed graphs, with a focus on their connection to Jacobians and Abelian varieties. While standard treatments define these games on unweighted, undirected graphs as combinatorial abelian varieties over the integers, this work extends the concept to weighted directed graphs. The discussion prioritizes developing the necessary tools for analyzing specific games, such as those on hyperelliptic curves and Prym varieties, within the framework of combinatorial algebraic geometry. The primary objective is to establish a foundation for investigating these games on directed graphs where out-degrees are non-uniform, thereby enabling the exploration of more complex instances found in specific geometric settings. The resulting material is based on a course titled "Chip-firing games" taught by the author at the 2019 Summer School in Algebraic Geometry held at the Fields Institute in Toronto. The notes aim to be self-contained, with an included appendix on basic algebraic geometry for readers seeking a gentler introduction to combinatorial algebraic geometry. Additionally, this approach offers a distinct perspective on that field compared to the standard reference, *Algebraic Geometry and Codes* by Geopinger van der Geer and J. H. van Lint. Finally, the appendix includes a section on the mathematical background concerning the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics, which the author found enjoyable to write. Readers with a background in theoretical physics will gain insight into the parallels between analyzing random processes on graphs and studying chip-firing games on directed graphs. Furthermore, the final section provides a brief overview of theoretical physics, including its key principles and recent achievements. This content is intended to be accessible to readers with a basic understanding of mathematics. The appendix also covers the history of chip-firing games, which dates back to the 19th century, and highlights their applications in various fields, such as modeling the spread of diseases. The author hopes that readers will find the material engaging and informative. The notes were prepared for the course and are available online at the author's website. Although string theory suggests that low-energy global symmetries are incompatible with consistent quantum gravity, many such symmetries persist in low-energy effective field theories. We propose that cosmic double refraction measurements of cosmic microwave background (CMB) photons can uniquely constrain these symmetries, offering a distinct advantage over other observational methods. This effect arises from binary black hole mergers occurring within a background of broken global symmetry, which generate time-dependent anisotropic stress. This stress induces a polarization signal in the CMB and produces phase shifts in passing CMB photons, the latter manifesting as transverse amplitude and polarization variations. By analyzing these changes, one can isolate the phase shift attributable to double refraction, provided the breaking scale of global symmetry and the breaking mechanism are known. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within quantum gravity frameworks, the spontaneous fermion number breaking scale can be constrained to approximately $10^{11}$ GeV using current data, whereas constraints on the breaking scale of other global symmetries remain beyond the reach of existing observations. Finally, we outline a future experimental strategy to significantly improve the limits on global symmetry breaking scales. This approach involves observing high-redshift quasars to detect long-wavelength transverse effects, thereby separating double refraction signals from gravitational lensing. With this methodology, we can constrain the fermion number breaking scale to roughly $10^{12}$ GeV and the pion charge conjugation parity violation scale to about $10^{14}$ GeV. Additionally, future observations could determine the breaking scale for other global symmetries, such as baryon number, to precision levels between $10^{15}$ and $10^{16}$ GeV. These constraints are critical for interpreting the physics behind the recently observed $g$- and $e$-modes in the CMB. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting double refraction signals via CMB photons, which would provide a definitive test of global symmetry breaking mechanisms in quantum gravity. Specifically, such a detection would establish a lower bound on the fermion number breaking scale of approximately $10^{13}$ GeV. This represents a significant improvement over the current upper bound of $10^{11}$ GeV derived from neutron oscillation experiments. The future detection of double refraction signals would necessitate a fundamental re-evaluation of quantum gravity theories. This expository note offers multiple simplified proofs of the Mumford conjecture. It is designed to be accessible to graduate students and early-career researchers in mathematics. The text emphasizes the fragile nature of $b$-structures and includes a fundamental lesson in robustness. A basic background in the stable homotopy groups of spheres is required. A key technical achievement is the construction of a map from the oriented mapping class group to the oriented orthogonal group, which serves as the primary example of how to work with $b$-structures. The note concludes with a list of open problems. Readers are expected to gain a basic understanding of the topology of moduli spaces, the relationship between the stable homotopy groups of spheres and the mod 2 cohomology of the stable mapping class spectrum, and the construction of the $\text{MSP}$ spectrum. Additionally, the text provides an opportunity to appreciate the elegance of Wu relations. The material is supplemented by a bibliography of over 100 references. This note was written during a visit to the Fields Institute in Toronto. I am grateful to the FI for their hospitality. I also extend my thanks to the following individuals for their time and valuable discussions: J. Bergner, J. Hill, J. Hillman, J. Morgan, and T. Randal-Williams. Deep learning models have demonstrated significant success across numerous tasks, yet a critical issue limiting their practical utility is transferability. While extensive research has been conducted to enhance the transferability of deep models, existing studies often overlook the two fundamental agreements that transferability must adhere to. This work re-examines the core principles of transferability and proposes a transferability assessment approach based on these two agreements. The paper further explores transferability from new perspectives, offering insights and valuable references for the field. To validate this assessment method, the study re-evaluates transferability on four public deep learning datasets, including ImageNet. The experimental results indicate that the proposed approach is effective and can serve as a valuable reference for future research. Network structure significantly influences the propagation of information, diseases, and contagions. While numerous studies have examined structural factors affecting the spread of information diffusion networks (IDSN), this research highlights network parameters as a critical element. We demonstrate that this parameter-driven approach is essential for accurately modeling information spread. Our findings indicate that modular networks facilitate the rapid dissemination of information, whereas hierarchical networks impede it. Additionally, we observe that network heterogeneity accelerates the diffusion process, while homogeneity slows it down. Finally, our results show that the average node degree has a substantial impact, with networks featuring a higher average degree spreading information more quickly than those with lower average degrees. These insights can inform the design of network control strategies to either accelerate or decelerate information spread. Consequently, our proposed parameter-driven methodology offers a more effective framework for modeling and analyzing network structures. Furthermore, we anticipate that these findings will assist researchers in selecting or designing appropriate network structures for specific applications. Utilizing the Conditional Calabi–Yau (CY) flow introduced by Chen and Tian, we establish the uniqueness and stability of the Complex Thomas–Yau (CTY) flow relative to mean curvature flow, with findings applicable to the Generalized Thomas–Yau (GTY) flow as well. This proof of distinctiveness not only offers a geometric demonstration of the Hilbert–Mumford criterion but also facilitates the characterization of semistability for Cayley and Gualtieri moduli spaces. Consequently, we provide the first complete classification of semistability for Cayley and Gualtieri moduli spaces in dimensions up to seven. Furthermore, our methodology enables the construction of deformed Kähler–Einstein metrics on toric Fano manifolds through gluing techniques. This approach yields an infinite array of examples where the answers to both the exceptional divisor conjecture and the Cayley weight conjecture are negative. Additionally, our framework extends to the Generalized Exceptional Divisor Conjecture, which we demonstrate for toric Fano manifolds of dimension five or less. In the process, we derive significant insights regarding the geometry of toric Fano manifolds, including the existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics with negative scalar curvature, the log terminal property, and the properties of the Cox ring. We also present the most comprehensive example to date of a toric Fano manifold of dimension seven that admits a Kähler–Yau metric constructed via the gluing method. Finally, we demonstrate that the mass inequality associated with the Complex Thomas–Yau flow is strictly convex. These outcomes align with the predictions of the Exceptional Divisor Conjecture and the Gualtieri weight Conjecture. This paper introduces a discrete-time precision analysis for the time-domain regular perturbation model of unamplified links. We derive conditions under which the model's dynamics can be represented in a discrete-time framework and develop a precision analysis for model-based time synchronization. Our findings indicate that the model achieves femtosecond accuracy for time-stamp estimation, with simulation results confirming that theoretical bounds on estimation error are met. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed precision analysis offers more conservative error bounds compared to existing methods. Finally, we show that the discrete-time analysis can be extended to a discrete-time approximation of the stochastic perturbation model for unamplified links. In this stochastic variant, the perturbation model is replaced by a linear regression model, and we derive corresponding precision guarantees. Numerical results confirm that this stochastic analysis also yields tighter error bounds than current precision analyses. The Android operating system, built on a Unix-like foundation, has become the world's leading mobile platform, with its inherent security flaws serving as the primary catalyst for various attacks. This paper reviews a specific subset of Unix-based security vulnerabilities known as issue-space evasion attacks, which have been documented in Android for over a decade. These attacks exploit a critical flaw in Android's permission model, allowing unauthorized access to system resources without requiring elevated privileges. We survey existing literature on this topic, categorizing the attacks into three main types: capability-based, race condition, and issue-space privilege escalation attacks. For each category, we provide a detailed examination of representative attacks, including their underlying mechanisms and mitigation strategies. Furthermore, we analyze the commonalities and distinctions among these attack classes and outline a unified framework for their detection and prevention. Finally, we discuss current research trends and our own contributions to advancing the security of issue-space evasion attacks. Given the severity of these vulnerabilities, we conclude that future research should prioritize developing effective countermeasures to mitigate their impact. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive table summarizing all known issues related to this attack category. We anticipate that this survey will facilitate a deeper understanding of issue-space evasion attacks and inspire further scholarly investigation. Accretion of pebbles by planetary embryos is a critical mechanism for forming super-Earths and the cores of gas giants. This study investigates how local density fluctuations in pebble disks influence planet formation. We developed a model that simulates stochastic pebble accretion onto planetary embryos, accounting for both spatial and temporal variations in disk density. Our framework incorporates a radial drift timescale for pebbles and a turbulent diffusion coefficient for density variations. Our results indicate that accretion rates are stochastic, with relative fluctuations increasing as expected when pebble surface density becomes low. Furthermore, the radial drift timescale significantly impacts stochasticity; lower drift timescales result in fewer pebbles reaching the planet's Hill radius and higher stochastic variation. Consequently, the power spectrum of mass accretion rates shifts from $k^{-1}$ to $k^{-2}$ as the drift timescale decreases. These stochastic accretion rates produce significant mass fluctuations in super-Earths and gas giant cores, with mass variance scaling linearly with the drift timescale. Ultimately, stochastic pebble accretion may hinder the formation of gas giants. Additionally, we demonstrate that this stochastic accretion process can explain the observed mass distribution of exoplanets with masses below 1 Jupiter mass. This model offers a straightforward explanation for the mass-radius correlation in small exoplanets and provides a potential explanation for the "radius valley" observed in transiting exoplanets. This stochastic accretion process is essential for planet formation models and must be incorporated into future research. A fundamental tenet of statistical learning theory is that models with excessive degrees of freedom are prone to overfitting the training data, thereby compromising their ability to generalize to unseen test samples. Consequently, it is typically advised to keep model complexity below the number of training samples. In contrast, modern machine learning practice frequently employs models with a far greater number of parameters, a phenomenon known as overparameterization, which has driven exceptional performance gains. This shift is possible because statistical theory assumes ideal optimization, whereas our computational reality involves limitations. We argue that the gap between theoretically optimal and computationally feasible solutions explains the disparity between classical statistical principles and current machine learning practices. Specifically, we demonstrate that the classical penalty on model complexity remains appropriate only when training data is fitted perfectly; however, when training error is constrained by computational limits, the optimal complexity of the training procedure must be reduced. This insight offers a novel perspective on the role of overparameterization, suggesting that it does not necessarily harm generalization. Instead, the free parameters in highly overparameterized models can be viewed as defining a training procedure that, when optimized, implicitly regularizes the learned function. This concept is illustrated through examples drawn from both classical statistics and contemporary machine learning. Finally, we present a new overparameterized model that leverages the trade-off between training and testing errors, yielding a classifier that achieves a more favorable training-testing error balance than state-of-the-art competitors. This classifier also trains significantly faster and demonstrates superior generalization on real-world data. This paper serves as a classical statistical examination of overparameterization, a topic that has become increasingly prevalent in machine learning. It is designed to complement existing literature, which predominantly focuses on the statistical characteristics of overparameterized models rather than the computational constraints of their optimization. Our work aims to inspire further research into the statistical implications of computational limits. Supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/andrewkulesza/overparameterization. This paper explores the pretraining of multi-modal models within the context of unstructured e-commerce data. Accurately predicting the transition to Alzheimer's disease (AD) is crucial for healthcare, as it enables early interventions to delay or prevent onset. However, the wide variability in individual progression makes this prediction challenging. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework that integrates anatomical and functional data to forecast AD progression. We developed a sequence-to-sequence model that utilizes a deep InfoMax autoencoder to extract latent features from longitudinal T1-weighted MR images, which are then merged with dynamic features from a convolutional neural network processing functional data. The model's latent representations are concatenated and fed into a regression layer to predict time-to-disease progression. Evaluated on the ADNI cohort, our approach achieved a concordance index of 0.672 for early-moderate stages and 0.642 for moderate-late stages. Compared to baseline methods, the model improved prediction accuracy by 10.5% and 11.4% in these respective groups, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting AD progression. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/DeepInfoMaxAD. Furthermore, we have released a pre-trained model for immediate use in predicting AD progression from anatomical and functional data, accessible at https://huggingface.co/chenyi1997/DeepInfoMaxAD. This resource can be integrated into medical decision-making systems to support clinical decisions. Additionally, we have made the model available for deployment on cloud-based AI platforms to facilitate its integration into healthcare systems. By leveraging the transferability of deep learning models, this work supports the broader goal of democratizing AI in medicine. This paper introduces a recurrent neural network architecture designed for comprehensive language semantics understanding. The model utilizes a language tree representation to facilitate deep comprehension of sentence structures and integrates a gating mechanism to regulate the flow of structural information. Interaction-based RNNs capture sentence semantics through the dynamic coupling of hidden states, while recurrent coupling enables cross-subtree information sharing. The proposed architecture was validated using the Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) task, with experiments conducted on the PropBank and Universal PropBank benchmarks. Evaluation metrics included argument F1 scores and predicate argument F1 scores. The results demonstrate that Interaction-based RNNs achieve state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks. Furthermore, an ablation study on the Universal PropBank revealed that the structural coupling mechanism is the primary driver of performance improvements. Finally, the study examines the model's performance on the CoNLG benchmark, a task focused on generating natural language from logical forms. The proposed architecture is highly effective for tasks requiring a deep grasp of sentence structure, and its scalability suggests potential applications in other language understanding domains. The utilization of recurrent coupling further suggests promising prospects for language generation tasks. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. Enhanced sampling of nucleic acid conformations is difficult due to their inherent rigidity. We introduce a method called Rigid Substrate Biasing (RSB), which modifies the potential energy of molecular dynamics simulations to bias nucleic acid conformations against their mean structure. The Ansitz entropy encoding (ANS) is a widely used technique in modern lossless compression formats, including AVIF, JPEG XL, and HEIC. This study evaluates its performance across various lossy image encoding pipelines, specifically within entropy coding stages of DenoiseAI (a colorization pipeline) and RealESRGAN (a super-resolution pipeline). The analysis compares ANS against the range entropy coding (REC) method used in the default JPEG XL encoder. The results indicate that substituting REC with ANS yields substantial improvements in the perceived quality of encoded images. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the effectiveness of ANS scales with the precision of the fraction bit depth. These findings are particularly relevant for the development of future lossless compression standards. The source code for this study can be found at https://github.com/CodeSourcery/ANSEffects. The dielectric properties of cement-based construction materials are closely tied to the electrical and dielectric features of their porous structures. At low frequencies, the polarization of both the solid and liquid phases dominates the dielectric response of these composites. To elucidate the connection between dielectric constants and electrical conductivity across various frequencies, we employ a generalized effective medium approach. This study examines how the dielectric constants of both phases vary with frequency relative to the porous material's frequency parameter. Our findings indicate that the relative dielectric constant of cement paste peaks at a frequency of 1 Hz. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the relative dielectric constant of the pore solution is influenced by the relative permittivity of water, which in turn depends on the salt concentration within the solution. Additionally, the relative dielectric constant of the cement paste filler shows dependence on both the relative permittivity of the pore solution and the frequency of the applied electric field. Finally, we provide an interpretation of how these factors affect the dielectric constant of cement-based materials under different frequency conditions. These results may assist in understanding the dielectric constants of such materials and could aid in developing non-destructive testing techniques for quality control in construction projects. Additionally, these findings could facilitate the detection of damage in existing structures. To validate our theoretical model, we compared our predictions with experimental data for cement paste and concrete, which showed good agreement. Our results also align with previously reported data for concrete. Ultimately, this research offers a comprehensive framework for investigating the dielectric constants of porous materials. We anticipate that these findings will prove valuable in future studies concerning the dielectric constants of porous composites, including biological tissues. The theoretical methodology presented here is applicable to any porous material containing a pore solution. We have also included a MATLAB code to calculate the dielectric constant of porous materials based on their frequency parameter, the dielectric constant of the cement paste filler, and the dielectric constant of the pore solution. This solution is determined by the relative permittivity of water and the salinity of the pore solution. The provided code can be found in the supplementary materials. We believe this work will be beneficial for researchers studying the dielectric constants of porous materials. We hope our findings will contribute to future investigations into these materials. Additionally, the theoretical approach presented may assist researchers in conducting further studies on the dielectric constants of porous composites. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable cosmological tool for mapping the distribution of intergalactic gas and constraining parameters related to dark matter and dark energy. In this study, we demonstrate that the three-dimensional spatial correlations of Lyman-$\alpha$ forest density fluctuations can yield precise measurements of the dark matter halo mass function, the linear matter power spectrum, and the baryon density parameter. By employing the Zeldovich approximation alongside a straightforward mapping between the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest and dark matter density, we calculate the theoretical correlation functions for both the matter and the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Our analysis indicates that these theoretical predictions align well with the halo model regarding halo mass function and with the linear theory concerning the power spectrum, provided the baryon density parameter is accurately known. Furthermore, we show that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest is capable of detecting the baryon density parameter with an accuracy of approximately 10% using a sample of $10^4$ quasar spectra. This level of precision is equivalent to the statistical uncertainty associated with the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Consequently, we conclude that the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest offers a direct and robust method for measuring the baryon density parameter. This represents a significant advantage over the traditional approach of comparing observed and simulated spectra. Additionally, we emphasize that the computational cost for calculating the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest is substantially lower than that of the traditional method. Finally, we suggest that the traditional method should be reserved for analyzing high-precision data, such as what will be provided by future large-scale spectroscopic surveys. This ensures that the full potential of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest as a cosmological probe is fully realized. These findings are based on a minimal theoretical framework, implying that the actual accuracy of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest as a cosmological probe is likely even greater. This is because the framework ignores the impact of radiative transfer, which can be modeled using the same simplicity. We anticipate that the accuracy of the baryon density parameter measurement will remain at the current level or improve further. This experiment marks the first time transverse emittance has been compressed by more than an order of magnitude and elevated to a higher energy level using a single device. These unprecedented capabilities significantly advance the fields of electron phase-space manipulation and free-electron lasers. By precisely controlling electron beam parameters, we have the potential to advance other areas, including particle accelerators, X-ray lasers, and electron sources. The technique's simplicity and broad applicability suggest it can be utilized in various electron beam manipulation contexts. This method relies on a straightforward interaction between a continuous-wave electron beam and a single cavity, where electrons are accelerated within a standing wave that is drift-compressed in a moving frame. The process is governed by the Doppler-shifted cavity frequency as observed from the moving frame. We have validated this mechanism through both experimental observations and particle-in-cell simulations. Furthermore, we have analyzed the limitations of this approach and outlined potential strategies for extending its capabilities. This paper introduces a Sliding Sequential CVAE (SSCVAE) designed to handle uncertainty in multi-modal trajectory prediction. Uncertainty manifests in two forms: uncertainty regarding a specific future path and uncertainty regarding the existence of that path. SSCVAE addresses both by employing a re-estimation mechanism. To incorporate social context, the model utilizes an uncertainty-aware social force field that adjusts future trajectories based on the uncertainty of surrounding agents. The study demonstrates that incorporating social context significantly enhances prediction accuracy, proving that a sliding window approach is essential for predicting long-term trajectories. Experimental results indicate that the proposed model surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in long-term trajectory prediction. The source code is available at https://github.com/SeongJinPark11/SSCVAE. This work is based on the paper by SeongJin Park, Seungryul Kim, and Sungho Lee, titled "Sliding Sequential CVAE with Time Variant Socially-aware Re-evaluation for Long-term Trajectory Prediction," published in the 2021 IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters. The full paper can be found here: https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/9443950. Additional resources are available at https://github.com/SeongJinPark11/SSCVAE. The research was conducted by SeongJin Park, Seungryul Kim, and Sungho Lee. The model's ability to produce socially aware outputs stems from its uncertainty-aware social force field, which re-estimates force fields considering both temporal and spatial uncertainty. Furthermore, the model re-estimates force fields at each timestep to maintain accuracy over long-term predictions. This approach enables the generation of multi-modal trajectories that reflect both the uncertainty of multiple possible paths and the uncertainty of whether a particular path exists. The results show that the proposed model significantly improves long-term trajectory prediction accuracy, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the model successfully predicts trajectories consistent with social norms and constraints. Source code: https://github.com/SeongJinPark11/SSCVAE. This study introduces a comparison of three distinct metrics designed to quantify the complexity of probabilistic neural networks. These metrics are evaluated through numerical simulations and an analysis of the Minimum Description Length principle. Furthermore, the research extends these concepts to a "liquid" framework, examining how they evolve during the glass transition in simple spin models and, more significantly, in a new Boltzmann machine simulation of a glass-forming liquid. This approach offers a unique perspective on both simple and complex liquids, yielding promising outcomes. Specifically, the findings indicate that these metrics can elucidate the nature of the glass transition and its associated singularities. Additionally, the results suggest that these measures may prove valuable in distinguishing between the recently proposed scenarios for this transition. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the practical utility of these metrics in addressing complex problems within machine learning and artificial intelligence. A Python implementation of a Boltzmann Machine simulating liquid silica, along with the code used to generate the simulation results, is available at https://github.com/alejo-fernandez/BoltzmannMachine. This paper introduces a novel, vision-based Human-in-the-Loop control framework designed to facilitate natural hand-swipe interactions between human operators and autonomous swarm agents. By integrating a deep neural network trained to identify sequential hand gestures, this system enables an operator to direct multiple agents simultaneously by swiping across the field of view. Upon detecting these actions, the agents interpret the sequence of movements to derive the operator's intended direction and distance. The researchers have implemented a proof-of-concept study involving a fleet of four quadcopters and an operator. The findings demonstrate that the proposed hand-sweeping interaction mechanism is both intuitive and effective for modifying the agents' collective behavior. Furthermore, the study indicates that the vision-based recognition approach remains robust even under conditions of limited lighting and minor occlusions. Ultimately, this solution offers a promising avenue for facilitating decentralized interactions between humans and robotic swarms. Automated classification of rare and abnormal blood cells is a critical component of medical diagnostics. This study investigates the performance of deep learning models applied to this task, specifically examining the advantages of ensembling multiple networks. We trained and evaluated various architectures, including ResNet, VGGNet, and DenseNet, on a dataset of 1,000 images spanning 11 cell types. Our ensembling approach combined model outputs using both uniform averaging and performance-weighted methods. The results indicate that the ensemble consistently surpasses individual models, with the average-ensemble achieving the highest accuracy of 94.1%. Furthermore, we observed that the performance gap between our ensemble and the best single model diminished as the number of images per class increased. The source code for this study is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta12345/bloodcellclassification. This work is based on the paper submitted to the 2020 Medicine Processing Challenge of the International Conference on Image Analysis and Recognition. Additional code and resources are available at https://github.com/abhishekgupta12345/bloodcellclassification. Our findings suggest that ensemble methods are highly effective for blood cell classification and that increasing the count of rare class images can further enhance results. The challenge dataset is planned for release in the near future. We hope this work inspires future research in blood cell classification and contributes to the development of computer-aided diagnostic tools for medical professionals. This paper introduces a novel and computationally efficient tone-mapping approach grounded in the principle that human vision perceives high-contrast scenes as having altered color tones. We mathematically formulate this phenomenon as a high-contrast, color-temperature-driven discoloration. Our method calculates local contrast and discoloration on a pixel-by-pixel basis, yielding a perceptually uniform shift in color temperature. This approach was applied to high-dynamic-range imagery and video, demonstrating superior tone-mapping performance compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, our method is more computationally efficient than previous solutions, making it ideal for real-time applications. The method is implemented in both OpenCL and CUDA formats. Experimental results indicate execution times of approximately 1.5 microseconds per pixel for CUDA and 2.5 microseconds for OpenCL. Additionally, the method is fully parameterized, allowing users to adjust tone-mapping characteristics to suit specific needs. This paper introduces a new approach to exponential Taylor expansions that provides deeper insights into the error term. It further investigates the application of these expansions to bound the error in Euler-Mascheroni's harmonic sum series. Additionally, the work examines their utility in deriving sharper bounds for the gamma function and in proving Landau's asymptotic formula for the zeta function. Finally, the text offers an elementary demonstration of a specific property of the zeta function that was previously established by Titchmarsh.

This paper presents a proof of the uniformization theorem for CAT($m$) spheres with $m > 2$, originally proposed by J. Geoghegan and S. Weinberger. Specifically, it establishes the following result: Let $X$ be an orientable, connected, regular $q$-fold covering CAT($m$) sphere of a compact triangulated surface $M^2$, where the triangulation of $L$ consists of finitely many 2-simplices, and $q \ge 2$ is a natural number. Then $X$ is homeomorphic to the $q$-th harmonic branched covering of $M^2$ over the barycenter of the triangulation. Furthermore, if the sphere $X$ is locally Euclidean, then $X$ is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^2$. In this scenario, the covering map $p: X \to M^2$ is identified as the Euclidean harmonic branched covering of $M^2$. Additionally, for any compact triangulated surface $M^2$, the universal cover $\widetilde{M}^2$ is determined to be either $\mathbb{R}^2$ or the second symmetric power $S^2_{\infty}$ of the 2-sphere, and the covering map $p: \widetilde{M}^2 \to M^2$ is proven to be the harmonic branched covering of $M^2$ with degree equal to the order of the triangulation. This finding extends the Euclidean uniformization theorem to all triangulated surfaces. Finally, the authors suggest that this approach can be adapted to prove the spherical uniformization theorem for all triangulated surfaces. The proof relies on the Euclidean uniformization theorem, properties of harmonic branched coverings, and the Euclidean isometric group action on the universal cover of a triangulated surface. The authors intend to address the Gauss-Bonnet theorem and the Spherical uniformization theorem using this method in a subsequent paper. We introduce a theoretical framework for photon-photon interactions within laser-plasma environments. This approach integrates the most recent advancements in strong-field QED with contemporary models of laser-plasma interaction, enabling the prediction of new regimes and phenomena. Specifically, our methodology is applied to laser-solid collisions, revealing that existing experimental data and upcoming studies at the European XFEL and LCLS-II are already operating within a novel, ultra-strong field regime. Furthermore, we identify potential sources of real-world photons and their interactions with intense electromagnetic fields, with implications for future experiments. Additionally, we highlight the existence of a highly energetic, ultra-strong field regime accessible through multi-color laser interactions with plasmas generated by intense laser-solids collisions. This phenomenon is particularly promising for experiments involving multi MeV electron beams generated via nonlinear Compton scattering and laser wakefield acceleration. Finally, we outline the future prospects of this emerging field. This work is dedicated to our friend and colleague, Dr. Alexander Pukhov, on the occasion of his 50th birthday. This study examines the sensitivity of the lower mass bound for the lightest Higgs boson, $m_h$, within a general two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) to the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$. By analyzing the model's parameter space under various assumptions regarding the heavier scalar spectrum and CP properties, we determine how $m_{12}$ influences the $m_h$ lower bound. Our findings reveal that for models featuring a light pseudoscalar or charged Higgs bosons, the $m_{12}$ impact on the Higgs lower bound is comparable to or exceeds that of models with a light-scalar spectrum. Furthermore, we identify a specific region in the $m_{12}$ parameter space where the standard analytical lower bound for $m_h$ becomes invalid. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for reconstructing the lightest Higgs boson mass from current experimental data. Shape expressions provide declarative frameworks for validating RDF data, enabling users to define intricate constraints on RDF graphs. Their primary utility lies in assisting knowledge engineers in documenting and disseminating the structural expectations regarding incoming data. However, merely declaring these target structures does not eliminate the need to manually convert source data into the RDF model, as one must still address how to handle information that falls outside the intended RDF vocabulary. This situation commonly arises when integrating legacy relational databases with contemporary RDF knowledge graphs, where legacy applications must be adapted to align with target RDF vocabularies. This article introduces a novel algorithm that automatically generates data migration scripts for such transformations. Given a relational schema and a target shape expression, the algorithm produces a mapping from the relational schema to shape expressions that guarantees: (1) every script-generated instance of the RDF model validates against the target shape expression, and (2) the resulting mapping is maximally expressive. We have implemented this algorithm in the open-source software RDF4J. Furthermore, we demonstrate its application in generating data migration scripts for a specific case study involving the conversion from RelationalDB to either SHACL Turtle or RDF Schema. A web application built using RDF4J is also presented, which enables users to upload a database schema and a target RDF model, automatically generate the mapping, and execute it on the uploaded legacy database. The system then generates scripts that transfer the legacy data into the specified target RDF model. We illustrate this process by describing a scenario where RDF4J-generated scripts migrate data from a DBpedia-style relational schema to the RDF Model Library (RML). The resulting scripts successfully produce a RDF graph that satisfies both RDF Schema and SHACL Turtle style constraints. We demonstrate that the generated RDF graph is maximally expressive when utilizing RDF Schema, and nearly so when employing SHACL Turtle. Finally, we show that achieving expressiveness over target SHACL Turtle constraints would necessitate additional shape expressions beyond what is available in our example. To our knowledge, this represents the first approach to automatically generating scripts for valid data migration from legacy relational schemas to a target RDF model defined by either RDF Schema or SHACL Turtle. Our results indicate that the algorithm is highly effective for generating valid migration scripts for knowledge graphs derived from relational databases, such as DBpedia. We also demonstrate that the algorithm can be extended to support RDF models that include optional properties, thereby generating migration scripts that are close to maximally expressive in those scenarios. We conclude that the algorithm is well-suited for producing valid migration scripts for a wide range of knowledge graphs, though some specific knowledge graphs

This paper presents a phenomenological analysis of top-quark associated production of a heavy scalar $\phi$ at the LHC, with the scalar subsequently decaying into various channels. The investigation examines all possible final states for a $\phi$ mass up to 100 GeV, covering decays into gluon pairs, photons, $Z$ bosons, $W$ bosons, Higgs bosons, and Higgs pairs. Utilizing ATLAS detector simulations, we estimate the production cross-sections and signal significance across various decay modes. Our findings indicate that Higgs pairs offer the most promising search channel for masses below 10 GeV, whereas for masses between 10 and 100 GeV, decays into $W$ bosons, $Z$ bosons, and gluon pairs yield the highest significance. Furthermore, we establish the mass range of 10–100 GeV as a viable target for future LHC searches. Additionally, we examine the impact of Higgs signal interference on the significance of the $H H$ channel. We also address the necessity of including $t \bar t \phi$ processes in Higgs pair searches, particularly for low-mass Higgs pairs, and provide a strategy for searching the $t \bar t H$ channel in the $b \bar b \gamma$ final state. Finally, we propose a search strategy for the $t \bar t \phi$ process at the high-luminosity LHC. These findings will be incorporated into a comprehensive study of heavy scalar production in association with top quarks, which is currently under preparation. This study will evaluate the potential of the HL-LHC to discover scalar particles with masses up to approximately 1 TeV. Additionally, we will outline a systematic search strategy for top quark associated production of the Standard Model Higgs boson, BSM Higgs bosons, and Higgs pairs. This study investigates the analyzing capability of language models, distinguishing it from the more commonly researched classifying ability. The distinction is significant because analyzing provides a deeper understanding of a model's knowledge, whereas classifying can be achieved through various strategies that do not necessarily reflect such insight. Furthermore, analyzing skills are crucial for few-shot and zero-shot learning, which are currently trending research areas. Consequently, this work examines the analyzing potential of language models using an unsupervised and few-shot framework. We evaluate existing language models based on their few-shot performance in detection and generation tasks. Our findings indicate that while recent models excel at few-shot detection, their few-shot generation potential remains largely unexplored. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the analyzing potential within language models is more closely linked to computational complexity than previously assumed. Finally, we explore the relationship between analyzing and classifying, revealing that certain models exhibit a strong correlation between the two, while others show that analyzing potential can exist independently of classifying. Overall, this research underscores the existence of analyzing potential in language models and establishes a foundation for future few-shot and zero-shot learning studies. Inverse text normalization (ITN) converts automatic speech recognition output from spoken to written form, making it a critical component in building data-driven systems. This study investigates data augmentation techniques to enhance ITN performance using a non-linguistic approach. We evaluated three methods—back-translation, random insertion, and copy-pasting—across English, German, and Russian. Our findings indicate that both random insertion and copy-pasting yield consistent improvements in generalizing to out-of-vocabulary words. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of such a non-linguistic data augmentation approach for inverse text normalization. This paper establishes a Faber-Krahn type inequality concerning the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator $\mathcal{L}=-\Delta+|x|^{2}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, subject to a Robin constraint on a ball $B_{r}$. By employing affine invariant characteristics and specifically the symmetric $A$-mean, we demonstrate that the eigenvalue $\lambda$ associated with an admissible eigenfunction $\varphi$ satisfies $\lambda \geq \lambda^{*}$, where $\lambda^{*}$ represents the optimal constant achieved by a radial eigenfunction. Furthermore, we provide a complete characterization of the eigenfunctions that yield this optimal constant. Along the way, we also derive the corresponding Weinberger inequality. Finally, we examine the corresponding problem for the Laplacian $-\Delta$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Our findings align with and extend the work of Benguria, de Faria, and Heinzle, as well as Wang, Wang, and Zhang. Additionally, we offer an alternative approach to the Weinberger inequality for the Laplacian, which utilizes a simplified version of the Sternberg-Monaco moving plane method. Bibliography not included.

Transfer learning has become a widely adopted method for addressing data scarcity in machine learning. Typically, data are grouped into non-overlapping clusters, and models trained on one cluster are transferred to another. This paper introduces an alternative transfer learning framework where groups are defined by proximity to individual samples rather than clusters. We derive the statistical properties of the estimator obtained by combining tangent kernels from all sample levels of a trained hierarchy. We demonstrate that this group-based approach is statistically equivalent to our sample-based method and validate the findings through simulations and a case study involving COVID-19 data. The NFT kernel is readily adaptable to various machine learning tasks, including classification, clustering, and regression.

Keywords: Transfer learning, tangent kernel, functional data analysis, COVID-19.

This study examines the impact of correlations on the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian one-dimensional (1D) systems. Using a generalized Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, we demonstrate that correlations can eliminate the non-Hermitian point-gap topology. Furthermore, we show that correlations can be precisely controlled by adjusting coupling strengths, offering additional flexibility in the design of non-Hermitian topological phases. Finally, we analyze how this non-Hermitian point-gap topology differs from its Hamiltonian counterpart. These findings are validated through numerical simulations. Additionally, our results indicate that non-Hermitian 1D point-gap topology can be observed in both microwave and photonic systems. Consequently, this research establishes a foundation for developing novel non-Hermitian topological phases and explores applications in non-Hermitian photonic and microwave platforms. Finally, we provide insights into the relationship between non-Hermitian point-gap topology and skin modes. Experimental verification of these results is expected to advance the study of non-Hermitian topology. This paper outlines our strategy for infusing social characteristics into synthetic speech. Although contemporary TTS systems can generate phonetically accurate and intelligible audio, their vocal outputs often lack the social cues necessary for specific user groups. Our technical approach involves modifying prosodic features, such as pitch, to embed desired social signals. To assess the resulting vocal quality, we employ both objective metrics and subjective evaluations. Our experimental results indicate that for a given social target, adjusting pitch alone is insufficient to fully realize the intended characteristics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that minor deviations in pitch value can produce significant shifts in perceived social traits. Finally, our experiments reveal that listeners are capable of detecting subtle variations in vocal characteristics generated by our proposed method. Given the ethical challenges associated with manipulating social signals in text-to-speech, our findings highlight the critical need for further research and more sophisticated synthesis techniques. We introduce a neutrino mass model grounded in the $A_4 \times U(1)_{B-L}$ flavor and symmetry structures, utilizing the real representation of $A_4$. To address the small neutrino mixing angle $\theta_{13}$, we extend the scalar sector with an additional triplet scalar. The neutrino mixing parameters are accurately predicted by this framework. To investigate dark matter, we add a fermion singlet to the scalar sector. Simultaneously, gauging the $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry ensures the smallness of the dark matter candidate's mass. The residual $Z_3$ symmetry from $A_4$ stabilizes a new neutral fermion, which is identified as dark matter. This neutral fermion interacts with the dark sector through a new $Z$ boson and with the visible sector via a kinetically mixed photon. The model is tested against relic density constraints, direct detection limits, and LHC results. Furthermore, we examine the model's implications for neutrinoless double beta decay and the muon $g-2$ anomaly. Finally, we explore the possibility of detecting dark matter at the LHC and highlight the phenomenology of a light dark matter candidate. This work is motivated by the recent identification of a stable dark matter candidate with a mass below 10 GeV, consistent with neutrino oscillation data. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed model can explain the recent muon $g-2$ anomaly and that the dark matter candidate falls within the parameter space favored by LHC data. Additionally, we show that direct detection constraints can be evaded through parameter choices, while the relic density can be satisfied through annihilation into both fermionic and bosonic channels. We conclude that the model predicts a dark matter mass near 7 GeV, with a primary annihilation mode into fermions, and we discuss the prospects for detecting this dark matter at the LHC. Finally, we highlight the phenomenology of a light dark matter candidate, with a mass below 10 GeV, that is compatible with neutrino oscillation data. This paper introduces the concept of polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PhGA). We establish construction methods for PhGAs of sizes $(N_1+N_2+N_3)\times P$ and $(N_1+N_2)\times P_1 \times P_2$ utilizing array expansions. Additionally, we provide a growth rule for PhGAs that maintains the polynomial autocorrelation property while increasing the array size. Simulation results demonstrate that PhGAs constructed via these array expansion methods exhibit low sidelobe levels and are robust against the deletion of up to 50% of the elements. This cycle repeats indefinitely, generating a series of consecutive universes. The initial conditions for each phase are established by the reverse time-evolution of the Big Crunch from the preceding cycle. We demonstrate that this process leads to an oscillatory matter distribution. Furthermore, we establish that the formation of structures such as galaxies and clusters within each phase is closely linked to the matter configurations established at the onset of that phase. Ultimately, we illustrate the potential for large-scale structures in the universe to exhibit negative time-reversal parity. These findings offer a novel perspective on the cosmic time-evolution of large-scale structures and may assist in interpreting various time-reversal parity violation phenomena. This work is founded on the premise that the cosmic matter distribution possesses time-reversal parity, which can be violated. Consequently, our model provides a new approach to investigating the nature of the Big Bang. A distinctive feature of this model is that it does not necessitate a Big Bang for the initial universe; instead, it posits that the Big Bang for any given phase results from the reverse time-evolution of a Big Crunch from the other cycle's phase. Additionally, our study indicates that the Big Bang cannot serve as the absolute beginning of the universe, thereby implying that the universe is eternal. Our analysis also suggests that the Big Bang may be a one-sided event, as we explore the possibility of a Big Crunch evolving into a new phase of the universe in reverse time. These conclusions are derived from the principle that the Big Crunch can trigger the reverse time-evolution of the universe. Finally, our study addresses the issue of the arrow of time. We also propose that the cosmic matter distribution is not random but is determined by the cosmic time direction. This assumption is reasonable because the cosmic matter distribution is not random, as random distributions would result in no observable Big Crunch or Big Freeze. This study investigates the applicability of superdeterminism, as seen in Tipler's work, to Bohmian quantum mechanics, a variant of the Copenhagen interpretation. By employing Bohmian mechanics, we demonstrate that the no-collapse superdeterministic framework known as Invariant-set theory can indeed function as a viable hidden-variable theory. This approach offers a solution to the Bell inequalities and restores local realism. Furthermore, we show that the quantum potential can be expressed via path integrals, suggesting that Invariant-set theory may constitute a new formulation of many-worlds theory grounded in superdeterminism. Additionally, the theory remains compatible with the recently proposed Many-Source Bohmian interpretation. Our findings indicate that both Invariant-set theory and Many-Source Bohmian theory are equivalent to many-worlds theory, differing only in their descriptive language. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for understanding the nature of time. In this context, we argue that time is not merely an emergent property but is instead intrinsic to the theory, with the Wheeler–DeWitt equation playing a crucial role in this framework. Automated keyphrase spotting involves detecting short phrases within a signal stream and generating non-redundant, sorted lists of those phrases. While Neural Networks (NNs) have shown superior accuracy compared to traditional methods, their high computational cost makes them unsuitable for IoT devices with limited resources. This paper introduces a novel Neural Network architecture designed to balance computational efficiency with accuracy. The proposed model achieves a reduction in both training and inference time by an order of magnitude on a Raspberry Pi 4, while maintaining a minimal accuracy trade-off of less than 1%. Additionally, we explore accuracy improvements by implementing knowledge distillation to train a smaller model, which further decreases inference time on IoT hardware without any loss in performance. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/DeepKeyphraseDistillation}. Given the significance of NNs in the IoT sector, we anticipate that the models introduced in this work will facilitate faster research and development cycles. Furthermore, we aim to support future research by enabling the deployment of neural networks for keyphrase spotting on IoT hardware. Our work demonstrates that these deployment options do not necessarily entail a significant compromise in accuracy. We hope that our research will inspire other scholars to investigate NN architectures for resource-constrained environments and that they will find our work valuable in their own endeavors. This work examines dimer models on a two-dimensional square lattice subject to non-abelian gauge fields, demonstrating their ability to simulate two-dimensional Dirac fermions coupled to gauge fields. The study begins by reviewing the free dimer model and its formulation via matrix product states (MPS). Subsequently, various gauge-invariant extensions are investigated, including formulations for both real and complex vector gauge fields. Within the MPS framework, the dimer model is shown to be equivalent to a fermionic lattice theory; consequently, the gauge-invariant dimer model corresponds to Dirac fermions interacting with the background gauge field. Numerical simulations are employed to analyze the large-scale behavior of these systems. The results reveal an area-law entanglement entropy and a gapless excitation spectrum, with a dynamical exponent of $z=1$ at zero gauge field, consistent with Dirac fermion theory. Furthermore, the presence of a background gauge field is demonstrated to induce a finite excitation gap when the flux is non-zero. Finally, the statistical dimer model is observed to satisfy the Weyl equation, describing Weyl fermions coupled to the background gauge field. These findings indicate that dimer models serve as a valuable tool for investigating quantum field theories involving fermions and gauge fields, as their Hilbert space scales exponentially more slowly than that of the corresponding fermionic theories. The methodology extends to other frustrated two-dimensional quantum spin systems, offering a means to study their non-abelian gauge-invariant behavior. Finally, the results suggest that the dimer model can be utilized to investigate fermion fractionalization. By mapping the dimer model onto a fermionic theory, it becomes possible to examine the topological aspects of Dirac fermions coupled to gauge fields, including the emergence of fermion zero modes and the relationship between these modes and fractional charge. This approach also facilitates the calculation of the renormalization group flow of the fermionic theory. The paper concludes by discussing potential future research directions. Group lasso methods are extensively utilized for performing structured variable selection, particularly for identifying a subset of highly correlated predictors. However, the standard approach relies on a Euclidean norm, which is ill-suited for categorical predictors. This study investigates the limitations of the Euclidean norm and proposes an alternative based on information theory. We demonstrate the advantages of this new norm, develop the corresponding group lasso framework, and provide an efficient algorithm for its optimization. The proposed method was evaluated using both simulated and real-world datasets. Simulation results indicate that the proposed approach surpasses existing methods in terms of variable selection accuracy and model prediction performance. Furthermore, an application to a real dataset demonstrates the method's effectiveness regarding computational efficiency. Embedded systems are increasingly diverse, often integrating multiple operating systems (OSes) to serve distinct purposes. However, the growing trend of OS consolidation is driven by the need to reduce hardware costs and power usage. While existing hypervisors can host general-purpose OSes, they lack support for high-assurance, real-time (RT), or mixed-criticality RT systems. To address this, we present T-Visor, a hypervisor designed for the coexistence of x86 RT and x86 general-purpose (GP) OSes. T-Visor offers near-100% CPU scheduling efficiency, deterministic RT performance, and minimal overhead. It has been validated on an x86 platform running Windows 7 alongside x86 RT Linux systems. The results show a hypervisor overhead of under 1% CPU time, with RT execution time variance below 10 microseconds. Furthermore, the RT Linux kernel was customized to ensure real-time determinism, and a preemptive RT Linux kernel was developed to facilitate the study of multiple RT configurations. Ultimately, T-Visor enables the efficient deployment of heterogeneous embedded systems, whether in standalone mode or within cloud environments. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of T-Visor's architecture, implementation details, and performance evaluation. We introduce a novel panoramic stitching algorithm grounded in image warping prior. Our objective is to create a seamless, wide-angle panorama from multiple images captured by a handheld device, such as a smartphone. The core methodology involves selecting optimal warping parameters for each image to ensure optimal Warped Image Blending (WIB) performance. These parameters are initially estimated using camera intrinsic parameters and camera pose data derived from SLAM. To achieve a smooth blend, we optimize camera poses by minimizing the total WIB error across all input images. We present an efficient optimization framework that rapidly converges to a local minimum. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach yields stitching outcomes with high visual quality and superior robustness compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we have released the corresponding source code.

This work examines a random tensor network (RTN) model defined on the boundary of an AdS spacetime, composed of tensor networks linked by nonlocal reflections. We derive an explicit formula for the network's probability density function (PDF) and utilize it to study correlations within random geometries. Specifically, we demonstrate that AdS/CTFT correlations in the boundary theory scale with the separation distance of the inserted points. Furthermore, we show that these correlations exhibit exponential decay governed by the ratio of the network's width to its length. Finally, we provide numerical evidence supporting the network's ergodicity and discuss the applicability of a quantum ergodic theorem regarding the convergence of geometrical observables toward their mean values. These findings suggest that the mechanism of nonlocal reflections is essential for establishing statistical equivalence between points across different RTNs. Additionally, the study explores the influence of tensor randomness on the equivalence of boundary points within the network. Notably, we find that AdS/CTFT correlations between points on distinct RTNs are suppressed by the tensor randomness strength, which is consistently explained by the tensor network geometry. The conclusions of this research are grounded in the explicit solution of the network's PDF. Finally, we extend our findings to scenarios involving multiple reflections and tensor networks of varying shapes. The methodology employed in this study holds significant potential for analyzing other classes of tensor networks. Furthermore, the study offers a comprehensive analysis of the statistical properties of these networks, including the distribution of geometrical observables, the existence of phase transitions, and the stability of the network. These insights are expected to facilitate a more profound understanding of the relationship between tensor network geometry and boundary theory. Ultimately, the analysis of RTNs serves as a valuable tool for elucidating the nature of quantum gravity. We investigate heritable information within stochastic dynamics, focusing on heritable random patterns (HRP). An HRP consists of random, time-dependent source-sink structures that maintain a persistent, dynamic pattern capable of indefinitely supporting the propagation of passive tracers. The persistent component of an HRP is defined as a dynamical variable that remains invariant under perturbations with sufficiently small support. To facilitate an unambiguous definition of HRP, we analyze a broad category of dynamical systems known as reactive turbulent dispersions (RTD), which model complex interactions between active chemical reactions and passive turbulent diffusion. In all RTD models, heritable information is abundant, as any HRP can be generated by a chemical reaction occurring within a bounded region. Furthermore, we demonstrate that heritable information is robust in both particle-based and field-theoretic descriptions of RTD, a property that extends to other systems, including biological development and neural activity. Finally, we explore the implications of HRP for modeling biological systems, which are often characterized by complex, non-equilibrium dynamics. This analysis reveals a significant discrepancy between field-theoretic and particle-based models of RTD, where heritable information is prevalent in the particle-based framework but absent in the field-theoretic one. The paper concludes by discussing the origins of this paradox and its potential relevance to biological systems. This study investigates the average spin-flip time of tunneling electrons using a spin-resolved Larmor clock. By measuring the spin-flip duration through the longitudinal spin component perpendicular to the sample surface, we employ the non-equilibrium Green's function method to calculate the full width at half maximum of the time distribution, which quantifies the spin-flip interval. Our results indicate that spin-fluctuation-induced phase shifts are more pronounced in the up-spin component, resulting in a shorter average up-spin flip time compared to the down-spin time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the chosen bias voltage is a critical parameter for accurately determining spin-flip time. Finally, our findings suggest that the proposed Larmor clock method is viable for future experimental measurements of spin-flip times. These outcomes are anticipated to offer new perspectives for future theoretical and experimental investigations into tunneling spin fluctuations. Additionally, the developed theoretical framework is applicable to various spin-dependent quantum transport phenomena. Finally, the code utilized in this work is publicly accessible. \newline

We examine the relationship between the asymptotic symmetries of four-dimensional gravity and the IR divergences of scattering amplitudes, specifically within the context of the celestial sphere. We demonstrate that a specific linear combination of soft theorem parameters functions as a symmetry parameter for amplitude functionals mapped to the celestial sphere, yielding a Ward identity that precisely reproduces the amplitude factorization formula for double soft graviton scattering. Furthermore, we outline the methodology for calculating lower-point partial waves and suggest a path toward determining complete wave functions. Continual learning (CL) aims to enable machines to sequentially acquire new knowledge from evolving data streams without losing prior capabilities. However, CL remains a significant challenge because standard machine learning approaches are optimized for batch learning with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data, making them prone to catastrophic forgetting. To address this, ensemble methods have been introduced, which maintain multiple neural networks to adapt incoming data while preserving past knowledge. Despite their effectiveness, existing ensemble CL techniques often struggle with the computational demands of training and storing several models. This paper presents a novel structure designed for online ensemble continual learning, utilizing a single neural network model. By implementing a dynamic partitioning strategy, the proposed approach automatically identifies data substreams and generates a specialized model for each partition. This method is evaluated across various substreams, demonstrating its effectiveness in both ensemble and batch continual learning scenarios. Experimental results indicate that the proposed structure surpasses state-of-the-art methods in classification accuracy and exhibits robustness against concept drift. Furthermore, it achieves these performance gains while utilizing approximately 50% less memory. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/Online-Ensemble-CL. Keywords: Continual Learning, Ensemble Learning, Concept Drift, Neural Structure.

The study examines a hypercomplex-like structure on a four-dimensional oriented Riemannian manifold that does not require associativity. This generalization of the associative form is defined by multiple characteristics, most notably the absence of co-closedness for the three forms. The focus shifts to examining the geometry of these generalized forms and their linked metrics across various dimensions. A key finding is that the Laplacians of the four forms are proportional to the Riemannian Ricci curvature scalar, meaning that if the metric is Einstein, every form is co-closed, and conversely, if any single form is co-closed, the Riemannian Ricci tensor vanishes. Furthermore, when a specific combination of the four forms constitutes a Hodge decomposition, the Riemannian Ricci tensor exhibits diagonalization. Additional insights are provided regarding the Laplacian and Hodge decomposition of the associative form within an Einstein metric. Finally, the text explores the geometry of the 4-form in the non-associative Einstein metric on twisted $SU(3)$ geometry, revealing that in this framework, the Laplacian of the twisted Einstein form is positive, and its decomposition into 2-2 and 11 components precludes the existence of a Laplacian cocycle. These findings hold significant implications for non-associative Einstein manifolds, particularly those underling non-geometric M-theory. Additionally, the text investigates the geometry of generalized forms in the non-Minkowski 3-form background of M-theory, demonstrating that in both Minkowski and non-Minkowski scenarios, the Laplacian of the non-Minkowski 3-form is negative. These results suggest that such forms may not satisfy the co-closedness condition, thereby influencing the construction of non-geometric M-theory. Finally, the text briefly addresses hypercomplex-like structures in six and eight dimensions, noting that while 6D forms retain co-closedness, this property is lost in 8D forms. These findings may impact the development of non-geometric M-theory frameworks beyond dimensions 5 and 7. Consequently, the construction of hypercomplex-like structures appears essential for understanding the non-geometric nature of M-theory. This study addresses a non-zero-sum stochastic differential game involving two insurers and one investment firm within a unified framework. The firms share the objective of optimizing the value function to maximize long-term growth. The two insurers' value functions are interdependent, creating a need to consider Nash equilibrium solutions. The proposed model incorporates two distinct economic environments that can transition between each other via a continuous-time Markov chain. Within this framework, the jump-diffusion processes governing the firms' value functions are defined by a system of nonlinear integro-differential equations. To address the lack of closed-form solutions, we develop finite-difference schemes to approximate these equations. Finally, we establish the convergence of these schemes toward the exact solution. Key findings include the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the nonlinear system, the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium, the existence of value function solutions, the convergence of the finite-difference schemes, and the continuity of this convergence. Furthermore, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the theoretical results. This model holds significant potential for practical application in both real-world investment and reinsurance scenarios and for future research. Additionally, the approach is adaptable to various other domains, such as insurance and finance. Our work also lays the foundation for extending the model to more complex scenarios, including those involving more than three agents. Future research could explore the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium for the generalized model and its associated value functions. Additionally, the value functions could be characterized using quasi-variational inequalities.
