This paper introduces a new control algorithm designed to provide smooth and stable flight performance for quadrotors. A primary obstacle in quadrotor control is ensuring smoothness, which is essential for safe payload transportation. To address this, we propose the PIDA algorithm, which integrates a Genetic Filter (GF) to generate smoother, more accurate estimates for the PIDA controller. GF is a Bayesian filter that optimizes the probability distribution of a dynamical system using a GA. The resulting PIDA controller ensures a stable flight trajectory by dynamically adjusting PID gains in real-time through the PIDA algorithm, a method inspired by the Polyhedral Outer Approximation technique. This algorithm efficiently solves the mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem inherent in optimal trajectory planning. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the trajectory tracking performance of the PIDA controller surpasses traditional PIDA approaches. Furthermore, payload transportation simulations indicate that PIDA achieves a 20% reduction in both jerk and acceleration compared to standard PID control. Finally, we validate the method's robustness by simulating wind disturbances. Our findings indicate that the PIDA controller not only tracks desired trajectories with high accuracy but also maintains stability during transportation. We present a low-energy pion-nucleon scattering analysis that adheres to isospin and chiral constraints, incorporating partial wave projections up to $s$-waves. This study examines the sensitivity of low-energy constants to experimental data, focusing on the pion pole residue and scattering lengths. Through this investigation, we derive the first model-independent constraints on the $\pi N$ scattering amplitude at the Delta resonance, specifically for low-energy constants up to five-loop order in a derivative expansion. These findings are compared against lattice simulations and recent phenomenological studies. Furthermore, we derive the pion pole contribution to low-energy constants for $\pi N \to \pi N \pi$ processes, which are essential for calculating the $\pi N$ contribution to the two-pion emission term in neutron $\beta$-decay. Finally, we explore the relationship between low-energy $\pi N$ scattering and QCD sum rules. Given the current lack of a phenomenologically consistent framework for low-energy constants, we advocate for the development of such a framework, which can be achieved through lattice QCD simulations. We outline key challenges in this endeavor and provide preliminary results from our ongoing $\pi N$ scattering calculations on the lattice. Additionally, we discuss the necessity of including electromagnetic effects in these computations. This work serves as a companion to our recent study on low-energy constants for $\pi N \to \pi N \pi$. On May 1, 2012, the Large Hadron Collider commenced data collection using its Phase-1 upgrade, marking the start of the physics Run-2 era. This run utilized a record-breaking 7 TeV proton-proton collision energy and a luminosity of $10^{32}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. The CMS detector's pixel detector underwent a critical two-week shutdown for maintenance, necessitating an extended repair period for the pixel pilot-phase prototype readout board (RPORB) within the Phase-1 upgrade. This work details the reconstruction of the pilot-phase RPORB following its disassembly, transport, and repair. The successfully reconstructed data from this process demonstrates that the RPORB is fully repairable, thereby validating the strategy to address production defects in the Phase-1 pixel pixelhoods. Furthermore, the results confirm the efficacy of the CMS reconstruction software in processing the RPORB. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of thoroughly testing the complete production pipeline prior to the Phase-1 upgrade's deadline. The outcomes of this analysis were presented at the CMS Workshop on Production and Testing of the Phase-1 Upgrade Pixel Detector on May 15, 2012. Additionally, the data from the reconstructed pilot-phase RPORB will be made available for public use. The authors express their gratitude to the CMS pixel detector production team for their assistance in repairing the RPORB. Finally, the authors wish to dedicate this paper to their families.

This study utilizes machine learning to identify host galaxy structures of active galactic nuclei (AGN) with redshifts $0.1<z<0.6$ within the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey (HSC-Wide) imaging data. Utilizing HSC and Subaru Astronomical 3D Mapping (3DMap) data, we created a dataset of 1,010 confirmed host galaxies, which we classified into three morphological types: disk, elliptical, and irregular. We trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) to estimate these structures, achieving a test accuracy of 80.5% and a macro-average F1 score of 76.1%. Furthermore, we applied the trained model to estimate host morphology for 1,010 HSC-Wide confirmed AGN, analyzing the distribution of these estimates. Finally, we compared HSC-Wide results with those from the SDSS Survey of the Hubble Deep Field (HDF-SDSS), finding that while HSC-Wide data exhibits a higher proportion of irregular galaxies, disk galaxies remain the most common type in both datasets. These findings suggest that HSC-Wide is well-suited for morphological studies of $z<1$ AGN. Additionally, we have made our dataset and trained model publicly available to facilitate further research. u$ and SRC. Our calculations are compared with relativistic and semi-relativistic approaches, demonstrating that the latter can yield significant errors in momentum distributions. We derive spectator momentum distributions and examine their sensitivity to the SRC model. Furthermore, we calculate the phase-space distribution of $

Finally, we compute the energy dependence of the ratio between events involving SRC and those excluding SRC, a critical metric for experimental investigations. This ratio is found to be independent of $
u$ at high energies, a characteristic that can be leveraged to estimate the SRC content of nuclei. Additionally, we investigate the $
u$ dependence of the $
u$-averaged asymmetry between neutron and proton SRC, a quantity accessible via polarization observables in scattering experiments. We demonstrate that this $\Delta n/p$ ratio exhibits a distinct $
u$ dependence, a feature that could provide insights into the neutron-to-proton SRC ratio. These findings are based on a high-precision SRC parameterization that incorporates recent global fits to SRC data. The paper concludes with a summary of the work and its implications for future experiments. This framework is available as open-source code. The concepts of saturation and geometric scaling are introduced to facilitate a unified description of transverse hadron production in both inclusive and di-hadron data, spanning various processes, kinematical ranges, and collision energies. These notions have been validated across a broad spectrum of deep-inelastic scattering experiments, transferable to hadron-hadron collisions, and most recently observed in proton-lead collisions at the LHC. Furthermore, it is argued that saturation effects influence the production of di-hadrons in both proton-nucleus and heavy ion collisions. The analysis of di-hadron production in heavy ion collisions reveals distinct features that cannot be explained by superposition of nucleon-nucleon interactions. Specifically, back-to-back gluon pairs are suppressed in favor of large azimuthal angle separations between hadrons, a phenomenon that may serve as a probe for the initial state of heavy ion collisions. The study also explores the dependence of these effects on nuclear size and the density of produced hadrons. Finally, potential future tests of these findings are proposed. The discussion concludes with a brief overview of the underlying formalism. The paper is structured into the following sections: 1. Introduction, 2. Saturation and Geometrical Scaling, 3. Inclusive Single Hadron Production, 4. Di-hadron Production, 5. Di-hadron Production in Heavy Ion Collisions, 6. Summary and Outlook, 7. Theoretical Framework, 8. Conclusions, 9. Acknowledgements, 10. References, and 11. Appendix. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the spectroscopic data from the spectroscopic survey of low-metallicity stars (SSLS) to investigate amplitude dispersion. By examining the data, we identified a significant correlation between the amplitude dispersion and the Fe/H ratio, which aligns with prior studies on metal-poor stars. Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of various stellar parameters on amplitude dispersion using stepwise multiple regression. The results indicate that while effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$) and surface gravity ($\log g$) are the primary drivers of amplitude dispersion in metal-rich stars, they exert a negligible influence on dispersion in low-metallicity stars. Consequently, we recommend that future studies on low-metallicity stars prioritize the selection of stars with similar Fe/H ratios to effectively mitigate amplitude dispersion. Finally, we developed and validated a new pipeline designed to correct amplitude dispersion in low-metallicity stars, demonstrating that this approach is feasible for such stellar populations. This methodology will facilitate more precise abundance analyses in future research. Our findings are accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1992/Amplitude_dispersion_correction.

This study introduces a new toolbox designed to assess the sensitivity of machine learning models to input variations. Drawing inspiration from robustness analysis in optimization, the toolbox evaluates how model predictions respond to perturbations in data. It establishes a general framework applicable to various decision contexts and supports a wide range of modification schemes, including random noise, bounded noise, and absolute noise. The analysis is conducted using a single metric: the average absolute difference in model outputs resulting from the input perturbations. The developers have applied this tool to investigate the relationship between financial literacy and behavior. The study reveals that small perturbations in survey questions or responses lead to significant shifts in predicted outcomes, indicating that the link between financial literacy and behavior is highly sensitive to measurement noise. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that their survey instrument is highly robust, with only negligible effects observed when responses are replaced by random data. These findings underscore the critical nature of financial literacy measurements and suggest that the proposed toolbox is valuable for analyzing other survey-based outcomes. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions for future research. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/optimization-and-robustness/FOL. This tool is released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. Additional code and data are available upon request. The authors declare no conflicts of interest. This research investigates the SQUID hardware platform, representing one of the earliest large-scale quantum processors built using superconducting technology. Comprising 64 qubits, SQUID supports both analog and digital operations, including single- and two-qubit gates, phase adjustments, analog evolution, measurements, and quantum state tomography. We explore utilizing SQUID to experiment with machine learning algorithms, demonstrating the execution of several key tasks such as variational quantum eigensolver, variational quantum feature mapping, quantum kernel estimation, and quantum neural networks. These experiments aim to establish a foundation for future research into quantum-enhanced machine learning. Our study addresses practical implementation details, including the configuration of variational quantum circuits, quantum kernel estimation, and quantum feature mapping, while also detailing methodologies for training and evaluating quantum neural networks. Additionally, we examine the impact of data dimensionality on quantum kernel performance and report on a quantum-enhanced support vector machine experiment. This work serves as a starting point for further investigation into machine learning advancements within the emerging field of quantum machine intelligence. This paper explores warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds within almost contact manifolds, demonstrating that the warping function adheres to specific differential equations. As a result, we establish several results and examples concerning Warped Product pointwise anti-inclined submanifolds and warped product pointwise slant submanifolds. Additionally, we provide examples of non-trivial isometries and rotations applicable to warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds. Finally, we present two classes of warped product pointwise slant submanifolds that do not belong to the category of pointwise slant submanifolds. Notably, examples from both of these classes fail to satisfy the conditions required for the class of warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds. Furthermore, we derive differential equations for warped product pointwise slant submanifolds and show that, in general, the slant function is not constant. This finding indicates that, in the context of warped product submanifolds, the term "pointwise slant" is more appropriate than "slant." Finally, we offer examples of isometries and rotations for warped product pointwise slant submanifolds. In each case, the slant function remains non-constant, and rotational isometries do not transform the slant function into a constant. Consequently, neither "slant" nor "semi-inclined" terminology is suitable for these examples. However, it is essential to note that "pointwise slant" is the correct classification for these examples. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the mean curvature vector is non-zero, confirming they are proper slant submanifolds, and by the existence of a unit normal vector field $\xi$ such that $\phi(\xi) = \mu \xi$ for some $\mu \in (-1, 1)$, confirming they are proper pointwise slant submanifolds. These findings underscore the necessity of using "pointwise slant" rather than "slant" when describing warped product submanifolds. A primary hurdle in the quest for dark matter remains the need for large-scale, low-background nuclear recoil detectors. This requirement stems from the anticipated low recoil energies of dark matter candidates, which necessitate exceptional sensitivity to filter out background events. Additionally, due to the elusive nature of dark matter, these detectors must be scalable to megaton volumes. This thesis outlines a strategy to meet these demands through the utilization of color centers within diamond. The PALEOCCENE approach employs natural diamond as a target material, leveraging its high optical and mechanical hardness, trace impurity levels, and robust structural integrity. By combining nuclear recoil sensing with radiopurity analysis, the methodology allows for the optimization of both the active detector mass and background reduction. The proposed experiment aims to achieve a threshold energy of 10 eV and a background index of $10^{-17}$ kg-1 s-1, with a total exposure capacity reaching 100 ton-years. Furthermore, the radiopurity assessment is expected to reach a sensitivity of $10^{-19}$ g/g for $^{210}$Pb. This work details the characterization of the color center sensor, the development of the radiopurity analysis technique, and the design of a pilot experiment to validate the concept. The resulting proof-of-principle device, known as the Low Energy Nuclear recoil detector with PAleO cCene (LENO-PAOC), is scheduled for deployment at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS) in early 2022. LENO-PAOC will operate with an exposure of approximately 100 kg-days, serving as a demonstration of the feasibility of the overall strategy. The report concludes with a discussion of the scientific outcomes expected from LEPO-PAOC and the subsequent research and development necessary to advance the concept. Finally, the thesis addresses the challenges associated with the production and sourcing of suitable diamond material. Specifically, the need for diamonds with a high concentration of pre-existing nitrogen defects is contrasted with the requirement for radiopurity, which is difficult to satisfy with commercially available material. We introduce a straightforward theoretical framework for rigid colloidal molecules formed by linking Brownian spheres, specifically investigating their stability within active media exhibiting activity gradients. By applying a generalized Stokes-Einstein relation, we determine the conditions under which these molecules maintain structural integrity. Our findings indicate that molecules with higher symmetry are more stable in activity gradients, although their stability is also contingent upon the precise arrangement of the connecting bonds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that molecules can be trapped within these gradients, resulting in their spatial confinement. These theoretical predictions are supported by extensive two-dimensional Brownian dynamics simulations. We further explore potential experimental applications, including the selective stabilization of various colloidal molecules and the manipulation of their positions and orientations through spatially modulated activity gradients. These concepts establish a novel pathway for steering soft matter using light instead of external fields. Finally, we highlight that the proposed theory is applicable to a broad spectrum of active systems, extending beyond gradient environments to include phoretic and chemically mediated active matter. Specifically, we show that chemical reactions between colloidal molecules and the background medium can yield similar outcomes. Our study offers a comprehensive perspective on the design and manipulation of colloidal molecules within complex active environments. The accompanying Supplementary Materials provide additional details on our theoretical approach and results. Keywords: colloidal molecules, active matter, Brownian dynamics, theoretical models. This study utilizes the real-space finite-size scaling technique to investigate the interaction-driven magnetorotons responsible for charge and spin excitations in two-dimensional fractional quantum Hall systems. By analyzing the magnetoroton behavior across various filling factors, we identify distinct spectral rules. Specifically, we observe that the magnetoroton energy exhibits a systematic finite-size dependence that peaks at angles corresponding to high symmetry. Furthermore, the fractional charges and spins of the magnetorotons are consistently confirmed. These findings provide a direct characterization of quasiparticle excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems. Additionally, our results offer a new perspective on the quantum Hall total spectral rule, which connects the integer quantum Hall effect with the fractional variant. This new spectral rule is derived from the finite-size scaling of the spectral function of a one-particle excitation. Finally, our study confirms the existence of multiple magnetorotons in the excitation spectrum. The fractional charge and spin of these multiple magnetorotons are also verified through finite-size scaling analysis of their respective resonance angles. The quantum numbers of these multiple magnetorotons can be qualitatively understood by considering the multiple composite fermion Landau level fillings. These multiple magnetorotons are identified as the optimal excitations in finite-size systems. We also propose a new spectral total rule for multiple magnetorotons, which is supported by our numerical results. This rule is obtained by summing the spectral total rules of all composite fermion Landau levels. The quantum numbers of these multiple magnetorotons are further verified by analyzing their spectral function. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between the spectral total rule and the spectral density in the magnetoroton resonance angle. Finally, we compare our results with those obtained from the finite-size scaling of the ground state. Our findings indicate that the spectral total rule is more accurate than the ground state total rule. This is because the spectral total rule relies on the fractional quantum number of the magnetoroton quasiparticle, whereas the ground state total rule is based on the Fermi level of the composite fermion system. Consequently, the spectral total rule is more suitable for describing quasiparticle excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems. This research significantly advances our understanding of quasiparticle excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems. It also provides a new perspective on the spectral total rule, which is essential for studying spectral properties in various quantum Hall systems. This paper addresses the challenge of understanding natural language goals within goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. We focus on the issue of referential ambiguity, which occurs when a sentence contains multiple nouns that could potentially refer to the object specified in the goal. To manage this during training, we introduce a method that trains agents on sentences containing unresolvable referential ambiguity. Our approach demonstrates that resolving this ambiguity is essential for achieving high performance on complex tasks, particularly in 3D environments. Furthermore, our results indicate that achieving robustness against such ambiguity requires specific capabilities in both the agent and the language model. Finally, we show that utilizing a training corpus with controlled referential ambiguity enables evaluation using metrics that directly measure performance in resolving this ambiguity. Finally, we demonstrate that creating a corpus with controlled referential ambiguity allows for evaluation using metrics that directly measure performance on this challenge. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexpampanini/RefAmbiguityRL. To our knowledge, this represents the first attempt to mitigate referential ambiguity in language-driven reinforcement learning. A key contribution of this work is highlighting a critical limitation in current reinforcement learning benchmarks, which typically rely on simple sentences with a single subject noun. We believe that developing benchmarks capable of testing the robustness of reinforcement learning agents to more complex sentences is a significant future research direction. This study employs scanning tunneling microscopy and density functional theory to examine the structural conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 when adsorbed on an Ni(111) substrate modified with an h-BN overlayer. Temperature variations induce distinct structural changes in the molecule: at room temperature, the N-type conformation predominates, whereas cooling to 4.2 K shifts the equilibrium toward the E-type conformation. These findings are corroborated by theoretical calculations, which indicate that the E-type conformation is more stable than the N-type. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the energy barrier for transitioning between these two states is sufficiently low to permit such a conversion. Finally, the second harmonic resonance Raman spectra of C80 derivatives confirm the ability to distinguish between the E-type and N-type conformations. Consequently, this research demonstrates the feasibility of manipulating the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 through thermal control. These results offer a foundation for future applications in molecular switches and memory devices. Additionally, the thermal regulation of molecular conformation on a semiconductor surface holds significant promise for advancing two-dimensional molecular electronics. Finally, the study underscores the critical role of the substrate in the stability and conformation of functionalized C80 derivatives. The experimental data indicate that the interaction between Sc2TbN@C80 and the h-BN layer is stronger than that between C80 and a bare Ni(111) surface, a conclusion supported by density functional theory calculations. This finding highlights the necessity of utilizing suitable substrates, such as h-BN, to achieve the optimal performance of C80 derivatives in molecular electronic applications. Keywords: Sc2TbN@C80, C80, conformation, substrate, harmonic resonance Raman spectroscopy.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly expanding field that facilitates communication between devices and the cloud, enabling access to a vast array of generated data. However, transmitting this data securely is a significant challenge, particularly for low-power devices with limited resources. Current high-security protocols are often too complex and energy-intensive, making them unsuitable for deployment on constrained hardware. This paper introduces a novel Compact Encryption (CE) protocol designed specifically for IoT devices. CE is implemented using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM), which is renowned for its robust security. We developed two versions of CE: one for low-power devices utilizing a 128-bit key and another for slightly more powerful devices using a 256-bit key. Both variants are lightweight, featuring a minimal footprint and low energy consumption. We created custom C implementations of CE and compared them against AES-GCM. Additionally, we developed a protocol stack based on CE and benchmarked it against the widely used MQTT protocol over TCP/IP. Performance was evaluated using the Message Throughput Rate (TMR) and Latency (TL). Testing was conducted on an embedded Linux system running an Ubuntu 16.04 environment with a Raspberry Pi 3. Results demonstrate that CE offers superior performance compared to MQTT, with both versions outperforming the standard AES-GCM implementation. CE is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Compact-Encryption. The source code for the protocol stack can be found at https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Compact-Encryption/tree/master/CE_Protocol_Stack. Our findings indicate that CE is ideal for low-power IoT devices, with the CE128 version being especially well-suited for the most resource-limited hardware. Furthermore, CE is versatile and can be integrated into various communication protocols, including MQTT, CoAP, and HTTP. Given its security and efficiency, CE represents a viable alternative to the Resource Public Key Cryptosystem (RPKC) for secure IoT communication. Future work will focus on deploying CE on diverse low-power devices and integrating it with multiple communication protocols. This study confirms that CE is highly effective for low-power IoT applications. We introduce a novel centrality metric grounded in the comparison of actual distances within a network against the path length inferred from node embeddings in a low-dimensional Euclidean space. By defining centrality through a metric distance, we maintain consistency with current geometric network theories. Specifically, we link to three excesses resulting from triangle inequalities: the stretch factor, embedding error, and inequality excess. Furthermore, we provide multiple applications across various network types, revealing a resolution-dependent, multi-scale behavior. Our findings indicate strong correlations with multiple existing centrality measures, highlighting a trade-off between computational efficiency and result accuracy. Our results suggest that Gromov Centrality offers a flexible, multi-scale approach for identifying key nodes in heterogeneous networks, with a focus on geometric and network structural properties. We introduce a generalized gravitation model grounded in an extended version of the Laplace equation for gravitational potential, applied within the cylindrical coordinate system. By utilizing this generalized potential, we derive the corresponding generalized field equation. Subsequently, we construct a non-relativistic framework to solve these generalized field equations under the assumption of azimuthal symmetry. This model successfully reproduces the observed rotation curves of galaxies and the gravitational redshift of spectral lines from the 30 Doradus galaxy. Furthermore, it accurately predicts the dynamics of planetary orbits, the precession of the perihelion of Mercury, and the gravitational redshift of spectral lines in the Sun. These results demonstrate that our model offers a viable alternative to the prevailing relativistic theories of gravitation. In our upcoming publications, we will extend this model into a relativistic regime. Our approach relies on the observation that both the field equations and the Laplace equation employed are fundamentally linear, facilitating the superposition of solutions. This characteristic suggests that the principle of superposition can be applied to the general solution of our model's field equations, thereby enabling a straightforward derivation of the dynamics for any specified matter distribution. Consequently, the computational complexity of our model is significantly lower than that of Einstein's general relativity. Additionally, we show that the field equations of our model can be transformed into those of the weak field approximation of general relativity, thereby establishing a direct link between our model and Einstein's theory. Our ultimate objective is to develop a framework that extends the linear nature of both the generalized Laplace equation and the generalized field equation into the strong field region, thereby creating a model that remains linear across all regimes of gravitational field strength. This linearity would facilitate the superposition of solutions, allowing us to describe the dynamics of any matter distribution. We anticipate that this model will facilitate a fundamental shift in the understanding of gravitation. Specifically, our method will enable the calculation of the gravitational field for any matter distribution, thereby overcoming the substantial complexity inherent in solving the non-linear Einstein equations. This capability is expected to lead to a more profound comprehension of gravitational phenomena. In this initial paper, we will solve the generalized field equations for a homogeneous cylinder of finite length, which possesses a finite surface mass density. This solution will yield the generalized potential, the generalized field strength, and the equations of motion for this configuration. Through this approach, we aim to elucidate the behavior of the generalized potential and field strength within the interior and exterior regions of the cylinder, as well as the dynamics of a particle situated on the cylinder

We introduce a new algorithmic framework designed to compute low treewidth tree decompositions for large graphs, provided their large-scale geometry is known. This approach relies on decomposing the graph into small, uniform components that can be arranged according to a specific domain map. We demonstrate that for any parameter $k$, metrics that are Euclidean in nature (such as those found in manifolds) or hyperbolic (such as those on surfaces) possess a constant-width decomposition relative to $k$. Consequently, these treewidths can be computed in linear time. Furthermore, we establish that minor-free graphs constructed from uniform embeddings under domain maps also admit low treewidth tree decompositions, which are efficiently identifiable, thereby creating new algorithmic opportunities for this graph class. We extend these findings to weighted metrics, which are relevant to random graph theory, and discuss how our results enable the efficient computation of various graph problems, including minimum spanning trees and maximum independent sets. The primary technical advancement is a novel, optimal bound on the local treewidth of major metric spaces, which is derived from domain maps and the properties of uniform embeddings. This bound is subsequently applied to derive efficient tree approximations for these metric spaces. Our work also yields new algorithmic outcomes, such as the first quasi-linear time algorithm for computing a constant-width decomposition based on hyperbolic domain maps. Additionally, we prove that minor-free graphs with a limited number of edges can be decomposed into a constant-width class identified via domain maps, and we show that uniform embeddings of Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces result in minor-free metrics with linearly bounded growth. Finally, we present an algorithm that, given a domain map, generates a sequence of graph approximations with controlled treewidth in quasi-linear time, where the treewidth is a function of the domain map's width. This sequence converges to the original graph, and the distance between successive approximations is bounded by a function of the prior level's treewidth. We establish that, under broad conditions, locally Lipschitz continuous discrete-time dynamical systems defined on convex compact sets exhibit specific behaviors near their fixed points: when linearized at these points, they converge globally within their domain of definition or diverge globally, regardless of initial conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for locally strongly monotone operators, the globally converging fixed points necessarily attract all initial conditions. These findings apply to a wide array of scenarios, notably encompassing all $C^1$ operators, and offer novel insights into the underlying mechanisms of the global convergence theorem for strongly monotone continuous-time dynamical systems and their associated Euler discretizations. Additionally, we identify key properties of the prevalent behavior in this context, characterized by the fact that the system either converges globally or diverges globally, with at most a measure-zero subset of initial conditions leading to non-trivial $\omega$-limit sets. We also examine the case of multivalued operators and explore examples of multivalley operator examples. Finally, we highlight that the multivalley example illustrates the optimality of our results, as multivalley functions are the sole class of functions where the convexity of the domain is essential for achieving this optimal behavior. In such instances, the prevalent behavior manifests as total divergence or convergence to a single fixed point, with at most a measure-zero set of initial conditions converging to the midpoint between the two fixed points. These outcomes are derived through the application of the recent theory of $\alpha$-nonexpansive mappings. Moreover, the prevalent behavior observed in globally converging fixed points of strongly monotone discrete-time dynamical systems represents a new phenomenon, as it contrasts with the behavior of their continuous-time analogues, where a set of initial conditions with positive measure can converge to the midpoint between two fixed points. We further establish the prevalence of this behavior for multivalued strongly monotone operators, thereby extending the phenomenon to this domain. Finally, we present several open problems concerning the application of our results to the study of discrete-time variational inequalities. Additionally, it remains unclear whether the prevalent behavior of strongly monotone operators extends to the case of weakly monotone operators, given that the latter is not applicable to multivalued operators. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) represent a promising method for executing noisy quantum computations, with their primary challenge being the identification of an optimal parameter set from an extensive search space. This work introduces the qubit-excitation-based adaptive solver (QEBAS), a technique designed to enhance VQA performance. By utilizing the excitation operator to define a qubit-based figure of merit, QEBAS optimizes parameters to minimize this metric, thereby reducing the total excitations within the variational state. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to the variational quantum eigensolver, showing an optimal parameter count reduction of up to 90% on hardware simulators. Additionally, a rigorous theoretical analysis is provided, and the method is tested on trapped-ion hardware, where it achieves a significant decrease in total excitations. These findings indicate that QEBAS can substantially shrink VQA parameter spaces, facilitating the execution of more complex algorithms on near-term quantum devices. The method is publicly accessible at https://github.com/quantumlib/QEBAS. Keywords: Variational quantum algorithm, quantum eigensolver, qubit excitation, near-term quantum device. We introduce a hybrid neural network architecture designed for dimensionality reduction and learning that integrates a deep generative model with a deterministic one. This generative component functions as a variational prior, enabling the concatenation of its maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates with deterministic low-dimensional representations. Furthermore, we show that the architecture can learn complex representations, such as those for CIFAR-10 and CUB-200, within a single network. The recent NANOGrav 15-year dataset hints at a common low-frequency background signal, while Hubble constant estimates derived from Cepheid-based Type Ia supernovae and Cosmic Microwave Background data remain significantly discordant. This study proposes that both discrepancies can be addressed by a gravitationally amplified gravitational-wave backdrop (GWB) with a stiff equation of state, which would also influence the Hubble constant. In the early universe, cosmic inflation could have generated such a backdrop, potentially explaining the low-frequency signal detected by NANOGrav. Although this GWB would decay rapidly at later times, a low-frequency component could be reinstated by a stiff fluid, such as dark radiation, which would subsequently decay into leptons. The persistence of dark radiation in the post-inflationary era would cause the Hubble constant to decline at a rate of $H \propto t^{-2/3}$, thereby resolving the Hubble tension. Furthermore, the decay of stiff dark radiation into leptons could account for the observed diffuse gamma-ray background. This framework offers a unified explanation for the low-frequency NANOGrav signal, the Hubble tension, and the diffuse gamma-ray background. Additionally, the high-frequency tail of this backdrop could be observable by current LIGO-Virgo detectors, with future observations expected to constrain its parameter space. The model also predicts a stochastic gravitational-wave signal at MHz frequencies, potentially detectable by the proposed AEDGE mission. Finally, the framework suggests a mechanism for dark matter production through dark radiation decay, with a viable parameter space that aligns with NANOGrav limits and remains consistent with LIGO-Virgo data. Consequently, the NANOGrav 15-year data could provide the first evidence of gravitational wave amplification in the early universe. This scenario is also applicable to other low-frequency GWB models, such as those involving supermassive black hole binaries or cosmic strings. In these cases, the low-frequency signal in NANOGrav data could serve as a probe for dark radiation, while the high-frequency tail could be investigated using LIGO-Virgo observations. Ultimately, the NANOGrav 15-year data could offer the first confirmation of dark radiation and a novel method for probing the early universe. Furthermore, the model predicts a GWB signal in the AEDGE frequency range, with NANOGrav data potentially providing the first evidence of dark radiation. This represents the first comprehensive analysis of the connections between NANOGrav data, dark radiation, and the Hubble tension

This study presents the first interferometric observations of a comet using a sub-millimeter telescope, specifically targeting the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array's Atacama Compact Array (ACA). We conducted a spectral survey of Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a geocentric distance of 2.0 AU, detecting emission from CS, HCN, and HNC. These detections mark the first identification of CS in a comet and represent some of the most sensitive HCN and HNC observations to date. The observed CS abundance is notably high, suggesting a parent molecule lifetime exceeding 100 years. This implies that the comet's nucleus may contain a reservoir of CS formed over extended periods, potentially within the early solar nebula or during previous perihelion passages. Additionally, we observed a diffuse CS source near the comet's position, which we attribute to the diffuse interstellar medium. This source exhibits a column density of $1.1 \pm 0.1 \times 10^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$ and a kinetic temperature of 2.0 $\pm$ 0.1 K. Our analysis indicates that CS is likely destroyed in the comet's nucleus, with a lifetime of less than 10 years, a finding that contrasts with recent studies reporting longer lifetimes. These results offer valuable insights for future observations of cometary nuclei and CS reservoirs in the interstellar medium. The ACA's ability to resolve the spatial distribution of cometary molecules and distinguish them from diffuse interstellar sources makes it an ideal instrument for such investigations. This paper examines the Tsallis holographic dark energy (THE) model, treating it as an essence model. The holographic energy density is defined as $\rho_{DE} = \frac{1}{R^{2(1+\lambda)}}C_{\lambda}$, incorporating a non-extensive statistical characteristic. To ensure consistency with the first law of thermodynamics, an complex form of THE is introduced. The cosmic evolution equations are then solved to determine the equation of state (EoS) parameter, $w_{DE}$. Furthermore, the stability of the model is assessed by calculating the squared speed of sound, $c_{s}^{2}$. Finally, the paper analyzes the temporal variations of the EoS and $c_{s}^{2}$ within a specific subclass of Tsallis models. Results indicate that the universe transitions from a contraction phase to an accelerated one, with the model remaining stable throughout. Additionally, the temporal behavior of the model is influenced by the parameter $\lambda$. Finally, the model is applied to two specific cases to derive their respective solutions. These applications demonstrate that the universe expands at an increasing rate, and the temporal variations of the model depend on the parameters $n$ and $\lambda$. Finally, the model fits the observational data well. This study extends the holographic dark energy model by introducing non-extensivity, thereby enriching its physical content. Furthermore, the essence model employed is novel, and the complex form of THE represents a new approach. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in numerous real-world scenarios. Although robust solvers exist for linear and non-linear variants, the combined category has garnered significant recent interest. This study addresses MO-MINLPs by relaxing integer constraints to generate a preliminary solution set, subsequently refining these solutions through the NSGA-II algorithm to eliminate redundancy and enhance efficiency. This refined set serves as the starting point for the BARON solver to identify the Pareto-optimal set. Extensive testing was conducted to evaluate the proposed method's performance. Results indicate that for moderate-sized problems, the method significantly reduces solution times while maintaining solution quality comparable to top-tier solvers. However, for large-scale problems, the approach remains less competitive. Additionally, the methodology demonstrates the ability to handle discontinuities in solution sets, a capability often lacking in leading solvers. The paper concludes with a detailed discussion of the method's strengths and limitations. The source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/AmirHosseinHajializadeh/NSGAII4MINLP. Keywords: Multi-objective optimization, Non-convex optimization, Mixed-integer optimization, Non-linear optimization, Pareto set.

Within a regular differential category, such as the global points of a smooth manifold model, we demonstrate that any connected Lie groupoid $\mathcal{G} \rightrightarrows M$ is internally linked and naturally equivalent to the monoid groupoid formed by the formal tangent germs of formal curves in $M$. This equivalence relies on the existence of a unique curve connecting the base of any two formal points. Furthermore, we establish that the integration functor mapping Lie groupoids to formal curves in monoid groupoids is both full and faithful when applied to connected Lie groupoids, as it preserves all essential categorical and differential structures. Additionally, we show that every connected Lie groupoid is locally integrable; its universal Lie groupoid is the bundle of its formal curves, and the exponential map for any such groupoid is the projection map of its formal curve bundle. Finally, we prove that the exponential map of a connected Lie groupoid is proper if and only if the groupoid is proper. These findings extend and refine earlier results by adapting categorical language and utilizing synthetic differential geometry. Specifically, we generalize the work of Moerdijk and Treibergs on manifold monoids and the findings of Bunge, Marmolejo, and Treibergs on exponential maps for Lie groupoids. A key advantage of this synthetic approach is that it circumvents the need for exponential maps on the groupoid's structure monoids. Additionally, we provide a categorical characterization of proper connected Lie groupoids in terms of the compactness of the space of formal curves in their associated Lie groupoid. As a consequence, we derive a characterization of proper connected Lie groups based on the compactness of the space of formal paths. Finally, we characterize exponential maps for Lie functors between connected Lie groupoids using the universal property of the exponential functor. These results are derived through elementary and direct arguments based on the differential category structure of Lie groupoids and the characterization of exponential maps via formal curves. We also present a characterization of exponential maps using a universal property involving Cartesian products and apply this characterization to establish the equivalence between connected Lie groupoids and formal curve groupoids in the context of any differential category. Finally, we characterize the functor that assigns to each connected Lie groupoid the monoid of its formal curves using a universal property involving Cartesian products. These characterizations facilitate the construction of the exponential map and the exponential map bundle for any connected Lie groupoid using universal properties. Moreover, the definition of the exponential map bundle is shown to be independent of the chosen monoid structure

Secure and effective communication is fundamental to the success of scientific endeavors. As researchers increasingly rely on cloud computing and distributed data services, new challenges emerge regarding how to securely facilitate data exchange while maintaining compatibility with existing software ecosystems. Traditional security methods, such as SSL encryption, are insufficient for large-scale data transfers, and the application of fine-grained access controls within cloud environments often hinders scientific progress. This paper introduces a novel model for secure biomedical data sharing, leveraging the capabilities of Cyberinfrastructure Gateways. We demonstrate the implementation of this model using the DataONE global biodiversity data network, which has recently expanded to include clinical and genomics data. Through a proof-of-concept clinical trial, we evaluate the model's efficacy and performance. Our results indicate that this approach offers a practical solution for facilitating secure data sharing among researchers. Furthermore, we discuss the potential implications of this model for enhancing research productivity and proposing strategies for its future adoption. Finally, we outline key challenges that must be addressed to realize the full potential of this data sharing model. Aspect-based sentiment analysis enables the extraction of emotion-intense aspects and their respective opinions from user feedback, a capability that is vital for enterprises to gauge product and service quality. While prior research has leveraged large-scale corpora to derive contextual embeddings for emotion-specific tasks, this paper introduces a novel pre-training approach that explicitly learns the relationship between aspects and emotions. By incorporating a new task that predicts the supervision signal of an aspect's emotional label, the proposed method utilizes a supervised contrastive loss to generate distinct representations for different emotion categories. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields superior representation learning compared to models relying solely on supervised classification losses, achieving state-of-the-art performance in identifying emotional aspects and emotions within benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the paper offers valuable insights into the value of the proposed supervised contrastive loss and the characteristics of the new prediction task. Given the growing availability of large-scale data, this research holds significant potential for driving future advancements in the field. Finally, the authors release the newly created Large-scale Emotion-specific Data (LED) to further facilitate future research. LED comprises 1.1 million sentences annotated with both emotional aspect labels and the emotions governing those aspects, sourced from publicly available online reviews. This study addresses the identification and estimation of mediation parameters within a causal model featuring a binary exposure, a binary mediator, and an outcome that may be continuous or categorical. A key contribution is demonstrating that the probability of the joint exposure and mediator states can be explicitly recovered from data collected via case-control sampling, even when the study design involves sampling cases and a control group without matching. Our proofs rely on a large body of set-theoretic inequalities. We illustrate the practical application of this identification result using data from a case-control study of ovarian cancer. Additionally, we introduce a g-computation estimator that leverages the specific structure of case-control data, which is shown to be consistent under weak assumptions. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that this estimator remains valid even in scenarios where a naive application of g-computation would fail. Finally, we discuss the extension of these results to models with multiple mediators. The core findings are supported by proofs and supplementary materials available at https://github.com/alexisgustafson/MediationCaseControl. Furthermore, we have developed a software package named `mediationCaseControl` to facilitate mediation analysis with case-control sampling; its installation instructions and documentation can be found at https://alexisgustafson.github.io/MediationCaseControl/. The package is available at https://github.com/alexisgustafson/MediationCaseControl. We conclude that the strategies and software presented here are applicable to case-control studies investigating the impact of a risk factor on a disease-related outcome. Our approach offers a valuable alternative to methods requiring the selection of appropriate sampling fractions, a topic that has seen recent renewed interest. Specifically, we show that standardizing analysis to account for sampling fractions does not introduce bias, provided the fraction applies uniformly to all strata of a specific covariate. This finding broadens the scope of an earlier method designed for continuous outcomes to accommodate binary mediators. Furthermore, our work extends previous research limited to models with a single mediator to allow for the simultaneous analysis of multiple mediators. Finally, we demonstrate that the sampling fraction needed to be specified for each stratum of the confounder does not need to be known exactly; it suffices to know that it is constant across the strata, even if the specific stratum identities are unknown. This represents a significant practical advantage, as it eliminates the need to measure sampling fractions for every stratum of a confounder, a requirement that often leads to bias in mediation analyses. In summary, we argue that mediation analysis can be conducted without bias

This study examines a secure, multi-user radio over Gaussian channel utilizing a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) to distribute reflection coefficients across the surface. The system operates under the constraint of a total transmit power, which is further restricted by an information leakage threshold to ensure security. Additionally, the analysis incorporates first-order circular complex hardware impairments. The primary objective is to design an RIS-assisted robust transmission strategy that minimizes the mean square error (MSE) for legitimate users while adhering to these hardware and security limitations. To achieve this, the problem is modeled as a Multi-Objective Non-Linear Programming (MONLP) challenge. Since this optimization involves jointly optimizing discrete RIS reflection coefficients and continuous transmission strategies, it is inherently non-convex. To address this, the MONLP is decomposed into two distinct sub-problems: one for optimizing RIS discrete coefficients and another for transmitting optimized signals. The paper introduces a novel algorithm to solve both sub-problems, thereby generating a robust transmission design capable of meeting both security and hardware impairment requirements. Simulation results confirm that the proposed approach effectively reduces the MSE experienced by legitimate users. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that accounting for hardware impairments is essential to prevent excessive power allocation to legitimate users, which could compromise the privacy of eavesdroppers. Finally, the RIS configuration is shown to significantly enhance the performance of legitimate users. This improvement is particularly pronounced when RIS is deployed, as it enables the derivation of a non-convex optimization problem, allowing the algorithm to identify optimal solutions that would be unattainable without RIS. Ultimately, the RIS configuration is demonstrated to substantially reduce the noise introduced by hardware impairments, thereby significantly improving the performance of legitimate users. Drawing from human cognitive science, this paper introduces a new AI framework called "Executive Function" (EF). Functioning as a meta-layer above standard machine learning algorithms, EF employs a contrastive value strategy to re-sample and re-label perceptual experiences through hindsight summarization. By utilizing hindsight, EF can retrospectively reconstruct an agent's value function from its raw perceptual data. The strategy's core insight is that an agent's true "mind" is not defined by any single perception, but rather by the long-term memory of its perceptual history, which is summarized by the agent's past actions. Consequently, the agent's value function is derived from the contrastive value of its action history relative to its perceptual history. We provide a formal definition of the contrastive value strategy and demonstrate its effectiveness in solving fundamental reinforcement learning challenges, including the exploration-exploitation dilemma, the credit assignment problem, and the frame of reference issue. Furthermore, we show that the contrastive value strategy can be integrated into existing methods like Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Deep Q-Network (DQN) to form new, effective solutions. Finally, we present experimental results that validate the efficacy of the EF approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/Executive-Function.

The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) has provided the first in-situ measurements of solar breeze energy flux within the inner heliosphere. These PSP findings align with existing in-situ observations from the Helios, Ulysses, and Wind missions, as well as remote sensing data from the SOHO/LASCO coronagraph and the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI). By utilizing the Parker Solar Probe, we have established the energy flux of solar breeze plasma as a critical parameter for modeling and forecasting solar wind conditions. This capability is essential for understanding the energy and momentum transfer between the Sun and the heliosphere, as well as for developing space weather forecasts. We define the concept of a noncommutive countable principal bundle generated by a group action on a C*-algebra. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, this construction encompasses both classical countable principal bundles with a compact base space as well as certain significant examples found in noncommutative geometry. Furthermore, we establish that countable principal bundles arise naturally from noncommutative G-actions on C*-algebras, provided the group G satisfies specific properties. Finally, assuming the group G acts amenably on the C*-algebra, we prove that every noncommutative principal bundle is isomorphic to an associated bundle formed from a noncommutative space and the discrete group G. Additionally, we explore applications within the context of quantum groups. In this application, we demonstrate the existence of noncommutative principal bundles derived from discrete quantum groups that do not possess the Hilbert-Schmidt property. This finding stands in contrast to the case where discrete groups are considered, as discrete principal bundles over finite-dimensional compact manifolds always admit a bundle metric. We also investigate the relationship between this phenomenon and the property of being a weakly amenable discrete group. Finally, we establish that any principal bundle arising from a strongly amenable quantum group admits a bundle metric. This conclusion follows from the fact that strongly amenable quantum groups are both amenable and have discrete groups that are Hilbert-Schmidt. Consequently, principal bundles over finite-dimensional compact manifolds generated by strongly amenable quantum groups always admit a bundle metric. In the appendix, we provide examples of principal bundles that admit a bundle metric even when the quantum group is not strongly amenable. These examples include the quantum flag manifolds associated with Kac algebras and certain quantum groups arising from free probability theory. The construction method utilized here is also applicable to other types of principal bundles. We illustrate this by examining bundles over quantum groups derived from free actions of free discrete quantum groups on quantum spaces. In these instances, the principal bundles admit a bundle metric despite the quantum groups not being strongly amenable. This is because their discrete groups are still Hilbert-Schmidt. This approach also enables the construction of principal bundles over quantum groups that are both amenable and Hilbert-Schmidt, which are not strongly amenable. The bundles over these examples admit a bundle metric, consistent with the general principle that principal bundles over such groups admit a bundle metric. This work presents a simplified analysis of R-parity violation within a Two-Rotors Model featuring two levels of granularity. The model's efficacy is demonstrated through the reproduction of the "adverse" event observed at LHCb, which involved a final state comprising a B meson and 40 X events. By treating R-parity violation as an "adverse" occurrence, we establish upper limits on the associated coupling constants using LHC data. Furthermore, we propose experimental signatures that could distinguish between the Standard Model and R-parity violating scenarios. These signatures include the production of B mesons in the initial state alongside 40 X events in the final state, as well as B mesons generated in association with a single X event. Such signatures are anticipated to provide the most sensitive constraints on R-parity violating couplings. Finally, we suggest that the LHCb experiment should conduct a search for these signals, as they would yield the tightest bounds on the R-parity violating coupling constant. Additionally, the LHCb collaboration could investigate these signatures in future runs, potentially uncovering new physics beyond the Standard Model. This would be particularly significant if the resulting limits surpass those derived from the LHCb analysis of the adverse event. Ultimately, the ultimate test of this model will depend on the observation of these signatures and the decay of B mesons into X final states. Such findings would necessitate the construction of a detector capable of identifying X events and conducting a thorough investigation of B meson decays. We hope that the LHC experiments will soon be able to explore these possibilities. This document serves as a proof of concept, and we welcome further discussion and collaboration. This study introduces an innovative cell-mean-based neural network algorithm designed to address various hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations. Unlike traditional finite difference or finite element methods that rely on discretizing the domain into cells, this approach discretizes the input and output layers of a neural network. By applying the finite difference method to the cellular structure within the hidden layer, the partial differential equation is transformed into a system of ordinary differential equations. The proposed cell-mean-based neural network effectively solves these ordinary differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the resulting cell-mean-based neural network solutions achieve high accuracy for both hyperbolic and parabolic equations. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of this cell-mean-based neural network solution is comparable to that of finite difference or finite element methods. Finally, the paper concludes with an analysis of the proposed method's advantages and its potential future applications. **Keywords:** hyperbolic equations, parabolic equations, neural networks, cell mean. **AMS Subject Classification:** 65M20, 65L20, 68T07. **Citation:** J. The ALICE experiment's primary mandate is to investigate the conditions of the early universe and the characteristics of heavy-ion collisions. To ensure its scientific goals remain aligned with the accelerator programme following the LHC's upgrade and across the subsequent three years of Run 3, an ALICE Future Technical Proposal (TFP) was developed. This proposal examines the physics potential of ALICE across all LHC phases and details the necessary upgrades to sustain the experiment's core objectives. It also addresses the funding requirements and implementation strategies for these upgrades. This text serves as a non-technical introduction to the content of the TFP.

The Unruh effect predicts that uniformly accelerated detectors perceive the Minkowski vacuum as a thermal bath, a phenomenon closely linked to the separation of future and past light cones, which creates unbalanced entanglement between these regions. This study demonstrates that a Unruh detector undergoing accelerated motion exhibits the Berry phase induced by this unbalanced entanglement. Consequently, the Berry phase offers a novel method for Unruh detectors to identify the thermalization of the Minkowski vacuum field, providing an alternative to the change in internal state density typically used by standard Rindler observers. Furthermore, we show that the Unruh effect can be detected through Berry phase interference even when the detector's acceleration is finite. These findings suggest that the unbalanced entanglement of future and past light cones can be probed through the coherent rotation of the internal state density of uniformly accelerated observers. Finally, we explore a potential experimental realization of this proposal by simulating the Unruh effect within a circuit QED setup. This work advances the understanding of how future and past light cones shape the entanglement structure of the Minkowski vacuum and suggests a new pathway for observing entanglement-induced effects in the accelerated Unruh scenario. Additionally, it underscores the significance of Berry phase interference as a tool for investigating fundamental physics. Our research thus establishes a new framework for exploring the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity. Finally, we propose that this proposal can be tested using existing circuit QED technology. Simulating the Unruh effect has significant implications for quantum information science, as it enables the investigation of entanglement harvesting and manipulation, thereby deepening our understanding of entanglement and its relationship with spacetime geometry. Furthermore, this approach may offer a pathway to experimentally verify phenomena such as entanglement teleportation. These findings offer a promising avenue for uncovering new physics and deepening our comprehension of the universe. The proposed method for detecting the Unruh effect could also contribute to advancing our understanding of black hole physics. By demonstrating that uniformly accelerated observers can detect horizon entanglement through Berry phase interference, this proposal may offer a means to explore the information paradox associated with black holes. Ultimately, this research may help unravel some of the most profound mysteries of the universe. The findings presented in this proposal may also inspire a new field of research dedicated to experimentally verifying fundamental concepts in quantum physics. By suggesting a method for detecting the Unruh effect through Berry phase interference, this proposal may pave the way for future experimental tests of quantum phenomena. We introduce the Multilingual Incident Extraction (MEE) dataset, which supports English, German, and Spanish. We outline the data collection methodology and demonstrate its utility through the construction of the MEE dataset. Finally, we explore the application challenges associated with incident mention extraction in multilingual environments. The concept of a vector bundle extends to any globally defined complex. This paper investigates the relationship between the characteristic forms of a complex and its direct image components. We establish that, given a holomorphic vector bundle on a complex manifold equipped with a Hermitian metric, the form embodies the curvature properties inherent in the bundle. Applying this finding, we generalize the Grauert-Riemenschneider and Gilkey push-forward formulae to the context of global bundles. Furthermore, we examine the positivity and mixed type nature of these forms, demonstrating that bundle curvature is not invariably positive, even when the underlying complex is a bundle of positive type. Consequently, we derive a novel criterion for the positivity of these forms based on the cohomology of the bundle. Our approach begins with a review of the definition and fundamental properties of global vector bundles, followed by an exploration of their connections to cohomology theories. We then present the definition and primary results concerning the characteristic forms of such bundles, concluding with the development of the theory for their direct images. This framework yields generalizations of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch, Grauert-Riemenschneider, and Gilkey theorems, alongside new insights into the positivity of characteristic forms. The study is grounded in the work of various mathematicians, including Grothendieck, Groisser, Riemenschneider, Gilkey, and others. Additionally, we introduce the concept of a "bundle of positive type," which serves as a global analogue to the positivity of differential forms and may hold independent significance. Finally, we outline several open problems and conjectures regarding the positivity of characteristic forms for global vector bundles. The hard spectral state of Cyg X-1 is characterized by a dominant steeper power-law component in its X-ray spectrum, which is hypothesized to originate from the accretion flow surrounding the black hole. This study investigates the extent to which material from the stellar breeze influences the emission from the black hole's accretion flow during this state. We conducted a joint analysis of NuSTAR and XMM-NTT X-ray data from observation ID 4001040101, utilizing the reprocessing spectra of the primary source. Our results indicate that the soft X-ray component derived from the stellar breeze significantly impacts the high-energy emission from the hard state, as evidenced by the correlation between the soft and hard X-ray fluxes. Furthermore, we identified a lag between the soft and hard X-rays, with the soft band preceding the hard band by approximately 1.5 ms. These findings suggest that the stellar breeze contributes to both the spectral and timing properties of Cyg X-1's hard state. Additionally, we observed a strong correlation between the soft and hard X-ray count rates, supporting the hypothesis that the breeze feeds the inner accretion flow around the black hole. Finally, we propose that the observed soft-hard lag arises from the time required for breeze matter to travel from the outer regions of the accretion flow to the inner regions. These results offer new insights into the physics governing the hard state of Cyg X-1. Future observations of the source are necessary to further explore these phenomena. We investigate the impact of an ether-like, dimension-5 operator, scaled by a mass, on the Standard Model. Originally formulated as a non-abelian dimension-5 derivative term for a non-zero background vector, this operator is equivalent at tree-level to a dimension-5 mass term for the same background vector. This study details how to determine the parameters of this operator from both the mass of the background vector and its coupling to the Standard Model. Furthermore, we analyze how this operator modifies the thermal masses of electroweak gauge bosons and fermions, as well as the spectrum of electroweak gauge bosons at finite temperature. Our findings indicate that the background vector mixes with the electroweak gauge bosons, a phenomenon that could be observed in thermal environments. Additionally, we show that fermions acquire non-zero Majorana masses at finite temperature, a result that could be detected in thermal environments. Finally, we demonstrate that this operator does not affect the electroweak phase transition. These effects on particle masses and the particle spectrum within hot environments offer a distinct signature for this operator, potentially observable in the early universe. We outline the necessary experimental observables to constrain this class of operators. Finally, we briefly discuss the possible quantum mechanical origin of this ether-like operator. These conclusions are based on a previous study by the same authors, which focused on the cosmological implications of this ether-like term. See arXiv:1909.00072 [astro-ph.CO]. In the present work, we limit our scope to finite-temperature effects, specifically regarding thermal masses, spectra, and phase transitions. We omit detailed quantum mechanical derivations, as our focus remains on phenomenology. Instead, we provide the necessary references for readers interested in the quantum mechanical origins of this class of operators. We introduce a joint model that simultaneously parses syntax and semantics, leveraging the shared dependencies within an extended abstract syntactic structure. This unified approach enhances learning efficiency for both syntactic and semantic tasks while ensuring complete and consistent structural coverage. Experimental results show that our method matches current state-of-the-art performance in individual syntax and semantics tasks and achieves a new state-of-the-art in combined syntax and semantics parsing. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model is resilient to variations in underlying syntactic labeling standards. Finally, we illustrate how storing intermediate results enables efficient joint inference across multiple tasks and corpora. This study investigates how the postmerger dynamics of a binary neutron star system are influenced by an accretion disk and its inherent magnetic fields. We perform three-dimensional general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, utilizing neutrino cooling models for the merger phase derived from our prior neutrino-spherically symmetric simulations. Our results indicate that the resulting magnetized accretion disk generates significant outflows, which are primarily driven by neutrino cooling. These post-merger outflows substantially impact the dynamical evolution of the system, including the contraction of the merger remnant and the growth of the magnetized disk. Furthermore, they significantly alter the final gravitational-wave signal by redistributing energy and angular momentum, thereby modifying the characteristics of the outflows. Consequently, these outflows could be detected as a bright electromagnetic counterpart to the merger. This underscores the critical role of accretion disks in shaping both the gravitational and electromagnetic signatures of neutron star mergers. Finally, we outline the implications of these findings for future multimessenger astrophysics research. This study examines the characteristics of massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) exhibiting prominent tidal features, such as giant elliptical galaxies with bright tidal tails, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). We identified 1,000 ETGs displaying flux features exceeding 10% of the total flux within 100 kpc, a sample roughly 100 times larger than previous investigations. By analyzing their color, luminosity, and surface brightness distributions, we confirmed that these galaxies are intrinsically similar to standard massive ETGs. Furthermore, we quantified the flux fractions of their tidal structures and found a correlation between these fractions and the surface-to-edge brightness ratios, indicating that HSC-SSP-prompted mergers are more likely to produce visible tidal tails. Finally, we estimated the merger rates for these "giant" ETGs by comparing their tidal feature properties with numerical simulations. The results suggest that significant tidal features are typically generated by mergers with a mass ratio greater than 1:3, though this threshold may be lower for galaxies with very large tidal flux fractions. Additionally, the current star formation rate in these giant ETGs is approximately 10% of that observed in star-forming galaxies at the same redshift, implying that mergers do not substantially trigger star formation in these systems. These findings align with existing literature and provide a quantitative assessment of the tidal features of ETGs. The HSC-SSP dataset offers a unique opportunity to investigate the tidal features of galaxies across a broad mass range, thereby enhancing our understanding of the relationship between prominent tidal structures and galaxy evolution. The identified sample of "giant" ETGs is expected to be valuable for analyzing the impact of mergers on early-type galaxies. The data and analysis code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/taiki-ito/ETG_tidal_features. This research is part of the "Toward a New Era of Galaxy Evolution" initiative. This study introduces a novel gravitational framework, the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), which extends the well-established General Theory of Relativity (GTR) to accommodate azimuthal symmetry. Unlike GTR, which relies on spherical symmetry, ASTG provides a new mathematical description for the bipolar outflows observed in young stellar objects and active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Within this model, angular momentum creates a centrifugal force that generates a negative gravitational field, resulting in a repellent gravitational effect. This mechanism offers a fresh perspective on understanding outflow generation. Furthermore, ASTG predicts that gravitational force diminishes with the cube of the distance, a distinct departure from the inverse-square law of Newtonian gravity. The paper concludes by outlining the specific applications of ASTG regarding these stellar and galactic outflows. We conducted a thorough search for optical counterparts to four well-defined fast radio burst (FRB) bursts from the repeating FRB 20201124A, which occurred between November 2020 and May 2022. This source, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud at a distance of 50 kpc, was previously identified with a radio flare at 1.4 GHz exhibiting a luminosity of $L_{1.4\rm GHz} \sim 10^{30}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and a duration of $\sim 1$ ms. Our analysis yielded no optical detection, establishing an upper limit of $L_{V} \lesssim 10^{31}$ erg s$^{-1}$ for emission at 5500 \AA. This limit is approximately 10 times lower than the highest optical luminosity observed in FRBs to date. Additionally, we investigated for delayed optical emission within 100 seconds of the radio bursts and found no evidence of such activity. These findings suggest that FRBs in the Galactic Center may be intrinsically distinct from those in the Magellanic Clouds, and they underscore the necessity of future observations with greater sensitivity and broader wavelength coverage. Furthermore, our results indicate that the compact binary scenario for FRB 20201124A is less favored, as it would likely produce an optical signal comparable to the radio emission. Finally, we propose that the radio emission from FRB 20201124A may be partially or wholly attributed to the plasma sheath surrounding a neutron star. Future studies should prioritize simultaneous and high-cadence radio and optical monitoring of FRBs to better constrain their emission mechanisms. We have created free open-source software designed to address the design, optimization, and enhancement of high-power laser systems, incorporating features for generating human-readable reports. Additionally, this tool is utilized in educational settings to teach laser physics concepts, including the design and optimization of high-power laser systems. Furthermore, we present a methodology for modeling and reverse-engineering laser systems based on their spectral characteristics. The value of our software is demonstrated through the enhancement of a commercial laser-by-number system and the reconstruction of a Yb-doped laser spectrum, which were experimentally validated. The software is freely accessible at https://lasersim.io.
