Experimental data from the National Ignition Facility (NIF) indicate that heat transport during the stagnation phase of direct-drive implosion is approximately $10^3$ times greater than the classical value. This study examines the implications of such high thermal transport on the stagnation phase of direct-drive impactions, focusing on the interaction between turbulence and thermal disturbances. We demonstrate that at the dissipation scale, fluid turbulence reaches a state of equipartition with thermal disturbances, resulting in a total energy flux that is roughly $10^3$ times larger than the classical Spitzer-Härm flux. This finding aligns with the NIF experimental observations. Furthermore, we show that the energy flux at the dissipation scale is $10^3$ times higher than the energy flux at the integral scale, implying that the majority of energy is transferred from fluid turbulence to thermal disturbances before reaching the dissipation scale. Finally, the $10^3$-fold enhancement in heat flux significantly impacts the stagnation phase of direct-drive impactions, leading to an early collapse of the stagnation point and a reduction in achieved compression. These conclusions are supported by the hydrodynamic code FLASH. Our research suggests that the primary mechanism driving anomalous heat flux is the transfer of energy from fluid turbulence to thermal disturbances at the dissipation scale. Additionally, we propose a new theoretical framework for the implosion process that incorporates this enhanced heat flux. Our analysis indicates that, under the assumption of anomalous heat flux, the stagnation phase is limited by the Rayleigh-Taylor (RT) instability growth rate, whereas in the classical regime, it is limited by the RT saturation time. Consequently, the implosion process is shortened by a factor of $10^3$ when anomalous heat flux is considered. These conclusions are derived from the radiation hydrodynamic code. Our findings highlight the critical role of the interaction between fluid turbulence and thermal disturbances in high-energy density physics. Specifically, this interaction governs the implosion process, determining both the attainable compression and the resulting hotspot temperature. Our theoretical framework offers a comprehensive description of the implosion process, accounting for both heat flux and the energy spectrum across all scales. This work underscores the necessity of accurately modeling the interaction between fluid turbulence and thermal disturbances in radiation hydrodynamic simulations. We conducted an extensive numerical investigation of laser heating within a liquid medium to elucidate the origin of intricate diffraction patterns observed in experiments. This approach enabled us to pinpoint errors in prior numerical models and to examine how heat diffusion and the specific heat capacity of the liquid influence the resulting thermal profiles. Our simulations demonstrate that laser heating generates a highly non-linear thermal profile, characterized by elevated temperatures at the focal volume's center and a sharp gradient extending outward. We further show that both heat diffusion and the liquid's specific heat capacity are essential for accurately modeling the complex experimental diffraction patterns. Finally, we developed a compact analytical model of the thermal profile that relies on the laser's focal volume size and the maximum temperature attained at the center. This model is robust and effectively captures the physics underlying the liquid's thermal response to laser deposition. Collectively, these findings establish a solid foundation for future research into laser heating in liquids. Specifically, they facilitate the design of experiments utilizing self-diffraction, such as those measuring liquid viscosity or investigating phase transitions. More broadly, this work offers a framework for numerically modeling laser heating in any liquid by incorporating its specific physical properties. The model is also applicable to other systems where laser heating induces a non-linear temperature profile, including gas plumes generated by nanosecond laser ablation of solids. Designers frequently resolve issues through discussion, yet capturing the relevant information within this dialogue remains a significant challenge. This study addresses the problem of identifying information relevant to decisions during design discussions. We propose a new task, conclusion stability, which evaluates the consistency of information extraction across various natural language models. To our knowledge, this is the first work to analyze how model generalization is affected by changes in both context and features. Our experiments reveal that while models can effectively extract relevant sentences, they struggle to generalize when sentence structures vary. Furthermore, we demonstrate that models are more likely to select conclusions containing technical details rather than those reflecting the designer's intent. Finally, we validate the utility of this task by showing that it assists in generalizing models trained on a specific corpus to design discussion data from another company. This study investigates the production of top and bottom quark partners at the LHC and the future FCC-hh through the associated production of $t\bar b$, $\bar t b$, $t\bar t b$, and $\bar t \bar t \bar b$ events. The analysis covers both associated production via vector boson fusion and Drell-Yan mechanisms. Employing a one-loop order calculation for the relevant scalar form factors, we examine how variations in the spectrum influence the cross sections. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the cross sections of events with opposite and like-sign charges for top and bottom quark partners. These findings may assist in the future discovery of such particles. Additionally, we provide numerical results for these events at the future 100 TeV FCC-hh collider. Finally, we generate rapidity distributions for these processes and compare them with those of the standard model top and bottom quarks. These results may aid in the future identification of vector boson fusion events involving top and bottom quark partners. Our findings are presented in the form of JETSET cards for event generation using the MiNNLOPS framework. All relevant files, including numerical results, are available at https://github.com/Ankit-12345/TopBottomQuarkPartners. Knowledge Base (KB) Machine Translation enables users to translate query results from one knowledge base to another using SPARQL. However, existing systems fail to address a common issue where entities, such as country names, appear multiple times within a single knowledge base, leading to redundant query construction and evaluation efforts. This paper introduces the Copy System, a novel mechanism designed to handle repeated elements within knowledge bases. The system operates by copying these repeated elements during query construction and storing them in knowledge base registers to prevent duplication during translation. Experimental results demonstrate that the Copy System successfully reduces the number of queries translated from one knowledge base to another. The system is available at https://github.com/ailab-tau/sparql-kbmtl-copy-system. Furthermore, the authors have released a dataset of knowledge bases containing repeated elements for testing purposes, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ailab-tau/sparql-kbmtl-copy-system/blob/master/datasets/test_kb.jsonld. This dataset was utilized in the evaluation experiments, which show a 40% reduction in translated queries compared to baseline methods. The Copy System represents a foundational approach for translating repeated knowledge base elements, a capability that will be integrated into the CBT tool for translating knowledge base-coupled natural language questions. This integration is anticipated to be completed by the end of 2021. Additionally, the authors intend to explore applying the Copy System to other translation challenges, such as translating partial queries or handling translation errors. Future research will investigate the use of knowledge base registers to resolve translation errors and improve the accuracy of partial query translations. The Copy System serves as a foundational solution for translating repeated knowledge base elements and is expected to enhance the efficiency of SPARQL-KBMT tools. The authors anticipate that this tool will contribute to the broader community's ability to more efficiently translate and interact with knowledge bases. The authors extend their deepest gratitude to the community for its unwavering support and collaboration. We introduce a new approach for assessing scientific research that relies solely on venue-based metrics, offering a viable alternative to citation-counting methods. This solution employs a two-tier classification system to categorize venues and utilizes their reputations for venue-specific paper evaluation. We demonstrate that our approach effectively mitigates the well-documented biases inherent in citation metrics. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness of this method across three distinct domains, illustrate its simplicity regarding implementation and analysis, and compare its performance against two established citation metrics. Ultimately, we show that the proposed solution outperforms these existing metrics in minimizing venue and author-specific biases while enhancing accuracy. Additionally, we explore the limitations of venue-based metrics, including their susceptibility to temporal dynamics and their potential discouragement of authors from targeting specific venues. Finally, we outline directions for future research to further refine venue-based evaluation and address these constraints. The code and data required to replicate our findings are accessible at https://github.com/venuemetrics/venue_analytics. This study examines the validation of neural networks employed in control systems. We first outline the two primary approaches: absolute validation, which establishes a guaranteed performance bound independent of the specific neural network implementation, and relative validation, which determines a performance bound based on the characteristics of the implementation. Subsequently, we detail the resources necessary for each approach and analyze the properties of neural network validation for both. Finally, we connect these control-focused validation methods to their counterparts in machine learning. Regarding absolute validation, we concentrate on the lattice structure of the neural network parameter space; this allows us to define the essential information required for validation and to bound the approximation errors of the neural network functions. The required parameter for this analysis is a measure of the variation within the function class, which can be computed via volume-based and function-based metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to extend absolute validation from static to dynamic scenarios. In the case of relative validation, we focus on standard deep learning techniques, including cross-validation and generalization error estimation. We conclude by highlighting the challenges and open questions associated with validating neural networks in control applications. Specifically, we address the need for a unified framework that harmonizes absolute and relative validation methods and examines the trade-off between computational cost and accuracy in validation procedures. Overall, this survey aims to offer a comprehensive reference for researchers entering the field of neural network validation for control. By bridging machine learning and control theory, we identify significant opportunities for future advancements in both domains. Additionally, the insights gained may assist practitioners in making more informed decisions when implementing neural networks for control purposes. Given that this field is in its nascent stage, we anticipate it will evolve into a substantial and vibrant research area in the coming years. Object detection and segmentation are critical yet challenging tasks in computer vision, where identifying all instances of a target class within an image constitutes the goal. Current leading methods rely on a greedy approach: individual predictions are made for image regions, and a metric like Intersection over Union (IoU) determines if regions overlap; if they do, they are grouped together. However, this process is non-deterministic and lacks a clear categorical hierarchy. To address these limitations, we propose a hierarchical grouping framework that simultaneously recovers a categorical hierarchy and optimizes grouping based on predicted scores and IoU. We also present a novel loss function that encourages the simultaneous optimization of detection performance and hierarchical recovery. Experimental results demonstrate that this end-to-end framework effectively reconstructs a categorical hierarchy, outperforms existing methods, and achieves competitive performance on standard benchmarks. Furthermore, we validate the framework's efficacy on tasks beyond standard detection and segmentation, specifically addressing hierarchical classification and zero-shot learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb22/FunHGr. Our results indicate that the hierarchical grouping framework is versatile and can recover categorical hierarchies across various domains. Additionally, we explore applications in hierarchical object detection and image classification, showing that our approach can recover unknown hierarchies and outperform current state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in few-shot learning, where it outperforms existing few-shot hierarchical classifiers. Overall, our work shows that the proposed hierarchical grouping framework is versatile and capable of recovering categorical hierarchies in diverse scenarios. By viewing these problems through a unified lens, we show that our framework can recover categorical hierarchies and outperform current state-of-the-art solutions. Streaming recovery of data missing in motion (DMIM) is vital for numerous applications, including surveillance, traffic monitoring, and video conferencing. This paper introduces a new method called patch tracking-based streaming tensor loop completion (PTSLC) for visually recovering DMIM. The proposed framework first estimates the optical flow between two consecutive frames to visually link and extract corresponding patches from large-scale tensors. Subsequently, these extracted patches are reconstructed using loop completion, which iteratively applies a least squares solver and a patch selection operator. The process continues until the estimated patches converge. We evaluated the PTSLC framework across various datasets with different sampling rates and block sizes, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Furthermore, the PTSLC framework achieves superior performance with significantly lower computational costs compared to existing solutions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1997/patch-tensor-loop-completion. This paper establishes that, for every finite traditional complex reflection group, the Nichols algebras of certain rank 2 types are finite-dimensional, with the exception of 14 specific cases. These exceptions correspond precisely to the list of 14 non-real finite traditional complex reflection groups. Additionally, the finite-dimensional Nichols algebras associated with the remaining rank 2 types are explicitly described. Notably, the algebra linked to a finite traditional group of rank 2 is finite-dimensional if and only if the group itself is real. This result provides an alternative proof of a theorem by Shepler and Zhang. Furthermore, the finite dimensionality of Nichols algebras for all rank 2 diagonal types was previously demonstrated by He, Zhang, and Li. The methods employed in this work are expected to be applicable in proving diagonal type exceptions for higher ranks. Finally, the text addresses an inquiry raised by He and Zhang. This study presents direct numerical simulations of two-dimensional, randomly forced and damped nonlinear Schrödinger equations across various turbulence regimes. Our primary objective is to gather evidence supporting the Zakharov-Kolmogorov (ZK) spectrum within turbulent wave turbulence regimes characterized by weak, quasi-resonant, and strong interactions. We demonstrate that energy spectra in the inertial range align with the ZK spectrum $E(k)\sim\kappa^{-2/3}$ under weak and quasi-resonant conditions. Furthermore, our findings indicate that even when quasi-resonance is violated, the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum persists. These results corroborate the predictions of the resonant and non-resonant wave kinetic equations concerning the zonal flow damped wave turbulence regime. Additionally, we show that the inverse cascade of enstrophy, previously hypothesized by Nazarenko, is also observed in these simulations. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the strong wave turbulence regime. This paper introduces a novel iterative approach to solving the maximum weight independent set problem on undirected graphs with non-negative vertex weights. Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ and a non-negative weight function $w:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, the goal is to identify an independent set $I\subseteq V$ that maximizes $\sum_{v\in I}w(v)$. We define a series of polynomial-time algorithms, denoted $\mathcal{A}^k(G,V,E,w)$ for $k\geq 0$, which iteratively normalize the graph and weights. Each algorithm $\mathcal{A}^k$ maps the input to an output graph $G'=(V',E')$ and a weight function $w':V'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, followed by an independent set $I'$ in $G'$ that is optimal for the transformed weights. The process is designed so that a maximum weight independent set in the output can be directly translated back to one in the original graph. The algorithm $\mathcal{A}^0$ serves as the base case. Subsequent algorithms $\mathcal{A}^k$ for $k\geq 1$ are constructed by applying $\mathcal{A}^{k-1}$ to the graph and weights produced by $\mathcal{A}^k$. This framework enables the application of any single $\mathcal{A}^k$ to find the desired set. We demonstrate that for any $k\geq 0$, the algorithm $\mathcal{A}^k$ achieves an approximation ratio of $\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{2^k}}$. Furthermore, we establish that the sequence of ratios is strictly increasing and converges to $\frac{1}{e-1}$, which is the optimal ratio achievable by any polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. Additionally, we provide a polynomial-time method to verify the termination of the $\mathcal{A}^k$ algorithm for any fixed $k\geq 0$. Finally, we examine the algorithm's behavior when the graph is restricted to specific graph classes. For each class, we analyze the infinite sequence of graphs generated by repeatedly applying the algorithms. This study investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of electrically modulated monolayer graphene. Specifically, we examine the temperature-dependent electrical and thermal conductivities within the low-temperature regime, focusing on scenarios where the chemical potential is comparable to or lower than the thermal energy ($T$). Our findings indicate that, under these conditions, the temperature dependence of thermal conductivity is primarily determined by the external perpendicular electric field ($E_{\perp}$). Additionally, we observe that low-temperature thermal conductivity can exceed that of bulk graphite by an order of magnitude when the applied electric field is weak. These results are expected to be valuable for modeling low-temperature devices utilizing electrically tunable two-dimensional materials. Finally, our theoretical predictions align closely with existing experimental data. \textbf{Keywords}: Graphene; Thermal conductivity; Low temperature. This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the binary system CR Draconis, conducted using the LOFAR Low-Band (L-band) and Wideband (W-band) receivers. We monitored the system over a period of 1.5 years, detecting maser-like emission at 115 MHz from the active M dwarf CR Draconis A. This event exhibited a duration of 1.5 hours and a peak flux density of 100 mJy, with a circular polarization of 90%. The maser emission was detected only during the active phase of CR Draconis A, which is part of a close binary pair with an M3.5V primary and an M3.5V secondary. The observed characteristics of the emission align with the electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) model, suggesting that the maser is triggered by magnetic reconnection within the star's magnetosphere. This is the second confirmed ECM emission event from a close binary system, following the 2018 detection on the M3.5V component of TV Virginis. The identification of these two ECM events from close binaries supports the hypothesis that such events are more common in binary systems than in single stars. Additionally, the detection of maser-like emission from CR Draconis A at 115 MHz indicates that this star is capable of producing long-duration, high-intensity ECM events at low frequencies. This finding is significant for upcoming low-frequency radio observatories, such as the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) and the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) Low-Band, which are expected to observe numerous such events. Furthermore, the discovery of high-intensity, long-duration ECM emission from close binaries may facilitate the investigation of magnetic reconnection processes in magnetospheres and the study of stellar magnetic fields. Finally, the detection of ECM emission from two different active M dwarses suggests that these stars may be valuable targets for studying the differences between solar and stellar magnetospheres. The Articulated Neural Visualization (ANR) network addresses a critical yet underexplored challenge in neural radiance field rendering: virtual avatar rendering with a novel camera using an articulated model trained from a single-image multi-viewpose sequence. Unlike standard neural rendering, this process requires a trained model to be retrained for every new camera position, a step that is computationally expensive and often unnecessary since the original geometry is already visible. ANR efficiently resolves this by integrating model articulation into neural rendering, enabling the use of a single-image model across multiple camera views. The method consists of two core components: (1) a neural radiance field conditioned by skeleton joints to generate novel camera views for a specific pose, and (2) an image warping strategy that aggregates warped images from various poses to produce a single-view synthesis for a new camera position under articulation. Additionally, the approach incorporates a novel single-shot skeleton tracking technique to enhance rendering performance. As a neural radiance field method, ANR avoids the need for dense 3D surface sampling, thereby reducing memory requirements and accelerating rendering. Furthermore, the framework is flexible enough to be adapted for other neural rendering tasks involving articulated objects. Experimental results demonstrate that ANR accelerates rendering by approximately 100 times compared to traditional neural rendering methods while maintaining comparable image quality. Humans and machines typically interpret visual information in distinct ways. This study investigates how these differences manifest specifically under severe image transformations. We constructed a diverse collection of semantic image pairs linked by severe transforms, which participants annotated for object class and scene class. Our findings indicate that human and machine responses diverge significantly, particularly in object class predictions. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the distributions of image features perceived by humans and machines differ markedly. These results offer valuable insights for enhancing machine performance through the integration of human knowledge and for leveraging machine capabilities to inform human decision-making. Large pre-trained language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, frequently surpassing task-specific models even with limited data. While few-shot learning has been extensively researched, this study investigates zero-shot learning using pre-trained models. We observe that standard natural language inference datasets, when adapted for zero-shot tasks, yield suboptimal results due to dataset bias. To address this, we introduce a straightforward yet effective method that involves meta-training on custom prompt assemblies. Additionally, we examine the impact of tweaking prompt assemblies and explore potential dataset biases. Our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot tasks across the SuperGLUE and CLEVER benchmarks. Furthermore, results indicate that meta-tuning on prompt assemblies derived from a specific dataset introduces corresponding biases, highlighting the need for more diverse prompt assemblies during the meta-training phase. Finally, we highlight the promising potential of zero-shot learning as a means to evaluate language models. Our findings indicate that the $Z_3$-invariant NMSSM is incompatible with LHC limits; however, relaxing these constraints allows for a first-order EPT and a WIMP dark matter candidate with masses between 100 GeV and 200 GeV, yielding a P-wave annihilation cross-section of approximately $1.5 \times 10^{-26}~\mathrm{cm}^3/\mathrm{s}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a high-frequency signal from the LISA mission could potentially be observed, offering a promising avenue for confirming the EPT scenario. We introduce a new diagnostic tool designed to evaluate the robustness of submillimeter redshifts, offering an alternative to the traditional Sudoku method. This instrument relies on the statistical likelihood that a galaxy's emission originates from the peaks of the spectral energy distribution (SED) at specific (1.6 mm, 1.25 mm, and 0.85 mm) wavelengths. By utilizing a comprehensive catalog of publicly available spectral data from over 1000 galaxies, we established this new metric and benchmarked its effectiveness against the Sudoku technique. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is more effective at distinguishing reliable redshifts from unreliable ones, particularly for sources detected at wavelengths longer than 1.1 mm. This improvement stems from the method's dependence on the two most reliable redshift anchors, whereas Sudoku requires three. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method's superiority persists even when using shallower spectral data. Consequently, this tool is particularly advantageous for galaxies with redshifts greater than z = 3, where the separation between (1.6 mm, 1.25 mm, and 0.85 mm) wavelengths is most pronounced. We provide a user-friendly Python package to facilitate the application of this method to individual galaxies or samples. The package is accessible at https://github.com/brunomachado/highz-sudoku. We anticipate that this approach will assist in identifying the most robust redshifts for the (sub)millimeter galaxies discovered by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). We present lattice simulations of $N_f=3$ Abelian-Higgs theory featuring an $SU(3)$ gauge group. By analyzing the behavior of the deconfinement-deconfinement shift, string tension, and Polyakov loop, we track the system's transition from a deconfined to a confined state as the string coefficient $g_{\lambda}$ increases. Our findings indicate that confinement emerges at $g_{\lambda}\simeq 0.15$, a result that aligns with predictions derived from a recent effective model. Furthermore, we observe that the string tension exhibits a step-like increase across the phase transition, whereas the deconfinement-deconfinement shift remains largely constant, maintaining a value near one throughout the transition. These results suggest that the confinement mechanism within the effective model is robust and extends to higher dimensions. Finally, our simulations demonstrate that the string test, a key feature of the effective model, remains valid for $N_f=3$. These observations collectively support the conclusion that the low-energy dynamics of this multi-Abelian Higgs theory are well-described by the $SU(3)$ E-C model. Additionally, we show that the string coefficient $g_{\lambda}$ serves as a valuable order parameter for identifying the confinement-deconfinement phase transition. In the deconfined phase, the system displays a first-order transition characterized by a string test, while in the confined phase, it undergoes a crossover. The transition point is marked by a sharp peak in the kurtosis of the string correlation function. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the string coefficient in both the confined and deconfined regimes. Specifically, we demonstrate that the convergence of the string test toward the large $N$ limit is significantly accelerated in the confined phase. This observation is attributed to the presence of a non-trivial fixed point in the renormalization group flow of the string coefficient. We also explore the broader implications of this phenomenon for other physical theories. Our results confirm that the string test is not merely a qualitative indicator of the effective string description but also provides a precise quantitative tool for investigating the string dynamics of multi-Abelian Higgs theories. This approach is particularly valuable for probing the string dynamics of theories that exhibit a string description only within a limited parameter range. In this context, the string test enables the identification of the precise boundary between the string and non-string regimes. The present study investigates the magnetic structure of Cr$_2$Al via first-principles calculations. We identify a novel in-plane antiferromagnetic arrangement where Cr atoms occupy alternating ferromagnetic layers that are coupled through antiferromagnetic interactions. This configuration is determined to be the ground state, with an energy significantly lower than that of previously reported magnetic structures. The strength of the antiferromagnetic coupling between adjacent layers is quantified by the exchange interaction J$_{c}$, which is derived from the energy differences between various magnetic configurations. Furthermore, the exchange interactions J$_{11}$ and J$_{12}$ corresponding to the nearest and next-to-nearest neighbors are found to be antiferromagnetic. The values of these exchange interactions are analyzed in relation to the orbital and spin structures. Finally, the study examines the potential for Cr$_2$Al to exhibit exchange bias effects. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the magnetic properties of Cr$_2$Al, a material with a Curie temperature of approximately 300 K. Additionally, the results may assist in the design of materials capable of displaying the exchange bias phenomenon. This is achieved by utilizing the calculated exchange interactions to select appropriate Cr$_2$Al-based materials and by engineering their interfaces with other magnetic materials. Such combinations are essential for applications including magnetic sensors, permanent magnets, and spin valves. To further support these applications, the study provides guidance on tailoring the magnetic properties of Cr$_2$Al through strain engineering and chemical substitution. Specifically, we demonstrate that applying tensile strain and substituting Cr atoms with Co atoms can enhance the exchange bias of the material. These conclusions are based on calculations of the exchange interactions resulting from the proposed modifications. Ultimately, this research establishes a robust foundation for the future development of Cr$_2$Al as a functional material for spintronic devices. This is evidenced by the detailed analysis of its intrinsic magnetic properties and the identification of viable strategies for modifying them. The findings presented herein are expected to contribute significantly to the ongoing efforts to advance the understanding and utilization of Cr$_2$Al in cutting-edge technological applications. These efforts are underscored by the material's high Curie temperature and its potential for exhibiting exchange bias, both of which are critical factors in the pursuit of next-generation magnetic technologies. The conclusions drawn from this study are expected to have a profound impact on the field of materials science, particularly in the context of developing advanced functional materials for use in magnetic sensors, permanent magnets, and spin valves. Semantic grounding involves determining the natural language meanings of symbols within an artificial language. Recent progress in training semantic interpreters has been driven by methods like Minerva, which utilize training data featuring extended vocabularies to foster generalization through compositionality. However, these approaches necessitate substantial data to establish a baseline vocabulary of size $k$ before interpreting the remaining vocabulary $G \setminus k$. We introduce Data Efficient Semantic Grounding (DESG), a method that interprets the full vocabulary of an artificial language with minimal training data by leveraging established connections between the symbol sets of two related artificial languages and their corresponding natural languages. DESG achieves this through a two-stage process: first, training an semantic interpreter on a restricted subset of the artificial language using limited human-annotated data, and second, employing an induction algorithm to train a mapping between the two symbolic systems. We demonstrate that DESG successfully grounds an entire vocabulary of $10^4$ unique symbols using only a few hundred annotated examples. Furthermore, we show that this approach can interpret the complete vocabulary of a second artificial language, which shares a large portion of its symbol set with the first, without requiring any additional annotated data. Finally, we validate the generalization capabilities of DESG by testing its performance on various unseen natural languages. These results highlight the potential of DESG to significantly reduce the data requirements for semantic grounding tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepMind/semantic_grounding. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is designed to investigate the internal structure of protons and nuclei, as well as the interactions between them. Powered by an energy level of 10–20 GeV per beam, the collider is expected to commence operations in the 2030s. To achieve this, the EIC will utilize a compact, high-luminosity, and precision detector capable of measuring charged particles, photons, and neutrons across an energy spectrum of 0.1 GeV to 100 GeV. The Forward Silicon Tracker (FST) serves as the detector's innermost sub-system, designed to trace and identify charged particles with high precision. This paper outlines the current design and development status of the FST, which relies on unstructured silicon sensors featuring an active region of 100 um and a thin overall thickness of 200 um. These sensors were fabricated using the reverse vertical epitaxial growth (rvege) method. Additionally, the findings from a recent test beam experiment are presented. Results indicate that the FST's spatial resolution and radiation tolerance meet the EIC's requirements. Furthermore, the readout system has been successfully tested and is currently being integrated into the detector. The EIC is anticipated to be the premier facility for exploring the proton's structure and the interactions between protons. Consequently, the FST is expected to deliver crucial data for understanding the internal structure of protons and the production mechanisms of various particles. This study examines the variability in the continuum luminosity of the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LAGN) PDS 457, utilizing a dataset of 118 observations collected between 2014 and 2016. The data were gathered using the Swift UVOT at 2530 and 2600 Angstroms, alongside the Swift XRT and the Keck 2.0 m telescope at 5500 Angstroms. The observed flux variations span three orders of magnitude in the ultraviolet and 1.5 orders of magnitude at 5500 Angstroms. We demonstrate that the ultraviolet (UV) and optical (O) fluxes correlate positively, with a time lag of approximately 1000 seconds where O follows UV. These fluctuations are attributed to the accretion disk, as the UV emission is thought to originate from the disk's outer regions while optical emission arises from the inner regions. The observed fluctuations align with the gravitational time scale of the accretion disk at these radii. Furthermore, we analyze the light curves to identify and remove a single, significant eruption event. This event, detected simultaneously in both UV and O bands, occurred on 2016-01-10 and is believed to stem from a sudden increase in accretion rate onto the disk. Finally, we compare the variability characteristics of PDS 457 with those of other LAGNs. Ultimately, we conclude that PDS 457 exhibits both accretion disk fluctuations and occasional eruptions, a behavior shared by other LAGNs. This suggests that low accretion rates do not preclude fluctuations and eruptions, and that the mechanisms driving them may be similar across different accretion rates. Consequently, the low accretion rate alone cannot explain the differences in spectral energy distribution (SED) and variability between high and low accretion rate AGNs. The primary distinction between LAGNs and HMSAGNs likely lies in the accretion disk's temperature, thickness, and the prevalence of magnetic fields. Future research should focus on investigating these factors and their impact on AGN accretion disk physics. Additionally, we recommend that future observations of PDS 457 employ instruments with higher time resolution to better understand the accretion disk structure and dynamics in this system. The magnetic architecture of rapidly rotating stars is governed by a dynamo mechanism driven by the interaction between their rotation and internal convection. This study investigates the magnetic field morphology of HD58260, a rapidly rotating star exhibiting a dipole field strength of approximately 1.5 kG, by analyzing spectropolarimetric data collected with ESPaDOnS. The dataset comprises 1,000 spectra, with 100 selected around the maximum of emission for the emission-sensitive lines Fe i 6166 Å and Fe i 6172 Å. By applying the Inverse Differential Doppler Effect (IDDE), we derived longitudinal and radial magnetic field components as functions of stellar latitude. The data reveal a negative slope in the longitudinal magnetic field, a signature of a dipolar field, with a magnitude of roughly 3 kG krad$^{-1}$. This value aligns with expectations for a dipolar field and matches findings from other rapidly rotating stars. Furthermore, the radial magnetic field displays a positive slope, indicating a poloidal component. The derived radial field strength reaches approximately 2.5 kG krad$^{-1}$, suggesting a strong poloidal contribution. These results support the conclusion that the dynamo generating magnetic fields in rapidly rotating stars produces a dipolar field with a significant quadrupolar component. Additionally, the paper discusses the potential impact of the sloped magnetic field on the interpretation of longitudinal magnetic field measurements obtained via the Zeeman-Doppler Imaging technique. Finally, the observed radial magnetic field slope is interpreted as a manifestation of the dynamo mechanism, which establishes a correlation between the longitudinal magnetic field slope and the rotational shear rate. This insight may aid in refining future models of stellar magnetic fields. We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in NGC 5253, a low-metallicity galaxy ($Z$=0.3$Z_\odot$) known for its intense star formation. These observations reveal a compact, bright emission region centered on the galaxy's nuclear starburst, with a size of approximately 1.5 kpc and a peak intensity of 1.5 Jy/beam. By comparing these findings with observations of H2 and CO lines, we demonstrate that the H30$\alpha$ line serves as a robust tracer of star formation in low-metallicity galaxies. Furthermore, we compare the H30$\alpha$ line luminosity with the far-ultraviolet (FUV) continuum, utilizing the H30$\alpha$/H41$\alpha$ ratio to derive the ionization parameter. This ratio yields an ionization parameter of $\log(U)$=-3.1$\pm$0.1, which aligns with values derived from the [OIII]5007/[OIII]4959 ratio. Finally, we conclude that the H30$\alpha$ line is an effective tool for determining the star formation rate in low-metallicity galaxies. The derived star formation rate density for NGC 5253 is $\dot{M}_*$=1.3$\pm$0.1 M$_\odot$/yr, consistent with earlier estimates based on H$\alpha$ and UV data. This study introduces a new kernel-based method for estimating conditional expectation operators (CEOs) within Hilbert spaces, advancing beyond traditional regression techniques that rely on parametric or semi-parametric assumptions. By utilizing data-dependent bandwidths, the proposed operator estimator achieves optimal minimax rates for pointwise mean squared error (MSE) and demonstrates near-optimal rates for operator norm MSE. Furthermore, it establishes a novel optimal rate for strong convergence. These findings are supported by finite sample asymptotics, specifically weak convergence for the operator and its eigenvalues/eigenvectors, along with almost sure convergence for the operator. Applications include testing for orthogonality and independence, as well as eigenvalue consistency. The methodology is validated through extensive simulations and an empirical analysis of the German Credit dataset. The paper also features an R package, `Ceost`, which implements the estimator and provides code for all theoretical proofs alongside the examples. This study addresses the creation of reduced-order Luenberger-type observers for a standard SIR epidemic model. The infection dynamics are governed by a system of nonlinear ordinary differential equations, with parameters representing biological and social factors that are difficult to quantify precisely. Consequently, the analysis focuses on designing a reduced-order observer dependent only on two measurable outputs: the count of infected individuals and the total population size. It is demonstrated that, under the assumption of a constant natural death rate, these reduced-order observer errors converge exponentially to zero, ensuring a precise estimate of the susceptible compartment. This approach offers a straightforward alternative to full-order observers, which require numerical integration. Additionally, a numerical simulation validates the proposed method's effectiveness. Finally, the study explores applications in model reduction and model identification, which are essential for analyzing epidemic dynamics. Integrating time into knowledge graph embeddings has recently become a focal point of research, driven by the need to capture the timing and evolution of facts. This paper investigates the application of time to link prediction within knowledge graphs, specifically temporal knowledge graphs (KGs). We introduce a novel approach that leverages pre-trained static knowledge graph embeddings to forecast both future and potential historical facts in temporal knowledge graphs. Our evaluation, conducted on two benchmark temporal KG datasets, shows that utilizing static models enhances link prediction performance, achieving an mAP score of 0.4330. Furthermore, factor graph analysis indicates that embedding time into static models is sub-optimal, suggesting that re-parameterizing time relative to the current moment is a more effective strategy. Finally, we explore leveraging static model performance for relation extraction in temporal knowledge graphs, yielding promising results with an F1 score of 0.8122. Overall, this work underscores the value of static models in temporal KGs and establishes a robust baseline for future research in temporal knowledge graph embedding evaluation. Although Federated Learning (FL) is primarily designed to safeguard data privacy, it also facilitates distributed computation, enabling FL models to be trained across distributed devices equipped with Central Processing Units (CPUs). Given the computational constraints of these devices, training FL models nonlinearly and asynchronously while honoring device CPU resources becomes crucial for achieving practical performance. This paper introduces Resource-Conscious Asynchronous Online Federated Learning (RC-AOL), a novel framework that enhances computational efficiency in CPU-bound devices. RC-AOL employs an asynchronous online learning mechanism to adapt to dynamic computing resources and incorporates a CPU-aware update rule to optimize the utilization of recruited devices. Simulation results based on nonlinear regression demonstrate that RC-AOL surpasses existing asynchronous online FL methods in CPU-intensive environments by improving computational efficiency and reducing training time. Furthermore, comparisons with synchronous online FL methods reveal that, in CPU-intensive settings, RC-AOL matches the performance of synchronous methods while achieving superior computational efficiency and shorter training durations. Consequently, RC-AOL is particularly suited for CPU-intensive applications within resource-limited FL environments. Simulations were conducted using MATLAB. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Resource-Conscious-Asynchronous-Online-Federated-Learning. The study evaluates the light absorption capabilities of silicon films ranging from bulk material to monolayers by integrating them with three-dimensional photonic band gap (3D-PBG) structures as back reflectors. These 3D-PBGs function as mirrors at wavelengths within their photonic band gap, thereby enhancing total absorption across the entire solar spectrum. By strategically positioning absorbers at specific locations inside the 3D-PBG, the system supports strong standing waves at the surface, leading to superior light trapping. The analysis utilizes the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method to calculate absorption rates. Results indicate that the absorption of thin silicon films (such as those 1 µm thick) approaches bulk-level efficiency, while the absorption of ultrathin films (such as silicon monolayers) reaches approximately 90%. These findings hold significant promise for the development of ultra-thin solar cells and other light-absorbing devices. This paper introduces multiple asymptotic approaches for deriving solutions to the exponential equation, with primary focus on the full asymptotic series and Stokes phenomenon within the subfactorial context. We employ Riemann surface analysis to examine the asymptotic behavior of these solutions and investigate the associated branching phenomena. Furthermore, we outline various approximation methods for exponential equations, compare them against known asymptotic solutions of the Gamma function, and present solution sets for the equations $x^x = a$ and $x!\ = \ a$. Finally, we offer several applications, including the solution of Weber's equation, to demonstrate the utility of these techniques. Notably, the full asymptotic series for the subfactorial exhibits an algebraic singularity at zero, a feature absent in the Riemann zeta function, and its description of the Stokes phenomenon relies on Bessel functions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the asymptotic solutions of the exponential equation possess a branching point at zero, whereas those of the Gamma function do not display such behavior. The appendix provides a comprehensive list of all special functions encountered in this study. We present extender models for highly transitive permutation groups in dimension $n$ where the action on the $n$ points corresponds to a cover of the group's cosets on a subgroup of index 2. This approach recovers the extender model originally developed by the authors for dimension-2 transposition groups, which correspond covers of braid groups, and also applies to the original formulation of Mathieu groups as groups of coset actions. Specifically, a closed formula for the size of the extender is derived for the little octahedral group, while upper bounds for the size are established for the little icosahedral group and the two small Mathieu groups. The extender size for the little octahedral group is calculated to be 20 times the size of the center of the free braid group. Furthermore, this result supports the conjecture that the extender size for any dimension-2 transposition group is the product of the group size and the size of the center of the corresponding braid group. Finally, the paper concludes with several open problems. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a new antiferromagnet, GdInO$_3$, which features a centered honeycomb lattice composed of slabs separated by van der Waals gaps. Using bulk magnetization and specific heat measurements across a temperature range of 0.35–300 K under external fields up to 9 T, the research establishes the antiferromagnetic nature of the material and details its magnetic phase diagram. The data indicates that GdInO$_3$ exhibits anisotropic magnetic behavior, with easy magnetization aligned along the $c$ axis. Additionally, a sharp peak in specific heat at 2.85 K corresponds to the Néel temperature, while a kink at 2.5 K in both magnetic responses signals a metamagnetic transition. This transition is attributed to a change from the basal plane to the $c$ axis as the easy axis of magnetization. Finally, the magnetic behavior of GdInO$_3$ is analyzed using a Heisenberg model. This analysis confirms that the material is quasi-two-dimensional, displays ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interactions, and is governed by single-ion anisotropy. Graph embedding methods are extensively utilized to transform network nodes into dense vector representations, which are critical for various downstream applications. This study introduces a novel and streamlined graph embedding technique named Sparse-SNE (SSNE). SSNE is a streamlined variant of Spectral Neighbourhood Embedding (SNE) that optimizes the embedding of sparse graphs by incorporating both the adjacency matrix and the degree diagonal matrix $D$ into the weight matrix $W=D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}$. This approach effectively mitigates the influence of tail nodes in sparse topologies. The efficiency of SSNE is evaluated through link prediction tasks, where it is benchmarked against leading embedding algorithms on both real-world datasets and synthetic topologies. The experimental results confirm that incorporating node degrees enhances representation quality, particularly for sparse graphs. Furthermore, SSNE surpasses current state-of-the-art embedding techniques in link prediction performance across most datasets. Additionally, SSNE demonstrates superior execution speed, being orders of magnitude faster than competing methods. Finally, the results indicate that SSNE successfully identifies and assigns greater weights to edges with higher probabilities of existence. We introduce a novel micro-fabricated silicon silicon-vacuum (SiSi) process designed to construct atomic vapor cells containing up to 10 cm of multiple gaseous atomic species. This approach utilizes silicon as a material for both the substrate and the primary structural component. Silicon's high melting point and chemical stability make it ideal for withstanding the high-temperature conditions necessary to introduce and retain alkali and alkaline-earth atoms at elevated pressures. Additionally, the SiSi process is compatible with other micro-fabrication techniques, such as dicing and anisotropic etching of silicon wafers, which facilitate the integration of atomic vapor cells with optical resonators, photonic waveguides, and photodetectors. These features position SiSi as a highly adaptable method for building atomic ensembles within hybrid quantum systems. We demonstrate the fabrication of these vapor cells and their application in high-fidelity quantum memory for both single-photon absorption and collective atomic resonance enhancement. Furthermore, we illustrate the potential of SiSi to develop advanced hybrid quantum systems featuring atomic and photonic qubits by employing these cells in the creation of a solid-state, photonic crystal cavity. This work underscores the versatility of the SiSi process in advancing quantum information science and engineering. This paper introduces a model for nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization wavelength-division multiplexing (DP-WDM) systems carrying two 4D formats: dual-polarization quadrature amplitude phase 16D (DP-QAP16) and dual-polarization quadrature amplitude phase 64D (DP-QAP64). The proposed model demonstrates that the impact of cross-polarization mixing on these 4D formats is comparable to its effect on the corresponding single-polarization (SP) quadrature amplitude phase formats (QAP16 and QAP64). Additionally, simulations reveal a slight reduction in the nonlinearity penalty of SP-QAP16 and SP-QAP64 when polarizations are mixed, indicating that moving to higher-order formats like SP-QAP64 or DP-QAP16/DP-QAP64 is more advantageous for mitigating nonlinear impairments. Finally, this proposed model is shown to be more efficient than the generalized split-step Fourier method (GSSFM) in terms of computational efficiency.

Detecting wildfires and smoke plumes is critical for safeguarding human life and property. Deep learning-based smoke detection in video streams has become increasingly popular, yet it remains highly susceptible to variations in illumination and camera quality. To address these challenges, we introduce a deep learning architecture that integrates infrared and visible light imagery. This hybrid approach leverages the complementary strengths of infrared imaging, which excels in fire detection, with visible light cameras, which offer superior smoke plume identification. Our proposed Fusion-Infrared-GAN (FIRe-GAN) combines these modalities to achieve enhanced smoke detection performance. The network utilizes a novel fusion layer that integrates a weighted fusion of infrared and visible images with the feature maps from the visible light branch of a standard Gen-DAN network. Evaluations on the Rainier dataset demonstrate a 1.5% increase in mean Average Precision (mAP) compared to the original Gen-DAN network. Furthermore, an ablation study confirms that the fusion layer is the primary driver of this performance gain. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/FIREGAN. The proposed method involves having participants complete a depression symptom checklist, followed by the collection of their profile details and historical posts from platforms like Facebook and Twitter. We introduce a random compartmental model designed to capture the spatial propagation dynamics of COVID-19. The system is constructed by randomly assembling various propagation mechanisms, where the underlying probability space represents a collection of cities or regions. For infection parameters, we apply a log-normal distribution to adhere to the principle of invariance under coordinate change. To address the stochastic nature of transmission, we utilize a Cox process. Furthermore, the model incorporates a term for social distancing, acknowledging that reduced human mobility significantly impacts the spread of COVID-19. Finally, the random compartmental model is resolved into a series of independent stochastic differential equations. This paper provides numerical simulations of the model and compares its results with the COVID-19 pandemic in China. Additionally, the model's predictions for the COVID-19 outbreak in California are compared against actual data. The findings indicate that, absent strict social distancing, the COVID-19 epidemic in California would have escalated rapidly. These results underscore the necessity of strict social distancing to mitigate the pandemic. Additionally, we examine the model's properties and explore its potential applications. The model's parameter can be estimated using epidemiological data from various regions. Consequently, this framework serves as a valuable tool for analyzing COVID-19 propagation dynamics and forecasting future outbreaks. The model can be adapted to study other diseases, such as Ebola and HIV, and to predict the spread of emerging infectious diseases. This work examines stick-slip phenomena and trajectory convergence in feedback-controlled motion systems featuring Coulomb friction, a common scenario in position control. A key challenge in this area is the non-Lipschitz continuity of Coulomb friction near zero velocity, which causes standard Lipschitz-based convergence results to fail. To address this, we model convergence using comparison systems that incorporate Lipschitz continuous approximations of non-Lipschitz functions. Our primary objective is to determine appropriate parameters for these comparison systems to ensure results that accurately reflect the original system's behavior. We establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing that the comparison system's trajectories either (i) converge to the same limit as the original system or (ii) experience infinite repeated stick-slip cycles, whereas they would experience finite cycles in the original system. Additionally, for linear original systems, we derive sufficient conditions for the comparison system to share the same exact limit. These findings are supported by numerical examples. Notably, the methods proposed are applicable to Lipschitz continuous friction models, such as viscous friction and dry friction with velocity-dependent signum functions. Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items to users based on their past consumption history. However, these recommendations often fail because users hold specific intentions regarding the items they want, intentions that previous consumption patterns do not necessarily address. To address this, we introduce a sequential recommender system that incorporates an explicit model of user purpose into the recommendation process. We develop a Bayesian latent Dirichlet allocation model that infers topics from web content related to items, using these topics to estimate the user purpose from a user-item interaction sequence. This purpose model then informs the recommender system, allowing it to prioritize items that align with the user's current intent. We evaluate our model in two settings: online search and online shopping. In the search domain, we demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms baseline methods. Additionally, we show that the model is effective in the shopping context, where its performance matches that of leading sequential recommender systems. Finally, we provide an analysis of our search model's performance across various user interaction sequences. Our code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1996/LUP.

This approach relies on the monodromy representation of the source term's differential equation, which is subsequently linked to the automorphism group of a specific algebraic curve. We investigate the estimation of a low-rank matrix from noisy, partially observed data entries that exhibit groupwise heteroskedasticity. This framework generalizes the established spiked covariance model to apply to general rank-one matrices. We establish minimax lower bounds for the best possible estimator and introduce a computationally efficient method that attains these lower bounds asymptotically, achieving optimal convergence rates across all entry-wise and low-rank parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the success of our procedure depends on the effective sparsity of the groupwise heteroskedasticity, rather than the total number of observed entries. This insight enables the extension of our findings to high-dimensional settings. Additionally, we present a procedure that asymptotically recovers all positive eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, even when the separation between eigenvalues is non-asymptotic. Our findings indicate that sample complexity for accurate reconstruction scales with the effective number of observed entries, which accounts for the varying noise levels of different groups. Finally, we present numerical results comparing our approach against existing methods for related problems. Our contributions are particularly relevant to applications involving heterogeneous data, such as those found in high-dimensional statistics, high-dimensional dynamical systems, and network analysis. Specifically, we demonstrate that our findings can be applied to problems where data is collected via sampling without replacement. In this context, we derive a sampling scheme where the probability of observing each entry is proportional to its true value, a scenario that has garnered significant interest in recent literature. We show that the sampling probabilities in this scheme yield the same asymptotic behavior as additive noise, thereby allowing our results to apply to this setting as well. Moreover, we illustrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments on both this sampled-without-proportional-to-values scheme and a new one we propose. In this alternative scheme, the probability of observing an entry is proportional to the sum of that entry and those of its neighbors. We show that this neighboring-proportional sampling scheme also produces asymptotically equivalent behavior. Our results further suggest that this form of "value-weighted sampling" is more effective than sampling proportional to value alone. Finally, we show that our procedures converge to the optimal estimator as the effective number of observed entries increases. This convergence holds even when the effective observed number of entries is significantly smaller than the total number of entries, provided the total number of entries is sufficiently large. We present a distinct topological model that lacks inherent symmetry, distinguishing it from the standard topological insulator. In this framework, the Hamiltonian for low-energy excitations is defined as $H(k_x, k_y) = \sigma_x k_x + k_y(\sigma_y\cos\phi+\sigma_y\sin\phi)$. The resulting band gap, given by $2|k_x|\sin\phi$, vanishes only when $k_x=0$, leaving a two-dimensional gap. This model is topologically equivalent to the conventional topological insulator when $\phi=0$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this insulator remains topologically non-trivial for any $\phi$ within the interval $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. This study introduces a decentralized architecture for linear multi-channel systems, where each channel operates as an independent entity managing its own design and estimation. The approach utilizes a distributed estimation framework, enabling channel independence and autonomy, alongside a distributed design mechanism that facilitates the formation of linear multi-channel systems without requiring a central design unit. Additionally, the design and estimation processes are distributed across multiple control centers, allowing the architecture to tolerate failures in any single control center. Furthermore, the design and estimation algorithms are formulated using distributed methods, enabling easy adaptation to various distributed estimation techniques. Finally, the design and estimation procedures for the entire system are executed in a distributed manner. Simulation results demonstrate that this decentralized design achieves performance comparable to centralized design while delivering the benefits of distributed estimation. The primary advantage of the proposed decentralized architecture is its flexibility and compatibility with diverse distributed algorithms. The paper also explores a novel plug-and-play design method for multi-channel systems, which supports the dynamic addition and removal of channels. This enables the application of distributed estimation algorithms to linear time-varying systems and extends the framework's applicability to nonlinear systems. The study also addresses distributed design for nonlinear systems, designing observers for each channel and integrating them into the overall system in a distributed fashion. Simulations illustrate that the performance of this distributed observer design rivals that of centralized observer designs. These findings collectively enhance the flexibility and robustness of the proposed decentralized architecture. The paper concludes by discussing the application of this decentralized design to distributed data fusion. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and devastation, affecting millions globally. While early detection of the virus is critical for containing its spread, the high cost of RT-PCR testing creates a dilemma: conducting it on every individual is financially prohibitive, yet relying solely on it risks missing cases. This necessitates a cost-effective screening mechanism to identify potential patients before they undergo RT-PCR validation. This paper introduces a two-stage deep learning framework that integrates clinical features with BERT-derived features to predict whether a patient is positive or negative for COVID-19. In the first stage, a neural network analyzes demographic and clinical data to generate an initial prediction. The second stage employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network that processes the contextual embeddings of clinical test findings from the input dataset to refine the outcome. The final prediction is derived by combining the outputs from both stages. Experimental results demonstrate that this multi-modal approach surpasses state-of-the-art single-stage models in accuracy. The proposed model is expected to significantly aid in early detection, thereby facilitating timely treatment and ultimately saving lives. Eco-evolutionary dynamics describe how ecological and evolutionary processes interact across various spatial and temporal scales. While ecology typically operates on shorter timescales than evolution, the two domains are deeply intertwined, with each influencing the other. This paper examines the timescales of ecological and evolutionary change and explores the mechanisms driving these dynamics, specifically focusing on eco-evolutionary feedbacks. We highlight the roles of eco-evolutionary rate modulators, including phenotypic variation, generation time, and the intensity of biotic interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the temporal and spatial dimensions of these timescales and the resulting dynamics. Finally, we propose an empirical research agenda aimed at advancing the field of eco-evolutionary dynamics. Key topics include defining and measuring timescales, investigating the causes and consequences of these interactions, and modeling the duality of ecology and evolution. The discussion also addresses the challenges posed by spatial and temporal heterogeneity, as well as the necessity for long-term research initiatives. We conclude by emphasizing the significance of eco-evolution as a unifying framework that harmonizes evolutionary and ecological research. The paper is supported by two supplementary sections: one detailing the mathematical foundations of timescales and another outlining the theoretical basis for timescale duality. Additionally, we provide a glossary of terms to ensure clarity for readers from both ecological and evolutionary backgrounds. This study examines the conditions under which a blockchain-enabled exchange can attract significant users. It constructs a blockchain-based decentralized exchange (dEX) model and compares the conditions for its adoption with those of a traditional centralized exchange (cEX). The findings indicate that a dEX will gain a substantial number of users when either the number of trading pairs is limited or when the risk of price manipulation is high. Conversely, when price manipulation risks are low, the dEX will fail to attract a large user base. These results are validated through a simulation. Given that most current blockchain exchanges operate as dEXs, this research underscores the necessity of further analyzing the trade-offs between decentralization and price discovery. Additionally, it offers a framework for designing the number of trading pairs in a new blockchain exchange. Finally, the work provides insights for investors evaluating whether to allocate capital to a specific blockchain exchange. Keywords: Blockchain, Decentralized Exchange, Price Manipulation, Liquidity, Liquidity Pools.

The E-value, originally developed by Diamond et al. (2013) to evaluate sensitivity to spurious associations in epidemiological research, has recently been adapted for other contexts. This study aims to suggest and assess a novel application of the E-value for sensitivity analysis in missing data issues. We begin by reviewing the standard method for calculating the E-value in the presence of unmeasured confounding, which involves determining the minimum effect size an unseen confounder would need to possess to alter a study's finding from non-significant to significant at a 0.05 level. Subsequently, we translate this concept into a missing data framework. By linking the E-value to the T-value and integrating it with Bayesian false lead probability concepts from Chen et al. (2020), we demonstrate its utility in sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, we show that the E-value can be computed for a broad range of effect sizes, extending beyond the binary nature of the original formulation. Finally, we illustrate the method through a simulation study and a practical example drawn from an epidemiological investigation. This work introduces a new, effective approach for conducting sensitivity analysis regarding missing data. Additionally, we have created an R package to facilitate the implementation of the E-value in sensitivity assessments. The package is available on CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=eval. This paper investigates the Laurent extension of quantum surfaces and examines their symmetries governed by the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. We demonstrate that the Laurent extension possesses a complete set of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries precisely when the quantum surface is either odd or satisfies $c_1 = -c_2 = \frac{q+q^{-1}}{2}$. Furthermore, we outline the action of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ on these extended quantum surfaces and determine the spectra of the generators $E$ and $F$. Additionally, we explore the quotient construction of these quantum groups, revealing that the quotient of an odd quantum surface yields a quantum group distinct from the quotient of an even one. Finally, we detail the spectrum of the symmetric operator $K$ for odd quantum surfaces, which is derived from the $R$-matrix. This spectral information is subsequently utilized to construct a complete set of mutually commuting operators. Finally, we establish the conditions under which a quantum surface is odd based on the coefficients of its quadratic form. Specifically, a quantum surface is odd if and only if its quadratic form can be expressed as $c_1\left(\frac{d\theta}{\theta}\right)^2+c_2\left(d\phi-\frac{q\theta^{-1}d\theta}{2}\right)^2$. The complete list of odd quantum surfaces is provided in Appendix A. The findings presented herein were previously announced in [arXiv:2101.01002]. However, training ML models on such large-scale data often raises privacy concerns, as it necessitates the sharing of sensitive user information. Federated Learning (FL) offers a solution to this challenge by enabling the training of a global ML model without the need to exchange private user data. Nevertheless, FL faces inherent vulnerabilities, including various attacks that can compromise the integrity of the global model. To address these issues, this paper surveys the integration of Blockchain and Federated Learning within the IoV ecosystem. We present a systematic literature review of 24 selected papers, analyzing their contributions, methodologies, and frameworks. Furthermore, we outline FL challenges specific to IoV and propose a Blockchain-enabled FL framework designed to mitigate these problems. Finally, we discuss how Blockchain can enhance FL in IoV environments, considering its contributions, methodologies, and frameworks. This study aims to offer valuable insights for researchers and practitioners operating within the intersection of these three domains. Additionally, we identify open research problems and propose future directions for Blockchain and FL in IoV. Given the dynamic nature of these technologies, this work is expected to remain relevant for an extended period. The large millikelvin system at Fermilab is purpose-built for quantum computing applications, featuring a room for up to 200 qubits and the flexibility to add various experimental tools. This paper details the design and performance of the cryogenic infrastructure, which utilizes a 12 kW, 4 K helium refrigerator equipped with a 12 kW, 10 mK still. The coldplate, measuring 150 mm in diameter and 100 mm in height, maintains a temperature below 10 mK with a thermal conductance exceeding 1000 W/K. The system also includes a vacuum chamber with a 400 mm diameter and a working volume of 0.4 m³, both situated within a magnetic shield that provides greater than 100 $\mu$T of magnetic shielding. This work presents a design report on the infrastructure, documenting a stable temperature of 7.8 mK and a magnetic field of 0.1 $\mu$T. Furthermore, a test of qubit scalability was conducted by cooling four qubits to 4.2 mK and achieving two-photon entanglement at 7.8 mK. The cryogenic system is currently being readied for the Q*Sense experiment at the Fermilab P*SCALE test facility. The P*SCALE platform is designed to investigate the impact of thermal and electromagnetic interference on quantum processors, including thermal annealing, entanglement, and decoherence. This paper also outlines the design of a cryogenic system intended for general quantum computing use. The P*SCALE facility will serve as a benchmark to evaluate the utility of this design for quantum computing applications. The system is expected to achieve a temperature below 10 mK, a vacuum superior to 10$^{-5}$ Torr, and magnetic shielding better than 1 $\mu$T. The P*SCALE facility is scheduled to begin operations in 2023. The authors extend their gratitude to the Fermilab Cryogenics Division for their assistance with the millikelvin system. This study examines a sample of 1,000 Python projects hosted on Bitbucket, GitHub, and GitLab to identify instances where Python cryptography is misused. The analysis focuses on four key areas: weak or absent authentication, weak ciphers, weak key lengths, and weak random number generators. By integrating application security standards with Python-specific characteristics, the research identifies on-demand, adaptive, and user-friendly code that allows developers to assess their projects and implement corrections. The findings include specific code snippets that enable the detection of up to 40% of security vulnerabilities in Python-based projects. Additionally, the work proposes a novel metric for measuring the vulnerability of Python code. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. This research is funded by the Ministry of Education, Science and Technological Development of the Republic of Serbia, Grant No. 174023. Keywords: Python, Cryptography, Vulnerability, Detection.

This paper introduces a robust, automatic tagging system for vast collections of images depicting urban settings. Our approach relies on a training dataset comprising 1.2 million images featuring 250,000 distinct tags. Image encodings are derived from a pre-trained ResNet50 network, while image-tag associations are established through a voting mechanism. To mitigate noise in the raw tagging data, we filter out spurious tags and suppress double-counting errors. Furthermore, we expand the dataset via a self-training process that propagates encodings and annotations to a large volume of unlabeled images. The final system is deployed as a REST API, capable of returning up to 250 tags per image. We assess the method's performance using two metrics: recall at various threshold levels and the distribution of tag counts across the dataset. The results demonstrate that our approach effectively identifies common objects and scenes present in the images. Additionally, we explore potential applications for this technique, including visual place recognition and place recommendation systems. The dataset and API are accessible at https://vision.cs.washington.edu/value/. The source code is available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/ashishgarg1996/VALUE. This thesis examines semigroups of composition operators acting on BMOA-type spaces and investigates integral operators linked to the Cauchy transform. The work is structured into two distinct parts. The first part, authored by J. L. Vázquez, introduces a novel class of analytic function spaces termed $M_{\beta}$ ($\beta>0$), of which the space of Bloch-type functions serves as a subset. Following the verification that the Cauchy integral operator maps $M_{\beta}$ into BMOA, the focus shifts to analyzing semigroups of composition operators on $M_{\beta}$. The study establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for a composition operator to be bounded or compact on $M_{\beta}$ and explores the compactness of the Cauchy integral operator. Furthermore, the asymptotic behavior of the semigroup is examined, with the main findings presented in an operator-theoretic framework. The second part, written by A. A. Kharazishvili, addresses integral operators related to the Cauchy transform within the spaces BMOA and Dirichlet. It is demonstrated that the Cauchy integral operator is bounded and compact on BMOA, whereas the Volterra integral operator is neither. The analysis concludes by determining the norm of the Cauchy integral operator on BMOA. Additionally, the relationship between the operators $Vf(z)=\int_{0}^{z}f(\zeta)d\zeta$ and $ Cf(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma}\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z)}d\zeta$ is explored in the context of the Dirichlet space.
