We introduce a universal formula for the first subleading correction to wavefunction overlaps in cylindrical geometries, applicable to models exhibiting cusp-like behavior at the maximum of the probability density P(k). Utilizing this formula, we examine the fusion of holomorphic and anti-holomorphic Haagerup operators across various spin sectors. Our findings indicate that the spin-1 operator corresponds to the identity operator in the dual CFT, whereas the spin-2 operator maps to the K(3) operator in the bulk. Additionally, we establish that the spin-3 operator's map relies on the specific model. By analyzing operator fusion in the bulk, we demonstrate that the bulk spin-3 operator is not primary. Furthermore, we compute the bulk spin-3 operator's scaling dimension, operator algebra, and fusion rules, revealing a non-trivial structure. Finally, we calculate the first subleading correction to the scaling dimension, finding it to be universal and consistent with the bulk spin-3 operator's non-primary nature. These results align with the analytic predictions of bulk conformal field theory. Our study also examines the fusion of operators with odd spin in spin sectors, showing that the resulting operators are non-primary with non-universal scaling dimensions. The calculated corrections to these dimensions are consistent with the analytic predictions of the non-primary operator in the bulk. This work enhances our understanding of operator fusion and scaling dimensions in non-rational conformal field theories. Our findings suggest that bulk conformal operators can be identified through wavefunction overlaps in specific geometries, even when the boundary CFT is non-rational. This approach is particularly valuable for models lacking a conventional operator product expansion. We anticipate that these findings will facilitate further research into the structure of conformal operators in non-rational CFTs. Finally, we propose that this method will aid in the identification of conformal operators in other non-rational conformal field theories. Supplementary material is available at [1]. Keywords: Conformal Field Theory, Non-Rational Conformal Field Theory, Operator Product Expansion, Scaling Dimension, Fusion Rules. Historical corpora exhibit significant linguistic variability due to evolving conventions in spelling, word usage, and part-of-speech tagging over time. To address this, we introduce a dependability-enhancement technique for POS tagging historical texts, which boosts confidence in the tag sets produced by a standard Tag-and-Validate (TV) algorithm. This method employs a modified version of the TV algorithm that outputs a set of potential POS tags for each word, accompanied by a confidence score reflecting the likelihood that the true historical tag is included. The approach integrates multiple historical corpora and re-ranks the confidence scores of the initial outputs. Experiments conducted on various modern German texts and three distinct Old High German corpora demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves dependability across different tagging scenarios. Furthermore, the results indicate that the dependability enhancement achieved on modern texts is fully replicable when applied to historical corpora. Consequently, the algorithm's robustness and reliability on modern data suggest its effectiveness in improving historical corpus tagging. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SebastianSchroeder99/Depandable-TV. Our findings also have broader implications for POS tagging across other domains, such as the tagging of ancient languages. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. This paper presents non-continuous integrability as a generalized integrability framework designed to resolve specific singularities in classical integrability theory. It defines the non-continuous integrability structure on open subsets of the Euclidean plane and introduces the concept of $\mathcal{N}$-continuity, which extends the standard notion of continuity. A central result demonstrates that any function possessing an $L^p$-derivative is $\mathcal{N}$-continuous for a particular class of null sets $\mathcal{N}$. The study also investigates the relationship between $\mathcal{N}$-continuity and Lipschitz continuity, proving that $\mathcal{N}$-continuity holds a pivotal role within noncontinuous integrability theory. Furthermore, it establishes that Riemann integration is viable for non-continuous functions, thereby broadening the scope of applicability for Riemann integration. These findings have significant implications for Green's theorem and the calculation of the area of plane regions. The work includes multiple examples and counterexamples to illustrate the distinctions between continuous and non-continuous integrability structures. The material covered is intended for undergraduate students and researchers in non-continuous integrability theory. This paper introduces a new approach to Formal Specification by developing a smart assistant capable of translating user needs regarding urban services and facilities into precise, formal definitions. This tool assists human designers in producing accurate formal specifications that eliminate ambiguity and facilitate effective communication between designers and stakeholders. We illustrate the functionality of this software assistant through the analysis of requirements for a real-world project: a mobile application designed to support tourists in Rome. The findings demonstrate that the assistant successfully converts natural language input—specifically user requirements from urban design projects—into formal specifications, thereby establishing formal requirements for urban services and facilities. Ultimately, this research expands the scope of formal specification beyond traditional computer science applications, such as software and hardware systems, into broader domains. The resulting tool assists human designers in generating accurate formal specifications for projects involving urban services and facilities. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of software-based assistants in formal specification that transcends the realm of computer science. The design and development of this tool are grounded in our theoretical framework for formal specification, which is detailed in a separate project report [1]. Furthermore, this tool has the potential to influence the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) by generating formal specifications that serve as formal language translations of natural language texts. The tool is accessible online at https://formal4urban4u.herokuapp.com/.

This study introduces a novel quantum error correction approach for superconducting quantum devices utilizing hidden inverses, termed the Hidden Inverses Protocol (HIP). We demonstrate that HIP can effectively detect and rectify arbitrary errors occurring during quantum computations. The protocol's design is straightforward, requiring minimal additional qubits and avoiding complex operations like measurements or inverses. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of HIP through simulations of experiments conducted on the Sycamore processor. These results confirm that HIP can substantially boost the success rates of quantum computations on superconducting hardware. Consequently, HIP serves as a valuable supplement to existing quantum error correction techniques for near-term quantum devices. In a regular category $\mathcal{C}$ lacking finite coproducts, an $X$-cocartesian representation of a set $S$ is defined as a functor $\mathcal{C}_X: \mathcal{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ that maps $X$ to the set $S$ and sends $X$-indexed product objects to disjoint unions of singletons, while preserving finite products and quotients of epimorphisms. This concept extends the idea of a strongly cartesian representation originally proposed by J. Adámek and S. Lack. The existence of such representations for objects in $\mathcal{C}$ enables the realization of certain universal constructions within $\mathcal{C}$ that would otherwise be unattainable. Specifically, we demonstrate that if $\mathcal{C}$ possesses $S$-cocartesian representations for some set $S$, then both partial preorders on $S$ (interpreted as $S$-indexed subobjects of the terminal object in $\mathcal{C}$) and equivalence relations on $S$ (interpreted as $S$-indexed objects of $\mathcal{C}$) can be expressed as cocartesian colimits of diagrams formed by these subobjects. This result relies on a newly established theorem regarding the existence of these $S$-cocartesian representations. Furthermore, we generalize findings by B. Jurík and Š. Maciá, proving that every set $S$ admits a cocartesian representation that is functorial with respect to $S$-indexed morphisms in any category $\mathcal{E}$ possessing enough projectives. Finally, applying these results to the category $\mathbf{Grp}$ of groups, we show that a functor $F: \mathbf{Grp} \to \mathbf{Set}$ admitting a $S$-cocartesian representation must map every free group to a free group of rank at least $|S|$. Consequently, we derive that both partial preorders and equivalence relations on any non-empty set $S$ cannot be represented as cocartesian colimits of their corresponding subobjects in $\mathbf{Grp}$, due to the free nature of subgroups within free groups. The offshore marine sector is increasingly concerned with the interplay between sea level rise and the frequency of extreme events, such as storm surges and storminess, which are projected to rise due to climate change. This study introduces a new spatial multivariate conditional extreme value model grounded in a stochastic process within a domain, designed to forecast extreme marine conditions at specific locations. The methodology is validated using a multivariate tide gauge dataset from the North Sea. Results indicate that the model can accurately replicate the spatial and multivariate extremes observed in the North Sea. Furthermore, the model demonstrates its ability to predict extreme conditions at unmonitored sites based on readings from nearby observed tide gauges. Finally, the paper explores potential applications in assessing future extreme conditions under various sea level rise scenarios. This paper introduces a general framework for operator transitioning to address noisy matrix systems, encompassing both operator Markovian and operator non-Markovian scenarios. The transitioned operator serves to eliminate the impact of system noise, thereby restoring controllability to the original quantum system. We present two distinct methods for transitioning operator noise: the first applies to systems where the noise operator commutes with both Hamiltonian and control operators, successfully transitioning both white and colored system noises; the second addresses cases where the noise operator does not commute with the Hamiltonian or control operators, specifically transitioning colored system noises. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transitioned noise operator inherently satisfies the local detailed balance condition. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to verify the study's theoretical findings and to compare the performance of two control methods: one without transition and one with transition under white noise conditions. These results indicate that achieving a transitioned noise operator significantly enhances control performance even in the presence of white noise. Additionally, we observe that the transitioned noise operator is independent of the specific choice of transition protocol. These findings hold significant value for the quantum control of noisy systems. As a practical application, we show that a transitioned noise operator can be derived from the original noise operator by applying a virtual rotation. This approach is effective for transitioning noise in a single qubit system, a quantum dot, and a quantum three-level atomic system. Notably, the proposed method is general and can be extended to various other quantum systems. We provide an explicit computation of the sections functor for the spectrum $X = Map(\mathbb{H}, MA)$, which represents four-dimensional integral homology. Our findings reveal an equivalence to an infinite product of generalized Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra. Consequently, we derive a spectral sequence that calculates the cohomology of the space $\mathbb{H}$ within the category $Map(\mathbb{H}, \mathbf{Sp})$ of quaternionic spectra. This spectral sequence converges to the cohomology $H^*(\mathbf{Sp}^{4\mathbb{Z}}; E)$, where $\mathbf{Sp}^{4\mathbb{Z}}$ denotes the full subcategory consisting of spectra with vanishing homology in degrees $k \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. This family of cohomology theories is novel and nontrivial for $k \leq -8$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this cohomology theory is nontrivial in the tensor-triangulated topology of $\mathbf{Sp}^{4\mathbb{Z}}$. This result establishes a counterexample to a conjecture by Balmer and Colpi regarding the classification of prime ideals in this triangulated category. Additionally, we establish that $\mathbb{H}$ is not representable in $\mathbf{Sp}^{4\mathbb{Z}}$ and investigate the obstructions to realizing it. Finally, we compute the homotopy groups of the sections functor up to degree 20. These computations indicate that the convergence of the spectral sequence is not reached until degree 16, suggesting that a more refined approach is necessary to determine the factors of the automorphism group of $\mathbb{H}$ in $\mathbf{Sp}^{4\mathbb{Z}}$. This paper is the third installment in a series of four, with the final part being forthcoming. Digital pathology and radiology are expanding at a rapid pace, driven by the increasing availability of high-resolution whole slide images (WSIs) and radiological scans alongside a surge in machine learning research. However, these fields currently lack a unified standard for sharing data and results. To address this, we introduce highdicom, a Python library that provides a high-level API for creating pixel-based annotations and outputs using the DICOM standard, which is the established industry standard for medical imaging. By utilizing well-defined, widely adopted formats, highdicom streamlines the sharing of pixel annotations among researchers and facilitates seamless integration into pipelines for machine learning and evaluation. The library is designed to be both simple and scalable, enabling the representation of complex annotations like polygons and free-form drawings through orthogonal fragments, while maintaining compatibility with existing DICOM resources and supporting future extensions for metadata and pixel encoding. This paper outlines the design principles behind highdicom and demonstrates its utility with examples from digital pathology and radiology. The library is released under the permissive Apache 2.0 license and is freely accessible at https://pypi.org/project/highdicom/ or via PyPI. Furthermore, additional documentation and usage examples can be found at https://highdicom.readthedocs.io/. We anticipate that this standardized approach will enhance interoperability and improve the reproducibility of pixel-based machine learning research in medical image analysis. The library's functionality is further validated by its adoption in established tools such as cuCIM and OpenPathology. Additionally, we demonstrate its application in digital medicine through a case study involving the prediction of adverse childhood experiences from brain MRI scans, which utilizes highdicom to share both data and model outputs. We believe these features will foster interoperability and reproducibility in pixel-based machine learning research. Feature learning has long been a central pillar of bioinformatics. This study introduces a feature learning technique that derives sequence representations from nucleotide patterns using unsupervised methods. Unlike many existing approaches, this technique avoids the need for sequence alignment, thereby broadening its applicability. The core method employs a dynamic programming-based motif search to identify and extract recurring DNA patterns, subsequently modeling the sequence based on these motifs. We demonstrate that representations extracted in this manner effectively capture fundamental sequence characteristics and prove their utility for downstream supervised classification tasks. Furthermore, we show that this approach can uncover representations that align with and surpass the information content of established sequence features. Finally, we confirm that these learned representations successfully identify biologically significant features, including those linked to chromatin accessibility and gene regulation. Overall, this method offers a robust, unsupervised strategy for sequence feature extraction that enhances both interpretability and predictive performance. The implementation is accessible via the open-source DMPFS package at https://github.com/GenomicsML/DMPFS. Additionally, we provide a Jupyter notebook that walks users through applying DMPFS to their own sequence data. Given that the method relies solely on the input sequence, it is readily adaptable to any genomic context. We anticipate that DMPFS will serve as a valuable, interpretable, and high-performing feature extraction tool for researchers in genomics and bioinformatics. Our hope is that this resource will facilitate the development of more effective machine learning models for genetic variant interpretation and gene regulation analysis. By enabling the discovery of novel sequence features, DMPFS is poised to significantly advance the field of computational biology. Supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/GenomicsML/DMPFS/tree/master/Notebooks. Keywords: DNA sequence, feature learning, motif search, dynamic programming, machine learning.

Notably, both VO$_2$ and rutile TiO$_2$ coatings suppress the metal-insulator transition in these thin films. These results offer valuable insights into nanodevice design, demonstrating that surface modifications can be utilized to control the metal-insulator transition. Furthermore, the ability to tune the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ nanoscale structures through surface engineering holds promise for the development of low-power, multifunctional devices. This paper introduces a specific canonical form, named the Clebsch form, designed for Lie-Poisson equations. By applying a change of variables and expressing the dynamics via an extended Lagrangian, one can derive this form, which typically features a reduced set of Poisson brackets. The study examines the conditions required for a Poisson structure to be reducible to this form and demonstrates its significant utility in simplifying the calculation of moments of motion. Furthermore, applying this reduction method to specific cases yields a novel reduced Poisson bracket on the co-adjoint orbit space of $so(4)$. Finally, the paper investigates whether this reduced bracket can be extended to the entire phase space of $so(4)$. These findings are validated through concrete examples, including the Euler equations for a heavy top and a symmetric body rotating within a fluid. Additionally, the role of Casimir functions in generating moment equations is illustrated. The techniques developed here are particularly applicable to systems exhibiting Lie-Poisson structures characterized by reduced brackets. The appendix provides a comprehensive set of formulas for an integrable $so(4)$ system, incorporating all necessary data for the calculations presented in this work. We introduce the conclusion of the 2018 sub-survey field planetary search conducted by the KMTNet Planetary Anomaly Search team. This report details the discovery of 10 new planets and the confirmation of one previously identified sub-planet, alongside the validation of 10 candidate signals that remain unexplained. This paper investigates the optimal control problem focused on minimizing conservation laws violations within compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Consistent with our prior work [1], we establish the existence of optimal pairs joining control and initial data, provided smallness conditions are met regarding the initial violation of conservation laws. Furthermore, for the specific case of the ideal gas equation of state, we demonstrate that violations to the first and second laws of thermodynamics can be completely eliminated. The proofs utilizing convex geometry techniques mirror those found in [2]. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of our methodology to an equation of state featuring a critical point, which results in conservation laws violations taking a distinct form. Finally, we present a numerical example illustrating the optimal control problem for a conservation law violation violation. This final example marks a departure from the methodology of [1], as it involves an initial value problem where data is prescribed on a subset of the domain. This shift necessitates a novel approach to proving the existence of optimal pairs and introduces novel issues concerning the existence of local minimizers. The strategy employed involves a penalization of the problem, followed by estimates and compactness arguments to derive weak convergence, ultimately passing to the limit in the first order condition to identify a minimizer. This final condition is constructed to ensure that the second law of thermodynamics is not violated. This strategy is inspired by [3], where a similar condition was utilized to prove the existence of a control ensuring strict positivity of density and velocity. However, this condition is not directly applicable here, as it is not guaranteed to yield a minimizer for the second law of thermodynamics. Instead, we prove the existence of a local minimizer for a penalized problem, which is subsequently converted into a local minimizer for the original problem. The existence of this local minimizer is established using a novel method that relies on the existence of a control ensuring the strict positivity of density and velocity. This existence is derived from a novel convexity argument, which is also applicable to the Euler equations. The paper concludes by discussing an alternative strategy for the optimal control problem involving the Euler equations. Banking institutions face significant challenges in managing non-performing loans (NPLs), as these assets drain liquidity and harm reputations. Consequently, there is a pressing need for effective early warning systems to identify and prevent NPLs. This study evaluates various machine learning models using a dataset of 1,000 customers, where each client is tagged with either a "good" or "bad" label. Feature importance analysis reveals that the most predictive variables are those related to the number of transactions, specifically "TotalDebitTx" and "TotalCreditTx." Among the algorithms tested, the Random Forest model demonstrates superior performance, achieving an accuracy of 80.00%. This paper aims to assist banking institutions in mitigating the risks associated with NPLs. The source code is available at: https://github.com/abdullahd/RF_Random_Forest. Future research will focus on expanding the dataset to include more than 1,000 customers. Additionally, given the model's high accuracy, we plan to integrate it into an NPL detection system for banking use. We will also explore the application of blockchain technology to enhance transparency and trust within the banking sector. Finally, we intend to incorporate explainable AI techniques to increase the transparency of the Random Forest model. Our goal is to establish a robust early warning system for NPLs, thereby enabling banks to minimize losses and generate revenue. Direction Convolutional Networks (DCN) are designed to enhance the receptive field of convolutional kernels by incorporating pixel or feature values from adjacent cells within the same input. This approach facilitates a more holistic image comprehension and has demonstrated superior performance in high-resolution image recognition tasks. However, the original DCN framework relies on sparse connections, which can cause information loss and a bottleneck effect during training. To address these limitations, we introduce the Multi-scale Aggregation DCN (MSDCN), which replaces sparse links with dense connections to enable full utilization of the input feature map and eliminate bottlenecks. Additionally, MSDCN employs multi-scale feature aggregation to further expand the effective receptive field of individual kernels. Experimental results confirm that MSDCN outperforms DCN and other state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks on PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 for object detection. Furthermore, we have released the source code for MSDCN to support future research and development in image recognition. The implementation is available at: https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/MSDCN. This work was presented at the 2019 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW). The corresponding author is Zhongyuan Wang. This study revisits the flavor dependence of the top quark mass within the framework of Dimensional Regularization. By employing an on-shell renormalization scheme, we demonstrate that the light quark correction to the top quark self-energy, which arises due to $V_{us}$, can be precisely calculated using self-energy methods. Furthermore, we prove that the flavor-dependent self-energy contribution involving the $W$ boson and top quon exactly cancels with a similar term in the vertex correction. Consequently, the flavor-dependent quark correction is suppressed by the mass difference between the $W$ boson and the top quark, a feature that persists in the tadpole diagram. This implies that the top quark mass exhibits a very weak dependence on the flavor of light quarks, a finding that is crucial for interpreting the recent lattice QCD determination of $M_t$ derived from the triple correlation function of $B$-mesons. Our analysis indicates that the mass difference between the $\overline{t}_{\overline{MS}}$ and $\overline{b}_{\overline{MS}}$ renormalized masses is approximately 1.3 GeV. In the $\overline{MS}$ scheme, the top quark mass displays an even weaker dependence on the flavor of light quarks. Finally, we examine the implications of this result for the recent lattice QCD extraction of $M_t$ from the $B$ meson's third correlation function. The findings suggest that the recent discrepancy between the top and $\overline{b}$ quark masses in the $\overline{MS}$ scheme is not influenced by the flavor of the light quark. We demonstrate that for any integer $k \geq 2$, a graph $G$ with degree $(1+o(1))n^{1-1/k}n^{1/k\epsilon}$ can be divided into $O(k)$ parts, where each part forms a subgraph with a maximum degree of $o(n^{1-1/k})$. The exponents governing these bounds are tight for the case where $k=2$ and $d=n^{1/3}\epsilon$. Furthermore, we prove that for $k\geq 2$, the power $n^{1/k(1-\delta)}$ is essentially the optimal degree bound for ensuring that every $k$-partite subgraph has a maximum degree of $o(n^{1/k(1-\delta)})$. Additionally, we establish that for $k=2$, a bipartite subgraph with a degree bound of $o(n^{1/2(1-\delta)})$ can be obtained from an $n^{1/2(\delta+1/4)}$ degree graph, confirming that the exponent $1/4$ is optimal. This result is achieved by deriving an upper bound on the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph that excludes a complete bipartite graph $K_{t,t}$. Our findings extend to hypergraphs, where the exponent $1/k(1-\delta)$ remains optimal. The paper also includes several applications, such as providing an upper bound on the maximum number of edges in a graph that admits a bipartite subgraph with degree $o(n^{2/3})$, and determining the maximum number of edges in a graph that can be 3-colored such that the maximum number of edges incident to any vertex within a color class is $o(n^{2/3})$. Additionally, we show that the exponent $2/3$ is optimal in this context. Finally, we generalize these results to the scenario where the maximum degree of a vertex in a color class is bounded by $n^{1/k(\epsilon+\delta)}$, yielding a maximum edge bound of $n^{1/k(\epsilon+\delta^2+\delta)}$. In this final context, the exponent $\delta$ is optimal. The primary tool employed is a variant of the Kőnig lemma. Our findings are closely linked to the concept of $k$-degeneracy. We also investigate the relationship between this concept and our results, showing that the exponent $1/k$ is optimal

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and has been managed through various testing methods, including PCR, rapid antigen tests, and CT-based medical imaging. Among these, CT scans are particularly valuable for diagnosing and monitoring patients with respiratory symptoms. However, the primary obstacle to utilizing CT imaging is the difficulty in accurately classifying the condition of a CT scan. To address this, we introduce a two-stage time-distributed capsule network (TD-CN) to extract features from CT scans. This architecture leverages the spatial and temporal data from a 4D CT scan to enhance classification accuracy. Specifically, a convolutional neural network (CNN) initially processes the CT scan to generate a 3D capsule set, which is subsequently fed into a 4D capsule network that captures temporal information to produce a 4D capsule set. The final capsule classification layer then determines the classification based on this comprehensive information. Extensive experiments were conducted on the LUNA16 and COVID-CT datasets, demonstrating that the proposed network significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1998/COVID-CT-Detection. The LUN16 dataset can be downloaded here: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/abhishekkumar1998/luna16-dataset. The COVID-CT dataset is available at: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/abhishekkumar1998/covid-ct-dataset. The results are posted at: https://www.kaggle.com/abhishekkumar1998/covid-ct-classification/results. Our findings indicate that the proposed network achieves human-level performance in classifying CT scans. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model can accurately detect COVID-19 using low-dose CT scans, offering a cost-effective alternative to standard CT imaging. This capability is crucial for facilitating early detection and treatment of COVID-19. We hope our research will contribute to the global fight against the pandemic. Future work will focus on enhancing classification performance through advanced data augmentation techniques and developing a more lightweight model for deployment on edge devices. We anticipate that these efforts will aid in the long-term battle against COVID-19. Finally, we express our gratitude to the community for their continued support. Thank you. God bless. 🙏🙏🙏. 🥰🥰🥰. �

This paper introduces a mathematical framework for spatial efficiency within low-Earth orbit, designed to facilitate a systematic analysis of the strategic and operational dynamics governing the deployment, operation, and termination of LEO constellations. The model incorporates key variables such as orbital altitude, orbital and equatorial inclination, and the counts of active and de-orbited satellites. By generating three-dimensional representations of occupied orbital space, we can comprehensively quantify the volume utilized by a constellation throughout its operational lifespan. We present results for various existing and proposed constellations, including Iridium, Globalstar, and Starlink, and discuss implications for future space traffic management. Additionally, we address limitations in current international legal frameworks regarding the management of orbital and frequency resources. Finally, we propose a computational game theory approach to model the strategic interactions between multiple constellation operators, aiming to identify stable equilibria in fleet size and space requirements. This methodology could provide a scientific basis for regulatory decisions concerning multi-constellation deployments. The findings of this study are applicable to a broad range of LEO missions, including those for global communications, remote sensing, and space-based surveillance. The code used to develop this model is publicly accessible on GitHub. Our methodology and model are also available on arXiv-preprint servers. This study introduces a novel framework for generating coarse quadrilateral meshes on CAD models by mapping them onto a quadrilateral integer grid. The process begins with an initial coarse quadrilateral mesh created through the segmentation of CAD model faces into rectangular regions. To address any inconsistencies between these pre-segmented faces and the connecting bridges, the vertices of the initial mesh are mapped to grid points via an integer linear programming problem, resulting in a valid quadrilateral mesh on the CAD model. The methodology is validated through several numerical examples. The primary innovation lies in the use of integer linear programming to bridge local and global meshing efforts, thereby producing high-quality quadrilateral meshes on CAD models. Furthermore, the paper provides a detailed theoretical analysis of the algorithm's computational complexity. Given its high quality, the generated mesh is suitable for finite element analysis. The proposed technique offers several advantages: (1) it produces direct quadrilateral meshes without requiring triangulation; (2) it ensures a one-to-one vertex mapping between the initial and final meshes, preserving element connectivity; (3) it maintains the initial mesh's quality; (4) it allows for the specification of arbitrary vertex and element densities; and (5) it facilitates the creation of specific features, such as quadrilateral patches. Additionally, the method is highly adaptable to various CAD model topologies. The study begins by outlining the mathematical background and formulating the core problem, followed by a detailed description of the proposed algorithm and its implementation. Finally, computational experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The paper concludes with a discussion of the results and potential future research directions. This paper introduces a systematic approach to determine the exact values of sample moment coefficients for the sample correlation across all 72 distinct datasets formed by the arrangements of three variables. Our approach is grounded in an analytical formulation for the expected value of the sample correlation raised to an even power, which is derived through two primary methods: first, by expanding the even power into a summation of even-power cross-product terms and evaluating their expected values; and second, by applying the properties of the multivariate normal distribution. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the bias of the sample correlation and calculate its magnitude for each of the 72 cases. Finally, we provide R code to compute both the theoretical and empirical moment coefficients for these 72 datasets. This work extends our prior research (2021a), where we developed analogous methods for the 12 possible cases resulting from the arrangements of two variables. The N-S equation includes a low-order internal localized observation, while the ODE incorporates a boundary detection term. This feedback control is designed to stabilize the Navier-Stokes equation uniformly across all Riemannian metrics, which is essential for applications on bounded domains with moving boundaries.

The stabilization achieves uniformness within a specific framework of maximal $L^p$-regularity for Navier-Stokes equations on the whole space $\mathbb{R}^3$. This framework encompasses various Sobolev and Besov spaces, covering a broad range of dimensions. Consequently, the moving boundary induced by the feedback control decays to zero at a rate determined by the observation localization and the selected function space dimension. Furthermore, this work extends uniform stabilization results from Navier equations to the Navier-Stokes equations. Notably, the observed boundary observation is permitted to be non-localized in the temporal direction. These findings offer new insights into the uniform stabilization of the Navier-Stokes equation and its connection to the Hilbert invariant principle. Additionally, the observed boundary does not require localization near the origin. A significant portion of this research was conducted during the second author's visit to the University of Nice-Sophia Antipolis. The core methodology involves a fixed point argument, leveraging the compactness of finite-dimensional projection operators and specific properties of the Navier-Stokes equation. Recent studies have explored interpretable machine learning, with LIME (Local Interpreted Model-agnostic Explanations) emerging as a prominent approach. LIME generates post-hoc local approximations to uncover interpretable insights into black-box models. However, when applied to recommendation systems, it is unclear whether the human-centric evaluation metrics of fairness, stability, and actionability are suitable for assessing LIME's local models. This paper addresses the adherence and consistency of LIME explanations specifically for recommendation systems. We validate our methodology using the publicly available MovieLens 1M dataset. Our findings indicate that LIME explanations for recommenders exhibit high adherence but low consistency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that LIME can effectively explain state-of-the-art recommenders while maintaining robustness against adversarial attacks. Finally, we explore directions for future research regarding explainable recommendation systems. The code supporting this work will be made publicly available.

This study examines how the Fermi level pinning parameter varies with well width in an infinite barrier near-surface quantum well within inAs. By employing the Fermi-level-pinning model, we determined that pinning weakens as the well width diminishes. Utilizing the envelope function formalism, we calculated the pinning parameter for wells ranging from 1 to 100 monolayers. Our results indicate that a 3-monolayer well exhibits low pinning, whereas a 100-monolayer well shows strong pinning comparable to bulk inAs. Furthermore, we explored methods to lower pinning in wider wells by incorporating surface states. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for designing near-surface quantum wells. These outcomes are anticipated to facilitate the development of novel quantum well structures for advanced nanotechnological applications. Ensuring robustness against adversarial input perturbations is a critical objective for deploying machine learning models in high-stakes, safety-sensitive environments. This study investigates a decentralized learning framework involving multiple agents that face two distinct adversaries: one introducing distribution shifts in the input space, while another targets the learning process by selectively withholding data from individual agents. We address binary classification tasks using linear models and propose a distributed algorithm incorporating a novel local inquiry mechanism, which enables each agent to sample points from any other agent's training set. Our findings demonstrate that, under certain conditions, the combination of local inquiries and selective data withholding allows attackers to degrade model performance to random chance levels. Furthermore, we analyze the interplay between these local inquiries and data withholding, proving that increasing the inquiry rate can actually enhance the robustness of models trained on Debiased Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGDM). Finally, we extend these insights to real-world datasets. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/LocalInquiryAttack. The source code for robust learning algorithms is hosted on our lab's GitHub at https://github.com/robust-ml-lab. Our results indicate that models trained with local inquiry methods outperform those using standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in realistic scenarios. Additionally, we observe that while local inquiry algorithms are effective in binary classification tasks, they offer diminished benefits in multi-class settings. Our contributions include: (1) a new algorithm for decentralized learning with local inquiry robustness, (2) a novel attack vector for decentralized learning, and (3) a demonstration of the trade-off between local inquiry and adversarial data withholding. This paper introduces Fast Sinkhorn II, a precise and collinear transport algorithm grounded in the triangular matrix method. It achieves linear computational complexity, O(n), for both the Sinkhorn iterations and the update of the optimal cost, alongside linear storage requirements. Unlike the collinear method, which relies on a sorting-based greedy approach, the sorting step in Fast Sinkhorn II is utilized solely to zero out a triangular matrix. The primary innovation lies in the triangular matrix formulation, which enables the accurate and linear time computation of the optimal transport cost. Furthermore, the algorithm leverages the fast exponential function evaluation method. Experimental results demonstrate that Fast Sinkhorn II is up to 100 times faster than the original Sinkhorn algorithm for transport problems involving 10,000 points. Additionally, it matches the performance of a recent linear time approximate method while delivering precise optimal transport costs. The algorithm is publicly accessible at https://github.com/leopoldo-ortega/fast-sinkhorn2. Future research will explore extensions to high-dimensional problems. The discovery of exoplanets has driven significant research into the impact of stellar activity on planetary atmospheres. This study examines the frequency and intensity of far-ultraviolet (FUV) flares from the active M dwarf AU Mic, a star known to host two planets within its habitable zone. Utilizing data from the Far Ultraviolet and Extreme Ultraviolet Explorer (FUSE), we identified 13 previously unknown flares and detected 10 confirmed flares. The remaining two excess FUV flux events were likely caused by stellar rotation rather than eruptive activity. The cumulative rate of all FUV flares observed is $0.15 \pm 0.03$ per day, which is approximately 100 times higher than the rate for inactive M dwarfs. The highest activity observed occurred on 2008 June 10, when AU Mic emitted $1.2 \times 10^{29}$ erg of energy in just 1.5 hours. We observed no significant correlation between optical and FUV fluxes, indicating that FUV flares are independent phenomena. Furthermore, the observed flare rate in the FUV is roughly 100 times greater than in the optical band. These FUV flares dwarf the flux received by AU Mic b and c from the Sun, and their associated ionizing radiation could severely affect the atmospheres of these planets. Finally, we propose that the excess FUV flux detected during quiescent periods may result from the decay of magnetic energy stored during active phases. These findings suggest that future studies of M dwarf exoplanets must account for the potential effects of intense FUV flares. Additionally, we recommend that atmospheric scientists incorporate the effects of energetic particle precipitation into their models, as this mechanism may be a primary driver of FUV emission in active M dwarfs. This study examines the motion of charged particles through an ionized gas under extreme electric fields, focusing on scenarios where relativistic effects and radiation reaction are significant. Our analysis reveals that the relative impact of radiation reaction varies inversely to the square root of the medium's resistivity. Consequently, radiation reaction exerted by an ionized gas medium can be substantially weaker than that caused by a vacuum. We explore the implications of this finding for laser-wakefield acceleration techniques. Additionally, our research indicates that charged particles undergoing intense acceleration within an ionized gas can experience windage forces from the medium. When these windage forces dominate over radiation reaction forces, particle trajectories deviate significantly from radiation-reaction-free paths. We present these results as a foundational framework for investigating particle dynamics under intense electric fields in ionized gas environments. Ultimately, these findings suggest that experimental investigations into relativistic electron beam properties and X-ray generation via intense laser-matter interactions in ionized gases should incorporate ionized gas radiation reaction into their analytical models. This inclusion is essential for accurately interpreting experimental data and for designing future facilities. We have included a numerical simulation of electron motion in a laser-accelerated ionized gas to illustrate these effects. Specifically, we examine ionized gases with varying levels of resistivity and analyze how radiation reaction influences the generated electron beam. Our findings indicate that, compared to a non-resistive medium, an ionized gas with finite conductivity can suppress energy loss due to radiation by a factor of up to 100. Furthermore, we observe that electrons in an ionized gas can maintain their energy over longer distances, resulting in beams with higher energy and reduced emittance. These results are particularly relevant for laser-wakefield acceleration experiments conducted in aerogel targets. Finally, we discuss the potential application of these results to laser-wakefield acceleration studies utilizing deuterium plasmas. In this specific case, we demonstrate that an ionized gas with low electron concentration can serve as an effective medium for mitigating energy loss caused by radiation reaction. Additionally, the ionized gas generates a windage force that further enhances the electron beam's energy. Ultimately, these results suggest that plasmas with low electron concentrations could be valuable for laser-wakefield acceleration applications. Specifically, deuterium plasma, which exhibits low electron concentration, is a promising candidate for use in such systems. In classification tasks involving highly imbalanced datasets, where one class significantly outnumbers others, the majority class often dominates the learned statistical model. Consequently, standard algorithms like the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) classifier, which typically rely on uniform data distributions, frequently yield suboptimal results. This study introduces a modified kNN approach that leverages the non-uniform, skewed distributions inherent in imbalanced data to enhance classification performance. By employing the concept of score functions, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of these distributions and their corresponding density functions. Furthermore, we provide the large sample behavior of our proposed classifier and establish its minimax optimality. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to validate the theoretical findings. The results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing techniques, including the weighted kNN (wkNN) classifier, in terms of classification error rates. Specifically, the wkNN classifier, which assigns higher weights to minority classes, is shown to be optimal within a specific subset of the parameter space. Building on this insight, the paper presents a novel classifier that utilizes information from data points belonging to different distributions. This proposed method is proven to be minimax optimal across the entire parameter space. Extensive simulations confirm that the new classifier achieves superior performance compared to the wkNN classifier across the complete parameter space. Overall, this work offers a theoretical foundation for developing classifiers capable of effectively handling general imbalanced data sets. Additionally, real-world data applications are included to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed classifier. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/AniruddhaSarkar1992/Imbalanced-Data-Classification. Keywords: Imbalanced data, kNN classifier, Minimax optimality, Score function, Weighted kNN classifier. MSC 2010: 62H17, 62F12, 62H30.

We report the identification of 11 new quasars and confirm 11 previously known bright quasars, all detected via optical spectroscopy. These 22 objects were found within the SkyMapper Southern Survey (SMASS) footprint, which covers 18,000 square degrees of the southern sky. All 22 candidates exhibit broad H$\beta$ emission lines with widths exceeding 10,000 km s$^{-1}$, and their redshifts range from $z=0.8$ to $z=6.3$. Their absolute $g$-band magnitudes span $g^* - 24.5 \lesssim m^*_{AB} \lesssim m^*_{AB} - 20.5$, with an average value of $m^*_{AB} = -23.2 \pm 0.1$. The new quasars extend the SMASS luminosity function (LF) to the most luminous end, surpassing the prior record holder by a factor of 10. This achievement is significant because the new LF is derived from a statistically complete sample, whereas the old LF was based on serendipitously discovered objects. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the SMASS LF aligns with LF measurements from the SDSS and Mauna Kea. This study presents the largest sample of quasars with $m^*_{AB} < 22$ and $z > 2$ identified to date. Additionally, we show that the SMASS LF can be used to estimate the number density of luminous quasars, a critical value for calibrating future cosmological surveys. Our findings indicate that the comoving number density of quasars with $m^*_{AB} = -22$ and $z > 2$ is $1.1 \pm 0.1 \times 10^{-5}$ Mpc$^{-3}$, while for $m^*_{AB} = -23$ and $z > 2$, it is $1.1 \pm 0.1 \times 10^{-5}$ Mpc$^{-3}$. These results are consistent with measurements from SDSS and Mauna Kea. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the evolution of the bright end of the quasar LF. We conclude that SMASS has identified the brightest quasars ever discovered, and we anticipate that this survey will continue

We investigate charge tunneling between a quantum dot and a superconducting island by monitoring the superconducting island's charging energy via an adjacent gate electrode. By analyzing the dependence of the gate-sensing signal on the dot's size and its coupling to a reference quantum dot, we identify the mechanisms driving coherent transfer of superposition states between the dot and the superconducting island. Our findings indicate that even with weak dot-superconductor coupling, the dot's charge can tunnel into the superconductor, which acts as a charge sink, while the hole returns to the dot through a distinct pathway. This research offers a new approach to investigating charge transfer mechanisms in quantum systems, with potential applications in developing hybrid quantum devices that integrate quantum dots and superconducting islands. Furthermore, this study establishes a foundation for constructing a new type of charge pump. These advances are achieved using an enhanced version of the capacitance matrix method, which enables the calculation of gate-sensing signals for complex multi-terminal devices. This theoretical framework is expected to be a highly versatile tool for analyzing charge dynamics in future quantum devices. Our results were validated using the open-source Python package PyQEC. Finally, we outline potential future extensions of this work, including the calculation of non-equilibrium charge and current distributions in quantum circuits featuring multiple quantum dots and islands. These capabilities will facilitate the design and analysis of new charge-pumping devices based on quantum dot-superconductor hybrids. Additionally, the proposed framework can be utilized to investigate the decoherence of hybrid quantum systems involving quantum dots, which is essential for advancing the field of quantum information science. To support these future directions, we have updated the PyQEC package to incorporate the ability to compute the decoherence rate of a quantum dot connected to a superconducting island, accessible via the PyQEC website. This functionality was implemented in collaboration with Dr. Alexander Blais. The package is available at https://github.com/alexanderblais/pyqec. Finally, we demonstrate the versatility of the PyQEC package by calculating the dynamical response of a capacitively-coupled double quantum dot system to a microwave pulse, a capability that will facilitate the design of new quantum information protocols. The source code for this calculation is available in the PyQEC package repository at https://github.com/alexanderblais/pyqec. This work introduces contraction conditions applicable to entropic solutions of scalar conservation laws and offers relevant findings for a scalar balance law featuring a source term. The concept of contraction is defined relative to $L^1$-functionals weighted by entropies associated with these laws. Notably, the proof demonstrates that entropic contractions imply uniqueness for scalar conservation laws. The analysis extends to scalar balance equations with source terms, where the weighting entropy is modified to incorporate the $L^1$-distance between entropies of two distinct solutions at the same time, adjusted to remain non-increasing over time. Both scenarios are addressed within a framework where entropies may be extended-valued, taking values in $(-\infty, \infty]$. Furthermore, when initial data are admissible—meaning they satisfy the contraction estimate against any entropy solution—the proofs show that any two entropic solutions must coincide. This approach unifies and streamlines existing proofs of uniqueness for entropy-admissible weak solutions in scalar conservation laws, as well as the derivation of regularity and local-in-time uniqueness for entropy-admissible weak solutions to scalar balance equations. Additionally, specific sufficient conditions for contraction are derived for both scalar conservation laws and balance equations. Finally, the theory is applied to specific scalar balance equations arising in porous medium flows, namely the Henry equation and the van Genuchten equation. For the Henry equation, the $L^1$-contraction property holds for entropy-admissible weak solutions, whereas for the van Genuchten equation, it is established that the contractivity condition is satisfied by any two entropy solutions. These findings rely on a priori estimates for entropy-admissible weak solutions, specifically the contractivity with respect to entropies, which are derived using a weighted relative entropy method. The validity of these estimates is confirmed through the construction of contraction variables. Consequently, the contractivity property for entropy-admissible weak solutions follows directly from the proof of the contraction principle. This outcome underscores the fundamental role of contractions in the theory of conservation laws and balance equations. Moreover, the proof of the contraction principle is simplified by the availability of the contraction property for entropy-admissible weak solutions. Finally, the paper concludes with remarks on the relationship between the contraction condition and the uniqueness of entropy-admissible weak solutions. These conclusions are achieved without requiring any a priori regularity assumptions on the flux function. Single-view 3D rendering, often termed perpetual view generation, aims to create new 3D images from a limited set of input views. Although recent approaches utilizing neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D diffusion models have achieved strong results, they often suffer from unreliable sampling and degraded quality. NeRF-based techniques depend on training complex scene-specific representations, which are sensitive to occlusions and produce inconsistent sampling. Conversely, 3D diffusion models, despite their global sampling capabilities, frequently generate incorrect samples. To address these issues, we introduce DiffDreamer, a novel method that enhances both the reliability and quality of sampling. First, we develop a conditional diffusion model to boost sampling reliability, achieving superior performance over state-of-the-art methods on the COLMAP benchmark. Second, we propose a two-stage training strategy that leverages the complementary advantages of NeRF and 3D diffusion models, resulting in significantly improved rendering quality. Our approach also demonstrates superior generalization on the challenging ShapeNet dataset. Project page and code are available at https://diffdreamer.github.io.

This paper introduces a data-driven prediction, optimization, and control framework designed for networked processes. The approach relies on a graph representation of these networks and utilizes a novel data-driven method to estimate the network's transition matrix. This transition matrix is subsequently used to construct network dynamics, which are applied to prediction and optimization tasks. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the application of these dynamics in controlling networked networkx processes. To validate the approach, the authors apply the model to networked Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemics and networked linear systems. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in modeling network dynamics for both the SIS epidemic model and linear systems. Additionally, the application successfully shows the control of networked SIS epidemics and systems using network networkx. The findings suggest that this approach is well-suited for network processes that exhibit linearity and local connectivity. Ultimately, the work provides a comprehensive framework for prediction, optimization, and control of networked processes that depends solely on graph information and data. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1995/DDFOC. Keywords: Data-driven, Network Process, Prediction, Optimization, Control, Network Epidemics.

This study theoretically examines the Rayleigh-Plateau instability of a viscous liquid film on a series of cylindrical fibers, accounting for differential slip at the liquid-air interface versus no-slip at the solid surface. The resulting dispersion relation for the wave speed of growing capillary waves is derived under the assumptions of high Bond number and high internal viscosity relative to external viscosity. The analysis demonstrates that slip significantly accelerates the growth rate, with the slip-enhanced growth rate scaling linearly with the ratio of slip lengths to fiber radius. Furthermore, the influence of this ratio on growth rate, wave speed, and wavelength is illustrated through numerical results. These findings are validated by an experimental investigation into the dripping of a viscous silicone oil from a series of fibers. The experimental data aligns well with the theoretical predictions, confirming that slip markedly enhances the growth rate of capillary waves and the subsequent coalescence of adjacent drops. Consequently, the filament connecting consecutive drops becomes shorter, leading to a more prolate droplet shape. The proposed theoretical model is applicable to any viscous liquid film where partial slip occurs at the internal solid boundary while differential no-slip and slip conditions exist differentially at the liquid-air interface. Such scenarios are relevant in various industrial and biological contexts, such as liquid films on fiber bundles or within blood capillaries. Additionally, the study addresses the drop detachment process, showing that increased slip accelerates detachment. This has potential implications for controlling droplet size and optimizing coating processes. Finally, the analysis indicates that the entire dripping process is governed by capillary and viscous forces, rendering surface tension the sole relevant length scale. Thus, the theory is broadly applicable to any viscous liquid film where the Bond number is sufficiently high. These insights are particularly pertinent to understanding the dripping behavior of viscous substances like saliva, which plays a crucial role in the transmission of pathogens. Understanding the factors influencing droplet size and shape is essential for mitigating disease transmission. The theoretical framework presented in this work is based on the high Bond number and local analysis of Rayleigh-Plateau instability. Future research could extend the theory to cases with low Bond numbers and explore the effect of fiber elasticity on droplet formation. Additionally, the impact of shear flow on droplet formation warrants further investigation. These extensions could enhance our understanding of droplet formation in various industrial and biological systems. Finally, the theoretical model can be utilized to predict the impact of surface hydrophobicity on droplet formation, which is critical for the design of self-cleaning surfaces. This paper investigates the initial-boundary value problem for the Hunter-Saxton model. We demonstrate that the model exhibits local Lipschitz stability in the Sobolev space $H^1(\mathbb{R})$. Furthermore, our model is confirmed to be Lipschitz stable for periodic initial data belonging to $H^1(\mathbb{R})$. These findings represent the first establishment of stability for the Hunter-Saxton model within Sobolev spaces. Additionally, we obtain corresponding stability results for periodic boundary conditions. Our methodology relies on a novel a priori estimate derived from an integral identity. Finally, we present a global existence theorem for initial data satisfying $u_0 \in H^2(\mathbb{R})$. The outcomes regarding global existence and stability under periodic boundary conditions are novel and mark the first proof of the well-posedness of the Hunter-Saxton model in $H^2(\mathbb{R})$. Notably, the techniques employed in this work are applicable to other evolution equations, such as the Camassa-Holm equation. Given the model's significance in both theoretical and applied mathematics, these results hold substantial practical value. To facilitate future research, we have provided a comprehensive set of a priori estimates alongside their complete derivations. This paper serves as a foundation for the theses of both authors. Specifically, the first author completed their doctoral dissertation under a periodic setting, while the second author completed their doctoral work in a whole space context; consequently, the theoretical results presented here differ slightly from those in their respective dissertations. Finally, we acknowledge that our primary objective was to prove stability, so we did not pursue the sharpness of the result. We intend to address this in subsequent research. **Background:** Ultrasound (US) imaging is increasingly utilized in clinical practice for diagnosing and monitoring scoliosis. However, the efficiency of scoliosis assessment via US relies on both the reliability of robotic systems and the expertise of operators. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of robotic US imaging for scoliosis evaluation compared to manual scanning.

**Methods:** The reproducibility of robotic US imaging for scoliosis was assessed in 20 scoliosis patients. Using a US robotic system, each patient underwent three consecutive scans, and the inter-scan reliability was quantified by calculating the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC). Additionally, the effectiveness of robotic US imaging in scoliosis assessment was compared against manual scanning. Ten patients were recruited, and each participant received 10 manual scans performed by an experienced operator. The correlation between manual and robotic US measurements was calculated using the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC).

**Results:** The average ICC for robotic US imaging was 0.92 ± 0.04, indicating high reproducibility. The average CCC for the comparison between manual and robotic US was 0.87 ± 0.05, demonstrating a strong correlation.

**Conclusion:** The findings suggest that robotic US imaging offers a reliable and effective approach to scoliosis assessment when compared to traditional manual scanning techniques. Consequently, robotic US imaging shows significant potential for clinical application in scoliosis evaluation. Future research should expand the sample size and incorporate comparisons with other scoliosis assessment methods, such as X-ray and MRI.

**Key Words:** scoliosis, ultrasound, reliability, robotic system.

Accurately generating speech duration traces is essential for Speech Synthesis systems to produce natural-sounding output. This study explores a non-parametric method for duration prediction that leverages linguistic features and previous word durations. The approach employs a conditional duration generator informed by the current word and an additional generator for the subsequent word. To enhance naturalness, the model incorporates a conditional generator for the final word in a sentence. By utilizing these integrated models, the paper demonstrates how to construct a synthetic median duration curve. Evaluations using both automatic metrics and human assessments reveal that the proposed non-parametric method surpasses a parametric alternative, with human ratings indicating superior performance. Furthermore, listeners perceive sentences synthesized with the median curve as more natural than those generated using the parametric approach. Finally, the study illustrates how the synthetic median curve can be integrated into a speech synthesis system. When the median curve is applied, the resulting synthesized speech is judged by humans to be more natural than the baseline parametric version. However, no significant differences were found between the natural and synthetic median curves based on either automatic evaluation or human perception. Overall, this work highlights the benefits of employing a synthetic duration curve to enhance the naturalness of synthesized speech. The paper concludes by discussing the advantages and limitations of the proposed method and suggesting future research directions. The molecular continuum is an emerging concept that extends the molecular graph approach to model the distant and diffuse regions of molecules. By applying physical laws to the data of the outermost electronic shell, this continuum seamlessly integrates with the atomic core, thereby unifying current descriptive methods for near and distant molecular regions. However, due to their physicochemical origins, molecular graphs and the molecular continuum exist as separate entities that require a specific interface to merge into a cohesive framework. This study introduces a method for defining a continuum across multiple atoms to facilitate such integration. The approach is validated through an analysis of the geometric properties of the sodium dimer. Ultimately, this work paves the way for a more comprehensive and accurate topology theory applicable to the entire molecule. Additionally, the research explores the potential for a new type of molecular descriptor. A resolving set for a graph $G$ is defined as a vertex set $R$ such that every vertex $v$ outside $R$ has a distinct distance vector to the elements of $R. The minimum size of such a set is termed the metric dimension of $G$, denoted by $\beta_d(G)$. This paper presents an exact formula for $\beta_d(G)$ when $G$ consists of a directed cycle with an attached graph. Leveraging this formula, we develop a feedback vertex set parameterized algorithm for graphs $G$ with a feedback vertex set of size $k$, achieving a running time of $O^*(2^k)$. Furthermore, we establish that the problem is fixed-parameter intractable when parameterized by clique-width, tree-depth, or path-width. Finally, we demonstrate a fixed-parameter intractability result based on the size of a minimum vertex cover. The latter conclusion follows from a more general finding: for any integer $t \geq 1$, determining the metric dimension is fixed-parameter intractable when parameterized by the minimum number of vertices required to reduce the graph to one with a maximum degree of at most $t$. Additionally, we prove fixed-parameter intractability under the parameters of maximum matching size, maximum edge-disjoint cycle packing size, and maximum branch-packing size. Notably, the fixed-parameter intractability with respect to clique, tree, and path-width is derived from the minimum vertex cover parameter, meaning no separate proofs are required for these specific cases. Finally, we examine the metric dimension of graphs formed by the disjoint union of $n$ graphs, showing that computing it is NP-hard even when each component graph contains at most one edge. However, we also provide an algorithm with a running time of $O(n^{t+1})$ for determining the metric dimension of the disjoint union of $n$ graphs, where $t$ represents the metric dimension of the sum of their metric dimension and domination numbers. Furthermore, the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the disjoint union of $n$ graphs' domination numbers. Lastly, the graph annihilation number is defined as the smallest size of a vertex set whose removal reduces the connected components to an acyclic graph. We show that the metric dimension problem is fixed-parameter intractable when parameterized by the graph annihilation number. In the final section, we explore the metric dimension of graphs $G$ containing a large clique, proving fixed-parameter intractability for parameters including clique number

We extend the theory of power domains to directed metric approximation spaces, specifically focusing on the approximations of directed metric spaces, which generalizes the concept of directed complete metric spaces. We demonstrate that both lower and upper power constructions satisfy the four fundamental axioms for power frameworks. Additionally, we show that lower and upper powers derived from the topological and Hausdorff- Hausdorff completions of directed sets align with those from the directed metric approximation spaces of the original set. Leveraging these observations, we present directed metric spaces that demonstrate the existence of power frameworks that cannot be realized within the scope of directed complete metric spaces. Furthermore, we prove that for any directed set, its lower power is homeomorphic to the space of lower sets within its upper power. Finally, we examine the topological characteristics of lower and upper powers of specific examples, including digital intervals, directed subsets of Euclidean spaces, and directed metric spaces modeling various types of networks. These findings highlight the utility of powers in digital topology, the topology of specialized domains, and the topology of networks. Notably, our results indicate that lower powers of directed metric approximation spaces of digital images may fail to be discrete, even when the original space is discrete. This reveals a significant distinction between discrete sets and discrete metric spaces, as well as between discrete topological spaces and discrete metric spaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that the lower power of a compact directed metric approximation space is compact, whereas the lower power of a compact directed set may lack compactness. These findings have implications for the topology of digital images and the topology of compact domains. Specifically, our findings regarding the non-compactness of the lower power of a compact directed set suggest that the lower power of a digital image could be non-compact, implying that the topology of lower sets of digital images may differ from that of the image itself. This contrasts with the case of compact directed metric spaces, where the lower power of a digital image is known to be compact. Consequently, our findings suggest that the topology of digital images may be more complex than previously thought, potentially necessitating the use of digital approximation spaces rather than discrete sets for the study of digital topology. This could have significant implications for the theory of digital topology. Finally, we show that lower and upper powers of directed metric approximation spaces can be non-Hausdorff, even when the original space is Hausdorff. This contrasts with the case of discrete sets, where powers are always Hausdorff, and implies that the theory of powers may require revision when applied to digital approximation

As planetary temperatures rise, the frequency of precipitation events is expected to increase. This study examines how the occurrence of extreme precipitation events (EPEs) evolves as a function of temperature in simulated hothouse climates. Utilizing the Community Climate System Model version 3 (CCSM3) under high CO2 concentrations, we analyzed a temperature range spanning from 340 K to 400 K. Results indicate that the frequency of EPEs rises with temperature, with a particularly steep increase observed between 340 K and 360 K. Furthermore, the relationship between EPE frequency and temperature is found to be independent of the specific CO2 levels. These findings are interpreted through the lens of the Precipitation-Temperature (P-T) relation, which describes how precipitation rates vary with temperature in a climate at radiative equilibrium. We demonstrate that the accelerating slope of the P-T relation at higher temperatures drives the observed rise in EPE frequency. Consequently, the rate of change in EPE frequency is directly linked to the rate of change in the P-T relation's slope. These conclusions are supported by an analytical model of EPE frequency, which incorporates the P-T relation, the vertical structure of the atmosphere, and the vertical profile of temperature changes. The model accurately replicates the numerical model's results across the entire temperature spectrum. Ultimately, this research confirms that the P-T relation serves as a robust predictor for the frequency of extreme precipitation events in hothouse conditions. This insight is crucial for anticipating how Earth's hydrological cycle may respond to global warming. Deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable success in medical image classification, yet they are highly susceptible to label noise, which can severely impair their performance. Although various label denoising techniques exist, they often demand substantial computational resources or specialized hardware. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective strategy to reduce the impact of noisy labels during training. Our approach leverages Bayesian statistics to design a mechanism that periodically refreshes labels based on the model's confidence in previous predictions. By integrating this method with the Graph Label Propagation algorithm, we demonstrate that it significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art denoising methods. Our results indicate that the proposed technique is both computationally efficient and effective, yielding substantial improvements in the accuracy of deep learning models for medical image classification. Extensive experiments on two public datasets confirm the superiority of our method over current state-of-the-art approaches. This paper introduces a novel method for calculating transition probabilities $P_{ij}^{(t)}$ within the standard basis framework of a simple associated random walk on a graph. We express $P_{ij}^{(t)}$ as a determinant involving a matrix $A_{ij}^{(t)}$, where the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian are essential to the definition of $A_{ij}^{(t)}$. We investigate self-dual vortex solutions within the V-model framework of a Born-Infeld type of p-form Skyrme model. Specifically, we present self-dual solutions featuring arbitrary topological charge $n$ and investigate their stability. Given that this is a non-linear field theory, we demonstrate that its dual form is also highly non-linear, indicating that the conditions for self-duality are not straightforward to satisfy. Furthermore, we establish that no self-dual solution with topological charge $n$ can exist if the $U(1)$ charge is fixed at $m$. Finally, our analysis of stability reveals that all known self-dual solutions are stable. In the context of the "V-model," the Skyrme term simplifies to a sum of squares, a feature that significantly facilitates the determination of both self-duality and stability conditions. Consequently, this model serves as an effective laboratory for exploring self-duality and stability across various non-linear field theories. Additionally, we outline a method for numerically solving such theories when the Skyrme term is not expressible as a sum of squares. Our findings regarding self-duality and stability are expected to be applicable to a broad spectrum of non-linear field theories. This Hofstadter Weyl metal features four Weyl points, which are the intersections of the lowest Landau bands of opposite chirality in momentum space. These points arise in pairs at the edges of the Brillouin zone, aligned with the field direction, and can be interpreted as Landau levels with zero index (LZLs) of opposite chirality at the boundaries of the Hofstadter supercell. The field direction serves as the normal vector to the momentum plane containing these LZLs. The positions of the Weyl points remain stable as long as the supercell dimensions stay constant, even if the field directions are interchanged. Furthermore, the spectral gaps between Hofstadert LZLs are determined by the product of the field strengths, not their specific orientation relative to the Brillouin zone. Optimizing the dielectric particle's size and position relative to the plasmonic nanoparticle allows the hybrid structure to emit light at the same frequency as the plasmonic resonance, but with superior light extraction efficiency. This approach enables the creation of a new class of nanoantennas that facilitate efficient, unidirectional, and luminous energy and light emission.
