To elucidate this behavior, we conduct discrete element method (DEM) simulations that confirm the experimental findings. Crucially, a novel theoretical framework is introduced to derive a comprehensive set of balance equations from first principles, incorporating a nonlocal term in the stress tensor. This nonlocal component stems from a bias in particle velocity distributions and is directly calculated using specific particle-scale parameters. Both numerical simulations and experiments validate the resulting extended anomalous balance equations, demonstrating that the stress-level dependent velocity distribution bias is the primary driver of the anomalous screening effect. Consequently, this research establishes a rigorous kinetic theory for granular matter that accounts for nonlocal stress effects. The developed model is designed to be computationally efficient, facilitating its application in large-scale direct numerical simulations of complex granular flows. Furthermore, the model's general framework can be extended to incorporate other significant microscopic details, such as particle rotation and shear-induced segregation. Finally, the model's predictive capabilities are leveraged to forecast the rheological response of granular matter under high-frequency vibrations. These findings provide a robust foundation for future research into granular matter physics, enabling the systematic design of granular systems with tailored rheological properties. Additionally, the proposed framework is applicable to other complex media, including biological fluids and colloidal suspensions. All findings are supported by comprehensive supplementary data. Sgr A East, situated in the Galactic Center, is a remnant nebula lacking a visible supernova (SN) site. This study investigates the age and origin of Sgr A East by analyzing its morphology and comparing it with supernova models. We determined an age of $2.6^{+0.7}_{-0.5}$ kyr using the Rayleigh criterion and the ratio of the shell's thickness to its radius. By employing 3D hydrodynamical simulations of supernovae within a dense molecular cloud, we identified the optimal explosion site. Our findings indicate that the supernova likely exploded within 0.1 pc of the Galactic Center. Furthermore, the interaction between the supernova remnant and dense molecular material may have shielded Sgr A East from the supermassive black hole's intense X-ray radiation. Finally, we propose that the Sgr A East nebula was formed by a Type Ia supernova. These results offer a comprehensive framework for understanding the origin of Sgr A East and its subsequent evolution. Our methodology can be applied to other nebulae to determine their origins. The primary goal of text classification is to assign a topic or category to a text based on its content. In practical scenarios, sufficient data often exists for the majority of categories, while some remain underrepresented. This imbalance can hinder models from learning the characteristics of rare categories. This study evaluates four strategies for generating synthetic data to address imbalanced multi-class text classification. Experiments were conducted using a classifier and four datasets derived from the SemEval-2016 Task 11. The findings indicate that back-translation is the most effective approach for multi-label classification. Conversely, when treating the multi-label task as a multi-class one, all four synthetic overampling methods yielded improved results. Ultimately, the simplest technique—random sampling—proved to be the most effective for balancing a multi-class dataset. This suggests that leveraging existing data is a viable and practical solution for various text classification tasks. Finally, the authors seek to collaborate on implementing pre-trained language models for multi-class and multi-label classification to enhance performance. This study examines the relationship between local news online (LNO) consumption, COVID-19 metrics including cases, fatalities, and audience engagement, utilizing U.S. county-level data. We construct a panel of U.S. counties and track the evolution of various LNO indicators from 2019 to 2020. Our findings indicate that higher LNO presence correlates with reduced COVID-19 cases and deaths, whereas increased LNO LNO audience attention is associated with higher case counts and at-risk populations. Additionally, we observe that counties with greater LNO LNO audience reach demonstrate more favorable outcomes regarding COVID-19 mortality rates. These results remain robust across multiple model specifications and control variables. Our conclusions suggest that local news online can serve as a valuable instrument for disseminating critical health information, potentially aiding in the containment of future pandemics. Finally, we offer policy recommendations for news organizations to enhance their public service roles during crises. Given the significance of these findings, we anticipate that our methodology and data will inspire further research into the impact of news media on public health.

The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is a fundamental technique for accelerating the calculation of pairwise interactions, which are common in physics simulations. However, the basic FMM approach is not entirely exact and suffers from both accuracy and efficiency limitations. The approximate FMM (AFFM) enhances speed by exploiting the asymptotic behavior of the Green function, while the hierarchical FMM (HFM) improves upon this by retaining higher-order terms to achieve greater precision. This study demonstrates that, when properly implemented, the L2-norm conservation of angular momentum in AFFM and HFM matches that of the exact method. Furthermore, we establish the exact conservation laws for the energy and center of mass within these algorithms. Finally, we validate these theoretical findings using a test case involving a collection of point particles. Our results indicate that both the theoretical and numerical computations for angular momentum conservation in AFFM and HFM align perfectly with the exact calculations. Additionally, our numerical analysis confirms that both methods maintain the exact conservation of angular momentum across all time steps. Finally, we illustrate that both AFFM and HFM achieve the same order of accuracy as the exact method. Notably, HFM demonstrates superior performance compared to AFFM. These findings are corroborated by numerical tests conducted on a collection of particles. All code required to reproduce these results is publicly accessible. Specifically, the code for calculating the L2-norm conservation of angular momentum is available at \url{https://github.com/akshaykumar2001/FMM/tree/master/Angular_Momentum_Conservation}, and the code for computing energy and center of mass conservation is available at \url{https://github.com/akshaykumar2001/FMM/tree/master/Center_of_Mass_and_Energy_Conservation}. Both repositories also include a test case for AFFM and HFM. This study examines two distinct proton polarization configurations relative to the scattering plane: longitudinal and transverse. Our results indicate that the proton polarization component perpendicular to the initial target polarization lies in the scattering plane; specifically, the transverse proton polarization component parallel to the scattered electron direction exhibits a notable dependence on the scattered electron angle. Experts in a specific domain often possess valuable but incomplete information, which can be formalized as a probabilistic model defining their knowledge. This paper introduces a method for automatically generating synthetic data from experts by sampling from their underlying distribution. This approach enables supervised learning using only expert queries, eliminating the need for human annotation. We validate this technique across various domains, demonstrating that it facilitates rapid deployment of models trained solely on expert-derived data. This study investigates Higgs boson pair production occurring in association with either a single vector boson (W or Z) or a pair of jets (VBF or QQ). Under the Standard Model framework, the observed (expected) upper limit for the Higgs boson pair production cross section is determined to be 3.2 (2.9) times that of double Higgs boson production. Furthermore, constraints on various new physics models are derived. In a scenario involving a light scalar produced via gluon fusion and decaying into Higgs bosons, the production cross section is constrained to be less than 1100 (700) fb. For a vector-like top quark model, the lower bound on its mass is found to be greater than 800 (750) GeV, assuming a branching fraction of 50% for its decay into the Standard Model top quark and a new, heavier top quark. Finally, the search for pair production of a new CP-odd Higgs boson yields a lower mass limit of 450 (400) GeV when considering its decay into a pair of photons. We introduce a protocol for generating a polarized thermal mixture of $^{133}$Cs atoms within an optical dipole trap using a laser tuned to excite hyperfine transition $|F=4, m_{F}=4\rangle \leftrightarrow |F=5, m_{F}=5\rangle$. Thermalization is achieved through evaporative cooling with a trap depth significantly lower than the laser detuning, preventing scattering losses while allowing control over atom number. Hyperfine and magnetic sublevel polarization are maintained by tuning the laser frequency and trap center relative to a 5 G/cm$^2$ magnetic field. The resulting atoms, confined in traps with radii as small as 10 $\mu$m, constitute a "spin laser." This device offers a stable, high-flux source of atoms in a hyperfine and magnetic sublevel specific spin state, suitable for applications in quantum information, atom interferometry, and cold atom chemistry. Furthermore, these spin-laser atoms can be directly loaded into standing-wave optical optical-lattice clocks. We also outline a method to generate lattices of atoms in the $|F=4, m_{F}=4\rangle$ state, which exhibit splitting due to dipole-dipole interactions, for use in spin-exchange optical lattice clocks. This system, capable of operating in the 5 D/cm$^2$ regime, can also function as a source of spin-squeezed states. This study examines the stability of neutralinos as dark matter candidates, with particular focus on scenarios where they decay into dark matter particles. By analyzing the decay of light and resonant neutralinos, we investigate decay channels involving dark photons, dark matter, and their lighter fermionic or bosonic supersymmetric partners. We demonstrate the existence of a effective polynomial-time approximation scheme (EPSAS) for the function $n\mapsto \textsf{genus}_n(\alpha)$, which denotes the minimum genus of a graph on $n$ vertices with a density approaching $\alpha\in (0,1]$. This function is monotonically decreasing and concave. Our approach is grounded in a recent random graph result by Krivelevich and Yehudiy [J. Eur. Math. Soc. 2020], which we apply to construct a graph family with precisely calculable genera. Furthermore, we establish that the EPSAS is indeed achievable. This finding complements our prior joint work with Krivelevich and Yehudiy [arXiv:2001.00300], which utilized EPSAS to derive significant bounds regarding the asymptotic behavior of the maximum genus of graphs with a specified density. Additionally, we provide an explicit upper bound for $\textsf{genus}_n(\alpha)$ and propose a conjecture that would allow for the calculation of an exact asymptotic formula. We demonstrate that this conjecture holds true for the case where $\alpha=2/3$. Finally, we present an EPSAS for the function $n\mapsto \textsf{nonplanar}_n(\alpha)$, representing the proportion of graphs on $n$ vertices that possess a genus of at most $\alpha\binom{n}{2}$. This resolves a question posed by Krivelevich and Yehudiy [arXiv:2001.00300]. Our findings are achieved through a combination of probabilistic and constructive methods. Specifically, we employ the probabilistic method to derive sharp asymptotic bounds, while the construction technique involves modifying Krivelevich and Yehudiy's random graph model to facilitate the calculation of genera. This paper is an expanded and refined version of our earlier study [arXiv:2001.00300]. This paper introduces a stochastic Newton approach designed for large-scale distributed convex optimization. Building on recent advances in parallel Newton techniques, the method leverages specific problem structures—such as the separability of objective and constraint functions—to minimize communication overhead between workers and a master node. Concurrently, it addresses computational limits by executing multiple iterations on each node before sharing results, thereby generating a biased yet diminishing estimate of the Hessian. We analyze the convergence properties of this algorithm under conditions where both noise and bias in the Hessian estimates are non-zero. The study incorporates both synchronous and asynchronous execution models and demonstrates that the method achieves an $O(1/k)$ convergence rate, indicating $k$ iterations are necessary to reach a first-order optimality measure of $1/k$. This performance matches that of full Newton methods and surpasses existing stochastic Newton, proximal bundle, and proximal gradient linearized BFGS (PG-LBFGS) for quadratic programs. Additionally, we present a parallel implementation capable of running multiple subproblems on worker nodes and evaluate the approach on real-world datasets. The results highlight the method's superior scalability and reduced runtime compared to current state-of-the-art solutions. Finally, experimental comparisons with a custom asynchronous implementation confirm the advantages of synchronous execution in this context. Finally, we compare our proposed approach with PG-LBFGS, demonstrating its superior performance. This study introduces the world's first publicly available dataset for detecting hate speech in Hindi and Bengali, a task previously unexplored. We developed this dataset by aggregating data from two English sources, employing a multilingual approach to ensure cultural relevance. The resulting collection features carefully screened and verified examples of hate speech alongside instances of non-hate speech. We subsequently trained various neural network models on this data and assessed their performance on both datasets. Additionally, we investigated transfer learning by utilizing pre-trained Indic language models, RoBERTa-IN and BERT-IN, which yielded significant improvements in performance. Our analysis indicates that transfer learning has substantially reduced the gap between non-hate and hate speech classifications in both languages. The data can be accessed at https://github.com/abhishekgupta12345/Indic-Hate-Speech-Detection. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishekgupta12345/Indic-Hate-Speech-Detection. This work was conducted while the first author was a student at the University of Central Florida. The second author is currently a student at IIT Delhi, and the third author is a faculty member at IIT Delhi. Correspondence regarding this work should be directed to abhishekgupta12345@gmail.com. Keywords: HATE SPEECH DETECTION, HINDI, BENGALI, NLP, NEURAL NETWORKS, TRANSFER LEARNING.

A time projection chamber (TPC) is a particle detector that utilizes a gas medium to trace the paths of charged particles. By combining drift time measurements with two-dimensional spatial data from a readout plane, a third dimension is derived from the drift time of ionization electrons. Gas TPCs offer superior particle tracking resolution compared to other technologies, though they historically suffer from limited readout granularity. The recent introduction of high-definition gas TPCs, featuring a readout plane with a pixel density roughly 100 times greater than earlier versions, enables new experimental avenues. These include enhanced pattern recognition, track reconstruction, and vertex finding capabilities. This paper introduces novel observables for the high-definition Bullpad TPC, designed to identify and characterize ionization ion tracks by analyzing energy and momentum conservation. These new methods aim to improve the precision of position reconstruction, track finding, and vertex reconstruction. Furthermore, these techniques are applicable to other physics scenarios, such as dark matter searches, where they could aid in distinguishing signal from background. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods using data from a $^7$Be $\beta^+$ decay source. The results show that track reconstruction accuracy is significantly improved, with position resolution reaching approximately 100 $\mu$m. Additionally, we present results for a Dalitz plot reconstruction of the $\beta^+$ decay, achieving an energy resolution of roughly 1%. These findings indicate the potential of high-definition gas TPCs to achieve unprecedented levels of tracking precision. Finally, we discuss the applicability of these techniques to future experiments, specifically the XENONnD dark matter search. In this context, we demonstrate that the proposed techniques can achieve a signal reconstruction resolution of approximately 1 keVee, which is comparable to the detector's energy resolution. This suggests that these methods could significantly enhance the ability to distinguish WIMP signals from background noise in such experiments. Keywords: Gas TPCs, Track Reconstruction, Vertex Reconstruction, Dark Matter Detection. PACS numbers: 29.40.Hs, 29.30.Nx, 29.30.Kv, 29.40.Lw. This study examines the use of machine outputs for evaluating performance in commercial driving. It presents a new approach to assessing these outputs through a two-stage top-tier driver rating system. The first stage involves an AI algorithm that generates performance scores and a set of indicators designed to assist human moderators in the subsequent evaluation. The second stage consists of expert moderators who review the AI-generated scores and indicators to make a final decision. The authors assess the fairness and accuracy of this novel assessment framework. To ensure fairness, the indicators proposed by the AI are selected based on their ability to assist human moderators. To evaluate accuracy, the performance of this new system is compared against baseline methods. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed two-stage system achieves a higher rate of correct ratings compared to baseline approaches, thereby enhancing the overall fairness of the assessment process. Furthermore, this system is more scalable than baseline methods, making it particularly suitable for the large-scale assessment of commercial drivers. The methodology and findings can be applied to other rating tasks involving machine outputs. Additionally, the authors have made their code and data available on GitHub to facilitate the reproduction of these results. Finally, the code is open-source, allowing for the replication of the experiments and the customization of the proposed rating system. Keywords: Intelligent Transportation Systems, Machine Learning, Assessment, Expert Moderation, Commercial Driving.

In recent years, Gaussian random fields have gained significant traction within the machine learning community. This paper examines the application of manifold learning to Gaussian random fields by deriving the geodesic equation on these manifolds. We demonstrate that the geodesic distance between two points represents the minimum distance required to transform one mean function into another, utilizing growth rates characterized by both polynomial and exponential behaviors. Furthermore, we establish that as the dimensionality of the Gaussian random field increases, the random field converges to a free manifold. Finally, numerical simulations are employed to validate the theoretical findings presented in this study. Our work aims to facilitate the investigation of manifold properties within the context of machine learning. Additionally, Python code implementing the algorithms described in this paper will be made available. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/ahmetkarakus/geodesic-random-field. A video of the presentation is also available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=42222222222. Geometric properties of random fields have garnered substantial interest in the field of statistics. This study seeks to extend existing research by employing a machine learning approach. Specifically, we investigate geodesic paths and associated distances between two point sets. Our methodology relies on the concept of measuring the distance between two mean functions. This approach is highly relevant to machine learning, where the primary objective is to identify the optimal model that best approximates a given function. To achieve this, we require the ability to quantify the discrepancy between two functions. This paper addresses the challenge of determining the shortest path between two mean functions. Our methodology involves applying manifold learning to Gaussian random fields. We derive the geodesic equation and calculate the associated cost function. The cost function is defined as the expected value of the norm of the difference between two functions. The optimal solution to this cost function yields the shortest path between the two mean functions. This research is grounded in the principle that the distance between two functions can be defined as the expected value of the norm of their difference. This concept is widely utilized in machine learning to quantify function discrepancies. Our findings indicate that the geodesic distance between two functions exhibits polynomial growth rates. Additionally, we observe that Gaussian random fields approach a free manifold as the number of basis functions increases. These results have significant implications for manifold learning. Our work contributes to the broader field of manifold learning by elucidating the geometric properties of Gaussian random fields. The paper is structured into two sections. The first section introduces Gaussian random fields and their fundamental characteristics.

We examine a real-time algorithm designed for string pattern matching, defined by the property that for any string $T$ of length $n$ and pattern $P$ of length $m$, the algorithm completes in $O(mn)$ time. This approach necessitates $O(mn)$ space and utilizes heuristics to accelerate pattern matching when $m$ is significantly smaller than $n$. Although such real-time methods have existed since the 1970s, the specific variant presented here has only emerged within the last few years. Despite its recent formulation, this algorithm is notably efficient, as is its naturally dual application to text compression. In this compressive context, a dictionary of $m$-mers is constructed for a given text $T$, resulting in a compression ratio of $n/(mn) = 1/m$ when $m \ll n$. Furthermore, our algorithm can be interpreted as length-based pattern matching, where the goal is to identify all occurrences of pattern lengths within $T$. This perspective enables the development of a real-time movie for length-based pattern matching that mirrors the text compression movie derived from the algorithm's dual role. This work extends the length counts method, originally proposed by Crochemore et al. (2001), and builds upon the length-based pattern matching framework established by Crochemore and Lecroq (2004). The resulting method is highly practical, offering real-time performance with $O(mn)$ space requirements. Additionally, it serves as a powerful tool for text compression, supporting a dictionary size as small as one-tenth that of the text. Furthermore, the movie for length-based pattern matching can be derived from the text compression movie, which itself is a real-time algorithm capable of performing both pattern matching and text compression simultaneously. Consequently, this approach is both highly practical and effective, with the text compression movie functioning as a real-time algorithm for both tasks. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the existence of a real-time movie for length-based pattern matching, thereby completing the full set of movies for this problem. Notably, the text compression movie stands out as the only real-time algorithm that simultaneously addresses both pattern matching and text compression. This achievement underscores the existence of a text compression movie that is both real-time and comprehensive, fulfilling all four dimensions of the text compression problem. The text compression movie represents the culmination of efforts to develop a real-time algorithm capable of handling pattern matching, text compression, dictionary size, and dictionary size relative to the text. This study investigates spin-dependent transport within armchair graphene nanoribbon (GNR) structures by applying a simultaneous, staggered, and tunable electric field. By adjusting the field strength, one can selectively activate or deactivate a quantum phase transition (QPT) between the filled and empty subbands, thereby enabling precise management of electron transmission. These findings not only deepen the understanding of spin-dependent transport mechanisms in GNRs but also highlight the potential for developing efficient spin devices using this material system. Furthermore, the research suggests the creation of new devices, such as spin filters, by incorporating additional gating to fine-tune the applied electric field. Finally, the study explores the design of a controllable spin oscillator based on GNRs, which could serve as a promising component for future spintronic applications. All simulations were conducted using the tight-binding model. These results are expected to inspire further investigations into spin-dependent transport phenomena in graphene-based nanoribbons. The source code for this research can be accessed at: https://github.com/abdullah-aydin/Spin-Filter-and-Oscillator-Graphene-Nanoribbons. Additionally, the accompanying video is available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. Keywords: Graphene nanoribbons, Spin filter, Spin oscillator, Quantum phase transition, Tight-binding model, First-principles calculations.

This study establishes Korovkin-style theorems concerning the weak convergence of operator sequences acting on Banach spaces of continuous functions. These sequences involve monotone operators that may be weakly nonlinear; such concepts are frequently encountered in the analysis of nonlinear partial differential equations. The resulting theorems provide a unified framework for various results found in existing literature. Furthermore, the proof method can be extended to broader contexts, including vector-valued function settings. An application demonstrating the utility of these findings in nonlinear PDE analysis is included. The findings of this work have also been generalized to higher dimensions by other researchers. Additionally, the concepts employed here find application in the theory of generalized difference operators. This generalization is essential for addressing problems in fractional calculus, a field that has seen significant recent growth. The theoretical framework is also valuable for investigating the convergence of finite difference schemes used to solve nonlinear PDEs. Specifically, it aids in analyzing the local stability and convergence of finite difference methods applied to nonlinear problems. This includes schemes for finding weak solutions to equations like the Hamilton–Jacobi equation, the Burgers equation, and the porous medium equation. The analysis of these schemes often relies on weak compactness arguments and monotonicity properties inherent to the difference operators. This paper establishes the theoretical foundation for these approaches, which are elaborated upon in a related work. Finally, the methods are also applicable to the analysis of the convergence rate of these schemes. This aspect is explored in another related study. Collectively, these works offer a comprehensive theoretical basis for analyzing the convergence of finite difference schemes for nonlinear PDEs, a topic that has received substantial attention over the past few decades. The relevance of these results is underscored by the fact that numerous significant problems in applied mathematics rely on PDEs featuring nonlinear operators. Examples include the Navier–Stokes equations, the Schrödinger equation, the Yamabe equation, the Monge–Ampère equation, the Euler–Lagrange equation, the Ricci flow equation, and the Ricci soliton equation. The analysis of the convergence rate for finite difference schemes addressing these equations has been extensively studied in the literature. This work contributes to that area by providing a rigorous theoretical foundation. Specifically, it establishes the conditions required to derive quantitative error estimates for the convergence rate of finite difference schemes for nonlinear PDEs. This achievement is realized through the application of the theory of monotone operators and the theory of $\alpha$-concave functionals. A graph $G$ is defined as independent-$\theta$-free if the count of independent sets within $G$ does not exceed $\theta$. This paper demonstrates that for any $\theta \geq \binom{n-1}{2}$, a connected, pancyclic, independent-$\theta$-free graph $G$ of order $n$ must be Hamiltonian. Furthermore, even when $\theta \geq \frac{(n-1)^2}{4} + 1$ and $G$ is assumed to be 2-connected, the same conclusion holds. The study also examines the conditions under which the second assertion remains valid in the absence of the pancyclicity requirement. Additionally, the authors establish a sufficient condition ensuring that $G$ contains a path of every length ranging from $2$ to $n$. These findings extend and refine numerous related results presented in the paper. A comprehensive survey of existing literature regarding the Hamiltonicity of independent-$theta$-free graphs is included as an appendix. Specifically, the appendix addresses the validity and associated conditions of independence number constraints for various types of $\theta$-graphs. Finally, the appendix concludes with a detailed discussion of the conditions required for the strong conjecture by Chvátal and Hammer concerning the sufficiency of the condition $\theta \geq \binom{n-1}{2}$ to guarantee Hamiltonicity in $G$. This discussion further clarifies the relationship between the independence count condition and Chvátal and Hammer's condition, ultimately demonstrating that the former is a stronger condition than the latter. Additionally, the appendix provides examples of $\theta$-graphs where both the independence number of $G$ and the size of the largest independent set in $G$ are strictly less than $\theta$. These examples illustrate that the conditions proposed by Chvátal and Hammer are not sufficient to ensure Hamiltonicity in $G$ when $\theta \geq \binom{n-1}{2}$. The appendix concludes with several open problems and a bibliography of relevant literature. The bibliography includes a detailed discussion of Hamiltonian graph theory, the history of the Hamiltonian problem, and the history of Chvátal and Hammer's conjecture. It also references independent-$\theta$-free graphs, $\theta$-graphs, Hamiltonian graph theory, Hamiltonian cycle conditions, and the history of Hamiltonian cycle conditions. Additionally, the bibliography covers Hamiltonian graph theory, the Hamiltonian problem, the Hamiltonian cycle problem, the pancyclic problem

This study examines the directed flow of forward and backward luminosity hadrons as a function of transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$) and centrality, derived from relativistic heavy-ion collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}=19.6$ GeV. The data originate from the Forward Silicon Vertex Tracker (sVNT) and Forward Calorimeter (FEMC) at the Normal Energy Beam Energy Facility (nSTAR), utilizing Au+Au collisions across $10 \leq p_{\mathrm{T}} \leq 10$ GeV/$c$ and 0–60% centrality, alongside isobar collisions for $2 \leq p_{\mathrm{T}} \leq 6$ GeV/$c$ at 0–20% centrality. Theoretical frameworks incorporating hydrodynamics, hydro+ray, and hydro+Glauber models are employed to interpret these findings. Results indicate that forward $\pi^{\pm}$ exhibit opposite directed motion compared to neutral and charged pions, with a notable shift in the momentum range $4 \leq p_{\mathrm{T}} \leq 6$ GeV/$c$ where the sign of the directed flow reverses. Furthermore, the directed flow of forward $\pi^{\pm}$ demonstrates a stronger dependence on centrality than that of neutral pions. Theoretical predictions align well with the observed directed flow of forward $\pi^{\pm}$, supporting the hypothesis that the parton medium's equation of state influences the directed flow of charm quarks. Additionally, the directed flow of forward $\pi^{\pm}$ in Au+Au collisions shows a distinct dependence on $p_{\mathrm{T}}$ compared to isobar collisions, suggesting a potential dependence on the number of participants. Finally, the comparison between nSTAR Au+Au and Xe+Xe data reveals a difference in the slope of the directed flow, which may be attributed to differences in the number of participants. These insights offer a deeper understanding of the directed flow of forward luminosity hadrons in heavy-ion collisions. The full dataset and findings are accessible at https://nsf-pub.nsthar.org/. This study introduces a sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral (SSA-SK) framework designed to address the "curse of dimensionality" within the Adaptive Spectral Koopman Method (AS-KM). The SSA-SKM utilizes sparse grids for initial state estimation and subsequently refines the domain through targeted sampling. To enhance spectral accuracy, the kinetic energy-based metric (KBM) is employed to quantify the discrepancy between AS-KM predictions and system dynamics. Furthermore, the closure of Koopman modes is dynamically adjusted based on KBM values, ensuring that the model concentrates on the essential features of the system. SSA-SKIMs demonstrate superior scalability, extending AS-KIMs from 2 to 6 dimensions with a computational cost increase of no more than 20%. Additionally, these models exhibit enhanced generalization capabilities, achieving up to a 30% improvement in accuracy compared to AS-KIMs. Finally, we illustrate the application of SSA-SKIMs in anomaly detection, showing detection rate gains of up to 15% relative to AS-KIMs. These findings underscore the potential of SSA-SKIMs for effectively modeling complex dynamical systems. The development of a strong-field theoretical framework for atoms and molecules is introduced. This approach relies on expanding the outer electron wave function using a complex-scaled basis set. By employing a non-orthogonal outer-valence configuration space, the method ensures size consistency. The resulting framework is applied to helium and the hydrogen dimer to calculate ionization rates for helium and bond dissociation and survival probabilities for H₂⁺ across a broad range of DC fields. The method demonstrates robust performance, yielding results that align well with existing data. Additionally, the approach addresses a significant issue in strong-field ionization theory: the unphysical interaction between the continuum and bound states of ions within strong DC fields, which can artificially elevate ionization rates. This problem is effectively resolved by employing a shifted Coulomb potential. Finally, the study examines the ionization rates of helium under alternating current (AC) fields, showing that the derived expression for AC rates remains consistent with the DC formulation. Urban environments are renowned for their vibrant social interactions and high levels of income and class diversity. However, the global pandemic led to reduced outdoor activity and stricter social distancing, thereby diminishing the variety of social contacts. This study examines changes in the diversity of urban encounters across 15 U.S. cities from January to October 2020, focusing on how diversity varied by household income and the specific type of interaction. We discovered that the pandemic's impact on interaction diversity was not uniform; rather, it varied by city and declined as city income levels rose. Furthermore, inter-pandemic diversity was driven more by changes in the diversity of different income groups rather than being evenly distributed across all income brackets. These findings underscore the critical role of urban diversity in mitigating pandemic effects and the necessity of fostering diverse social connections within cities. Additionally, our results indicate that the interplay between income and social interaction policies significantly influenced diversity changes, offering valuable insights for urban planning. Finally, we explore how these interconnections can inform the design of future smart cities. Chiral optical resonators are capable of distinguishing between left- and right-handed objects, which is a fundamental requirement for applications like chiral sensing. In this study, we introduce a theoretical framework for chiral resonators centered on a helical object. We establish a set of necessary and sufficient conditions for chirality within the object itself, as well as for the formation of bound states, the resonant scattering of light, and the achievement of asymmetric spectral peak splitting. We contend that the principles outlined in this work are universally applicable to chiral optical resonators in general. Furthermore, our theoretical predictions regarding both the intrinsic chirality of the helical object and its response to incident light are validated through three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations. Finally, we discuss the potential of helical objects as a viable platform for high-performance chiral sensing. The code used for the simulations is available at \url{https://github.com/alexei-panov/chiral-optical-resonators}. Additionally, the theoretical findings presented here can be experimentally realized using metallic helices. The sample metallic helices employed in our simulations were previously fabricated and utilized in studies on chiral sensing \cite{Kuznetsov2013, Panov2015}. The sensing performance of these fabricated helices has been demonstrated in works such as Panov et al. (Opt. Express 24, 2016) and Panov et al. (Sci. Rep. 6, 2016). In summary, our work establishes a comprehensive theoretical foundation for chiral optical resonators, with significant experimental evidence supporting these findings. The concept of a warp drive involves warping spacetime to enable superluminal travel. In the warp drive metric, the shape function $f$ determines the geometry of the bubble, while the width function $b$ controls the rate of local spacetime expansion. This study examines ideal fluid solutions for both the Mandal-Mehta and Alcubierre warp drive metrics, incorporating the cosmological constant. For the Mandal-Mehta form, we derive the solution for any equation of state, yielding new results that reveal both phantom and non-phantom matter configurations. Regarding the Alcubierre form with an arbitrary equation of state, we identify two distinct solution types: one featuring a singularity and another that is non-singular. These findings indicate that various warp drive geometries can be sustained by diverse forms of matter. Furthermore, for the Alcubierre solution with an arbitrary equation of state, we demonstrate that the geometry can be maintained by a single perfect fluid. Finally, we establish that the geodesic equation for warp drive metrics is independent of the functions $b$ and $f$. Consequently, particles follow the same paths regardless of the warp drive configuration, implying that for any particle trajectory, there exists a corresponding warp drive geometry. This insight may facilitate the construction of new warp drive geometries. Additionally, we show that within warp drive geometries, there exist timelike geodesics that are not causal. These findings have significant implications for warp drive research. Specifically, our results suggest that the requirement for exotic matter to sustain warp drive geometries is not absolute. Cities are increasingly complex, heterogeneous environments that are expanding rapidly and facing numerous challenges. Consequently, there is a growing demand for innovative, cost-effective, and sustainable solutions to address urban issues. A primary driver of this shift is the widespread availability of data, which has enabled the creation of new data-driven methods and tools. This presentation outlines our ongoing research on GUIDES (Geospatial Urban Infrastructure Information Engineering Solutions), a flexible, data-driven framework designed to facilitate data-driven planning and management. We will demonstrate how GUIDES can be applied to various domains, including the analysis of urban growth patterns, the management of underground infrastructure, and the management of social networks within city populations. Finally, we will highlight the commonalities and differences among these specific application areas. The ultimate goal is to show how a unified, integrated approach grounded in urban data analysis can provide a solid foundation for addressing diverse and often unrelated city challenges. To illustrate these concepts, we will present selected case studies. All examples will be drawn from the city of Zurich. We experimentally investigate the relationship between dephasing times and motional mode temperatures in a 2D Paul trap, employing both dephasing measurements and an optimized dephase-amplitude-dense-reading sequence to characterize dephasing and the initial temperature distribution of the fundamental mode. These findings are compared against a theoretical model of dephasing driven by thermalized, non-thermal, and non-integrated laser cooling noise. Our results indicate that dephasing is primarily caused by thermalized laser cooling shot noise, which facilitates the efficient transfer of laser energy into the fundamental mode. Furthermore, we measure the heating velocity of motional modes, revealing a strong dependence on the Rabi frequency, with higher rates yielding lower heating velocities. Finally, we demonstrate the application of a tailored dephase-amplitude-dense-reading sequence for state preparation, successfully generating a 2D ion crystal in the 2-photon Dicke state $|2,1,1\rangle$ with a probability of 20%. This sequence establishes a new record for multi-ion Dicke state generation, achieving this through the parallel dephasing of all ions. Collectively, these experiments and state preparations advance the development of large-scale, robust, and scalable quantum simulators and processors based on trapped ions. This research was conducted within the EU-funded Quantum Engineering Technology Support Unit (QETSC) project. Additionally, we introduce a new method for dephasing multiple ions in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, enabling the generation of Dicke states with higher fidelity than previously reported. This approach leverages thermalized laser cooling, which ensures that motional energy is efficiently and collectively distributed across all modes of the trap. We validate the thermalization of the mode population by analyzing the correlation between dephasing and mode temperatures. The paper concludes with a discussion on the utility of dephasing as a diagnostic tool for quantum simulators, specifically addressing issues such as mode heating and non-thermal state distributions. Finally, we demonstrate the creation of a 2D Dicke state $|2,1,1\rangle$ using a tailored dephase-amplitude-dense-reading sequence, marking a new record for multi-ion Dicke state generation. This technique holds significant promise for advancing large-scale quantum simulators and processors. **Background:** Humans and other animals frequently face repeated decisions, requiring the integration of prior knowledge with new information to select optimal actions. This study investigates whether variations in the extent to which individuals employ prediction errors (PEs) during learning are linked to differences in the midbrain's encoding of PEs.

**Methods:** We utilized a decision-making task involving repeated choices between two options, where reward probabilities fluctuated over time. Participants exhibited distinct tactical differences: some rapidly incorporated new information into future choices, while others did so more slowly. We then employed functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to examine the relationship between these tactical variations and midbrain activity related to PEs.

**Results:** Our findings indicate that the degree to which individuals adapt their choices following reward outcomes correlates with the magnitude of PEs encoded by the midbrain. Specifically, participants who swiftly adjusted their behavior after new information demonstrated a more robust midbrain response to subsequent PEs compared to those who adapted more slowly.

**Conclusions:** These results suggest that suboptimal tactics in decision-making may stem from idiosyncratic reinforcement learning strategies, which are associated with altered midbrain representations of PEs. This highlights the significance of behavioral variability in cognitive neuroscience research. Furthermore, our results support the hypothesis that the basal ganglia utilize distinct mechanisms for processing positive versus negative PEs, as the putamen showed a stronger correlation with the use of new information than the caudate nucleus.

**Discussion:** Our findings underscore the value of accounting for behavioral variability when interpreting neuroimaging data. They also offer support for the theory that the putamen specializes in learning from positive PEs, while the caudate handles negative PEs. Finally, our results bolster the theory that the striatum integrates new information into its prediction error signals. This study addresses the task of identifying the nearest previous point in a query sequence $t_q$ within a database of $n$ time series, each of length $k$, based on $\epsilon$-equivalence under the Fréchet distance. The goal is to construct a data structure occupying $O(k^\alpha n \log n)$ space for some $\alpha > 0$ and to design an algorithm that, given a testing point $p_q$ on $t_q$, efficiently retrieves the point $t_d \in \mathcal{D}$ containing the time instant $t^*_q$ closest to $p_q$ under the Fréchet metric. We establish a lower bound of $\Omega(k n^{2/3} \log \log n / \log n)$ on the space required for any such structure. Furthermore, we introduce a data structure with space complexity $O(k^2 n \log n)$ that achieves a query time complexity of $O(\log \log \log n)$. Finally, for the practical scenario where the temporal resolution $k$ is fixed, we present an algorithm with time complexity $O(\log n)$ and space complexity $O(1)9$. These results are derived by integrating techniques from computational geometry, including the application of $\gamma$-coverings to manage the non-metric nature of the Fréchet distance, alongside methods from the Euclidean metric embedding literature. Additionally, we demonstrate how to leverage existing lower bounds for the Euclidean Closest Pair problem to derive lower bounds for the Fréchet Closest Pair problem. Our most significant technical advancement is a novel reduction technique that transforms lower bounds established for the Euclidean Closest Pair problem into corresponding lower bounds for the Fréchet Closest Pair problem. This approach yields new lower bounds for the Fréchet Closest Pair problem, thereby establishing lower bounds for the space complexity of any data structure capable of solving the Fréchet approximate close neighbor search problem. The effectiveness of our reductions is further evidenced by the fact that the lower bounds we derive for the Fréchet Closest Pair problem are identical to those for the Euclidean Closest Pair problem. To facilitate this research, we have developed an open-source software package for performing Fréchet distance computations. This package is available at: https://github.com/akshaykumar1998/frechet-computation. The source code for the implementation can be found at: https://github.com/akshaykumar199

Historically, measurement error correction was addressed using ad-hoc techniques, primarily Bayesian unfolding, which function well on small datasets but fail to scale effectively to large ones. This paper introduces a scalable solution by applying iterative unfolding in a manner analogous to the parallelized gradient descent used in stochastic gradient descent for deep learning. The proposed algorithm, named Parallel Unfolding Descent (PUD), supports on-the-fly data streaming and can be implemented across distributed computing environments. We evaluated PUD against stochastic and Batch Gradient Descent variants of the Bayesian unfolding approach. Our results indicate that PUD surpasses the stochastic variant in accuracy while matching its computational efficiency, and it achieves performance comparable to the Batch Gradient Descent method. Furthermore, we demonstrated that PUD successfully scales to datasets of any size. Finally, we validated the utility of PUD for measurement error correction in a real-world scenario: predicting COVID-19 cases in the United States. In this application, PUD enabled accurate predictions using only a small subset of data from the CDC's COVID-19 Tracking Tool, which feeds into our prediction model. This capability is essential for the real-time prediction service we are developing. The PUD implementation is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/ashokkumar1/PUD. Our implementation of PUD is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/ashokkumar1/PUD. A demonstration video of PUD scaling to 100GB data is hosted on YouTube at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=11422222222. In conclusion, PUD is a highly scalable, general-purpose algorithm for iterative Bayesian unfolding that is well-su for large-scale measurement error correction tasks. Future research will explore its application to other domains, such as image processing and recommendation systems. We also plan to extend PUD to handle nonlinear scenarios, which are common in machine learning applications involving large datasets. The PUD algorithm is now available as an open-source library for measurement error correction. This work was conducted while the first author was a Master's student at the University of Florida. The second author served as the primary supervisor, and the third author contributed to the project. The first author thanks the University of Florida for providing the computational resources necessary to scale PUD to 100GB datasets. The second author acknowledges the University of Florida for supporting the research that led to the development of PUD. The third author thanks the University of Florida for facilitating the collaboration that brought PUD to fruition.

The proliferation of robot technologies has led to a diverse ecosystem of manufacturers, each developing proprietary hardware and software architectures. This fragmentation creates significant barriers to entry, as new players must invest heavily in specialized development tools and internal software frameworks to integrate with existing hardware. Furthermore, the lack of a unified framework for shared decision-making among multiple robots and humans hinders the widespread adoption of shared autonomy. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a novel communication protocol that allows decision-making architectures to be portably deployed across heterogeneous robot platforms. We demonstrate the protocol's efficacy by implementing it on two distinct commercial robots equipped with different sensing and decision-making architectures. Our experimental results show that, when guided by the proposed protocol, these heterogeneous systems can successfully perform shared autonomy tasks, such as cooperative object tracking. Additionally, we explore how the protocol facilitates smooth shared control between human operators and commercial robots. Our findings indicate that both robot-to-robot and human-robot interactions can be seamlessly managed through this protocol, thereby lowering the barrier to entry for new players and fostering a more inclusive robot ecosystem. Finally, we discuss how the protocol can serve as a foundational framework for future research into multi-robot systems. We introduce HiTMap, a novel topological navigation framework designed for exploration in unknown settings. This system maintains a hierarchical map composed of room-level and point-level (metaball) submaps. A pathfinding algorithm utilizes these submaps to determine routes from start to goal, dynamically integrating new submap information as the robot explores. The method was tested in both simulated and real robotic environments, demonstrating successful navigation without requiring manual input. Furthermore, when compared to existing topological navigation algorithms, HiTMap proves to be more robust and efficient. Computed Tomography (CT) images are reconstructed by inverting the physics-governed measurement equation, a process that is typically ill-posed and demands the application of image reconstruction techniques. While prior research has primarily addressed noise reduction or decomposition individually, this study integrates these capabilities into a unified framework. Specifically, we develop a joint approach to mitigate sensor noise, enhance image quality, and execute material decomposition. By incorporating a data fidelity term, a variational noise filtering method, and a material decomposition term, we formulate a non-convex optimization problem. We subsequently introduce a split Bregman-based algorithm to resolve this problem, demonstrating through numerical experiments that the method effectively manages polyenergetic CT noise while achieving material decomposition. The results indicate that the proposed framework surpasses existing techniques in both image denoising and decomposition performance. Furthermore, numerical findings suggest that the proposed decomposition approach yields superior outcomes compared to conventional methods that perform decomposition independently. Finally, the efficacy of this framework is validated using real CT data. Our results demonstrate that the method is capable of handling real-world noise, including quantum noise, and successfully executes material decomposition. Additionally, the framework exhibits robustness against varying noise levels. This work offers a novel and effective strategy for reconstructing CT images in the presence of noise, with the added benefit of simultaneous material decomposition. Ultimately, this has the potential to enhance imaging quality and enable more accurate material quantification. Future research will explore extensions of this framework for other imaging modalities. This study examines how electron spill-out influences surface plasmons in nanostructures featuring a dielectric gap using time-dependent density functional theory. The impact of nonlocality was assessed by substituting the local kernel in the electron exchange-correlation potential with an analytical long-wavelength approximation of the Tran and Reining kernel. Our findings indicate that for metallic nanocubes separated by a dielectric spacer, the shift in the surface-plasmon-mode resonance caused by electron spill-out is comparable to the shift resulting from the local versus nonlocal description of exchange-correlation. However, the spatial decay of the electric field into the vacuum gap differs significantly between these two cases. Consequently, the agreement between local and nonlocal models for surface-plasmon resonances and their field distributions into the vacuum gap is poor in the limit of vanishing gaps. This discrepancy is attributed to a strong nonlocal response, which necessitates a rigorous treatment of the induced charge density via the Poisson equation. These results suggest that future investigations into gap plasmons must explicitly account for electron spill-out and the associated nonlocal effects. Furthermore, the substantial differences observed between the local and nonlocal descriptions of electron spill-out into the vacuum gap may have significant implications for the interpretation of electron energy loss spectroscopy experiments. Finally, the methods employed to calculate the electromagnetic response of nanostructures can be utilized to derive the quantum correction to the dielectric permittivity of metals. This approach is expected to facilitate the development of nonlocal, semi-empirical dielectric functions that incorporate quantum corrections for the dielectric permittivity of metals. Such advancements are crucial for enhancing the accuracy of the electromagnetic description of light-matter interactions in nanostructures with extremely narrow gaps. The dynamic nature of language necessitates a shift from traditional static word matching to a context-aware approach known as contextual named entity retrieval. This method involves identifying entities that align with a specific query within a given context, such as replacing the underlined entity in "I like to eat \textit{salmon} for dinner" upon receiving the query "What are your healthy food options?" We introduce a new training objective designed to generate responses to such queries by leveraging entity representations enriched with contextual information. Our proposed objective is formulated as a rank-based contrastive learning task, utilizing term term-level relevance judgments to learn representations for contextual entities and their modifying terms. We demonstrate the efficacy of our objective in an open-domain assistant scenario, showing that it enables the model to generalize effectively to contextual named entity retrieval tasks. Furthermore, we establish a correlation between this learning objective and natural language inference, highlighting the model's capacity to perform reasoning regarding semantic relationships. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the objective's behavior across various dimensions, including response specificity, term sensitivity, and entity type sensitivity. Temporal data is inherently longitudinal, yet it is frequently represented in cross-sectional formats like tables. This paper introduces a framework designed to highlight the temporal dimensions of such data. We present three human-subject study findings: first, temporal data is best represented as multivariate time series rather than longitudinal datasets; second, this format is generally unengaging for most end-users; and third, integrating interactive, non-linear time axes significantly enhances user engagement. These insights offer valuable guidance for the design of data visualization tools and applications. The framework is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/mbeyer12/TimeSeriesEngagement. We introduce a novel heterogeneous graph neural network designed for patient similarity based on electronic health records (EHRs). This approach constructs a heterogeneous graph from EHR instances and utilizes a heterogeneous attention mechanism to capture both structural and feature information, thereby enhancing the modeling of patient similarity. The primary innovation lies in our graph construction method, which employs a hybrid feature encoding strategy to effectively handle diverse data types within EHRs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the model's efficacy in a clinical task by applying it to multi-class patient diagnosis across four distinct EHR datasets. Additionally, we introduce a new mechanism for automatic patient classification that relies on representation learning rather than manual feature engineering. Our results indicate that the model achieves robust performance in patient similarity modeling, offering a solid foundation for future clinical support systems. This study employs classical molecular dynamics simulations to examine how solvent polarization influences the structure of electric double layers (EDLs) near charged soft surfaces within electrolyte solutions. Our findings indicate that the significant polarizability of methanol molecules at the interface causes a shift in the zeta potential ($\zeta$) at different surface charge densities. Furthermore, we observe that the sign of $\zeta$ reverses when the surface charge density increases from $-20$ mC/m$^2$ to $+20$ mC/m$^2$. Additionally, our results demonstrate that methanol's polarization amplifies the overscreening effect, thereby enhancing charge oscillations within the EDL. Finally, we note that these observations are specific to the combined system of a soft surface and a polar solvent. These insights offer a deeper understanding of how surface charge density and the nature of the solvent interact to shape the structure of the EDL. This phenomenon is particularly relevant to applications involving highly charged surfaces in contact with polar solvents, such as biological membranes and water. Our conclusions are supported by data from both molecular dynamics simulations and Poisson-Boltzmann calculations. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for surface electrokinetics. Specifically, we predict that methanol's polarization can induce electro-osmotic flow in the opposite direction compared to the case where polarization is absent. These results are corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of how solvent polarization affects the EDL structure and its potential impact on surface electrokinetic phenomena. This conclusion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of results with and without polarization effects. Finally, we suggest that these findings have broad implications for various applications, including microfluidics and energy harvesting. Our conclusions are further validated by a sensitivity analysis of the simulation parameters. Software repositories typically contain structured specification documents in languages like LaTeX, Word, or PDFs, which clearly separate code from text. However, many developers have shifted toward using unstructured text platforms such as GitHub READMEs, GitLab Wikis, or Web IDEs for specification tasks. Automatically parsing unstructured text to extract specifications is difficult because it lacks the consistent formatting found in traditional documents. This paper introduces GSpecs, a system that utilizes a generative adversarial network to learn the characteristics of software specifications from historical data, enabling it to create specifications for new projects based on their code. Evaluation on datasets of repositories and specification documents shows that, given sufficient code, GSpecs can effectively extract common requirements, functional, and non-functional requirements. Furthermore, specifications generated by GSpecs are highly valuable to developers, improving their ability to identify new requirements in unfamiliar repositories and helping them understand existing ones. The code for this paper is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/GSpecs. GitHub stars are welcome.

This paper introduces a network coding-based cooperative communication framework designed to minimize total transmit power by jointly optimizing relay selection, network coding strategy selection, and power allocation. Within the cooperative network, a relay selects a source from which to decode a specific packet; once decoded, the relay transmits the signal. The selected relay then chooses between two network coding strategies: amplify-and-forward (AF) or decode-and-forward (DF). To ensure reliable delivery, the source retransmits the same packet until the receiver successfully decodes it. A general model is established to calculate the end-to-end outage probability for any given strategy combination, relay selection, and power allocation. This model serves as the basis for a joint optimization problem aimed at reducing the network's total transmit power. Due to the combinatorial nature of the problem, a brute-force search is employed to identify the optimal solution. Finally, a comparative analysis is conducted between the proposed scheme and conventional protocols, including selective relaying, non-selective relaying, and a network coding-based selective relaying approach. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves a power reduction of up to 30% compared to selective relaying and up to 15% compared to amplify-and-forward based cooperative transmission. Furthermore, the study confirms that the proposed scheme saves more power than DF-based selective relaying when the number of relays is small, but saves less power when the number of relays is large. Finally, the computational complexity of the proposed scheme is analyzed. To address this, a suboptimal scheme is developed, which achieves a power reduction of up to 10% compared to DF-based selective relaying. The paper concludes by discussing the advantages and limitations of the proposed approach. Keywords: Network coding, amplify-and-forward, decode-and-forward, relay selection, power allocation.

We present a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical investigation of magnetic impurity states, specifically Mn adatoms and clusters on an Nb(110) surface. Our methodology utilizes a slab model for the superconducting Nb(110) and employs the local spin density approximation within the density functional theory framework to accurately account for the magnetic moments of the impurities. Our results indicate that both the adatom and clusters generate Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states on either side of zero energy. The splitting energy between these paired YSR states is notably greater than that observed in previous studies of an Fe adatom on Nb(110). Furthermore, the spatial distribution of the YSR states exhibits distinct characteristics for the adatom versus the clusters. Finally, we calculate the exchange coupling between the Mn impurities and the Nb(110) superconductor, finding that it scales proportionally with the YSR splitting. These findings are anticipated to be applicable to other magnetic adatoms and clusters situated on superconducting substrates. Our theoretical predictions regarding YSR states in these systems can be experimentally verified using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. This study is part of a broader experimental and theoretical initiative aimed at investigating the YSR state in a superconductor-adatom-superconductor junction. Specifically, we examine an adatom located between two normal metal leads on a Mn(110) superconductor substrate, a configuration that can be investigated using a normal tunneling spectroscopy setup. Our calculations demonstrate that a tunneling current can be induced by a time-varying voltage, with a resonance occurring at the level splitting energy. This effect is expected to be detectable using normal tunneling spectroscopy and may be observable in current experimental setups. This represents a significant advancement in the theoretical understanding of magnetic adatoms and clusters within normal metal junctions placed on superconducting substrates. Finally, our work offers a pathway to understanding the recently reported observation of a Yu--Shiba--Rusinov state in a normal tunneling junction featuring a magnetic adatom on a Mn substrate. This specific system was previously considered unobservable in the Meissner state of the superconductor. We show that such a state can be detected in the superconductor when a bias voltage is applied, with the conductance peaking at the exchange coupling energy. Bias mitigation remains a persistent challenge in distribution-based Scan Matching (SSM), where metric biases cause significant errors even when point clouds are geometrically similar. Although Deep Learning (DNN) offers a solution by learning optimal correspondences, it struggles with bias because biasing artifacts are absent during the training phase. To address this, we propose a novel approach that extends distribution-based SSM by integrating a DNN into a traditional iterative framework. Specifically, the DNN serves as a corresponding point estimator to mitigate bias, while a traditional SSM algorithm refines the DNN output for accuracy. This combined method enables the traditional algorithm to operate effectively on DNN-generated results. Furthermore, we introduce a new SSM cost function that regularizes the distribution-to-distribution mapping, enhancing the robustness of the scan-matching process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses traditional SSM techniques and successfully solves long-range bias issues that DNN-only approaches fail to address. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYuan1996/DNNFilter. Additionally, the code is available in our open-source repository: https://github.com/ChenYuan1996/dl_slam. Our related work can be found at: https://github.com/ChenYuan1996/dl_slam. Finally, our research is also hosted in this repository: https://github.com/ChenYuan1996/dl_slam.

We introduce a model for fluence-dependent, non-linear X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) utilizing an extension of the standard rate equation. This equation governs three population levels: ground-state atoms, ground-state electrons, and excited-state electrons. By applying this framework to synchrotron-based non-linear XANES data from liquid water collected at the K-edge, we demonstrate that the proposed model offers superior fits compared to those derived from linear absorption theory. Furthermore, our results indicate that these non-linear measurements are predominantly driven by electronic absorption. Finally, we suggest that such non-linear XANES techniques could enhance the sensitivity of contrast agents in medical imaging. This sensitivity improvement arises from the model's ability to isolate the primary source of non-linear signal generation, thereby facilitating the development of more effective contrast agents. Additionally, this finding underscores the critical necessity of employing K-shell electrons as contrast agents rather than L-shell electrons. These conclusions are supported by synchrotron-based non-linear measurements of Gold at the K-edge and the L$_3$-edge. The latter data reveal that L-shell electronic absorption is the dominant contributor to the K-shell signal, whereas L-shell ionization accounts for only a minor portion of the L$_3$-shell signal. Consequently, Gold at the K-edge represents an optimal choice for medical contrast agents. In summary, this work establishes a foundation for non-linear XANES as a tool for evaluating the efficacy of potential medical contrast agents. We anticipate that this approach will enable the discovery of novel materials with enhanced non-linear contrast capabilities. To achieve this, we must identify substances that exhibit minimal L-shell ionization while maintaining strong K-shell absorption. Our findings suggest that organic molecules, which are well-suited for K-shell excitation, may be ideal candidates for use as medical contrast agents. This conclusion is reinforced by synchrotron-based non-linear measurements of Carbon in methanol at the K-edge, which show that electronic absorption is the primary source of the signal. These results align with the hypothesis that non-linear XANES could offer a pathway to ultra-low-dose medical imaging. Such an advancement would be realized by harnessing electronic absorption to generate contrast, thereby eliminating the need for non-linear laser intensities and mitigating associated risks such as plasma formation and sample damage. Ultimately, this could pave the way for medical imaging with unprecedented sensitivity. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, which involve adding carefully engineered noise to signal samples to induce misclassification. This paper introduces a resiliency approach to mitigate such attacks, centered on training a robust classifier using adversarial training. Drawing inspiration from image denoising, the method employs a generator network to eliminate noise from adversarial inputs before processing them by a discriminator classifier. To address the difficulty in generating realistic training data, the study proposes a blend Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) that merges multiple image samples to produce high-quality outputs. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed GAN successfully generates realistic image samples, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the discriminator classifier in adversarial scenarios. Furthermore, the study confirms that the resiliency strategy is effective across both real-world and simulated environments. The findings indicate that the approach yields significant improvements in communication systems, regardless of the specific GAN or discriminator classifier employed. Additionally, the resiliency mechanism exhibits transferability across different communication systems and DNN classifiers. Finally, the research illustrates that the strategy is applicable to various modulation schemes, including QPSK, 16-QAM, and higher-order modulations. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/BlendGAN}. The work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological condition characterized by demyelination within the central nervous system. MS lesions, which appear as hyperintense areas on T2-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, are categorized into two types: periventricular lesions adjacent to the ventricles and subcortical lesions located away from them. Periventricular lesions are typically more common in patients with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), whereas clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) patients often present with subcortical lesions. The size, count, and location of these lesions serve as critical indicators for assessing disease progression and predicting outcomes. Consequently, lesion segmentation is a vital step in clinical research. However, acquiring large, diverse datasets for training segmentation models is difficult. To address this, researchers often train models on small, high-quality datasets from a single site and subsequently fine-tune them on limited data from other sites. This paper evaluates the efficacy of continuous learning versus training from scratch using data from three hospitals. The results indicate that training from scratch yields superior performance compared to continuous learning. Furthermore, transfer learning strategies that incorporate subcortical lesion segmentation from one site and periventricular lesion segmentation from another outperformed all other experimental configurations. Finally, the study demonstrates that training from scratch is essential for developing robust MS lesion segmentation models. The code and models used in this research are accessible at https://github.com/DeepBrainTechnologies/datalab-lesion-seg. This work is part of the DeepBrain Technologies research initiative. We introduce a new metric for studying the contrast between two groups, offering intuitive support for political applications. This polarized contrast is defined as the difference between the distance from the origin to the hyperplane equidistant from the group means and the norm of the ratio of the group mean covariance matrices. We demonstrate that maximizing polarized contrast is equivalent to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). By leveraging the connection between QCQPs and robust portfolio optimization, we create an efficient algorithm to identify directions of maximal polarized contrast. Our numerical experiments illustrate the method's effectiveness in various contexts, including recovering the contrast between two means in polarized politics, identifying the most polarized directions in a high-dimensional space, and performing polarized PCA. Additionally, we present a general approach for polarized analysis of means and directions, which enables the measurement of polarization between any two groups. Finally, we apply this framework to the analysis of US Senate voting records.

Although data-driven techniques have made significant strides in modeling, the underlying physics of many systems remains poorly understood. Consequently, data-driven models often struggle to generalize beyond their training datasets. This paper introduces a data-driven framework capable of correcting model errors by leveraging auxiliary information from physics and/or simple structural assumptions. We illustrate the application of this method to a single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper system. Furthermore, the proposed approach is versatile and can be extended to other domains, including dynamical systems and the modeling of spatially distributed phenomena. Finally, the concept of "model mistake" is demonstrated within the context of dynamical systems. The intended outcome is a more profound understanding of the inherent limitations of data-driven modeling. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion on the potential of this proposed methodology. Keywords: Data-driven modeling, Dynamical systems, Error correction, Limitations of machine learning. The application of machine learning and data-driven modeling to engineering and physical systems has gained considerable traction in recent years. This trend is primarily driven by the high cost and time consumption associated with creating mechanistic models from first principles. However, the primary motivation for this work stems from the observation that these data-driven models frequently fail to generalize effectively beyond their training data. This limitation is particularly pronounced in modeling dynamical systems. This paper aims to address this issue by presenting a data-driven framework that utilizes additional information from physics and/or basic structural assumptions to correct model errors. To demonstrate this, we apply the method to a single-degree-of-freedom mass-spring-damper system. Additionally, the approach is highly general and can be extended to other fields, such as dynamical systems and spatially distributed phenomena. Finally, the notion of "model mistake" is illustrated in the context of dynamical systems. The ultimate goal is to achieve a deeper understanding of the inherent limitations of data-driven modeling.
