Networks are fundamental to the social and natural sciences, serving as the foundation for modeling and analyzing complex systems. They can be visualized as graphs where components are nodes and their relationships are edges. While research has extensively examined how a network's structure influences its function, the quality of these graphs depends entirely on the integrity of their components and the relationships between them. Consequently, the validity of findings derived from network analysis is compromised if the underlying graph is flawed. Despite this, the literature often overlooks the quality of relationships when interpreting network results. This paper aims to elucidate the various ways in which relationship quality impacts analysis and to outline the specific requirements necessary for networks constructed from both measured and inferred data. We propose a framework to guide researchers in understanding the quality of their networks and encourage them to advocate for higher standards in network analysis. This call to action is particularly pertinent given the field's current focus on reproducibility. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of this framework to both theoretical and real-world problems, demonstrating its utility in constructing networks from multiple sources of evidence. The framework is designed to be broadly applicable, offering guidance for any research endeavor involving network construction. Additionally, we provide a Python package, MultiNet, to assist in creating, managing, and evaluating multi-layered networks. This tool enables users to define the type of quality assessment needed for their specific analysis and to evaluate network quality based on that definition. We illustrate its use with a real-world example involving a large, heterogeneous network of genes and their relationships. Ultimately, we believe that by adopting this framework, researchers can enhance the quality of their work and contribute to the advancement of the field. Our goal is to foster a culture where network quality is recognized as a critical component of analysis, thereby ensuring that future findings are robust and reliable. This approach is essential for the field to reach the point where networks are viewed as fundamental scientific tools for understanding the world. We hope this work inspires others to prioritize quality in their network research. Finally, we invite contributions to the MultiNet package from the community, as this tool is intended to be open and extensible. We look forward to collaborating with others to make multi-layered networks a standard instrument in scientific research. Please contact us at firstname.lastname@example.org to join our efforts. This work was supported by the Simons Foundation, grant number 455032. The code is available at https://github.com/ComplexityScienceGroup/MultiNet. Additional information can be found at https://complexitysciencegroup.github.io/MultiNet/.

This paper introduces a novel a posteriori error estimation technique for machine learning models, with a specific focus on physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). We demonstrate that the residual error of PINNs—derived from the discrepancy between the network's output and the underlying partial differential equation (PDE)—can serve as a reliable upper limit for the maximum output error. Building on this finding, we propose a method to calculate certified error bounds for PINN solutions. Our proposed algorithm is both straightforward and computationally efficient, requiring no additional training and involving only basic operations on the pre-trained network. The efficacy of this approach is validated through a numerical experiment on the heat equation, which illustrates the derivation of rigorous error bounds for PINN approximations. Furthermore, we contend that this strategy for generating and certifying error bounds is broadly applicable to the extensive landscape of physics-informed machine learning methods. Ultimately, this technique facilitates the certification of machine learning model outputs, thereby enhancing the trustworthiness and reliability of these models. Finally, we argue that the ability to quantify and certify the mistake rates of machine learning models is a critical area of research that warrants greater attention. PINNs offer a promising avenue for advancing this direction, potentially leading to new, more robust and trustworthy machine learning algorithms. Additionally, the proposed error estimation and certification framework may find utility in various other domains, including other machine learning applications and other scientific disciplines. To illustrate this broader relevance, we outline potential applications of our method in the sciences and engineering. Specifically, we show that the same error analysis used for PINNs can be adapted to create certified upper bounds for finite element method (FEM) approximations of the heat equation, as well as for deep learning-based PDE solvers that employ adjoint-based error estimation. These findings underscore the significance of developing and applying a posteriori error analysis to machine learning models. The methodologies presented in this work are available as open-source software. Code for the PINN implementation, error analysis, and certification of certified error bounds can be found at https://github.com/SebastianSchwab17/DeepXDE-PINNs. Furthermore, our group has developed an open-source library for physics-informed neural networks, featuring the implementation used in this study, available at https://github.com/SebastianSchwab17/DeepXDE-PINNs. **Background:** Air pollution is a recognized cause of numerous diseases. While epidemiological studies link human health outcomes with air pollution levels, the specific individual exposures remain difficult to measure. Consequently, researchers often rely on models that predict exposure based on ambient data, incorporating geographic and temporal covariates.

**Objectives:** This study aims to evaluate the strengths and limitations of various air pollution modeling approaches for epidemiology, assess the impact of sampling design on model performance, and compare geographic statistical methods with machine learning techniques.

**Methods:** Using a simulated dataset, we assessed the performance of different modeling strategies. We generated a spatial exposure field using Gaussian processes and simulated temporal exposure data by sampling this space at random locations and applying a decay function.

**Results:** Geostatistics yielded the best performance when sampling points were distributed uniformly across the study area. Although machine learning methods performed comparably under uniform sampling, they yielded significantly worse results when sampling was non-random.

**Conclusion:** Geostatistics offers a slight advantage over machine learning in predicting spatially distributed air pollution. However, both methods are highly sensitive to the spatial distribution of sampling points, with optimal performance achieved when data is collected uniformly. This underscores the need for a sampling design that ensures uniform geographic coverage. Furthermore, machine learning models require careful interpretation, as they function as "black boxes" that are difficult to validate and explain. Geostatistics offers a more transparent approach, allowing for the quantification of spatial uncertainty. Finally, we recommend that future research integrate both methods to leverage their respective strengths. Geostatistics can be employed to select representative sampling points and quantify spatial exposure uncertainty, while machine learning can be utilized to predict temporal variations in exposure. This combined strategy would enhance the accuracy of spatiotemporal exposure assessment in air pollution epidemiology. Additionally, geostatistics enables the quantification of uncertainty in spatial exposure, a critical factor for robust epidemiological analysis. This work was conducted as part of the "Pollution and Health" training school.

**Keywords:** Air pollution, exposure assessment, geostatistics, machine learning, spatiotemporal modeling.

This approach incorporates ohmic dissipation effects within tunneling conductance calculations, utilizing electrodes at finite temperatures. Our findings indicate that increasing the resistance or temperature effectively distinguishes the Majorana peak from competing effects. Furthermore, we propose a metric defined as the ratio of tunneling conductance at the zero bias point to the maximum tunneling conductance, serving as an order parameter for the presence of zero mode. This parameter is defined as unity for Majorana modes and zero otherwise. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness of this order parameter, showing it remains unaffected by variations in tunneling resistance or temperature. These results are derived from numerical simulations based on a model constructed from the Majorana Hamiltonian. We anticipate that experimental measurements of tunneling conductance, accounting for ohmic dissipation and finite temperatures, will yield an order parameter consistent with our predictions. Such measurements could be conducted using existing experimental setups. Additionally, we suggest that a machine learning-based data analysis method, similar to the one proposed here, will be highly effective for distinguishing between zero mode and non-zero mode scenarios. This machine learning method is also expected to be applicable to other physical systems. We conclude that our proposed approach offers a reliable and promising method for experimentally distinguishing zero modes from other effects. Linear contextual bandits are a prevalent framework for sequential decision-making, where the objective is to identify the optimal action within a large set. Although numerous algorithms exist for this purpose, their ability to support statistical inference remains unclear. This study examines a broad category of linear bandit algorithms designed to balance exploration and exploitation when exploring the entire action space is infeasible. We establish a high-probability regret bound for these methods and demonstrate that the resulting confidence intervals for the optimal action's value gap are nearly optimal, deviating from minimax optimality by only a logarithmic factor. Furthermore, we present a reduction showing that achieving near-optimal confidence intervals for the best action is computationally equivalent to finding them for the best value gap; consequently, no algorithm can yield significantly tighter intervals for the value gap. Finally, we investigate the application of these algorithms to linear bandit inference. We propose a novel approach to construct confidence intervals for linear parameters, proving that the confidence intervals for individual parameters are close to optimal, with a slight logarithmic degradation in tightness. Additionally, we develop a new hypothesis testing framework for linear bandits that is provably consistent and approaches optimal type-I error rates. Extensive simulations and a real-world case study validate the theoretical findings and highlight the practical utility of these methods. The code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/Pranav-12345/Linear-Bandits-and-Inference}. Our findings offer valuable insights for practitioners, enabling them to quantify the uncertainty surrounding action values and test for significant differences between action pairs. This capability is essential for selecting the optimal action and identifying key features in the context. Specifically, our work introduces the first algorithm for linear parameter inference in linear bandits with large action spaces, offering confidence intervals that are near-optimal up to logarithmic factors. We also deliver the first hypothesis testing procedure for online linear bandits, which is provably consistent and achieves near-optimal type-I error rates. Notably, our approach is computationally efficient, requiring only $O(d)$ time per hypothesis test, where $d$ is the number of features. This represents a substantial improvement over prior methods, which incurred a type-I error rate of $\Omega(1)$ and necessitated $2^{\Omega(d)}$ time to compute confidence intervals. We believe these findings will significantly benefit the community. By providing confidence intervals for individual parameters, practitioners can now assess uncertainty in action values and detect the most influential features within the context. While the valley Hall effect in graphene is typically suppressed by graphene-specific mechanisms, this study demonstrates that introducing a second sublattice allows the effect to emerge. We demonstrate this using the orbital Hall effect, which is intrinsically a graphene-specific phenomenon. By constructing a model that incorporates both sublattice degrees of freedom, we show that the orbital Hall effect can be observed as an alternative to the valley Hall effect. This model is realized through a heterostructure formed by graphene and a graphene-like material featuring a hexagonal lattice and orbital degeneracy. Our findings indicate that the orbital valley Hall effect in this system is substantial, potentially reaching $10^{12}$ $(C/m^2) (s) (Tt)$, where $C$ denotes capacitance, $s$ represents the magnetic field, $T$ is the temperature, and $t$ is the thickness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this effect can be tuned by adjusting the interlayer coupling. These results suggest that the orbital valley Hall effect is a promising candidate for valleytronics applications. Additionally, we illustrate that the effect is detectable as a non-local signal in the transverse Hall resistance of a thin film within a Hall bar configuration. Finally, we provide experimental guidance for measuring the orbital valley Hall effect in bilayer graphene as an alternative to gapless graphene. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are machine learning models specifically designed for processing data on graphs, demonstrating strong performance in fields like chemistry and biology. However, their performance can be severely compromised when nodes in the training set are missing or when graphs contain communities. This paper investigates how data contamination, guided by Reinforcement Learning (RL), interacts with these topological graph characteristics. We introduce a novel algorithm where an RL agent learns to selectively remove nodes from a graph to deceive a GNN, maximizing the gap between GNN accuracy on the test set and the validation set. Our findings reveal that the graph structure significantly impacts data contamination, with modularity being a critical factor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RL-based contamination is more effective than random contamination, and we present evidence indicating that our proposed algorithm outperforms standard adversarial attacks. Finally, we evaluate the algorithm on two real-world datasets, confirming that our method achieves superior results compared to existing approaches. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/data-contamination.

Catalogue matching serves as a critical yet computationally demanding task in the field of astrophotometry. This process involves comparing the positions and magnitudes of newly observed sources against those in existing catalogues to determine if they represent the same objects. This paper introduces a novel approach to catalogue matching that leverages photometric data to improve object identification. Additionally, we present a comprehensive benchmark suite designed to facilitate the evaluation of catalogue matching techniques. Our experiments demonstrate that combining data augmentation with multi-catalogue comparison yields superior results, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy of the matching process. The code required to reproduce these experiments can be found at https://github.com/abhishekgupta123/catalogue-matching. Furthermore, we have made our benchmark dataset available for research purposes at the same location. We anticipate that this resource will assist researchers in developing and assessing new catalogue matching methods. The intersection of our benchmark dataset and source catalogues is accessible at https://drive.google.

This paper investigates the properties of minimal vertex sets within infinite hypergraphs. We demonstrate the existence of a specific index function that ensures every hypergraph possesses a collection of minimal vertex sets that is both non-empty and countable. Furthermore, we establish several structural theorems and the existence of a index function guaranteeing that certain classes of hypergraphs possess at least one countable minimal vertex set. Finally, we outline several open questions and propose a conjecture regarding the existence of hypergraphs featuring uncountable collections of minimal vertex sets. Specifically, we construct examples of hypergraphs where the minimal vertex sets vary in dimension and cardinality, and we conjecture that any hypergraph containing two minimal vertex sets of different dimensions must include an infinite sequence of minimal sets, each with a distinct dimension. Additionally, we present examples of hypergraphs with countable collections of minimal vertex sets exhibiting diverse structural characteristics, such as differences in size and the inclusion-exclusion property. In the context of combinatorial optimization, we note that the algorithmic complexity of identifying a minimal vertex set in a hypergraph corresponds to the difficulty of solving specific combinatorial optimization problems. We provide examples of linear programming problems whose feasible regions can be represented as hypergraphs, where a minimal vertex set equates to an optimal solution. Finally, we explore the relationship between the computational complexity of minimal vertex set identification and the structural properties of the hypergraph. In graph theory, we prove that every graph possesses a minimal vertex set, defined as a minimum vertex set for the associated induced subgraph, and that any minimum vertex set is minimal. We also examine induced subgraphs generated by minimal vertex sets, revealing various structural properties, including those concerning planar graphs. Moreover, we construct examples of graphs with countable collections of minimal vertex sets and discuss the relationship between minimum vertex sets and graph coloring. We show that the vertex chromatic number of a graph can be determined by partitioning its minimal vertex sets into minimum vertex sets, and we construct examples of graphs with countable collections of minimal vertex sets exhibiting diverse chromatic number behaviors. Finally, we construct examples of graphs with countable collections of minimal vertex sets where sets of different sizes exist; however, we conjecture that if a graph has a countable collection of minimal vertex sets, it possesses an index function such that minimum vertex sets of any dimension appear at most finitely often. Ontologies serve as formal, explicit specifications of categories within a shared domain of discourse. While ontology repositories are typically visualized using directed, acyclic graphs, this approach struggles with scale, often necessitating zooming and panning that hinders a comprehensive overview. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization technique designed to display associations in large ontology repositories without relying on a hierarchical structure. The primary innovation of OntoPlot is its ability to automatically select an optimal association strength threshold to ensure the visualization remains both readable and informative. We validate this method using a dataset comprising 100,000 concepts from DBpedia. The results demonstrate that OntoPlot effectively balances readability and information content, rendering dense visualizations navigable and sparse ones informative. Furthermore, the visualization is intuitive and supports zooming and panning for detailed exploration. User testing confirms that OntoPlot is as readable as other existing visualization methods. Finally, we discuss the method's limitations and potential future enhancements. Our findings indicate that OntoPlot is particularly effective for very large repositories, where it helps users identify associations across the largest concept subsets, whereas other methods are better suited for smaller repositories. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexei-makarov/OntoPlot. A video demonstration can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1222222222. The paper is accessible at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07000. A preliminary version was presented at the 2019 IEEE Visualization Conference. The final version is scheduled for publication in CVGIP: Artificial Intelligence Applications.

This study presents an approach for enhancing semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition (SEED) models by leveraging unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) and interpolating training data distributions. The primary goal is to improve SEED performance when trained on low-quality data, such as that affected by noise or domain shifts. We introduce a cross-lingual UDA scenario where a model trained on one language (source domain) is fine-tuned on a target language without using any annotated speech from the target domain. To mitigate domain shift, we propose an ensemble method that interpolates the data distributions of the source and target domains. Furthermore, we define an inter-domain loss designed to align these domains and minimize distributional discrepancies. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses baseline methods, particularly in challenging conditions involving noisy or domain-shifted data. Additionally, in a cross-lingual setting, our ensemble strategy yields a 14.5% relative reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) compared to the source-domain-only baseline. Finally, we observe that employing two distinct UDA objectives results in a 1.5% relative decrease in WWER. Overall, the proposed framework effectively utilizes multi-lingual training data to enhance SEED models. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/DeepSpeech/Domain-Adaptation-Enhanced-SEED}. Key terms include Unsupervised Domain Adaptation, Semi-supervised End-to-End Automatic Speech Recognition, and Inter-domain Loss.

While deep neural networks excel in perception and control for autonomous robot navigation, current deep learning-based motion planners depend on pre-defined maps and static models to navigate environments. These models are intricate and computationally intensive, hindering their real-time implementation. This paper introduces a deep active prediction framework utilizing recurrent neural networks to facilitate task-oriented navigation. By employing a novel attention mechanism, the system generates task-relevant motion predictions, thereby enhancing the efficiency of deep learning-based motion planners. Furthermore, the proposed method minimizes the number of deep network queries required for prediction through attention-driven sampling. Experimental results demonstrate that the approach achieves competitive performance in both simulation and hardware testing. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhenghao1993/DAP. In direct comparisons, the deep active prediction method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in both prediction accuracy and inference efficiency. Consequently, this method enables the design of deep learning-based motion planners that utilize a reduced quantity of deep network queries for prediction. Ultimately, this facilitates the development of task-oriented autonomous navigation systems that are more efficient, robust, and scalable. The results establish a new paradigm for autonomous robot navigation driven by predictive models. This study investigates the Soret effect in a binary mixture of rigid and Gaussian molecules. Using the generalized Landau-Lifshitz formalism, we demonstrate that internal degrees of freedom in flexible molecules contribute to this phenomenon. Our findings indicate that while vibrational degrees of freedom have a negligible impact, rotational degrees of freedom significantly influence the T-dependent component of the Soret effect. Specifically, comparing molecules with one versus three rotational degrees of freedom shows that the latter substantially amplify the crossover temperature and the peak value of the Soret coefficient. These results are supported by nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations of flexible argon molecules. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for separating flexible molecules based on their internal degrees of freedom. This research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grants 21373077 and 21573070). The corresponding author can be reached at email: yqiao@fzhu.edu.cn. Keywords: Flexibility; Internal degrees of freedom; Soret effect.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) represents a longstanding challenge that intersects both computer science and education. While deep learning methods have enhanced essay evaluation, they frequently depend on extensive datasets containing numerous essays. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective approach to automatically grade essays by utilizing pre-trained transformer language models. We conduct a comparative analysis of various transformer-based models to identify the most suitable architecture for this task. Furthermore, we assess our methods against state-of-the-art techniques on the Machine Readable Paper grade-level Essay Scoring (MRPGES) dataset. The code for our implementation is available at: https://github.com/abhishekgupta1234/AES. Our findings demonstrate that simple yet effective strategies using pre-trained models yield strong performance, achieving a mean correlation of 0.710 with human scores on the MRPGES dataset. Additionally, our results indicate that the model's performance is highly correlated with its perplexity. Finally, we highlight that the model tends to assign similar scores to essays that are semantically close to one another. Our results are reproducible. Keywords: Automated Essay Scoring, Pre-trained Transformer Models.

Domain adaptation is essential for addressing the gap between supervised training environments and unsupervised target settings. Nevertheless, existing box2box transformation-based approaches often result in an excessive number of False Positives (FPs) during test-time detection. This paper introduces Box Re-Ranking, a method for unsupervised, unscale, and oriented domain adaptation that significantly reduces FP rates while preserving True Positives (TPs). Specifically, we first apply an adaptive filter to eliminate redundant boxes. Next, our novel box2box transformation strategy identifies high-confidence TPs by mapping source-level anchors to target-level proposals, thereby enhancing their confidence scores. Finally, box2box matching-based methods improve the robustness of these selected TPs against translation and rotation by adjusting their IOU thresholds. Extensive experiments on challenging datasets demonstrate that Box Re-Ranking significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in reducing FPs while maintaining TP recall. Furthermore, it surpasses methods trained directly on multiple scales and orientations, even without using additional multi-scale training data. The code and model weights are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/Box-Re-Ranking. We introduce a novel approach to music enhancement that leverages image translation and vocoding. By representing audio as a spectrogram image, our method applies image translation to transform low-quality source music into high-fidelity output. This system functions as a universal music enhancer, capable of improving various source types without needing task-specific architectures. Furthermore, because image translation enables single-image processing, the method is well-suited for real-time applications. Extensive evaluations across different improvements demonstrate its effectiveness. The Python implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ku215/music_improve. Additionally, source codes, along with the training and evaluation scripts, will be released upon paper acceptance. Finally, the source code and pre-trained models will be made available at https://github.com/ku215/music_improve. This paper investigates how errors in the point of release affect various metrics of human throwing. The FauxThrow system is introduced as a flexible framework designed to simulate incorrect throwing scenarios by manipulating the point of release. Using FauxThrow, we conducted a study involving 12 participants to evaluate their reactions to simulated anomalies. Our findings indicate that while release height is easily detected and has minimal impact on perceived realism, errors in release timing and horizontal position are significantly harder to detect. These results offer a novel perspective on real-world throwing dynamics, where misjudging the point of release is common and can be more detrimental than other errors. Furthermore, this understanding is valuable for animators seeking to depict unrealistic throwing actions convincingly. To support this, we developed a simple yet effective method for animating incorrect throws. Additionally, we analyzed how real throwers adjust their motion to compensate for an incorrect point of release, revealing that they modify multiple parameters to mitigate such errors. This research is particularly relevant for researchers studying motion capture data, as it highlights how individuals compensate for mistakes, thereby improving the accuracy of synthesized throwing animations. Finally, we outline how these insights can enhance motion synthesis for virtual humans, resulting in more realistic animations. To demonstrate this, we present a novel metric for assessing the realism of synthesized throwing motions. Our results indicate that while most existing metrics fail to detect incorrect throws, our proposed metric successfully identifies them. We also show that incorporating incorrect throws into synthesized motions improves realism, as evidenced by a user study. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the development of virtual humans capable of reacting effectively to incorrect throws. This work is especially pertinent to researchers in human-robot interaction, as it underscores the importance of considering incorrect throws when designing robots to interact with humans. To support this, we introduce a new dataset featuring throw-catch interactions where throws are intentionally incorrect. This is the first of its kind, offering a foundation for researchers to develop robots that can better respond to human throws. The dataset includes both motion capture and physiological data, such as muscle activation, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of throwing mechanics. This paper is targeted at a multidisciplinary audience, including computer graphics, human-robot interaction, and sports science, with the goal of fostering interdisciplinary collaboration. To facilitate this, we have made the FauxThrow system, synthesized throwing motions, and the new motion capture and physiological throw-catch interaction dataset publicly available. We anticipate that this work will inspire researchers to explore incorrect throws from their respective disciplines and to foster greater cross-disciplinary collaboration.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) relies on beam decoding to enhance translation quality, yet this approach lacks a mechanism to regulate the order of word generation. This paper introduces a novel tree-structured NMT framework that integrates a top-down sequence generator with a tree-structured decoder. The top-down generator produces constituent structures and their sequencing, while the tree-structured decoder refines these into translations. Additionally, the framework employs syntactic links to enable mutual reinforcement between translation and parsing tasks. Experiments on bilingual English-French translation and joint English parsing demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms standard NMT models. Specifically, it achieves a 0.90 BLEOU improvement on translation and a 1.02 percentage point gain in UAS for joint parsing. Source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi2020/T2SDecoding.

The Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP) offers access to binding energy data for water, methane, and carbon monoxide on grain surfaces, calculated using high-level quantum chemical methods. BEAP is a web-based database that provides the binding energy distributions derived from these calculations. The platform is designed to support astrophysicists and astrochemists by enabling the selection of binding energies appropriate for their specific grain surface models. Access is free and unrestricted. The website is available at http://beap.chem.ox.ac.uk. Future updates will expand the database to include additional species. This paper outlines the background and rationale for BEAP and details the current database's contents. Furthermore, a tutorial is provided to guide users on how to select binding energies from BEAP. The selected energies can be exported in various formats, including JSON, to facilitate their use in computational models. The authors welcome any inquiries or comments. Contact can be established via email at chemox@chem.ox.ac.uk. Collaboration is encouraged. The study of multiplicative stochastic processes is essential for modeling the time evolution of physical quantities, particularly in the financial sector, where these models are typically defined by an initial value. However, the standard formulation assumes an initial value that is independent of time and random, as it is treated as a random variable. In this work, we demonstrate that in specific scenarios, the initial value can also be a random process, even if its randomness is deterministic. We subsequently analyze the properties of such processes and propose a method for calibrating this specific type of multiplicative stochastic process. This approach finds application in modeling the inflation rate, where we present a case study based on data from the last thirty years in Brazil. Furthermore, we also address the one-dimensional random walk with a lower bound. This random process is characterized by an initial position and a random velocity, both of which are assumed to be independent and random. We analyze this process, demonstrating that it can be interpreted as a stochastic process with a lower bound, and we also present an alternative interpretation. Finally, we analyze the one-dimensional random walk with a lower bound under this alternative interpretation. As an application, we present a model for the relative error between the inflation rate and its expected value, which we consider to be a random process with a lower bound. Through this model, we show that the inflation rate reaches a lower bound with high probability. Additionally, as an alternative application, we present a model for the absolute error between inflation rates, interpreting it as a one-dimensional random walk with a lower bound. This model indicates that the distance between two inflation rates remains above a lower bound with high probability. In both cases, the parameters of the process are estimated using the method of maximum likelihood. Finally, we demonstrate that these models are consistent with the available data. Keywords: Stochastic process, Lower bound, Multiplicative stochastic process, Method of maximum likelihood, Inflation rate. PACS numbers: 02.50.-r, 05.40.-a, 89.65.-a, 89.75.Fb. We introduce a random Clifford algorithm designed to evaluate an expectation value $Z$ for a $k$-local Hermitian operator $O$ under the $n$-qubit Gibbs distribution at inverse temperature $\beta$. Our method requires a quantum circuit of depth $d = \tilde{O}(n + k)$. When $k$ is small, this approach surpasses the $d = \Omega(n^2)$ requirement of existing expectation value algorithms. For the specific case of $k=1$, our technique is capable of determining $Z$ within additive error $\delta$ using $d = \tilde{O}(n)$, achieving this with a total failure probability of $\Delta$ across $\Delta$ independent runs. This represents a substantial enhancement over the $d = \Omega(n^2)$ depth of previous protocols for estimating individual Pauli terms within a $k$-local Hamiltonian. The core of our algorithm involves a "shadow-in-shade" strategy, which integrates random shadow tomography with the shadowless shadow tomography proposed by Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (arXiv:2004.09967). Our application to shadow tomography recovers $m$ target reduced density matrices of size $k$ qubits each with depth $d = \tilde{O}(n + \sqrt{k})$, surpassing the $d = \tilde{O}(n + k)$ depth of prior methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm's failure probability is exponentially suppressed by increasing the number of shots in each shadow tomography run. Finally, we examine the algorithm's performance on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. By selecting an appropriate circuit depth, the algorithm can achieve the desired accuracy even when noise levels are below the threshold required to execute a single layer of gates without significant data loss. This capability to obtain accurate results without data loss under noisy conditions suggests that the algorithm is well-suited for near-term experimental implementation. Additionally, we show that the algorithm can be implemented without data loss even when data loss occurs within individual data processing steps. These findings regarding the algorithm's robustness to noise are also expected to hold for current NISQ processors. Our proposed algorithm is broadly applicable to variational quantum algorithms, such as those for estimating expectation values in quantum chemistry simulations. In these contexts, our algorithm enables the accurate recovery of the reduced density matrices of individual molecular orbitals, thereby facilitating more efficient variational energy estimation. For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we establish that the reflection coefficient's behavior as $|k| \to \infty$ is governed by the $L^2$-norms of the x and y derivatives of the nonlinearity. This finding contrasts sharply with standard nonlinear Schrödinger equations, where the reflection coefficient is known to be analytic at $|k| = 0$. Consequently, our results provide a comprehensive description of the reflection coefficient's properties for one-dimensional steepest descent contours. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these findings are unique to Davey-Stewartson II equations and do not extend to Davey-Stewartson type III equations. These observations stem from the distinct nonlinear terms in each equation, which dictate the large-frequency asymptotics of the linear Green's function. As an application, we derive new large-frequency asymptotics for the linear scattering phase shifts of Davey-Stewartson II equations. These results are essential for constructing a steepest descent contour in the spectral plane that avoids the square-root branch cut along the imaginary axis, a task required by a specific application. Our derived asymptotics are significantly more accurate than the approximations obtained by simply combining the asymptotics of the individual one-dimensional steepest descent contours. This enhanced accuracy is a direct consequence of the specific large-frequency asymptotic behavior of the nonlinear term. We also note that while our asymptotic formulas are applicable to both Davey-Stewartson type I and type II equations, the lack of a linear scattering transform for Davey-Stewartson type I equations prevents us from deriving new results for that case. Finally, we show that our asymptotic formulas are optimal for the class of nonlinearity considered in this paper. This is because the derived asymptotics are the most singular term in the steepest descent expansion of the determinant, and the exponents of the matrix function are the least in the steepest descent expansion of the determinant equation. We further explain that these asymptotic properties are specific to Davey-Stewartson type II equations, as the least singular term in the steepest descent expansion of the matrix equation for other dsII variants is known to be of lower order. This implies that there are no other dsII equations capable of supporting a steepest descent expansion for the determinant. Although text classification is a well-researched area, many deep learning models lack robustness against adversarial attacks. To address this, we introduce Sibylvariant Modifications (SIM), a collection of novel, simple, and effective transformations designed to perturb text. These perturbations enable the joint training of a classifier and a Sibyl leader-followers model (SFL), which tracks follower leaders as a warning system to flag suspicious inputs for the leader. We evaluated our method on standard text classification tasks and found that SIM demonstrates superior resilience against adversarial attacks compared to baseline models. Furthermore, we present theoretical insights into the relationship between Sibyl and standard consensus models, revealing a trade-off between Sibyl's fault tolerance and its communication overhead. Finally, we propose various modifications to the learning process to enhance efficiency. Experimental results confirm that our proposed modifications significantly improve performance relative to the SFL baseline. To the best of our knowledge, this paper offers the first theoretical analysis of learning with Sibyl, alongside the proposal of Sibyl-based modifications for robust text classification. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Sibylvariant-Modifications.

Meta-learning has recently gained significant traction for its capacity to facilitate rapid adaptation to novel tasks. Although many methods have been developed to train models in this paradigm, it remains unclear how these approaches function internally. This paper introduces a method that can provably guarantee adaptation to new tasks given a sufficient training pool, assuming linear transformations and representations. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm provides a clear characterization of the learned model and offers a proof of its ability to generalize to tasks within the support of the training distribution. This work serves as a foundational step toward developing provably adaptable meta-learning techniques. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets underscore the importance of the algorithm's components and its robustness in handling various scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first provably adaptable method designed for meta-learning. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/DEMON-LR. Furthermore, we hope that establishing provably adaptable methods will pave the way for more complex meta-learning algorithms that offer guarantees of rapid adaptation to new tasks. Finally, we believe that elucidating the learned model in this manner will advance the field of interpretable machine learning. The paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01001. The source code is available at https://github.com/ashwinb/DEMON-LR. Our research indicates that the characteristics of the language pair significantly influence the efficacy of these techniques. Specifically, distillation proves more effective than quantization for low-resource languages, particularly in scenarios involving language pair swaps. Consequently, we propose a novel training strategy that integrates quantization and distillation, demonstrating its potential to enhance low-resource translation. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the newly developed models are capable of matching the performance of full precision models across various metrics. We introduce a mathematical framework for single hypergraphs that extends the Riemannian geometry of manifolds into the combinatorial realm of sets. This approach accommodates both odd and even sets, thereby supporting both odd and even hypergraphs. Leveraging this framework, we formulate a "density" for a single hypergraph, which functions as a Lagrangian density within a general variational formalism for single hypergraphs. This density is termed the hypergraph density. Subsequently, we compute the "divergence" of a specific type of vector field defined on a specific manifold associated with a single hypergraph. We term this the "hyperedge vector divergence." The divergence of a single hyperedge vector is derived from the divergence of a specific manifold vector field. The "Lagrange density of a single hypergraph," constructed from the hyperedge vector divergence and the hypergraph density, is called the hypergraph Lagrange density. The "equation of a single hypergraph" is generated by applying the Euler-Lagrange formalism to the hypergraph Lagrange density. This equation is termed the single hypergraph equation. The density of a specific manifold, derived from the single hypergraph equation, is called the manifold density. The "Lagrange density of a specific manifold," formulated using manifold density, is named the manifold Lagrange density. The "Lagrange density of a manifold," obtained by integrating the manifold Lagrange density over a specific manifold, is referred to as the manifold Lagrangian. We present a study on training a segmentation network for pneumonia detection using limited labelled data. To enhance network performance with small datasets, we implemented two image augmentation techniques: rotation and horizontal flip. These methods were evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 chest X-ray images collected from patients at the University of Malaya. The segmentation task involved isolating the lung region from each image. Our findings indicate that training the network with only 10% of the dataset, augmented via image flipping, yields the most promising segmentation outcomes. The resulting network achieves an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.8101 and a Dice coefficient of 0.8302. Furthermore, we observed that the network's performance is highly dependent on the selection of input images. To address this, we tested a combination of image augmentations, including rotation, flip, zoom, and shift. However, these additional augmentations did not improve the network's performance. We have made the network code and the trained model available on GitHub. This work holds significance for medical institutions that possess extensive unlabeled data but possess a small labeled subset, as it demonstrates that segmentation networks can be effectively trained on limited labeled data through appropriate image augmentations. Additionally, the network shows robustness to variations in input image quality. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/raufhassan12345/UNet-SE-Encoder-Decoder-UNet-with-Atrous-Spatial-Pyramid-Pooling. The trained model can be found here: https://github.com/raufhassan12345/UNet-SE-Encoder-Decoder-UNet-with-Atrous-Spatial-Pyramid-Pooling/tree/master/pneumonia_segmentation_model. Future research will focus on evaluating the network's ability to segment other pathologies, such as lung nodules and breast cancer. Given the network's dependence on specific image augmentations, further investigation is required to determine if a single set of augmentations can be applied universally across different medical domains. The source code is available at: https://github.com/raufhassan12345/UNet-SE-Encoder-Decoder-UNet-with-Athrous-Spatial-Pyramid-Pooling.

We introduce Prompt to Prompt (P2P), a two-stage framework designed to generate a diverse array of descriptions for a single image by leveraging a single prompting variable, the text embedding. In the first stage, we create Text-to-Text (T2T), which transforms the image feature into various unique textual descriptions using the same embedding as the descriptive signal. The second stage, Image-to-Text (I2T), is a standard text generation model that accepts the image feature and the specific text embedding as inputs to produce the final description. We demonstrate that this text embedding effectively controls the diversity of the generated descriptions. To evaluate our framework, we conducted a comprehensive set of experiments on the COCO dataset. Our results indicate that the generated descriptions are not only more diverse and rich in vocabulary but also maintain higher accuracy compared to baselines. Furthermore, we show that manipulating the text embedding allows for the exploration of multiple description styles within a single model. Finally, we present a method to generate an unlimited number of images from a single seed image, further extending the capabilities of our approach. The concept of harm is both intuitive and fundamental, yet its formal definition remains contentious. This paper investigates whether a unified definition can encompass all relevant causal considerations. We demonstrate that existing definitions fall into two categories: those emphasizing harm's causal priority and those highlighting harm's causal susceptibility. However, we argue that neither category adequately captures harm as a complete definition. To resolve this, we propose a definition grounded in actual cause, which accommodates harm across a wide range of scenarios. Furthermore, we examine how harm integrates with the counterfactual framework of actual cause and extend existing formal theories of harm to address new cases. Ultimately, our framework establishes a rigorous foundation for the study of harm within actual cause. Additionally, we introduce a formal theory of moral harm based on utilitarian principles and explore its relationship with actual cause. Finally, we apply our framework to analyze actual and moral harm in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. By clarifying the relationship between harm and actual cause, our work offers a valuable resource for understanding the nature of harm and evaluating actual cause-based legal theories. Additionally, a formal theory of moral harm provides a foundation for assessing moral utilitarianism. Furthermore, our framework elucidates the causes of harm and informs public health strategies, such as those used during the COVID-19 crisis. This represents a significant advancement in the formal study of harm. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to address actual harm through a formal lens and to utilize such methods in policy analysis. Ultimately, we believe that formal research on harm holds immense potential for contributing to societal well-being. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source machine learning library that integrates Spark and Python. By bridging these ecosystems, it allows developers to build models using existing Python algorithms and leverage Spark's scalability. The toolset offers both Python bindings for Spark algorithms and Spark UDFs for them, ensuring a seamless workflow. Additionally, the library includes Python bindings for Spark ML algorithms that match the API of popular Scikit-learn models. The authors demonstrate how to apply MMLSpark to train a deep neural network for image classification on a Spark cluster. Furthermore, they illustrate how to train the same model using either Python or Spark, highlighting the ability to switch between environments without modifying the code. Finally, the paper presents performance benchmarks comparing the Python binding to the MLlib implementation of the Python algorithm. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Azure/MMLSpark. Given its open-source nature, the library is continuously evolving, with new algorithms and functionality added regularly. Voice translation handles multilingual speech processing by directly converting spoken words from one language into another. Although voice translation systems have progressed significantly, most current models depend on extensive annotated speech data for every specific language pair, a resource that is frequently unavailable. This paper addresses the challenge of zero-shot voice translation, where audio from unseen language pairs is mapped to speech in known languages by training solely on data from languages present in the training set. We introduce a straightforward architecture capable of handling this task, achieving state-of-the-art results on the Librispeech and Multilingual Speech Corpus (MSC) benchmarks. Additionally, we evaluate performance on an evaluation set comprising 100 languages, each with only two sentences, to assess the generalizability of our model. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ashwinb/zero-shot-vt. To support the community, we have also made our dataset accessible: https://github.com/ashwinb/dataset. This resource includes 100 languages (covering both low and high resource) and 2 sentences per language, providing a total of 20,000 sentences. We have also provided a python script to facilitate the download of these data files. We hope this resource will be beneficial to the community. Please cite our paper if you utilize this resource. The data files are hosted on our github organization, and we kindly request that you not use them for commercial purposes. The organization's license prohibits commercial use. This study examines nonisothermal Coleman-Gurtin equations incorporating moving boundary conditions and deterministically evolving boundaries. The analysis provides a well-posedness result under the assumption of small data. Furthermore, an implicit finite element scheme is developed and proven to yield a priori estimates that guarantee its convergence. Finally, the convergence of the numerical solution to the exact solution is demonstrated. Additionally, the regularity assumptions imposed on data and boundary functions are justified through an inverse problem formulation. This approach involves determining evolving boundary conditions based on measurable boundary data, specifically the temperature and its normal flux. A Carleman estimate is derived to ensure the uniqueness of this inverse problem, thereby establishing the necessity of high regularity for both conditions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges involved in developing a direct method for this inverse problem. This study evaluates the impact of forecast fusion and energy storage on the accuracy of household energy consumption patterns. To achieve this, probabilistic load forecasts were generated using the Continuous Ranked Score (CRS) and coverage intervals for the T0 to T-15 minute horizons. The analysis incorporated both individual and fused forecasts, alongside scenarios with and without considering energy storage. Results indicate that while storage has a limited impact on peak loads, it significantly reduces the standard deviation of the CRS across all horizons. Furthermore, the combined use of multiple forecasts and storage can decrease the total duration of all intervals by up to 20% for the T0 to T15 horizons. However, the duration of peak load intervals remains largely unaffected by the inclusion of forecast fusion or storage considerations. This outcome is attributed to the inherent characteristics of household loads, which are primarily driven by the grid-supplied load profile rather than the specific features of the forecasting models or the presence of storage. Consequently, the research underscores the need for further research into the representation of peak loads. Additionally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for the planning and design of future low-voltage networks. Keywords: Smart Grid, Probabilistic Forecasting, Forecast Fusion, Energy Storage, Peak Load.

This paper outlines a systematic approach to embedding domain knowledge into machine learning models. We begin by defining domain knowledge as semantic or structural information derived from the data domain, distinguishing it from statistical information which is solely learned from data. We argue that structural graph information can be encoded into deep neural networks using a graph neural network layer, while semantic class relationships are best integrated via a Markov random field layer. Furthermore, we propose that incorporating this relational layer enhances robustness against distribution shifts caused by concept drift. To validate this method, we applied a knowledge-infused deep network to a real-world social network dataset, successfully embedding social network structure and role drift information to boost robustness. Our results demonstrate that models infused with domain knowledge achieve higher accuracy and greater robustness, particularly in scenarios involving concept drift. Finally, we discuss how this proposed architecture can be extended to integrate additional types of domain knowledge. Overall, this work establishes a blueprint for embedding domain knowledge into machine learning models, offering a clear roadmap for future research in this area. The associated code is available at: https://github.com/abhishekdatta1996/KnowledgeInfusedML. Keywords: Knowledge-infused machine learning, Graph information, Role information, Concept drift, Distribution shift.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented global loss of life, yet the scarcity of medical personnel and resources remains a critical challenge. Although recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the diagnosis and monitoring of COVID-19, the field still faces resource constraints and a lack of unbiased localization and segmentation. To address these issues, we introduce a weakly supervised framework that utilizes a single, unannotated CT scan to localize and segment COVID-19 lesions. Our approach employs a dual task head to simultaneously predict lesions and segment lung regions, followed by a contrastive loss designed to enhance the model's ability to distinguish between different lesion categories. Additionally, we implemented a weakly supervised strategy for data augmentation to further boost performance. Evaluated on the public LiSegCOVID-2020 dataset, our method surpassed the top-performing entry and compared favorably against other state-of-the-art techniques. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenLi1998/WeaklySupervisedLearning}. Given the single-CT-scan requirement, this method is highly promising for practical clinical applications. We anticipate that this work will contribute to the ongoing battle against COVID-19. Furthermore, our experimental results highlight the potential of contrastive learning for improving weakly supervised localization and segmentation tasks. We believe this approach will offer new insights and directions for future research in these areas. Finally, we hope this study inspires the computer vision community to assist medical professionals in their efforts to combat the virus. Accurate vertebra localization and identification (VL&I) are critical for numerous vertebral pathologies, including fractures, metastases, and deformities. This study introduces a novel CT-based VL&I framework that automatically refines the scan's orientation to align vertebrae horizontally and reconstruct missing slices from adjacent 2D images. Subsequently, vertebrae are identified by optimizing an anatomically-based cost function that minimizes inter-vertebral distances while ensuring compliance with established biological constraints. The system was rigorously validated using the publicly available OrthoSpine dataset, which contains 100 anonymized CT scans of the lumbar and cervical regions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art approaches, achieving an overall vertebra localization accuracy of 98.5% and an identification accuracy of 96.0%. Furthermore, the method successfully recovers lost vertebrae in 90% of the cases in the cervical dataset. The method has been implemented in an open-source software package. The source code and software are accessible at https://github.com/medialab/ASLAI, and the method is integrated into the medical imaging platform 3D Slicer (https://www.slicer.org/). The method is also incorporated into the spine module of the AI4Medic European project (https://www.ai4medic.eu/). The interplay between electromagnetic fields and charged particles is a cornerstone of physics, typically characterized by electromagnetic radiation emitted when charged particles scatter off intense electromagnetic fields. This study investigates single electron scattering within a finite volume under an ultra-intense field, highlighting the critical role of boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the scattering cross-section can be significantly diminished, a phenomenon attributed to the stabilization of the electron by vacuum fluctuations. Furthermore, we show that this stabilization is transient and can be lost when the electron's energy resonates with the spacing between cavity modes. These findings underscore the vital role of light-induced dressing of electron states in the context of ultrafast, non-adiabatic electron-cavity interactions. Consequently, these results are essential for interpreting ultrafast electron diffraction experiments involving intense light-cavity systems. Additionally, our findings offer a potential pathway to achieve dynamical confinement of electrons, with applications extending to fields beyond atomic, molecular, and optical physics. Specifically, we explore the implications of these findings for spintronics and the development of novel quantum devices. Finally, we address the relevance of these phenomena to current research on strong light-matter interactions in superconducting circuit QED. By extending our findings to a polarizable artificial atom, we uncover a new phenomenon of light-induced electron decay, which may be observable in superconducting circuit QED experiments. This suggests a novel approach to controlling the lifetime of excited states in quantum information processing. Ultimately, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics of electron scattering in the ultrafast, non-adiabatic regime of light-matter interaction. This research holds significant potential for advancing quantum information processing, nanotechnology, and spintronics. Additionally, it offers a fundamental understanding of the complex behavior of electrons in intense electromagnetic fields, with applications ranging from electron microscopy to particle accelerators. Our findings also have broader implications for the fundamental understanding of light-matter interactions and the development of new technologies for manipulating light and matter at the quantum level. Although numerous researchers have developed controllers for legged robots, the specific learning strategies used to handle elastic actuators remain unclear. This study investigates the benefits of learning-based control systems that utilize elastic actuators. We constructed a simulation environment featuring a 12-degree-of-freedom robot with series elastic actuators and trained a controller using reinforcement learning. The findings indicate that the actuator's elasticity can enhance both the robot's running speed and jump height. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that the mechanical power generated by the series elastic actuator is essential for achieving superior locomotion performance. These results offer valuable insights into the optimization of learning-based control for legged robots equipped with flexible actuators. Additionally, this work aligns with our broader objective of elucidating the mechanisms behind high-performance locomotion in legged robots controlled by deep reinforcement learning. To support this, we have released an OpenAI Gym-compatible simulation library known as SEF (Series Elastic Framework), which enables the design of simulation scenarios incorporating actuator elasticity. Inspired by the variational approaches employed in the quantum Monte Carlo algorithm, we introduce a method to examine whether an entangled pure state can be approximated by separable ones. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness using entangled states of both small and intermediate sizes, showing that it achieves exceptional performance even under noisy conditions. Additionally, the method proves applicable to mixed states, yielding optimal results with noiseless approximations. Our findings suggest that this algorithm is a valuable tool for investigating the quantum separability problem's phase diagram and for advancing methods to reduce quantum memory overhead. Furthermore, the approach may find utility in other domains, such as analyzing the phase diagrams of many-body Hamiltonians. This research appears in Physical Review Letters (2021). Ripping is a collisionless plasma instability that arises during the collisionless reconnection of current sheets, first identified by Bhattacharjee et al. (1999) and later analyzed in depth by Daughton et al. (2005). This study investigates the initial phase of the instability, which occurs prior to significant magnetic field line reconnection. We demonstrate that during this early phase, the primary effect of reconnection on the instability is to broaden the current sheet, thereby narrowing the range of wavenumbers in which the mode is active. This observation underscores the critical role of the sheet width in determining the onset of the mode. Additionally, we show that the initial phase is characterized by a current-density profile resembling an error function rather than a tangent function. Consequently, we conclude that the previously described ripping mode is more accurately termed the "tearing-ripping" mode. Furthermore, we find that the most unstable wavenumber of this mode is independent of the tearing-ripping scale, implying that the tearing-ripping interaction does not form a closed loop. Finally, we illustrate that the most unstable mode exhibits a magnetic field profile with a sinusoidal-like structure. These findings are supported by both numerical simulations and analytical theory. Our results indicate that the tearing-ripping mode is driven by a combination of tearing and kink instabilities, with the most unstable wavenumber reflecting a balance between these two mechanisms. This balance is quantified by a new mode growth rate that accounts for both effects. We also identify the critical conditions under which the tearing-ripping mode exists and provide an explanation for why this mode is more prevalent in smaller-scale current sheets. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the tearing-ripping mode is a fundamental component of the reconnection process in collisionless slabs. This conclusion is reinforced by recent numerical simulations of large-scale, three-dimensional, three-component slabs, which have observed the development of this mode. These simulations reveal that the tearing-riping mode is responsible for the formation of small-scale, thin current sheets, which are essential for the continued reconnection process. This insight is crucial for our understanding of the reconnection process in collisionless plasmas. Furthermore, we show that the most unstable wavenumber of the tearing-ripping mode is independent of the magnetic field magnitude, indicating that this mode is a fundamental feature of the reconnection process in collisionless slabs. The growing availability of digital fashion resources has spurred significant research into utilizing image data for fashion image retrieval (FIRe). However, a primary challenge remains the scarcity of labeled datasets, as annotating large collections of fashion images demands substantial human effort. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel approach for FIRe that employs a feature-level trait manipulation technique to train a robust deep convolutional neural network. By applying a deep autoencoder to latent features, the method learns a compact, informative representation of fashion items. This allows for the alteration of specific attributes, such as garment color, while keeping the identity intact. We validate our proposed method on the FIRe task using the Fashion-MNIST and Fashion-IQ datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we visualize the learned representation to illustrate its effectiveness in capturing fashion identity and its capacity to encode the target trait. Finally, we discuss how this technique could facilitate style transfer applications, such as changing a garment's color within a specific outfit context. This paper introduces a dual gradient approach designed for addressing first-order linear ill-posed equations within Banach spaces. The proposed method is both simple to implement and straightforward to analyze, generating dual iterates that converge strongly to the dual of the exact solution of the original problem. Subsequently, a dual approximate solution is generated through a simple pointwise projection. Applied to the problem of reconstructing a function from its Fourier transform, the method demonstrates superior performance compared to Nesterov's accelerated method. Furthermore, numerical experiments on recovering sparse signals via $\ell_1$-duality confirm that the dual gradient method outperforms the proximal gradient method. These findings indicate that dual gradient methods are highly effective for solving dual problems associated with convex ill-posed problems. The method's versatility extends to various applications, including image restoration, deconvolution, inverse problems, and function reconstruction from Fourier data. Additionally, the paper provides a comprehensive comparison between the primal (Nesterov) and dual (proposed) gradient methods in the context of function reconstruction from Fourier data. Finally, the efficiency of the dual gradient method in this context is benchmarked against the conjugate gradient method. These comparisons underscore that the dual gradient method serves as a robust and effective tool for solving dual problems arising from convex ill-posed scenarios. **Keywords:** Banach spaces, ill-posed problems, dual gradient method, primal gradient method, conjugate gradient method. **MSC 2010:** 47A50, 47H05, 47J05, 65J20, 65K10. **Authors:** M. This paper introduces a deep learning approach for light field depth estimation that prioritizes occlusion-aware cost volume construction and provides a novel 3D-2D convolutional depth estimation network. To address the challenge of incomplete cost volumes caused by energy concentration at high-frequency components, we propose a cost volume builder that integrates a 3D-2D convolutional layer with a frequency separator. This architecture separates low and high-frequency parts to enable independent, specialized processing. Additionally, we develop a frequency re-integrator to facilitate depth estimation on an expanded cost volume. To better capture high-frequency details, we design a 3D-2D convolutional depth estimator featuring a 3D convolutional layer, frequency separator, convolutional depth estimators, and frequency re-integrator. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenZhang1997/Occlusion-Aware-Cost-Builder.

This paper applies the bilinear method to the normal forms of the Fokas-Lenells equations, deriving novel bilinear representations, auto-bäckward transformations, and higher-order soliton solutions for both normal types. Additionally, we present auto-backward solutions for the all-definite equations and auto-forward solutions for the semi-definite equations, thereby resolving several open problems. Finally, we calculate double soliton solutions for the definite equations and calculate double and three soliton solutions for the semi-definite equations, which have not previously been reported in the literature. These results significantly advance the understanding of the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy. Notably, the three soliton solution for the semi-definite equation represents a new finding, as it involves two auto-backward waves and one auto-forward wave. Furthermore, we derive the double and three soliton solutions for the mixed-definite equation, which has not been addressed in existing literature. Finally, we calculate the double soliton solution for the all-definite equation, providing new findings that contribute to a deeper comprehension of the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy. The bilinear method is a highly effective and efficient tool for analyzing nonlinear evolution equations (NEEs), and we believe these findings will significantly contribute to a better understanding of the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy. Non-Riemannian gravitational theories offer valuable frameworks for investigating phase transitions away from standard Riemannian geometry, particularly in contexts involving a non-vanishing torsion tensor. This torsion is expected to emerge naturally in a string-theoretic formulation of gravity, specifically within the proposed double field theory. By examining a sequence of non-Riemannian geometries derived from double field theory, we demonstrate that certain torsion-induced actions can be derived from a dRGT-like torsion potential, while others require a double field theory-specific potential. Furthermore, we establish that these non-Riemannian gravitational theories satisfy the de Donder gauge condition. Finally, by calculating the equations of motion, we identify that describing torsion as a dynamical field leads to the emergence of a massive graviton. Ultimately, this approach not only validates that torsion can be dynamical in DFT gravity but also provides a viable mechanism for generating such dynamics through the torsion potential. These findings underscore the potential of double field theory to construct a consistent string-theoretic formulation of gravity incorporating both torsion and massive gravitons. Additionally, we explore the possibility of a holographic dual for these non-Riemannian geometries, revealing that torsion generates a finite temperature in the dual theory. This suggests that non-Riemannian geometries may play a crucial role in understanding thermal phenomena within quantum gravity. Given that these findings rely on the AdS/CFT correspondence, they also highlight the potential of non-Riemannian gravity to elucidate thermal aspects of quantum gravity. Consequently, this research may offer a pathway to uncovering the hidden symmetries of quantum gravity. Our findings are supported by numerical computations. The numerical code is available at \href{https://github.com/AlperenKaya/DFT-non-Riemannian}{DFT-non-Riemannian}. The proliferation of IEEE 802.11-based home WiFi has led to significant channel congestion and interference, resulting in degraded user experience. To address this, the 802.11k and 802.11v amendments were introduced to enable access points (APs) to share network topology details and facilitate clients in selecting APs with lighter channel loads. This paper introduces a novel extension to the 802.11k/v framework that allows signal extension devices (ECDs), such as extenders, to advertise their channel load. This innovation allows WiFi clients to account for ECD channel load during network selection, thereby reducing the likelihood of associating with over-loaded ECDs. A prototype implementation was developed to validate the proposed scheme, and extensive simulations were conducted to assess its performance. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively mitigates the selection of over-loaded ECDs, subsequently lowering the overall channel load within the network. Furthermore, the scheme exhibits rapid convergence, requiring only a few scans to identify an optimal AP. Finally, the study confirms that the additional overhead from 802.11k/v is negligible and does not impact network performance. Experimental data indicates that the proposed solution can reduce the average channel load by approximately 20% and the ECD's channel load by about 30%. Additionally, it successfully prevents around 40% of ECD over-loading events, compared to only 10% in the baseline scenario. These findings suggest that the proposed scheme is well-suited for deployment in next-generation home WiFi environments. To achieve this, both the AP and the ECD must support 802.11k/v capabilities. The paper also outlines the necessary modifications to the AP and ECD to enable this support. Finally, the AP's role in managing the Extender Control Document (ECD) is detailed, including the ECD selection algorithm and the Extender Selection List (ESL) generation process. The paper concludes by discussing potential future research directions. Finally, the study addresses the impact of the proposed scheme on the ECD's handover process, specifically examining associated latency and the number of required scans. It demonstrates that the scheme introduces only a minimal number of scans during handovers, ensuring that performance remains unaffected. Additionally, the scheme incurs only a few milliseconds of latency, which is negligible compared to the time required to switch from one ECD to another. Consequently, the proposed solution is deemed appropriate for implementation in next-generation home WiFi
